Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement BEST describes project management as PRINCE2 7 uses the term?
o: A temporary organization created to deliver business products under an agreed business case
Applying methods, tools, techniques and competencies to a project so it meets its objectives
Running the repeatable, ongoing operations that keep an organization's services available
Selecting and balancing an organization's whole set of change investments against its strategy
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Project management is the application of methods, tools, techniques and competencies to a project so that it achieves its objectives (see manual ch 1 and the glossary). The project is the temporary organization; project management is what is done to direct and control it.

n.0: This is the definition of a project, not of project management; the question asks about the management activity applied to the project.
n.2: Running repeatable, ongoing operations is business as usual, which a project changes rather than manages.
n.3: Balancing an organization's whole set of change investments against strategy is portfolio management, not the management of a single project.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about projects are true according to PRINCE2?
1. A project team is a permanent part of the organization's line structure.
2. A project continues after its change is implemented so that it can run the new service.
3. A project is created to deliver one or more business products.
4. A project is undertaken according to an agreed business case.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Statements 3 and 4 restate the PRINCE2 definition: a temporary organization created to deliver one or more business products according to an agreed business case (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Statement 1 is false because the project organization is temporary, and statement 2 is false because the need for the project ends once its change is implemented.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false: the project team is temporary and is disbanded when the project closes.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: running the new service is business as usual, which resumes once the change is in place.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A project delivers a new online booking system. After handover, staff start handling customer bookings in a different way. In PRINCE2 terms, what is the change in how staff work?
o: An outcome: the result of the change brought about by using the project's outputs
An output: the product that the project hands over to the business at the end
A benefit: the measurable improvement the business gains from the new way of working
A product description: the specification of what the team must build and to what quality
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects deliver outputs (products) that enable outcomes, the results of change in real-world behaviour, which in turn realize measurable benefits (see manual 1.3 and the business case practice). Staff working differently is an outcome.

n.1: The booking system itself is the output; the change in how staff behave after using it is the outcome.
n.2: A benefit is a measurable improvement, such as fewer missed bookings, that results from the outcome; the new way of working is not itself the measurable gain.
n.3: A product description specifies a product before it is built; it does not describe a change in how people work.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: An insurer pays out on claims each month using the same procedure and the same permanent team. How should this work be classed in PRINCE2 terms?
o: As a project, because each monthly run has a defined start and finish
As a programme, because it repeats over many months across several teams
As business as usual, because it is routine and introduces no change
As a stage, because it is planned and controlled one month at a time
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Routine, repeated work carried out by a permanent team is business as usual. A project is a temporary organization that introduces change and then ends (see manual 1.3).

n.0: A regular monthly cycle is not a project: it introduces no change and has no business case of its own, even though each run starts and finishes.
n.1: A programme leads several related projects to achieve outcomes; repetition of routine work does not make it a programme.
n.3: A management stage is a section of a project controlled by the project board; routine operations are not divided into project stages.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A hospital project brings together nurses, software developers and estates staff to introduce a new patient check-in system that will alter how reception teams across the site work. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: The project is unique
The project is cross-functional
The project is temporary
The project carries uncertainty
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Cross-functional means people with different skills working together, on a temporary basis, to introduce a change that affects others outside the team (see manual 1.3). Here clinical, technical and estates staff combine on a change that affects reception teams.

n.0: Unique means each project differs in some way, such as its team, customer or location; the stem stresses the mix of skills and the people affected, not how this project differs from others.
n.2: Temporary means the need for the project ends once the change is in place; nothing in the stem describes the project ending.
n.3: Uncertainty refers to the extra threats and opportunities projects bring; the stem describes who is working together, not risk.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A housing association has completed ten kitchen refurbishment projects. Its next one will use a different contractor, at a new site, for a different group of tenants. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: Temporary
Change
Unique
Cross-functional
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Every project is unique: even when an organization runs many similar projects, each one differs in some way, such as its team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Temporary is about the project ending once its change is implemented; the stem is about how this project differs from earlier similar ones.
n.1: Change describes projects as the means of introducing change; the stem highlights the different contractor, site and tenants, which shows uniqueness.
n.3: Cross-functional is about people with different skills working together; the stem compares this project with previous ones rather than describing the team's skills.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Why does PRINCE2 regard projects as riskier than business as usual?
o: Because projects normally spend more money than routine operations do
Because project teams have less experience than the staff who run daily operations
Because projects are directed by a project board rather than by line managers
Because their other characteristics bring threats and opportunities beyond routine work
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Uncertainty is the fifth characteristic: change, temporary teams, cross-functional working and uniqueness introduce threats and opportunities over and above those met in business as usual, so projects are riskier (see manual 1.3).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not link a project's riskiness to its budget; many projects are smaller than routine operations, yet they are still riskier because of their characteristics.
n.1: PRINCE2 does not assume project teams are less experienced; the extra risk comes from the nature of project work, not the people's experience.
n.2: The project board provides direction and control; having a board is a response to project risk, not the reason projects are riskier.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement BEST describes the 'temporary' characteristic of a project?
o: Once the change is in place, business as usual resumes and the project is no longer needed
Each project differs from others in some way, such as its team, customer, location or timeframe
People with different skills work together on a change that affects others outside the team
Projects bring threats and opportunities beyond those normally found in routine work
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects are temporary: when the desired change has been implemented, business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project is removed (see manual 1.3).

n.1: This describes the 'unique' characteristic: every project differs in some way from others, even similar ones.
n.2: This describes the 'cross-functional' characteristic: different skills working together on a change that affects others.
n.3: This describes the 'uncertainty' characteristic: projects are riskier than business as usual.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about the characteristics of a project are true?
1. A project that closely repeats an earlier one is not unique.
2. Projects are the means by which an organization introduces change.
3. Uncertainty makes projects less risky than business as usual.
4. Every project differs from others in some way, even when it is similar.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Statement 2 describes the 'change' characteristic and statement 4 the 'unique' characteristic (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is false: even a project that repeats an earlier one differs in some way, such as team, location or timeframe, so it is still unique.
n.1: Both are false: similar projects are still unique, and uncertainty makes projects riskier than business as usual, not less risky.
n.3: Statement 4 is true, but statement 3 is false: the uncertainty projects carry makes them riskier than business as usual.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Change, temporary teams, cross-functional working and the uniqueness of each project create [?], so projects bring threats and opportunities over and above those of business as usual.
o: uncertainty
governance
tolerance
sustainability
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Uncertainty is the fifth characteristic: the other four introduce threats and opportunities beyond those typically met in business as usual, which makes projects riskier (see manual 1.3).

n.1: Governance is how a project is directed and controlled; it is a response to project risk, not the characteristic that describes it.
n.2: Tolerance is the permitted deviation from a plan's targets under manage by exception, not one of the five characteristics of a project.
n.3: Sustainability is one of the seven aspects of project performance, not one of the five characteristics that distinguish projects from business as usual.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement about the 'unique' characteristic of a project is correct?
o: A project that closely resembles an earlier one is treated as business as usual
Uniqueness means the project's outputs cannot be reused by the organization later
Uniqueness means the project should not draw on lessons from previous projects
Similar projects still differ in some way, such as team, customer or location
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Every project is unique: an organization may run many similar projects with a familiar pattern of work, but each one differs in some way, such as its team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe (see manual 1.3).

n.0: A project that resembles an earlier one is still a project; it introduces change and differs in some way, so it is not business as usual.
n.1: Uniqueness is about each project differing from others; it says nothing to stop the organization reusing what a project delivers.
n.2: Similar projects create a familiar pattern of work, and PRINCE2's learn from experience principle expects lessons from previous projects to be used.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A council sets up a project team for nine months to move its library catalogue online. When the new catalogue is in use, the team is disbanded and staff return to their usual jobs. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: Unique
Temporary
Uncertainty
Cross-functional
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects are temporary: once the change is implemented, business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project ends, so the team is disbanded (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Unique is about how a project differs from other projects; the stem focuses on the project ending once its change is in place.
n.2: Uncertainty is about the extra threats and opportunities a project brings; the stem describes the team being disbanded at the end.
n.3: Cross-functional is about different skills working together; the stem does not describe the mix of skills, only that the team ends with the project.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Why do organizations commonly use project management to deliver change, rather than handling it through normal line management?
o: So that the project team can take permanent ownership of the changed operations
So that the business case can be approved once and then set aside during delivery
So that change is introduced in a controlled way while business as usual continues
So that line managers can direct each change as part of their routine duties
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects are the means by which organizations introduce change, and that change must be controlled while day-to-day operations keep running; project management gives the temporary organization the structure to do this (see manual 1.3).

n.0: The project team is temporary; once the change is in place business as usual resumes and the operations are owned by the business, not the project team.
n.1: PRINCE2 requires business justification to be checked throughout the project, not approved once and then set aside.
n.3: Project management sets up a separate temporary organization with defined roles because routine line management is not designed to control cross-functional change.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A project team is drawn from four departments. Nobody is sure who may approve changes to the design, and decisions keep stalling. Which challenge that PRINCE2 is designed to address does this BEST illustrate?
o: Uncertainty about which delivery approach the suppliers intend to use
Projects overrunning because tolerances have been set too widely
A lack of common vocabulary between organizations in different industries
Unclear roles, responsibilities and accountability in a temporary team
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Temporary, cross-functional teams often suffer from confusion about who is responsible for what and who can decide. PRINCE2 addresses this with defined roles, responsibilities and relationships and a clear project management team structure (see manual 1.4 and 2.3).

n.0: The stem says nothing about how products will be delivered; the problem is that nobody knows who has authority to decide.
n.1: Tolerances are not mentioned and no overrun is described; decisions are stalling because authority is unclear.
n.2: The departments belong to one organization and the problem is who decides, not the meaning of project terms.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement BEST explains why projects need a different style of management from business as usual?
o: Projects bring temporary, cross-functional teams together to make unique changes, which adds risk
Projects are smaller than routine operations, so they need less formal direction from senior managers
Projects repeat a proven pattern of work, so the same controls can be reused unchanged each time
Projects are funded from operating budgets, so they are best managed through normal reporting lines
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The five characteristics (change, temporary, cross-functional, unique, uncertainty) make project work riskier and harder to control than business as usual, which is why organizations use project management (see manual 1.3).

n.1: Projects are not defined by being small, and their uncertainty calls for clear direction from the project board rather than less direction.
n.2: Every project is unique and differs in some way from earlier ones, so controls are tailored to each project rather than reused unchanged.
n.3: PRINCE2 sets up a temporary project organization, separate from normal reporting lines, to direct and manage the change.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which challenge is PRINCE2's principle of ensuring continued business justification designed to address?
o: Teams working in different locations finding it hard to build relationships
Projects carrying on after they have stopped being worth the investment
Specialist products being built with unsuitable engineering techniques
Project staff being unsure what common project terms actually mean
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A PRINCE2 project must have business justification to start and to continue; if it is no longer justified it should be stopped. This tackles the common problem of projects continuing with few real benefits (see manual 1.4 and 2.1).

n.0: Building relationships across dispersed teams is addressed by the people element and the define roles, responsibilities and relationships principle.
n.2: PRINCE2 works alongside specialist, industry-specific models; it does not set the engineering techniques used to build products.
n.3: A shared vocabulary is a benefit of PRINCE2's common language and concepts, not of the business justification principle.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements are reasons why organizations use project management?
1. To keep a project team in place permanently after its change is implemented.
2. To remove the need for business as usual management.
3. To introduce change in a controlled way.
4. To check that an investment remains justified as the work progresses.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Project management lets an organization introduce change in a controlled way and keep checking that the investment is still worthwhile (see manual 1.3 and the ensure continued business justification principle, 2.1).

n.0: Both are false: a project team is temporary, and business as usual resumes in its new form once the change is in place.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false because the project organization is disbanded once the change is implemented.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: projects change business as usual, which continues alongside and after them.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which challenge is PRINCE2's principle of managing by exception designed to address?
o: Lessons from earlier projects being lost because they were not recorded
Senior managers being drawn into decisions that could be taken at a lower level
Products being delivered that do not meet the users' quality expectations
Projects starting before anyone has checked they are worth the investment
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Manage by exception delegates authority with tolerances so that senior managers are involved when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, making efficient use of their time without removing control (see manual 2.5).

n.0: Recording and applying lessons is the purpose of the learn from experience principle.
n.2: Meeting the users' quality expectations is the concern of the focus on products principle and the quality practice.
n.3: Checking that a project is worth the investment before it starts is the ensure continued business justification principle.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A project board hears about problems only when the project is already badly late and over budget. Which part of PRINCE2 is designed to address this challenge?
o: Defining the specialist techniques the team must use to build the products
Fixing the stage budget as one figure that the project manager may not vary
Setting tolerances so that forecast breaches are escalated to the board early
Having team members report directly to the board instead of to the manager
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Under manage by exception, tolerances are set for each level and any forecast breach is escalated to the next level as early as possible, so the board is alerted before the problem becomes severe (see manual 2.5).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not prescribe specialist build techniques, and these would not give the board earlier warning of delays or overspend.
n.1: PRINCE2 allows a range of variation through tolerances rather than a fixed figure; it is the forecast breach of that range that triggers escalation.
n.3: Team managers report to the project manager, who reports to the board; bypassing the project manager undermines the defined roles and does not create early warning.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which is a common reason organizations use project management?
o: To coordinate people from different functions working temporarily on a change
To run repeatable operational processes with a permanent team and fixed routine
To give each department full control of its own part of a cross-functional change
To pass accountability for the business case from the business to the supplier
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects are cross-functional: people with different skills work together temporarily on a change. Project management provides the structure, roles and control to coordinate them (see manual 1.3).

n.1: Repeatable operations run by a permanent team are business as usual, not what project management is used for.
n.2: A project is directed as one temporary organization under a project board; splitting control between departments is what project management aims to avoid.
n.3: The executive, representing the business, owns the business case; suppliers have their own justification but do not take accountability for the customer's business case.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which list gives the seven aspects of project performance that PRINCE2 7 manages?
o: Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and stakeholders
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and resources
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and governance
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and sustainability
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The seven aspects of project performance are benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (see manual 1.4). Sustainability was added in PRINCE2 7.

n.0: Stakeholders matter to the people element, but they are not one of the seven aspects of performance; the seventh aspect is sustainability.
n.1: Resources are planned and managed through the plans, but resources are not one of the seven aspects; the seventh is sustainability.
n.2: Governance is provided by the project board and the method as a whole; it is not an aspect of performance. The seventh aspect is sustainability.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Older PRINCE2 material lists six aspects of project performance. Which aspect did PRINCE2 7 add to make seven?
o: Sustainability
Benefits
Stakeholder engagement
Risk
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 7 added sustainability as the seventh aspect of performance: projects affect their environment, so teams need sustainability performance targets for the project work and its products (see manual 1.4).

n.1: Benefits was already one of the six aspects in the 2017 edition.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is covered by the people element, which is new in PRINCE2 7, but it is not an aspect of performance.
n.3: Risk was already one of the six aspects in the 2017 edition.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A new payroll system is delivered on time and within budget, but it calculates some deductions wrongly and cannot be used as specified. Which aspect of project performance has the project failed to meet?
o: Scope
Quality
Benefits
Risk
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The quality aspect is about products being fit for purpose: finishing on time and within budget is of little value if what is delivered does not work as specified (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope is about what the project will deliver; the payroll system was delivered, but it does not work as specified, which is a quality failure.
n.2: Benefits may later suffer, but the aspect describing a product that does not work as specified is quality.
n.3: Risk is about limits on the plan's aggregated risks; a product failing to meet its specification is a quality shortfall.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which aspect of project performance is concerned with when the project will start, when its key products will be delivered and when it will finish?
o: Scope
Costs
Time
Benefits
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The time aspect covers when the project starts, when key products are delivered and when it finishes (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope covers what the project will deliver, not when.
n.1: Costs cover affordability and any overspend or underspend against the budget.
n.3: Benefits cover who the project is for and what must be achieved to justify the investment.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which aspect of project performance is concerned with the project being affordable and with any possible overspend or underspend against its budget?
o: Costs
Scope
Risk
Quality
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The costs aspect recognizes that the project has to be affordable and that many factors can lead to underspend or overspend against the cost budget (see manual 1.4).

n.1: Scope is about what the project will deliver, not the money spent.
n.2: Risk is about limits on the plan's aggregated risks, not the budget itself.
n.3: Quality is about products being fit for purpose.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two are among the seven aspects of project performance in PRINCE2 7?
1. Stakeholders
2. Sustainability
3. Resources
4. Benefits
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Sustainability and benefits are both aspects of performance. The full set is benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Sustainability is an aspect, but stakeholders are not; stakeholders are addressed through the people element.
n.1: Neither stakeholders nor resources is one of the seven aspects of performance.
n.3: Benefits is an aspect, but resources are not; resources are planned within the plans practice.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The [?] aspect of project performance defines what the project will deliver, expressed through the products in its plan.
o: quality
scope
benefits
time
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Scope is what the project will deliver, represented by the products in the approved plan (see manual 1.4; scope tolerance is the permissible variation of the plan's products).

n.0: Quality is about whether the products are fit for purpose, not which products are delivered.
n.2: Benefits describe the measurable improvements that justify the investment, not the products in the plan.
n.3: Time concerns when products are delivered and when the project finishes, not what is delivered.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which aspect of project performance helps the project management team understand who the project is for and what must be achieved to justify the investment?
o: Scope
Quality
Sustainability
Benefits
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The benefits aspect asks who the project is for: the team must understand the project's purpose and what must be achieved to justify its investment (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope is about what the project will deliver, not who it is for or why the investment is justified.
n.1: Quality is about products being fit for purpose.
n.2: Sustainability is about the project's impact on its environment and the sustainability targets for its work and products.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which list gives the five integrated elements of PRINCE2 7?
o: Principles, people, practices, processes and the project context
Principles, themes, processes, people and tailoring to the environment
Principles, people, practices, processes and the business layer
Principles, roles, practices, processes and the project context
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The five integrated elements are principles, people, practices, processes and the project context (see manual 1.2, figure 1.1).

n.1: Themes and tailoring to the project environment belong to the 2017 model of four elements; PRINCE2 7 uses practices and the project context.
n.2: The business layer is the level of the organization that commissions the project, not one of the integrated elements; the fifth element is the project context.
n.3: Roles are covered within the organizing practice and the people element; 'roles' is not itself an integrated element, whereas people is.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which integrated element consists of the guiding obligations and good practices that determine whether a project is genuinely being managed using PRINCE2?
o: Practices
Principles
Processes
Project context
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The seven principles are the guiding obligations and good practices that decide whether a project is genuinely a PRINCE2 project; unless all are applied, it is not (see manual 1.2).

n.0: The practices describe aspects of project management that must be applied consistently throughout the lifecycle; they do not decide whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2.
n.2: The processes provide the activities to direct, manage and deliver the project from start-up to closure.
n.3: The project context is the setting the method is applied in, such as the organizational and commercial context, delivery method and scale.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which integrated element provides the activities needed to direct, manage and deliver a project, from before it starts through to its closure?
o: Practices
Principles
Processes
People
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The seven processes describe the whole project lifecycle, from the pre-project activities of starting up through to closing the project, with the activities needed to direct, manage and deliver it (see manual 1.2).

n.0: The practices describe aspects of project management, such as risk and quality, applied throughout; the lifecycle activities are set out in the processes.
n.1: The principles are guiding obligations that make a project PRINCE2; they do not set out lifecycle activities.
n.3: The people element is about the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved and their relationships, not the lifecycle activities.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which integrated element describes aspects of project management that must be applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle?
o: Processes
Principles
People
Practices
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The seven practices describe essential aspects of project management, such as business case, plans and risk, that must be applied consistently throughout the lifecycle so that the processes are effective (see manual 1.2 and 4.1).

n.0: The processes describe the lifecycle activities; the aspects of project management applied throughout them are the practices.
n.1: The principles are the guiding obligations that determine whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2.
n.2: The people element covers the needs, capabilities, motivations and relationships of those involved.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: In PRINCE2's figure of the five integrated elements, which element is shown as the foundation on which practices, people and processes rest?
o: People
Processes
Principles
Project context
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Figure 1.1 shows the principles as the foundation, with practices, people and processes built on them, all within the project context (see manual 1.2).

n.0: People are shown at the centre, above the principles, not as the foundation.
n.1: Processes are one of the three elements built on the principles.
n.3: The project context surrounds all the other elements; it is not shown as the foundation they rest on.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about the integrated elements of PRINCE2 7 are true?
1. There are four integrated elements.
2. Tailoring to the project environment is one of the integrated elements.
3. People is one of the integrated elements.
4. The project context is one of the integrated elements.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 7 has five integrated elements, two of which are people and the project context (see manual 1.2).

n.0: Both are false: PRINCE2 7 has five elements, and tailoring is covered by the principle tailor to suit the project rather than being an element.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 7 has five integrated elements, not four.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: tailoring is covered by the principle tailor to suit the project, not an element.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which integrated element recognizes that the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved, and their relationships, are crucial to how a project is set up and managed?
o: People
Practices
Principles
Processes
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: People are at the centre of PRINCE2 7: understanding the needs, capabilities and motivations of those working on or affected by the project, and the relationships between them, is crucial (see manual 1.2 and chapter 3).

n.1: The practices describe aspects of project management such as plans and risk, not the needs and motivations of those involved.
n.2: The principles are the guiding obligations that make a project PRINCE2.
n.3: The processes set out the lifecycle activities; people apply them, but the element about needs and relationships is people.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. PRINCE2 is designed to work within any [?], including its organizational and commercial setting, delivery method, sustainability requirements and scale.
o: programme structure
project context
delivery approach
management approach
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The project context element means PRINCE2 can work within any context, including organizational and commercial context, delivery method, sustainability requirements and project scale (see manual 1.2).

n.0: A programme structure is one possible setting for a project, not the element that covers every setting the method works in.
n.2: The delivery approach is one factor within the project context; it cannot contain the organizational setting, delivery method and scale.
n.3: A management approach sets out how one practice will be applied on the project, such as risk or quality; it is not the setting the method works in.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement about the organizational context of a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: PRINCE2 assumes the project sits within a programme that sets its objectives
PRINCE2 does not assume any particular organizational context for the project
PRINCE2 assumes the customer and the supplier belong to the same organization
PRINCE2 assumes the project reports directly to the organization's portfolio office
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The PRINCE2 method does not assume any specific organizational context: a project may be standalone, part of a programme or portfolio, or delivered in a commercial customer and supplier relationship (see manual 1.5).

n.0: A project may be part of a programme, but it may equally be standalone or in a portfolio; PRINCE2 does not assume a programme.
n.2: PRINCE2 explicitly allows for commercial contexts where the customer and supplier are separate organizations with their own business cases.
n.3: A standalone project may report to its business unit's management structure rather than a portfolio office; no single reporting line is assumed.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, which party ensures that the project investment can be justified and remains justified throughout the lifecycle?
o: Users
Suppliers
Business decision-makers
Specialist team members
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 describes users who specify the desired outputs, suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and business decision-makers who ensure the investment is justified and stays justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Users specify the desired outputs (products) and will use them; they do not hold the responsibility for keeping the investment justified.
n.1: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products.
n.3: Specialist team members build the products within work packages; they do not decide whether the investment is justified.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, which party provides the resources and expertise needed to deliver the products?
o: Users
Business decision-makers
Project assurance
Suppliers
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products, while users specify what is wanted and business decision-makers keep the investment justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Users specify the desired outputs; they do not provide the resources to build them.
n.1: Business decision-makers ensure the investment is justified throughout the lifecycle.
n.2: Project assurance monitors the project on behalf of the project board; it is not one of the three parties described in the organizational context.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A small charity runs a project to replace its donor database. The project is not part of any programme or portfolio and reports to the charity's management team. How is this project's context BEST described?
o: Standalone
Within a programme
Within a portfolio
Commercial customer and supplier
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A project may be part of a programme or portfolio structure, or it may be a standalone project reporting to the business unit's management structure (see manual 1.5, figure 1.2).

n.1: The stem states the project is not part of any programme.
n.2: The stem states the project is not part of any portfolio.
n.3: No contract with an external supplier is described; the defining feature here is that the project reports directly to the charity's own management.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A construction firm is contracted to build a depot for a logistics company. Which statement about this commercial context is correct according to PRINCE2?
o: The supplier is covered by the customer's business case and needs no justification of its own
The contract between the parties replaces the need for a project board to direct the project
The project must use one management system, which the supplier chooses
The supplier will have its own business case for taking part in the project
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: In a commercial context each party has its own reasons for taking part: the supplier has its own business case, and the project may need to align with two or more management systems (see manual 1.5 and 2.1).

n.0: All parties, suppliers included, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify their involvement, so the supplier has its own business case.
n.1: A contract governs the commercial relationship, but the project is still directed by a project board representing business, user and supplier interests.
n.2: A commercial project may need to align with two or more management systems, those of the customer and of the supplier.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: How is a programme BEST described in relation to the projects within it?
o: A temporary structure that leads several related projects and other work to achieve outcomes
A permanent function that runs all of an organization's routine operations and services
A single project large enough to need more than two management stages
The supplier's own management system for delivering contracted products
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A programme is a temporary structure that leads multiple interrelated projects and other work to progressively achieve outcomes and benefits; a PRINCE2 project may sit within one (see manual 1.5, figure 1.2, and the glossary).

n.1: Running routine operations is business as usual, which is permanent; a programme is temporary and exists to achieve change.
n.2: A project with many stages is still one project; a programme coordinates several related projects.
n.3: A supplier's management system is part of a commercial context, not a programme.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about projects in context are true?
1. PRINCE2 is designed for standalone projects and cannot be used in a programme.
2. A project can be part of a programme or a portfolio.
3. In a commercial context, suppliers share the customer's business case and have none of their own.
4. In a commercial context, a project may need to align with more than one management system.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A project may be standalone or part of a programme or portfolio, and in a commercial context it may need to align with the management systems of both customer and supplier (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 can be used for projects within a programme or portfolio as well as standalone projects.
n.1: Both are false: PRINCE2 can be used within a programme, and suppliers have their own business case for taking part.
n.3: Statement 4 is true, but statement 3 is false: each supplier has its own business case for its involvement.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, the [?] specify the desired outputs, which PRINCE2 refers to as products.
o: suppliers
users
executives
sponsors
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Users specify the desired outputs (products), suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver them, and business decision-makers keep the investment justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products; users specify them.
n.2: The executive is a project board role representing the business interest; the organizational context description names users as the party that specifies outputs.
n.3: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role; the party that specifies desired outputs is the users.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which list gives the three delivery approaches named in PRINCE2 7?
o: Predictive-sequential, adaptive-iterative and blended
Linear-phased, agile-incremental and combined
Linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid
Waterfall-sequential, Scrum-iterative and mixed
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 7 names three delivery approaches: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid (see manual 1.5.3).

n.0: These are not PRINCE2 7 terms; the method uses linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid.
n.1: These are not PRINCE2 7 terms; agile ways of working fall under the iterative-incremental approach.
n.3: Waterfall and Scrum are general industry terms, not the delivery approaches PRINCE2 7 names.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which delivery approach typically defines products in detail up front, with stages following one another, such as design, then build, then test?
o: Iterative-incremental
Hybrid
Agile
Linear-sequential
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: In a linear-sequential approach, work moves through a sequence of stages and products are defined in detail at the outset (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.3.1.1.3).

n.0: Iterative-incremental work evolves products through repeated cycles, refining criteria as it goes rather than fixing detail up front.
n.1: Hybrid mixes linear and iterative work; the description is of a purely sequential approach.
n.2: Agile ways of working are iterative-incremental and refine products in cycles, not in one sequence defined up front.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which delivery approach evolves products through repeated cycles, refining quality and acceptance criteria alongside development by using a product backlog?
o: An iterative-incremental approach
A linear-sequential approach
A hybrid approach
A stage-gated waterfall approach
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: In an iterative-incremental approach, products evolve through repeated cycles, and quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development using a product backlog; there may be several delivery stages (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.2.3.1).

n.1: A linear-sequential approach defines products in detail up front and moves through stages in sequence.
n.2: A hybrid approach mixes linear and iterative work; the description is of the fully iterative approach.
n.3: A stage-gated waterfall is a linear-sequential way of working, with detail fixed up front rather than refined in repeated cycles.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A project builds a new data centre using a fixed design, build and commission sequence, while the software that will run in it is developed in short cycles. Which delivery approach is the project using?
o: Linear-sequential
Hybrid
Iterative-incremental
Phased
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A hybrid approach combines approaches within one project, for example linear-sequential for infrastructure and iterative-incremental for software (see manual 1.5.3).

n.0: The building work is linear-sequential, but the software is iterative, so the project as a whole is not linear-sequential.
n.2: The software work is iterative-incremental, but the building work follows a fixed sequence, so the project as a whole is not iterative-incremental.
n.3: Phased is not one of the three delivery approaches named in PRINCE2 7.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about delivery approaches in PRINCE2 7 are true?
1. PRINCE2 7 can govern projects using any of the three delivery approaches.
2. PRINCE2 7 requires an iterative-incremental approach for software projects.
3. An iterative-incremental project may have several delivery stages.
4. A linear-sequential project refines its acceptance criteria in parallel with development.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 7 does not favour one delivery approach and can govern any of them, and an iterative-incremental project may use multiple delivery stages (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.2.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false: PRINCE2 7 does not require a particular delivery approach for any type of project.
n.2: Both are false: no approach is required for software projects, and refining acceptance criteria alongside development is a feature of iterative-incremental work.
n.3: Statement 3 is true, but statement 4 is false: linear-sequential projects define products in detail up front rather than refining criteria during development.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: How does PRINCE2 7 relate to the delivery approach a project uses?
o: It governs the project whichever delivery approach is used, without changing its principles
It replaces the delivery approach with its own processes for building specialist products
It requires a linear-sequential approach so that each stage can be approved in turn
It applies its principles to linear-sequential work and exempts iterative work from them
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 7 is not specific to any delivery method: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid delivery can all sit within its governance, and the principles always apply (see manual 1.1 and 1.5.3).

n.1: PRINCE2 works alongside specialist delivery methods; its processes direct and manage the project rather than replacing how products are built.
n.2: Stages are used with any delivery approach; PRINCE2 7 does not require linear-sequential delivery.
n.3: All seven principles must be applied for any PRINCE2 project, whatever the delivery approach.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: In a linear-sequential project, how detailed should product descriptions be when the work is planned?
o: Brief outlines, with detail added in each iteration from the product backlog
Limited to the project product description, with the rest written at closure
Detailed enough to show the delivery approach, but not to estimate cost or time
Detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated with appropriate confidence
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough for costs and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence (see manual 7.3.1.1.3).

n.0: Adding detail iteration by iteration from a product backlog is how iterative-incremental projects work, not linear-sequential ones.
n.1: Product descriptions are needed to plan and build products; writing them at closure would be too late to guide the work.
n.2: The point of the detail in a linear-sequential project is to estimate cost and time with confidence.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A simple project with a few well-understood products and a mature delivery method may need just [?] management stages: an initiation stage and one delivery stage.
o: one
three
two
four
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Every PRINCE2 project has at least two stages: initiation plus at least one delivery stage. A simple project may need only those two (see manual 7.2.3.1).

n.0: One stage is never enough: initiation is always a stage of its own, followed by at least one delivery stage.
n.1: Three stages would mean initiation plus two delivery stages; the sentence describes initiation plus one delivery stage.
n.3: Four stages would mean initiation plus three delivery stages, which is more than the sentence describes.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 means it can be applied to any project, of any scale, and used alongside specialist, industry-specific models?
o: Flexible
Proven
Outcome-focused
Universal
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 is universal: it can be applied to any project of any scale and implemented alongside specialist, industry-specific models (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Flexible means the method can be tailored to the needs of the organizations involved, which is a different feature from applying to any project.
n.1: Proven means it is based on established and proven practice and governance.
n.2: Outcome-focused means participants stay focused on the project's viability against its business case objectives.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: A software firm and a civil engineering supplier work on the same PRINCE2 project. Both use the same terms for stages, tolerances and work packages, which makes handovers between them smoother. Which feature of PRINCE2 does this BEST illustrate?
o: Common language and concepts
Universal
Part of an integrated suite
Increased organizational maturity
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 provides a widely recognized common vocabulary for all participants, supporting consistency, reuse of project assets, staff mobility and smoother handovers (see manual 1.6).

n.1: Universal is about PRINCE2 applying to any project of any scale; the stem stresses the shared terms the two firms use.
n.2: Being part of an integrated suite means PRINCE2 works with the programme, portfolio and risk management guides; the stem is about shared terminology.
n.3: Increased organizational maturity is about learning and continual improvement over time, not a shared vocabulary between parties.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 keeps project participants focused on whether the project remains viable in relation to its business case objectives?
o: Proven
Outcome-focused
Flexible
Common language and concepts
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 is outcome-focused: it keeps participants focused on the viability of the project against its business case objectives (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Proven means it is based on established practice and governance, not that it keeps attention on viability.
n.2: Flexible means the method can be tailored to the organizations involved.
n.3: Common language and concepts is about a shared vocabulary, not a focus on viability.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 means the method can be tailored to meet the specific needs of the organizations involved?
o: Universal
Proven
Flexible
Outcome-focused
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 is flexible: it can be tailored to meet the specific needs of the organizations involved (see manual 1.6 and the tailor to suit the project principle).

n.0: Universal is about applying to any project of any scale alongside specialist models; tailoring to the organizations involved is the flexible feature.
n.1: Proven means it is based on established and proven practice and governance.
n.3: Outcome-focused means keeping participants focused on the project's viability against its business case.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q:
Which two statements about the features and benefits of PRINCE2 are true?
1. PRINCE2 is designed for one industry and its engineering practices.
2. PRINCE2 is designed to work with PeopleCert's guides on programme, portfolio and risk management.
3. PRINCE2 replaces the specialist techniques used to design and build products.
4. PRINCE2 promotes learning and continual improvement across the organization.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Statement 2 describes PRINCE2 being part of an integrated suite of methods, and statement 4 describes increased organizational maturity (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 is not specific to any industry or engineering practice.
n.1: Both are false: PRINCE2 is not industry-specific, and it works alongside specialist techniques rather than replacing them.
n.3: Statement 4 is true, but statement 3 is false: PRINCE2 is used alongside specialist, industry-specific models rather than replacing them.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which is NOT a feature of the PRINCE2 method?
o: It can be tailored to suit the organizations involved
It is designed for one industry and its engineering practices
It provides a common vocabulary for all participants
It is based on established and proven practice and governance
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 is not specific to any industry, project type, delivery method or engineering practice; it is universal and works alongside specialist models (see manual 1.1 and 1.6).

n.0: This is a genuine feature: PRINCE2 is flexible and can be tailored to the organizations involved.
n.2: This is a genuine feature: common language and concepts give all participants a shared vocabulary.
n.3: This is a genuine feature: PRINCE2 is proven, based on established practice and governance.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: An organization adopts PRINCE2 as its standard. Over several years, lessons from its projects are shared and its ways of working steadily improve. Which feature of PRINCE2 does this BEST illustrate?
o: Universal
Flexible
Part of an integrated suite of methods
Increased organizational maturity
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Adopting PRINCE2 promotes learning and continual improvement, raising the organization's capability and maturity over time (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Universal is about PRINCE2 applying to any project of any scale, not improvement over time.
n.1: Flexible is about tailoring the method to the organizations involved, not improvement over time.
n.2: Being part of an integrated suite means PRINCE2 works with the programme, portfolio and risk management guides; the stem describes learning and improvement.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 reflects that it is based on established practice and governance for project management?
o: Proven
Outcome-focused
Universal
Flexible
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 is proven: it is based on established and proven practice and governance for project management (see manual 1.6).

n.1: Outcome-focused is about keeping participants focused on viability against the business case.
n.2: Universal is about applying to any project of any scale alongside specialist models.
n.3: Flexible is about tailoring the method to the organizations involved.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement BEST matches how PRINCE2 defines a project?
o: A temporary organization set up to deliver one or more business products in line with an agreed business case
A permanent team set up to run and continually improve an organization's routine business operations
A temporary structure set up to lead several related projects so that outcomes are achieved progressively
The whole of an organization's investment in the changes it needs to meet its strategic objectives
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: PRINCE2 defines a project as a temporary organization created to deliver one or more business products according to an agreed business case (see manual 1.3). The two defining ideas are that it is temporary and that it is justified by a business case.

n.1: Running and improving routine operations is business as usual, which is permanent; a project is temporary and ends once its change is in place.
n.2: Leading several related projects to achieve outcomes progressively describes a programme, which is the context a project may sit within, not a project.
n.3: An organization's total investment in change to meet strategic objectives describes a portfolio, not an individual project.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A project is a [?] organization that is created to deliver one or more business products according to an agreed business case.
o: permanent
temporary
line
commercial
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: The PRINCE2 definition describes a project as a temporary organization (see manual 1.3). It exists to deliver business products under an agreed business case and is no longer needed once the change has been made.

n.0: A permanent organization is the business as usual structure; a project is set up for a limited time and then closed.
n.2: The line organization runs business as usual; a project creates its own temporary organization alongside it.
n.3: A commercial customer and supplier relationship is one possible project context, not part of the definition of a project.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: According to PRINCE2, what happens when the change that a project was created to introduce has been implemented?
o: The project team becomes the new line management structure for the changed operations
The project carries on as a programme so that the expected benefits can be realized
Business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project ends
The project moves into a further delivery stage to maintain the products it has built
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: Projects are temporary: once the desired change has been implemented, business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project is removed (see manual 1.3). The project is then closed.

n.0: The project team is temporary and is disbanded at closure; running the changed operations is a business as usual responsibility.
n.1: A project does not turn into a programme when it finishes; benefits realized after closure are reviewed by the business, not by a continuing project.
n.3: Maintaining products after handover is business as usual work; a project closes within its final stage rather than adding a stage for maintenance.

Projects & PRINCE2 7.q: Which statement BEST describes how a project differs from business as usual?
o: A project repeats an established procedure to keep existing services running efficiently
A project is run by permanent line managers as part of their normal departmental duties
A project needs no business case once its funding has been agreed at the start
A project is temporary: it introduces a change and ends once that change is in place
Projects & PRINCE2 7.w: A project is a temporary organization that introduces change; when the change is in place, business as usual resumes in its new form and the project ends (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Repeating an established procedure to keep services running is business as usual, the opposite of a project.
n.1: A project creates its own temporary organization with defined roles; it is not run through the normal departmental line structure.
n.2: A project is delivered according to an agreed business case, and its justification is checked throughout, not just when funding is agreed.

The Seven Principles.q: Which list contains three of the PRINCE2 7 principles?
o: Manage by stages; focus on outcomes; learn from experience
Manage by exception; focus on products; tailor to suit the project
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships; manage risk; manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification; manage by tolerance; learn from experience
The Seven Principles.w: Manage by exception, focus on products and tailor to suit the project are all PRINCE2 7 principles. The other four are ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, and manage by stages (manual 2.1 to 2.7).

n.0: The principle is 'focus on products', not 'focus on outcomes': outcomes are a business case concept, not a principle (manual 2.6).
n.2: Risk is one of the seven practices, not a principle, so 'manage risk' is not a PRINCE2 principle (manual ch 4).
n.3: The principle is 'manage by exception'; tolerances are the means it uses, and 'manage by tolerance' is not a principle (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: A portfolio office wants a consistent test of whether each project in its portfolio is genuinely being run as a PRINCE2 project. Which part of PRINCE2 provides that test?
o: The seven processes, because each must be carried out as a separate step
The management products, because each must follow the standard template
The project context, because it defines how the method must be adjusted
The seven principles, because if one is not applied it is not PRINCE2
The Seven Principles.w: The principles decide whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2: if any of the seven is not applied, the project is not a PRINCE2 project (manual 1.2 and ch 2).

n.0: Processes can be combined or simplified when tailoring, so carrying each out separately is not the test (manual 2.7).
n.1: Management products can be merged, renamed or reformatted, so following a standard template is not the test (manual 2.7).
n.2: The project context shapes how the method is applied, but it is the principles that decide whether a project is PRINCE2 (manual 1.2).

The Seven Principles.q: An organization uses PRINCE2 on a small internal project and on a large project involving several suppliers. The two projects look very different in practice. Which statement explains this?
o: Both apply the principles, but the method is tailored to each project's context
The smaller project has dropped the principles that do not suit its size and risk
The larger project applies the principles, while the smaller applies the practices
Each project board has chosen a different edition of the method to follow
The Seven Principles.w: Every PRINCE2 project applies all seven principles, while the method itself is tailored to the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and risk, so projects can look very different (manual 2.7).

n.1: Principles cannot be dropped to suit a project's size: all seven must be applied on every PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.2: Every PRINCE2 project applies the principles and the practices; size changes how they are tailored, not whether they apply (manual ch 2, ch 4).
n.3: Differences between projects come from tailoring one method to each context, not from projects choosing different editions (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: Each PRINCE2 7 practice includes a table relating that practice to the principles. What does this table show?
o: That the practice can be used in place of a principle on small projects
That each principle belongs to a single practice and is applied there
How the principles are put into effect through that practice
Which principles may be set aside when that practice is tailored
The Seven Principles.w: Each practice chapter shows how the principles are applied through that aspect of project management, for example the business case practice supports ensure continued business justification and manage by stages (manual tab 5.2, 7.2, 8.3).

n.0: A practice never stands in for a principle; all seven principles apply on every project, whatever its size (manual ch 2).
n.1: Each practice relates to several principles, and each principle is applied through several practices, not through one (manual tab 5.2, 7.2).
n.3: Tailoring a practice does not set any principle aside; the principles are not tailored (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: Which principle requires a project to have a justifiable reason to start, with that reason remaining valid and being revalidated throughout the project's life?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Manage by exception
The Seven Principles.w: Ensure continued business justification requires a justifiable reason to start the project, which must stay valid and be revalidated throughout; if it lapses, the project should be stopped (manual 2.1).

n.0: Defining roles, responsibilities and relationships makes sure the business, user and supplier interests are represented; it does not require a reason for the investment (manual 2.3).
n.2: Focus on products is about defining and delivering products to agreed quality, not about the reason for the investment (manual 2.6).
n.3: Manage by exception sets tolerances to delegate authority between levels; it does not require a justifiable reason for the project (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: A government agency must update its licensing system to comply with new legislation by a fixed date. How does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle apply to this project?
o: It does not apply, because a compulsory project has no choice about proceeding
It applies at closure, when benefits are compared with costs to inform future work
It is replaced by the legal requirement recorded in the project mandate
It still applies, because the option chosen to meet the law must be justified
The Seven Principles.w: Even compulsory projects need business justification: the organization must still justify the option it chooses to meet the requirement, for example the one giving best value (manual 2.1, 5.2.3).

n.0: Compulsory projects are not exempt: the principle still requires justification of the chosen option (manual 2.1).
n.1: Justification must remain valid throughout the project, not just be considered at closure (manual 2.1).
n.2: A legal requirement explains why something must be done, but it does not replace the need to justify the option chosen (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: During the second delivery stage, a competitor launches a similar service and the forecast benefits fall so far that they no longer outweigh the remaining costs and risks. What does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle require?
o: The project should be stopped, as it no longer has a valid justification
The project should continue, as its business case was approved at initiation
The current stage should be extended so extra scope can recover the benefits
The project manager should close the project without involving the board
The Seven Principles.w: If the justification is no longer valid, the principle says the project should be stopped; stopping a project that is no longer viable is not a failure (manual 2.1).

n.1: Approval at initiation is not enough: justification must remain valid throughout the project, so it cannot rest on the original approval (manual 2.1).
n.2: Extending the stage to add scope ignores that the benefits no longer justify the investment; the principle points to stopping (manual 2.1).
n.3: Premature closure is triggered by the project board, not decided by the project manager alone; the PM then prepares the closure (manual ch 19).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'ensure continued business justification' principle are correct?
1. The justification is usually documented in a business case.
2. The justification is fixed once the project is authorized.
3. Suppliers also need their own justification for taking part.
4. It applies to commercial projects but not to compulsory ones.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: justification is usually documented in a business case. Statement 3 is correct: every party, including suppliers, needs a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify its involvement (manual 2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the justification can change during the project, and what the project delivers must stay consistent with it (manual 2.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: justification can change, and compulsory projects still justify the option chosen (manual 2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: compulsory projects still need justification of the chosen option (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Under the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, the justification for a project must remain [?] throughout its life, not only at the start.
o: unchanged
approved by the business layer
recorded in the project mandate
valid
The Seven Principles.w: The principle requires the justification to remain valid, and be revalidated, throughout the project (manual 2.1).

n.0: The justification can change during the project; the requirement is that it stays valid, not that it stays the same (manual 2.1).
n.1: The full business case is approved by the project board when it authorizes the project; the principle's test is continuing validity (manual 2.1, 5.3.1).
n.2: The project mandate triggers starting up a project; the justification is documented in the business case (manual 5.3.1).

The Seven Principles.q: A request for change would add a feature that users have asked for, at extra cost and with some new risk. How does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle guide the decision?
o: The extra benefit is weighed against the extra cost and risk of the change
The change is accepted if it falls within the project manager's tolerance
The change is rejected, as the business case cannot change once approved
The change is accepted if the senior user confirms the feature is wanted
The Seven Principles.w: Justification can evolve, but what is delivered must stay consistent with it, so a request for change is judged by weighing its extra benefit against its extra cost and risk (manual 2.1).

n.1: Tolerance decides who may approve, which is manage by exception; it does not show whether the change is justified (manual 2.5).
n.2: The business case is maintained and updated during the project, so it can change once approved (manual 2.1, 5.3.1).
n.3: User demand on its own does not justify a change; the benefit must be balanced against the cost and risk (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: Which problem does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle help an organization to avoid?
o: Stages running beyond their agreed tolerances without any escalation
Project teams repeating mistakes made on earlier, similar projects
Projects continuing with few real benefits or loose links to strategy
Products being delivered without any agreed quality criteria
The Seven Principles.w: Organizations that lack rigour in business justification may let projects go ahead with few real benefits or only loose links to strategy; the principle keeps the project aligned with the benefits sought (manual 2.1).

n.0: Escalation when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded is the concern of manage by exception (manual 2.5).
n.1: Avoiding repeated mistakes is the purpose of learn from experience (manual 2.2).
n.3: Agreeing quality criteria before delivery is part of focus on products (manual 2.6).

The Seven Principles.q: Which statement best describes how the 'ensure continued business justification' principle works together with the 'manage by stages' principle?
o: Business justification is checked once, at the end of the initiation stage
Business justification is checked by the board at each stage boundary
The length of each stage is set by the business case's payback period
Stage boundaries are used by the business layer to set stage tolerances
The Seven Principles.w: Decisions at each stage boundary include checking that the project is still justified before the board authorizes the next stage (manual tab 5.2, 5.3.1).

n.0: Justification is checked repeatedly, at the end of each stage and when assessing an exception plan, not just once (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Stage length reflects control needs, size, complexity and external influences, not the payback period (manual 2.4).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board; the business layer sets project tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: Which principle is being applied when a project team actively seeks, records and acts on lessons from earlier projects and from its own work as the project progresses?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
Learn from experience
The Seven Principles.w: Learn from experience means the project team seeks, records and implements lessons from prior projects and throughout its own project, and shares them so others can apply them (manual 2.2).

n.0: Manage by exception is about tolerances and escalation between management levels, not lessons (manual 2.5).
n.1: This principle is about agreed roles and stakeholder relationships, not seeking and acting on lessons (manual 2.3).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's context; gathering and applying lessons is learn from experience (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: In which process is the activity 'assess previous lessons' carried out, so that the project applies learn from experience before it is initiated?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
The Seven Principles.w: 'Assess previous lessons' is an activity in starting up a project: the lessons log is created and people with experience of similar projects are consulted (manual 13.4.2).

n.0: Initiating a project follows starting up; lessons are first assessed earlier, in starting up a project (manual 13.4.2).
n.2: Directing a project covers the board's decisions; the lessons activity named here belongs to starting up a project (manual ch 14, 13.4.2).
n.3: Lessons are recorded at stage boundaries, but 'assess previous lessons' is a starting up activity (manual 13.4.2, ch 18).

The Seven Principles.q: A housing association is starting its first ever project to fit heat pumps, a technology that its own staff have not worked with before. How does the 'learn from experience' principle apply?
o: Lessons cannot be sought, as there are no previous internal projects to review
Lessons should be gathered after the first stage, once the team has some experience
Seeking lessons is even more important, including from external organizations
Lessons should be left to the supplier, who has installed heat pumps before
The Seven Principles.w: When a project is a first for the business or includes novel content, learning from others is even more important, and that includes people and organizations outside the business (manual 2.2).

n.0: A lack of internal history does not stop learning: lessons can be sought from external people and organizations (manual 2.2).
n.1: Lessons should be sought when the project starts, not deferred until after a stage (manual 2.2, 13.4.2).
n.3: The project team as a whole seeks and applies lessons; it is not handed to one party (manual 2.2).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'learn from experience' principle are correct?
1. Lessons should be drawn from successes as well as from mistakes.
2. Lessons are gathered at closure rather than during the project.
3. Lessons are kept within the project rather than given to others.
4. Lessons should be shared so that other projects can apply them.
o: 1 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: the principle covers learning from both mistakes and successes. Statement 4 is correct: lessons are shared for others to apply (manual 2.2).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: lessons are sought before the project, throughout it and at closure, not left to the end (manual 2.2).
n.2: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong: lessons are gathered throughout the project and are passed on to others (manual 2.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the principle expects lessons to be shared with others, for example through a lessons report (manual 2.2).

The Seven Principles.q: Where are lessons recorded as they are identified during a PRINCE2 7 project?
o: In the lessons log, which is part of the project log
In the lessons report, which is part of the PID
In the risk register, as an opportunity to exploit
In the issue register, as a concern to be assessed
The Seven Principles.w: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log, one of the records held in the project log, and are later reported in a lessons report (manual 2.2, 4.3.2).

n.1: The lessons report passes lessons on; it is not part of the PID and is not where lessons are logged as they arise (manual ch 11).
n.2: The risk register holds uncertain future events, not lessons from experience (manual ch 9).
n.3: The issue register holds formal issues such as problems and requests for change, not lessons (manual ch 10).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Because behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to write down, much of this knowledge is best passed on through [?] learning.
o: formal
individual
social
classroom
The Seven Principles.w: Much valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem; behaviours, culture and relationships are best learned through social learning in a collaborative, knowledge-sharing environment (manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Formal learning suits documented knowledge; PRINCE2 points to social learning for knowledge that is hard to document (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Individual study does not draw out knowledge held across the ecosystem; PRINCE2 points to social learning (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Classroom training is a formal route; the knowledge described is best shared through social learning (manual 3.5.1).

The Seven Principles.q: How does the 'learn from experience' principle apply when a project is being closed?
o: Lessons are recorded in the end stage report for the final stage
Lessons are passed on in a lessons report so future projects can use them
Lessons are given to the senior user to manage in benefits reviews
Lessons are reviewed by quality assurance before the project is authorized
The Seven Principles.w: At closure, the project log is reviewed for lessons and a lessons report is produced so that lessons are passed on to future projects (manual 2.2, 19.4.4).

n.0: Managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage, so there is no end stage report then; lessons go into the lessons report (manual 19.4.4).
n.2: The senior user is responsible for the continued realization of benefits, not for managing the project's lessons (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.3: Authorizing the project happens at the end of initiation, not at closure, and lessons are passed on through the lessons report (manual 19.4.4).

The Seven Principles.q: A project's specialists work in three countries. The project manager sets up regular sessions where they share what has and has not worked, adapting the format to different learning preferences. Which principle is MAINLY being applied?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by stages
Manage by exception
Learn from experience
The Seven Principles.w: Sharing insights as the project progresses, and allowing for different learning needs and preferences, is how learn from experience is applied during the project (manual 2.2).

n.0: This principle is about agreeing roles and building stakeholder relationships, not sharing what has worked (manual 2.3).
n.1: Manage by stages concerns planning and deciding stage by stage, not sharing lessons between specialists (manual 2.4).
n.2: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and escalation, not knowledge sharing (manual 2.5).
