The Seven Principles.q: Under the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, which three primary stakeholder interests must be represented in the project management team?
o: Business, user and supplier
Sponsor, customer and contractor
Executive, project manager and team
Strategic, operational and technical
The Seven Principles.w: Every project has three primary stakeholder interests, business, user and supplier, and all three must be represented in the project management team, as reflected in the project board (manual 2.3).

n.1: Sponsor, customer and contractor are general terms; PRINCE2 names the business, user and supplier interests (manual 2.3).
n.2: These are roles or levels within the project, not the three stakeholder interests the principle requires (manual 2.3).
n.3: These are not PRINCE2 stakeholder interests; the three are business, user and supplier (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: PRINCE2 7 renamed the earlier 'defined roles and responsibilities' principle. What does the new wording add?
o: Tolerances agreed between each pair of management levels
A requirement for a full-time project manager
Building relationships with and between stakeholders
A separate role for each of the seven practices
The Seven Principles.w: PRINCE2 7 adds relationships: as well as defining roles and responsibilities, the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: Tolerances between management levels belong to manage by exception, not to the roles principle (manual 2.5).
n.1: The principle does not require a full-time project manager; it adds the building of relationships (manual 2.3).
n.3: Roles are not created per practice; the organizing practice defines the project management team roles (manual 2.3, ch 6).

The Seven Principles.q: Why does the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle call for a project organization structure instead of relying on the existing line management structure?
o: A project structure lets the project manager also act as the executive
Day-to-day line structures are often not suited to cross-functional project work
Line managers are not permitted to hold any role on a PRINCE2 project
A project structure removes the need for a project board on small projects
The Seven Principles.w: Line management structures may not suit project work, which is often cross-functional, spans several organizations, mixes part-time and full-time staff, and crosses locations and priorities (manual 2.3).

n.0: The project manager and executive roles are never combined, whatever structure is used (manual 2.7).
n.2: Line managers can take project roles; the point is that the line structure itself may not suit project work (manual 2.3).
n.3: The project board reflects the business, user and supplier interests the principle requires; a project structure does not remove it (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle are correct?
1. Stakeholders can be inside or outside the business.
2. The supplier interest is represented by the project manager.
3. Relationships matter within the project team and beyond it.
4. Roles are agreed once the first delivery stage has begun.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: stakeholders include internal groups and outside parties such as unions, customers, suppliers and communities. Statement 3 is correct: the team builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the supplier interest is represented on the project board, not by the project manager (manual 2.3).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the supplier interest sits on the board, and roles are agreed before delivery begins (manual 2.3).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: roles and responsibilities are defined and agreed as the project is set up, not after delivery starts (manual 2.3, ch 13).

The Seven Principles.q: How is the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle reflected in the make-up of the project board?
o: The board includes the project manager so that delivery is represented
The board has one member for each practice so that all practices are covered
The board brings together the business, user and supplier interests
The board is made up of line managers from each affected department
The Seven Principles.w: The principle requires the business, user and supplier interests to be represented, and this is reflected in the design of the project board (manual 2.3).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day for the board but is not a board member (manual ch 6).
n.1: Board membership follows the three stakeholder interests, not the seven practices (manual 2.3).
n.3: Membership is based on representing business, user and supplier interests, not on line positions (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Under the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, the project management team builds relationships with and between internal and [?] stakeholders.
o: senior
external
commissioning
operational
The Seven Principles.w: The principle says the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: The principle covers stakeholders inside and outside the business, not a seniority group (manual 2.3).
n.2: The commissioning organization is the business layer, which is internal; the pairing in the principle is internal and external (manual 2.3).
n.3: Operational staff are one internal group; the principle refers to internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: A new team member says she is unsure what is expected of her and what she can expect from others in the team. Which principle has been applied poorly?
o: Manage by stages, as her work has not been planned stage by stage
Focus on products, as her products have no agreed quality criteria
Learn from experience, as lessons from past teams were not shared
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, as roles are unclear
The Seven Principles.w: The principle aims to make sure the right people are involved and that each knows what is expected of them and what they can expect from others (manual 2.3).

n.0: Nothing in the situation concerns stage planning; manage by stages is about planning and deciding stage by stage, not who does what (manual 2.4).
n.1: The situation says nothing about quality criteria; the gap is unclear expectations between people, which focus on products does not address (manual 2.6).
n.2: The situation is not about lessons from past teams; it is about not knowing what is expected and what to expect from others (manual 2.2, 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: A project to build a new depot will affect local residents, and a trade union represents staff who will work there. How does the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle treat these groups?
o: As stakeholders with whom the project should build relationships
As members of the project board representing the user interest
As outside the project's concern, as they are not part of the business
As suppliers, as they influence how the products will be delivered
The Seven Principles.w: Stakeholders can be inside or outside the business, including trade unions and communities, and the project management team builds relationships with them (manual 2.3).

n.1: Being affected by a project does not make a group a board member; the board represents the business, user and supplier interests through its roles (manual 2.3).
n.2: External groups such as unions and communities are stakeholders the principle expects the project to engage (manual 2.3).
n.3: Suppliers provide expertise, people and resources; residents and a union are stakeholders, not suppliers (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: Under the 'manage by stages' principle, what is the minimum number of management stages in a PRINCE2 project?
o: One, covering initiation and delivery together
Three: initiation, delivery and a closing stage
Two: initiation and one or more delivery stages
Four: one for each level of management
The Seven Principles.w: A PRINCE2 project has at least two management stages: the initiation stage, which always comes first, and at least one further delivery stage (manual 2.4).

n.0: Initiation is always a stage of its own, so a single combined stage does not meet the principle (manual 2.4).
n.1: Closing a project is carried out within the final delivery stage, not as a separate stage (manual ch 19).
n.3: Stages are not linked to the management levels; the minimum is initiation plus at least one delivery stage (manual 2.4).

The Seven Principles.q: Which statement describes a benefit of the 'manage by stages' principle?
o: It removes the need for a project plan by relying on detailed stage plans
It lets the project manager set the tolerances for each stage
It allows team managers to report directly to the project board
It gives the board decision points to assess the project's viability
The Seven Principles.w: Stages give the project board review and decision points at which it can assess whether the project is still viable, rather than letting it run on uncontrolled (manual 2.4).

n.0: PRINCE2 uses both a high-level project plan and a detailed stage plan for the current stage (manual 2.4).
n.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board, not the project manager (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Team managers report to the project manager through checkpoint reports, not to the board (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: One project board wants tighter control over a high-risk project. Another wants to reduce the demands its project makes on busy senior managers. How should the stage lengths of the two projects differ?
o: Shorter stages for the high-risk project; longer stages for the other
Longer stages for the high-risk project; shorter stages for the other
Equal stages for both, as stage length is fixed by the business layer
One long delivery stage for both, to keep decision points to a minimum
The Seven Principles.w: Stage length is a trade-off: shorter stages give more control, while longer stages reduce the burden on senior management (manual 2.4).

n.1: This reverses the trade-off: longer stages mean fewer decision points and less control (manual 2.4).
n.2: Stage length is chosen for each project, considering size, complexity and control needs; it is not fixed by the business layer (manual 2.4).
n.3: A single long delivery stage reduces control, which does not suit the high-risk project (manual 2.4).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'manage by stages' principle are correct?
1. The first stage is the initiation stage.
2. Authority is delegated to the project manager one stage at a time.
3. Each stage must be the same length to allow comparison.
4. Closing a project is carried out as a separate final stage.
o: 2 and 3
1 and 2
3 and 4
1 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: initiation is always the first stage. Statement 2 is correct: the board delegates authority to the project manager stage by stage (manual 2.4).

n.0: Statement 3 is wrong: stage lengths vary with control needs, size, complexity and external events (manual 2.4).
n.2: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong: stages differ in length, and closure happens within the final stage (manual 2.4, ch 19).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: closing a project is part of the final stage, not a stage of its own (manual ch 19).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Because only the near future can be planned in detail, PRINCE2 combines a high-level project plan with a detailed [?] for the current management stage.
o: team plan
stage plan
exception plan
work package
The Seven Principles.w: The planning horizon limits detailed planning, so manage by stages pairs a high-level project plan with a detailed stage plan for the current stage (manual 2.4).

n.0: Team plans are optional plans for a team's work, not the detailed plan for the whole current stage (manual ch 7).
n.2: An exception plan is produced when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not as the normal detailed stage plan (manual ch 7).
n.3: A work package is a set of information for a team manager, not a plan for the stage (manual ch 7).

The Seven Principles.q: A retailer sets its budgets each April. The project manager proposes that a stage should end in March so the board can take the new budget into account. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, as a stage end is aligned with the budget-setting cycle
Manage by exception, as the board's stage tolerance must be reset each year
Ensure continued business justification, as benefits will begin in April
Tailor to suit the project, as stage length is set by the finance team
The Seven Principles.w: Stage ends can be aligned with external influences, such as the business's budget-setting cycle, to make their effect on the project clear (manual 2.4).

n.1: Tolerances are set for each stage by the board as it authorizes the stage; there is no yearly reset rule (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.2: The situation says nothing about when benefits start; the stage end is chosen to match the budget cycle (manual 2.4).
n.3: Stage length is decided within the project, considering control needs and external events, not set by a finance team (manual 2.4).

The Seven Principles.q: How does the 'manage by stages' principle support the 'manage by exception' principle?
o: Stage boundaries are when tolerances are first forecast to be exceeded
Each stage has its own exception report prepared by the team manager
The board sets project tolerances at the start of each delivery stage
The board delegates authority to the project manager one stage at a time
The Seven Principles.w: Manage by stages makes manage by exception workable: the board delegates authority one stage at a time, and while the stage is forecast to stay within tolerance the project manager can adjust as needed (manual 2.4).

n.0: A breach can be forecast at any time during a stage, not just at a boundary (manual 2.5, ch 11).
n.1: Exception reports are raised by the project manager when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not by team managers each stage (manual ch 11).
n.2: Project tolerances are set by the business layer; the board sets stage tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: How does PRINCE2 7 link the 'manage by stages' principle with the people involved in a project?
o: Each stage needs a new executive to bring a fresh view of the business
Each stage needs a new team so that working relationships stay simple
Stage boundaries are good points to review how people work together
Stage boundaries are when the business layer resets team tolerances
The Seven Principles.w: Stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so they are good points to review how people interact with each other and the wider organization (manual 3.5.1).

n.0: A project has one executive throughout; stages do not require a new appointment (manual ch 6).
n.1: Stages do not require new teams; they are points to review how people are working together (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The business layer sets project tolerances, and team (work package) tolerances are set by the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: Which principle establishes limits of delegated authority by defining tolerances for performance against plans?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by exception
Focus on products
Ensure continued business justification
The Seven Principles.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority by defining tolerances against plans, with escalation to the next level when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 2.5).

n.0: This principle defines who holds which role and builds relationships; it does not set tolerance limits (manual 2.3).
n.2: Focus on products defines products and quality expectations; the permitted variation is set through tolerances under manage by exception (manual 2.6).
n.3: This principle requires a valid reason for the project throughout; it does not set limits of authority (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: Under the 'manage by exception' principle, against which aspects of performance are tolerances set in PRINCE2 7?
o: Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk
Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope and risk
Cost, time, quality, scope, risk and stakeholder satisfaction
Cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and resources
The Seven Principles.w: PRINCE2 7 sets tolerances against seven aspects of performance: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (manual 2.5).

n.1: This is the older list of six; PRINCE2 7 adds sustainability as a seventh aspect (manual 2.5).
n.2: Stakeholder satisfaction is not a tolerance area, and the list leaves out benefits and sustainability (manual 2.5).
n.3: Resources is not a tolerance area, and the list leaves out benefits and risk (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: A stage is forecast to finish 2 weeks later than planned. The board set a time tolerance of plus 4 weeks for the stage. What should the project manager do?
o: Raise an exception report, as the stage plan's target date will be missed
Ask the business layer to widen the project's time tolerance
Ask the team manager to prepare an exception plan for the stage
Continue managing the stage, as it is forecast to stay within tolerance
The Seven Principles.w: Under manage by exception the project manager can take action within the delegated tolerance; escalation is needed when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, and a 2-week delay is within plus 4 weeks (manual 2.4, 2.5).

n.0: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not when a target is missed within tolerance (manual ch 11).
n.1: Project tolerances are not affected, and the stage is still within its own tolerance, so nothing needs escalating (manual 2.5).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager at the board's request after an exception report; none is needed within tolerance (manual ch 11, ch 18).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'manage by exception' principle are correct?
1. An exception exists when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
2. The project manager sets the tolerances for each stage.
3. It uses senior management time efficiently without removing their control.
4. Escalation waits until a tolerance has actually been exceeded.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: an exception is a forecast breach of tolerance. Statement 3 is correct: the principle reduces the burden on senior managers while keeping them in control (manual 2.5, ch 11).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: stage tolerances are set by the project board; the project manager sets work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the board sets stage tolerances, and escalation happens on a forecast breach (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the next level should be alerted as early as possible, when a breach is forecast (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: Under the 'manage by exception' principle, which management levels set stage tolerances and work package tolerances?
o: Project board sets stage; project manager sets work package
Business layer sets stage; project board sets work package
Project manager sets stage; team manager sets work package
Project board sets stage; team manager sets work package
The Seven Principles.w: Authority is delegated level by level: the business layer sets project tolerances, the project board sets stage tolerances and the project manager sets work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

n.1: The business layer sets project tolerances, not stage tolerances, and the board does not set work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The project manager works within stage tolerances set by the board and sets work package tolerances; team managers work within them (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances set by the project manager; they do not set them (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Applied to people, manage by exception means decisions should be made at the most [?] level where the knowledge to make and own them resides.
o: senior
central
formal
local
The Seven Principles.w: PRINCE2 7 applies manage by exception to people by placing decisions at the most local level where the knowledge resides, escalating when a decision could affect other areas (manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Pushing decisions to the most senior level would defeat delegation; the principle places them where the knowledge resides (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Centralizing decisions is the opposite of delegated authority under manage by exception (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Formality is not the test; the decision is made at the most local level with the knowledge to own it (manual 3.5.1).

The Seven Principles.q: What is the main purpose of the 'manage by exception' principle?
o: To make sure the board approves every change to the stage plan
To allow the project manager to change project tolerances when needed
To let each level manage within limits and alert the next level early
To make sure exceptions are reported at the end of each stage
The Seven Principles.w: Each level manages within its delegated tolerances, and the next level is alerted as early as possible when work is forecast to move outside them, which makes efficient use of senior time (manual 2.5).

n.0: Requiring board approval of every change would remove delegation; the PM can adjust within stage tolerance (manual 2.4, 2.5).
n.1: Project tolerances are set by the business layer; the project manager cannot change them (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Exceptions are escalated as soon as a breach is forecast, not held until the stage ends (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: A team manager forecasts that a work package will exceed its cost tolerance, although the stage as a whole is still forecast to stay within tolerance. How does manage by exception apply?
o: The team manager raises an exception report directly to the project board
The team manager raises an issue to the project manager to resolve
The project manager asks the business layer for an exception plan
The team manager continues, as the stage tolerance will not be breached
The Seven Principles.w: The team manager escalates a forecast breach of work package tolerance to the project manager as an issue; work package exceptions are handled by the project manager in controlling a stage (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).

n.0: Team managers escalate to the project manager, not the board; only stage or project exceptions go to the board (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: No exception plan is needed while the stage is within tolerance, and the business layer handles project-level exceptions (manual 11.2.6).
n.3: The team manager's own tolerance is forecast to be breached, so it must be escalated to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: Which principle centres on the definition and delivery of products, in particular their user quality expectations and requirements?
o: Manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Focus on products
The Seven Principles.w: Focus on products means the project concentrates on defining and delivering products, particularly the users' quality expectations and requirements (manual 2.6).

n.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and deciding stage by stage, not defining products (manual 2.4).
n.1: This principle concerns the reason for the investment remaining valid, not product definitions (manual 2.1).
n.2: This principle concerns roles and stakeholder relationships, not defining products and their quality (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: PRINCE2 says projects should be output-oriented rather than work-oriented. What is the main advantage of this?
o: Team managers can start building before the products have been described
Activities can be planned without needing to involve the users
Waste is avoided, as no more work is done than the agreed products need
Progress can be measured by hours worked rather than by products delivered
The Seven Principles.w: A product focus makes projects more efficient and avoids waste: the project does no more work than needed to deliver its agreed products, which also helps control scope creep (manual 2.6).

n.0: Products are defined and agreed before the work is done, not after building has started (manual 2.6).
n.1: Products are defined around user quality expectations, so users are involved rather than left out (manual 2.6).
n.3: Measuring hours worked is a work-oriented view; PRINCE2 tracks the delivery of products (manual 2.6).

The Seven Principles.q: Before a team starts building a new online booking form, the project manager agrees with the users what the form is for, what it consists of and how its quality will be checked. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Focus on products
Learn from experience
Tailor to suit the project
The Seven Principles.w: Agreeing a product's purpose, composition and quality criteria before work starts is the focus on products principle, applied through a product description (manual 2.6).

n.0: Manage by exception sets tolerances for permitted variation; agreeing what the product is comes under focus on products (manual 2.5, 2.6).
n.2: Learn from experience concerns lessons; nothing in the situation involves lessons (manual 2.2).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; defining one product's content and quality is focus on products (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the 'focus on products' principle are correct?
1. It helps to control scope creep.
2. Products are defined once the work to build them is complete.
3. Product descriptions include quality criteria or specifications.
4. It means each stage delivers exactly one product.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: doing no more work than the agreed products need controls scope creep. Statement 3 is correct: product descriptions include quality criteria or specifications and the quality method (manual 2.6).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: products are defined and agreed before the work to deliver them (manual 2.6).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: products are defined before the work, and a stage can deliver many products (manual 2.6).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: nothing in the principle limits a stage to one product (manual 2.6).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

A [?] sets out a product's purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and quality method.
o: work package description
project brief
product description
quality register
The Seven Principles.w: Under focus on products, product descriptions give clarity about each product: its purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality criteria or specifications and quality method (manual 2.6).

n.0: A work package description sets out work for a team manager; it refers to product descriptions rather than replacing them (manual ch 7).
n.1: The project brief describes the project as a whole for initiation, not each product's content (manual ch 13).
n.3: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities, not the product's definition (manual ch 8).

The Seven Principles.q: Which statement best explains how the 'focus on products' principle supports change control?
o: Changes are approved by the team manager who builds the product
Agreed product definitions give a baseline for judging changes
Products cannot be changed once their descriptions are written
Changes to products are deferred to the final stage for review
The Seven Principles.w: A product focus is the basis of planning, quality, scope and change control: with products clearly defined and agreed, a proposed change can be judged against that baseline (manual 2.6).

n.0: Team managers build products; changes are decided by the board or a change authority, not by the team manager (manual ch 10).
n.2: Agreed products can be changed through issue and change control; the definitions make change visible rather than forbidden (manual 2.6, ch 10).
n.3: Requests for change are handled as they arise through the issues practice, not saved for the final stage (manual ch 10).

The Seven Principles.q: How does PRINCE2 7 link the 'focus on products' principle with the people element?
o: Co-creating products with users and suppliers improves their adoption
Products are designed by the supplier to keep ownership clear
User involvement ends once the project product description is agreed
Team members are assigned by product rather than by skills or capacity
The Seven Principles.w: Co-creating products, using agreed product descriptions, with the business, user and supplier communities unites perspectives, improves development and adoption and reduces handover risks (manual 3.5.1).

n.1: PRINCE2 7 encourages co-creation across business, user and supplier communities rather than leaving design to the supplier (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Users stay involved, for example in co-creating and accepting products, not just in agreeing the project product description (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The principle's people link is co-creation and adoption, not a way of assigning team members (manual 3.5.1).

The Seven Principles.q: During delivery, a team adds several extra features that are not in any agreed product description because it believes users will like them. Which principle is this team weakening?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by stages
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Focus on products
The Seven Principles.w: Focus on products means doing no more work than needed to deliver the agreed products; adding unagreed features is scope creep, which the principle is meant to control (manual 2.6).

n.0: Learn from experience concerns seeking and sharing lessons; the problem here is work beyond the agreed products (manual 2.2).
n.1: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and decisions; the team is going beyond its agreed products (manual 2.4).
n.2: The team's roles are not the issue; it is delivering products that were never defined or agreed (manual 2.6).

The Seven Principles.q: Before drafting the project brief, a project manager reads the lessons reports from two similar projects and talks to their project managers about what went wrong. Which principle is being applied?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by stages
Focus on products
Ensure continued business justification
The Seven Principles.w: Seeking lessons from previous similar projects before the project begins is learn from experience, applied in starting up a project through 'assess previous lessons' (manual 2.2, 13.4.2).

n.1: Nothing here concerns stage planning or decision points; the PM is gathering lessons (manual 2.4).
n.2: The PM is not defining products or quality criteria; reviewing past lessons is learn from experience (manual 2.6).
n.3: The PM is not testing whether the project is worth doing; the action is gathering lessons from earlier projects (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: The project board agrees that the current stage may cost up to 5% more than planned before the project manager must escalate to the board. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by stages
Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Tailor to suit the project
The Seven Principles.w: Setting a cost tolerance for the stage, within which the PM can act without escalating, is manage by exception (manual 2.5).

n.0: Manage by stages provides the stage itself, but setting the permitted variation before escalation is manage by exception (manual 2.4, 2.5).
n.2: The board is not judging whether the project is still worthwhile; it is setting delegated limits (manual 2.1).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method; setting a tolerance for a stage is manage by exception (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: An organization renames the 'highlight report' as its familiar 'fortnightly update' and agrees that its widely dispersed board will review reports online. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
Learn from experience
The Seven Principles.w: Using the organization's own terminology and adjusting the format of reporting and reviews to suit the project are examples of tailoring the method to suit the project (manual 2.7).

n.0: No tolerances or escalation limits are being set; terms and reporting formats are being adapted (manual 2.5).
n.1: Roles and relationships are not being defined; the method's terms and formats are being adapted (manual 2.3).
n.3: No lessons are being sought or applied; the action is adapting the method to the organization (manual 2.2).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two of the following actions apply the 'focus on products' principle?
1. Agreeing quality criteria for each product before work starts.
2. Setting a cost tolerance for each work package.
3. Reviewing at a stage boundary whether benefits still outweigh costs.
4. Identifying the products needed before planning the activities.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 applies focus on products: quality criteria are agreed in product descriptions before work starts. Statement 4 applies it too: product-based planning identifies products before activities (manual 2.6, ch 7).

n.0: Statement 2 applies manage by exception, as it sets a tolerance for delegated work (manual 2.5).
n.1: Statement 2 is manage by exception and statement 3 is ensure continued business justification, so neither applies focus on products (manual 2.1, 2.5).
n.2: Statement 3 applies ensure continued business justification, checking that benefits still justify costs (manual 2.1).

The Seven Principles.q: First, the project manager agrees with the users which products are in scope. Second, the board agrees how much variation in those products is allowed before escalation. Which principles do these two actions apply, in order?
o: Manage by stages, then manage by exception
Manage by exception, then focus on products
Focus on products, then ensure continued business justification
Focus on products, then manage by exception
The Seven Principles.w: Defining what is in scope is focus on products; agreeing the permitted range of variation (scope tolerance) before escalation is manage by exception (manual 2.5, 2.6).

n.0: Agreeing which products are in scope is focus on products, not manage by stages (manual 2.6).
n.1: This reverses the pair: defining products comes under focus on products, and the allowed variation under manage by exception (manual 2.5, 2.6).
n.2: The permitted variation before escalation is a tolerance, which is manage by exception rather than business justification (manual 2.5).

The Seven Principles.q: Partway through a project, the board reviews whether the expected benefits still justify the remaining costs and risks before it approves the next stage plan. Which principle is the board applying by making this check?
o: Manage by exception
Learn from experience
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
The Seven Principles.w: Checking that benefits still justify the remaining costs and risks applies ensure continued business justification, which requires the justification to be revalidated throughout (manual 2.1, tab 5.2).

n.0: No tolerance is being set or breached; the board is checking whether the project is still worth doing (manual 2.5).
n.1: The board is not seeking lessons; it is revalidating the business justification (manual 2.2).
n.3: No roles or relationships are being defined; the check concerns the project's justification (manual 2.3).

The Seven Principles.q: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable way to tailor PRINCE2 to a project?
o: Combining the project brief and business case on a small project
Deciding not to apply the 'manage by stages' principle on this project
Adding an agile coach role to support an iterative supplier team
Using the organization's own names for some management products
The Seven Principles.w: Principles are not tailored: all seven must be applied, so deciding not to apply manage by stages would mean the project is no longer a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2, 2.7).

n.0: Small, low-value projects may merge the project brief and business case into one simple document, which is acceptable tailoring (manual 2.7, 5.4.5).
n.2: Roles can be added when tailoring, for example a coach to support an iterative way of working (manual 2.7).
n.3: Terminology can be tailored to use the organization's own terms (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: A project manager encourages a decision about a minor product feature to be made by the team member who understands it best, and asks for it to be escalated if it could affect other teams. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Learn from experience
Focus on products
The Seven Principles.w: PRINCE2 7 applies manage by exception to people: decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge resides, and escalated when they could affect other areas (manual 3.5.1).

n.1: The action is about where a decision is made and when it is escalated, which PRINCE2 links to manage by exception rather than to defining roles (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: No lessons are being sought or shared; the action concerns the level at which a decision is made (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The feature is a product, but the action concerns who decides and when to escalate, not defining the product (manual 3.5.1).

The Seven Principles.q: A project manager explains that her organization's projects use the PRINCE2 processes and management products, but the project board has decided not to apply the 'manage by exception' principle. How should this project be viewed?
o: It is a PRINCE2 project, because the processes and management products are in use
It is a PRINCE2 project, because principles may be tailored to suit the project's scale
It is not a PRINCE2 project, because all seven principles must be applied
It is not a PRINCE2 project, because every management product must be used unchanged
The Seven Principles.w: The principles are the guiding obligations of the method: unless all seven are applied, the project is not being run as a PRINCE2 project, however many processes or products it uses (see manual ch 2 and 1.2).

n.0: Using processes and management products is not enough: a project that leaves out any principle is not a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.1: Tailoring adapts processes, practices, roles, management products and terminology; the principles themselves are not tailored away (manual 2.7).
n.3: Management products can be merged, split, renamed or reformatted when tailoring, so unchanged use is not a requirement (manual 2.7).

The Seven Principles.q: Why does PRINCE2 give guidance through principles rather than prescribing exactly how the method should be fitted to each project?
o: So that the method can be applied differently to suit each project, even within one organization
So that every project in an organization follows an identical set of processes and documents
So that the project board can choose during initiation which principles suit the project
So that the method can take the place of the specialist techniques used in each industry
The Seven Principles.w: Because the method is guided by principles rather than prescriptive rules, it is flexible enough to be applied in different ways on different projects, including projects in the same organization (manual ch 2).

n.1: Principles exist precisely so that projects do not all have to look identical; the method is applied differently to suit each project (manual ch 2).
n.2: The board does not choose principles: all seven must be applied for the project to be a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.3: PRINCE2 does not replace specialist or industry techniques; it is a project management method that works alongside them (manual 1.1).

The Seven Principles.q:
Which two statements about the PRINCE2 principles are correct?
1. They are guiding obligations and good practices.
2. They may be left out on small, low-risk projects.
3. They are shown as the foundation beneath the practices, people and processes.
4. They are replaced by the practices once the project has been initiated.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
The Seven Principles.w: Statement 1 is correct: the principles are guiding obligations and good practices. Statement 3 is correct: the integrated elements figure shows the principles as the foundation, with the practices, people and processes built on them (manual ch 2, fig 1.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: small projects still apply all seven principles; it is the method, not the principles, that is scaled down by tailoring (manual 2.7).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: principles are never left out, and the practices put the principles into effect rather than replacing them (manual ch 2).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the principles apply throughout the project lifecycle and are not replaced by the practices after initiation (manual ch 2).

The Seven Principles.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

When PRINCE2 is tailored to suit a project, the [?] are not changed, so they still apply in full to every PRINCE2 project.
o: processes
principles
management products
role descriptions
The Seven Principles.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project, but the principles are not tailored: all seven must still be applied (manual 2.7 and ch 2).

n.0: Processes can be tailored, for example combined, simplified or carried out in more detail (manual 2.7).
n.2: Management products can be tailored, for example merged, split, renamed or given a different format (manual 2.7).
n.3: Roles can be tailored, for example combined, split or added to, so role descriptions change with them (manual 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of tailoring are correct?
1. Tailoring can make project controls lighter or more formal to suit the project.
2. Tailoring allows a principle to be dropped on a low-risk project.
3. Tailoring helps the method fit the business processes that support the project.
4. Tailoring removes the need for a project board on a small project.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 1 is correct: controls such as the frequency and formality of reports and reviews are fitted to the project. Statement 3 is correct: tailoring aligns the method with the business processes that govern and support the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the principles are not tailored, and all seven must be applied for the project to be a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: principles cannot be dropped, and a project board is still needed to direct a small project (manual ch 2, 6.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: tailoring may combine roles within the rules, but the project board still directs the project and is accountable to the business (manual 6.2.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Two PRINCE2 projects in one organization report differently: one has weekly formal highlight reports, the other brief monthly updates. What best explains this?
o: Each has fitted its controls to its own scale, complexity and risk
One of the projects has stopped applying 'manage by exception'
One is not a PRINCE2 project, as its reporting differs
Each reporting cycle is set by the team managers' checkpoint reports
Tailoring & Project Context.w: PRINCE2 guides through principles rather than prescribing one way of working, so it is applied differently on different projects, even in one organization; tailoring fits the frequency and formality of reporting to each project (see manual ch 2 and 2.7).

n.1: Different reporting frequencies do not mean a principle has been dropped; reporting is a control that tailoring adjusts (manual 2.7).
n.2: PRINCE2 is expected to be applied differently across projects in one organization, so different reporting does not stop a project being PRINCE2 (manual ch 2).
n.3: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager; how often the board receives highlight reports is agreed as a project control, not set by team managers (manual ch 11).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which statement about tailoring and the PRINCE2 principles is correct?
o: It lets the project board select the principles that suit the project
It is a practice, applied through the management approaches
It applies to the principles but not to processes or practices
It adapts the method, while all seven principles still apply
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Tailoring is itself one of the seven principles. It adapts the processes, practices, roles, management products and terminology, but the principles are not tailored: all seven must still be applied (see manual ch 2 and 2.7).

n.0: The board cannot select principles: if any principle is not applied, the project is not a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.1: Tailoring is one of the seven principles, not a practice; it is the practices that are tailored through the management approaches (manual 2.7).
n.2: This is the reverse of the rule: processes and practices can be tailored, but the principles cannot (manual 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A team manager suggests tailoring away 'manage by stages' on a small project by skipping the initiation stage and going straight into delivery. Why is this unacceptable?
o: Because stage numbers are fixed by the business layer in the project mandate
Because principles are not tailored, and initiation precedes the delivery stages
Because tailoring proposals have to come from the executive, not a team manager
Because a project with one delivery stage would first need an exception plan
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The principles cannot be tailored away, and manage by stages requires at least two stages: an initiation stage first, then one or more delivery stages, so the project is properly initiated before delivery work starts (see manual 2.4 and 2.7).

n.0: The business layer provides the mandate and project tolerances; the number and length of stages are planned for the project, not fixed in the mandate (manual 2.4, fig 6.2).
n.2: The problem is the proposal itself, not who made it: the principle cannot be tailored away whoever suggests it (manual 2.7).
n.3: A project with one delivery stage is valid if it also has an initiation stage; exception plans respond to forecast tolerance breaches (manual 2.4, ch 11).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which set lists factors that the 'tailor to suit the project' principle names as influencing how PRINCE2 is applied?
o: Environment, size, number of stages and benefits tolerance
Complexity, importance, executive's seniority and contract value
Delivery method, team capability, complexity and level of risk
Size, project mandate, quality register and level of risk
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The principle names seven factors: the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk. Delivery method, team capability, complexity and risk are four of them (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Environment and size are factors, but the number of stages and benefits tolerance are planning and control decisions, not named tailoring factors (manual 2.4, 2.5, 2.7).
n.1: Complexity and importance are factors, but the executive's seniority and contract value are not among the seven named factors (manual 2.7).
n.3: Size and risk are factors, but the project mandate is the business layer's trigger for starting up and the quality register is a record in the project log; neither is a tailoring factor (manual 2.7, 4.3.2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: While tailoring the method, a project manager notes that most of the project team have no experience of the delivery method being used. Which tailoring factor is she considering?
o: Team capability
Project importance
Project environment
Project size
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Team capability is one of the seven tailoring factors; the experience and skills of the team affect how controls such as reporting should be set (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Importance concerns how significant the project is to the organization, not how experienced the team is (manual 2.7).
n.2: Environment concerns the setting the project runs in, such as the organization, regulation or commercial context, not the team's own experience (manual 2.7).
n.3: Size concerns the scale of the project, not the experience of the people doing the work (manual 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
A PRINCE2 project is tailored to suit its environment, size, complexity, importance, [?], team capability and level of risk.
o: funding source
business case
stage plan
delivery method
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Delivery method is one of the seven factors named by the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, alongside environment, size, complexity, importance, team capability and level of risk (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Where the funding comes from is not one of the seven named tailoring factors; securing funding is an executive responsibility (manual 2.7, 6.2.4).
n.1: The business case is a management product that is itself tailored in format and detail; it is not one of the named factors (manual 2.7, 5.4.5).
n.2: A stage plan is a management product created for each stage; it is not one of the named tailoring factors (manual 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which situation may require a project to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems?
o: A project manager who is new to the business
A commercial customer-supplier relationship
A single internal team in one location
Updating the business case at stage boundaries
Tailoring & Project Context.w: A commercial customer-supplier relationship is an influence that gives cause to tailor: the project may need to align its processes, practices and documentation with both parties' quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.0: A new project manager may affect team capability, but it does not create a second quality system to align with (manual 2.7).
n.2: A single internal team in one location has one organization's quality system, so there is no second system to align with (manual 2.7).
n.3: Updating the business case at stage boundaries is normal practice in managing a stage boundary, not an influence that needs alignment of quality systems (manual ch 18).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project's product is central to the organization's strategy, and failure would be highly visible. How is this MOST likely to affect tailoring?
o: Some principles may be dropped so decisions are taken faster
Controls are likely to be more formal, given the project's importance
The business layer is likely to take over directing the project
Fewer management products are needed, as senior support is strong
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Importance is one of the tailoring factors, and project controls such as the formality of reports and reviews are fitted to the project's importance; a highly important project is likely to need more formal control (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Principles are never tailored away, whatever the pressure for speed; all seven must be applied (manual ch 2).
n.2: The business layer sets project-level tolerances and decides on project-level exceptions; the project board still directs the project (fig 6.2).
n.3: Strong senior support does not reduce the products needed; an important project is more likely to need fuller control (manual 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about the influences on tailoring are correct?
1. The level of risk is one of the factors that tailoring takes into account.
2. Tailoring factors are set by the business layer in the project mandate.
3. A project that is part of a programme does not need to consider tailoring.
4. A supplier's own iterative-incremental framework can be a reason to tailor.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 1 is correct: level of risk is one of the seven named factors. Statement 4 is correct: a supplier wanting to use its own iterative-incremental or agile framework is an influence that may lead to tailoring, for example adding a coach role (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the factors are features of the project considered when tailoring is agreed in initiating a project, not items set in the mandate (manual 2.7, 15.4.1).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: tailoring is agreed in initiation, and a programme context is itself an influence that may cause tailoring (manual 2.7, 15.4.1).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: being part of a programme is one of the influences that may cause tailoring (manual 1.5, 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Why is the delivery method one of the factors that influence how PRINCE2 is tailored?
o: Because quality activities need to suit how the products are delivered
Because PRINCE2 prescribes one delivery method for each type of project
Because the delivery method decides which principles the project applies
Because the delivery method replaces the need for a plan for each stage
Tailoring & Project Context.w: How the products are delivered affects which controls and activities fit; for example, the quality practice tailors by requiring the quality activities that are appropriate to the delivery approach and product characteristics (see manual 2.7 and 8.7 tab 8.3).

n.1: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method; it is tailored to whichever method the project uses (manual 1.1).
n.2: All seven principles apply whatever the delivery method; the delivery method affects how the method is tailored, not which principles apply (manual ch 2).
n.3: Manage by stages still applies whatever the delivery method, with a stage plan for each stage (manual 2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A government agency in a heavily regulated environment has its own mandatory project standards. How does this affect tailoring?
o: The project replaces the PRINCE2 principles with the agency's standards
The project uses PRINCE2 unchanged so it can prove compliance to regulators
The method is tailored to align with the agency's standards and environment
The project leaves tailoring until the first delivery stage is authorized
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The environment is a tailoring factor and organizational standards are an influence on tailoring: the method is aligned with the business processes and standards that govern the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Principles are not tailored or replaced; the method is aligned with the standards while all seven principles still apply (manual ch 2, 2.7).
n.1: PRINCE2 is meant to be tailored to its environment; using it unchanged ignores a named tailoring factor (manual 2.7).
n.3: Tailoring requirements are agreed in initiating a project, before delivery stages are authorized (manual 15.4.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project manager sets out how the risk practice will be applied on this project, with procedures and scales proportionate to its size and complexity. Which kind of tailoring is this?
o: Tailoring a principle through the risk register
Tailoring the terminology through the issue register
Tailoring the processes through the project mandate
Tailoring a practice through its management approach
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The practices are tailored through the management approaches; the risk management approach sets out how the risk practice will be applied on this project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.2).

n.0: Principles are not tailored, and the risk register holds specific risks rather than how the practice is applied (manual 2.7, ch 9).
n.1: Tailoring terminology means using the organization's own terms; the issue register records formal issues and does not set how risk is managed (manual 2.7, ch 10).
n.2: The mandate is the business layer's trigger for starting up a project; processes are tailored by combining or simplifying them, not through the mandate (manual 2.7, ch 13).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project manager renames the highlight report the 'monthly project update', matching the organization's usual terms. Which statement is correct?
o: It is not allowed, as management product names are fixed
It is acceptable tailoring of terminology
It turns it into a team-level checkpoint report
It needs an exception report, as a baseline has changed
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Terminology can be tailored: a project may use the organization's or industry's usual terms in place of PRINCE2 terms, and management products can be renamed (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Management products can be merged, split, renamed or given different formats when tailoring (manual 2.7).
n.2: Renaming does not change who the report is for: a highlight report still goes from the project manager to the board, while checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager (manual ch 11).
n.3: Exception reports are used when stage or project tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, not for agreed changes to terminology (manual ch 11).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which is an example of tailoring the PRINCE2 management products?
o: Setting no tolerances for the current stage to save the board's time
Leaving out the 'learn from experience' principle on a short project
Merging two management products into a single document
Letting the project manager take on the executive role
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Management products can be merged, split, renamed or produced in different formats to suit the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Tolerances are how manage by exception delegates authority; removing them abandons a principle rather than tailoring a product (manual 2.5).
n.1: Principles cannot be tailored away; all seven must be applied (manual ch 2).
n.3: Combining the executive and project manager roles breaks a role rule that still applies after tailoring, and it concerns roles, not products (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which is NOT an acceptable way to tailor the roles in a PRINCE2 project?
o: Combining the executive and project manager roles in one person
Having the project manager also perform the project support role
Adding a coach role to support teams that use an agile method
Having two people share the senior supplier role on the board
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Roles can be combined, split or added, but the role rules still apply: the executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role (see manual 2.7 and 6.2.4).

n.1: This is acceptable: depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity, the project manager may also perform the project support role (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: This is acceptable: adding a coach is a recognized way of tailoring roles where teams combine PRINCE2 with an agile method (manual 2.7).
n.3: This is acceptable: the senior supplier role may be held by more than one person (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about what can be tailored are correct?
1. Processes may be combined or simplified to suit the project.
2. Project assurance may be carried out by project support on a small project.
3. A project may use the organization's own terms in place of PRINCE2 terms.
4. The number of principles may be reduced on a low-risk project.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 1 is correct: processes can be combined, simplified or carried out in more detail. Statement 3 is correct: terminology can be tailored to the organization's usual terms (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: project assurance cannot be assigned to the project manager, team members or project support, whatever the project's size (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: assurance must stay separate from project support, and the principles are not tailored (manual ch 2, 6.2.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: all seven principles must be applied for the project to be a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: To reduce headcount, a project board proposes that the project manager also carries out project assurance. Why is this unacceptable?
o: Because it is a business layer role outside the project
Because it has to be done by the executive in person
Because it has to be independent of the project manager
Because it is a quality assurance function of the business
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Roles may be combined when tailoring, but the rules still apply: project assurance must be independent of the project manager, so it cannot be given to the project manager, team members or project support (see manual 2.7 and 6.2.4).

n.0: Project assurance is the project board's responsibility and is part of the project; it is independent of the project manager, not a business layer role (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Board members are accountable for assurance of their own area, but it can be delegated to others in the business or to an external party (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: This confuses project assurance with quality assurance; quality assurance is a business function independent of the whole project management team (manual ch 8).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which statement describes how the PRINCE2 processes can be tailored?
o: Processes are fixed by the business layer and are left unchanged by projects
Processes may be combined, simplified or carried out in more detail
Processes are tailored through the management approaches agreed in initiation
Processes are replaced by the delivery method chosen by the supplier
Tailoring & Project Context.w: When tailoring, processes can be combined, simplified or carried out in more detail to suit the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Processes are one of the things a project can tailor; they are not fixed by the business layer (manual 2.7).
n.2: The management approaches are how the practices, not the processes, are tailored (manual 2.7).
n.3: PRINCE2 works alongside any delivery method; the supplier's method influences tailoring but does not replace the processes (manual 1.1, 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project manager proposes splitting the senior user role between two department heads and adding a coach role. Which statement is correct?
o: Both break the rules, as PRINCE2 roles cannot be split or added
Splitting is acceptable, but adding a non-PRINCE2 role is not
Adding the coach is acceptable, but the senior user must be one person
Both are acceptable ways of tailoring the project's roles
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Roles can be combined, split or added when tailoring: the senior user role can be held by more than one person, and a coach role can be added, for example to help teams work with an agile method (see manual 2.7 and 6.2.4).

n.0: Tailoring explicitly allows roles to be combined, split or added (manual 2.7).
n.1: Adding a role, such as a coach, is a recognized form of tailoring (manual 2.7).
n.2: The senior user role may be held by more than one person; it is the executive that must be one person (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: In which process does the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity take place?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
Tailoring & Project Context.w: 'Agree the tailoring requirements' is the first activity of initiating a project, where the project manager works out how PRINCE2 or the business's standard method will be applied and tailored (see manual 15.4.1).

n.1: Starting up a project checks whether the project is viable and worthwhile and prepares the project brief; tailoring requirements are agreed afterwards, in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.1).
n.2: Directing a project is where the board makes decisions, such as authorizing the project and its PID; the tailoring itself is agreed in initiating a project (manual ch 14, 15.4.1).
n.3: Managing a stage boundary reviews and may update the PID, including how the project is tailored, but tailoring is first agreed in initiation (manual 18.2, 15.4.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Where should a project's agreed tailoring decisions be documented?
o: In the project brief from starting up
In the lessons log within the project log
In the project initiation documentation
In the project mandate from the business
Tailoring & Project Context.w: How the method is applied and tailored is documented and agreed during initiation and recorded in the project initiation documentation (PID), which the board approves when it authorizes the project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1).

n.0: The project brief is prepared in starting up a project, before the tailoring requirements are agreed in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.1).
n.1: The lessons log records lessons that may inform tailoring, but the agreed tailoring is part of the PID (manual 2.2, 2.7).
n.3: The project mandate is the business layer's trigger for the project and exists before any tailoring is agreed (manual ch 13).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which role works out, during initiation, how the business's standard project management method needs to be tailored for the project?
o: Project support
Project manager
Team manager
Senior supplier
Tailoring & Project Context.w: In the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity, the project manager may need to tailor PRINCE2 or the business's standard method to reflect internal and external factors; the result must be documented and agreed (see manual 15.4.1).

n.0: Project support provides administrative help, such as maintaining registers; it does not decide how the method is tailored (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Team managers deliver work packages in managing product delivery; they are not responsible for tailoring the project's method (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The senior supplier represents supplier interests on the board and commits supplier resources; working out the tailoring falls to the project manager (manual 6.2.4, 15.4.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: When does the project board approve the tailoring agreed for the project?
o: When authorizing initiation at the end of starting up
When giving ongoing direction during a delivery stage
When authorizing closure in the final stage
When authorizing the project and approving the PID
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID, which is assembled in initiating a project and approved by the board when it authorizes the project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.6).

n.0: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and initiation stage plan; the tailoring is agreed later, during initiation (manual ch 14, 15.4.1).
n.1: Giving ongoing direction responds to reports, requests and issues during a stage; approval of the PID and its tailoring comes when the board authorizes the project (manual ch 14).
n.2: Authorizing closure confirms the project can close; tailoring has to be approved before delivery begins (manual ch 19).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In initiating a project, any departure from the business's standard project management method must be documented and [?].
o: archived
escalated
reported
agreed
Tailoring & Project Context.w: In 'agree the tailoring requirements', how the method will be applied or tailored, including any deviation from the business's standard method, must be documented and agreed (see manual 15.4.1).

n.0: Archiving project information happens in closing a project, not when tailoring is set up (manual 19.4.1).
n.1: Escalation is for forecast breaches of tolerance; tailoring deviations are documented and agreed, not escalated as exceptions (manual 2.5, 15.4.1).
n.2: Reporting describes progress products such as highlight reports; the requirement for tailoring deviations is that they are documented and agreed (manual 15.4.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Why might the way a project has been tailored be revisited at a stage boundary?
o: Because tailoring is first agreed in managing a stage boundary
Because the PID, including approaches and roles, may be updated
Because the business layer re-approves tailoring at each stage end
Because each delivery stage uses a different set of principles
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if necessary, updates the PID, including the management approaches, project management team structure and role descriptions, so tailoring can be adjusted for the next stage (see manual 18.2).

n.0: Tailoring is first agreed in initiating a project; the stage boundary is where it may be revisited (manual 15.4.1).
n.2: The project board, not the business layer, authorizes each stage and approves an updated PID; the business layer is involved in project-level matters (manual ch 14, fig 6.2).
n.3: All seven principles apply in every stage; principles are not selected or tailored (manual ch 2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about who tailors PRINCE2 and how it is recorded are correct?
1. 'Agree the tailoring requirements' is an activity in starting up a project.
2. Tailoring decisions are recorded in the project initiation documentation.
3. Deviations from the business's standard method must be documented and agreed.
4. Once tailoring has been agreed, it cannot be changed later in the project.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 2 is correct: tailoring decisions form part of the PID. Statement 3 is correct: how the business's standard method is applied or tailored must be documented and agreed (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: 'agree the tailoring requirements' is the first activity of initiating a project, not starting up a project (manual 15.4.1).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: the activity is in initiating a project, and tailoring can be revisited when the PID is reviewed at stage boundaries (manual 15.4.1, 18.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the PID, including how the project is tailored, can be reviewed and updated in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: During initiation, the project manager finds that an external supplier's ways of working mean the business's standard PRINCE2-based method needs adjusting. What should happen to this adjustment?
o: It is documented and agreed during initiation
It is raised as an off-specification in the issue register
It is made informally and noted in the daily log
It is recorded in the lessons report at project closure
Tailoring & Project Context.w: In 'agree the tailoring requirements', the project manager may need to tailor the business's standard method for internal and external factors; any deviation must be documented and agreed, and it becomes part of the PID (see manual 15.4.1).

n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; a planned change to the method is not a product defect (manual ch 10).
n.2: Deviations from the standard method must be documented and agreed formally, not handled informally in the daily log (manual 15.4.1).
n.3: The adjustment is needed now, before delivery begins; the lessons report passes on lessons at the end and does not agree current tailoring (manual 15.4.1, 19.4.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A supplier wants to use its in-house iterative-incremental framework with agile approaches. To avoid confusion, what might the project manager propose?
o: Replacing the project board with the supplier's product owner
Adding a coach to help teams combine PRINCE2 with that framework
Removing stage boundaries so the supplier can work continuously
Asking the supplier to switch to linear-sequential delivery
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Where a supplier uses its own iterative-incremental, agile framework, the project manager might propose adding a coach role to guide teams in working effectively with the combination of PRINCE2 and that framework (see manual 2.7).

n.0: The project board directs the project and is accountable to the business; tailoring for a supplier's framework does not remove it (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Manage by stages is a principle and cannot be tailored away; an iterative-incremental project still has an initiation stage and delivery stages (manual 2.4, 2.7).
n.3: PRINCE2 is not specific to a delivery method; the aim is to tailor the method to the supplier's approach, not to force a different one (manual 1.1, 2.7).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which statement describes a project in a commercial customer-supplier context?
o: The supplier works to the customer's business case, with none of its own
The project must sit in a programme so the contract is managed
The supplier's management team replaces the customer's project board
The supplier has its own business case for taking part
Tailoring & Project Context.w: In a commercial context there are customer and supplier relationships, possibly under contracts, and the supplier has its own business case for its involvement; the project may also need to align with more than one management system (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Suppliers have their own justification for taking part, alongside the customer's business case (manual 1.5, 2.1).
n.1: A commercial project may be standalone or part of a programme or portfolio; a contract does not require a programme (manual 1.5, fig 1.2).
n.2: The supplier's interests are represented on the project board by the senior supplier; the board is not replaced (manual 6.2.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: PRINCE2 assumes no particular organizational context. Which parties does it describe as typically involved in a project?
o: Users, suppliers and business decision-makers
Sponsors, contractors and external regulators
Programme managers, auditors and end users
Shareholders, customers and team members
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The typical parties are the users who specify the outputs they need, the suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and the business decision-makers who make sure the investment is and stays justified (see manual 1.5).

n.1: PRINCE2 has no sponsor role, and regulators are stakeholders rather than one of the three typical parties (manual 1.5, 6.2.4).
n.2: Users are a typical party, but programme managers and auditors are not the other two; the typical parties are users, suppliers and business decision-makers (manual 1.5).
n.3: Shareholders and team members are not the typical parties named; the business, user and supplier interests are represented on the project board (manual 1.5, 6.2.1).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
A project that is not part of a programme or portfolio and reports to a business unit is described as a [?] project.
o: linear
commercial
standalone
hybrid
Tailoring & Project Context.w: A project may be standalone, reporting to a business unit, or part of a programme or portfolio (see manual 1.5 and fig 1.2).

n.0: Linear-sequential is a delivery approach, not a description of where the project sits in the organization (manual 1.5.3).
n.1: A commercial context is about customer and supplier relationships, which can apply whether or not the project sits in a programme (manual 1.5).
n.3: Hybrid is a delivery approach combining linear-sequential and iterative-incremental working, not an organizational context (manual 1.5.3).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A customer and its main supplier each have their own quality management system. Why might the project tailor PRINCE2?
o: To align its processes and documents with both quality systems
To let the supplier's quality system replace the principles
To make the supplier's senior manager the executive
To remove the need for a quality management approach
Tailoring & Project Context.w: A commercial customer-supplier relationship is an influence that gives cause to tailor: the project may need to align its management processes, practices and documentation with two or more quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Principles cannot be replaced or tailored; quality systems are aligned with, not substituted for, the principles (manual ch 2).
n.2: The executive represents the business interest and is accountable for the business case; the supplier is represented by the senior supplier (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: The quality management approach is still needed; tailoring adjusts it to align with both quality systems (manual 2.7, 15.4.2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about tailoring for suppliers and commercial relationships are correct?
1. A coach role may be added where teams combine PRINCE2 with an agile framework.
2. PRINCE2 is designed for use with linear-sequential delivery.
3. A commercial relationship can call for alignment with two or more quality systems.
4. A supplier's agile framework replaces the need for management stages.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 1 is correct: a coach can be added to guide teams combining PRINCE2 with a supplier's agile method. Statement 3 is correct: a commercial customer-supplier relationship may require alignment with two or more quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method and can be tailored to iterative-incremental, linear-sequential or hybrid delivery (manual 1.1, 1.5.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: PRINCE2 is not tied to one delivery method, and manage by stages still applies with an agile supplier (manual 1.1, 2.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the 'manage by stages' principle applies whatever framework the supplier uses (manual 2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Board members of a joint customer-supplier project work in different regions. The project manager proposes reviewing highlight reports in short online calls rather than formal meetings. What does this show?
o: The board's responsibility for direction has been removed
'Manage by stages' is applied by changing the stage length
A business case change has occurred that needs an exception plan
Reporting is tailored in format and formality to suit the project
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Tailoring makes project controls fit the project, typically by adjusting the frequency and formality of reports and reviews; holding highlight reviews online for a dispersed board is an example (see manual 2.7).

n.0: The board still directs the project; only the way it receives and discusses reports changes (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: Stage length is unchanged; the proposal concerns how reports are reviewed, which is a tailoring decision (manual 2.4, 2.7).
n.2: No business case change or tolerance breach is involved, so there is no need for an exception plan (manual ch 11).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project is one of several within a programme run by a regional health trust. How does this context affect how PRINCE2 is applied?
o: The project stops applying principles the programme covers
The programme is an influence on how the method is tailored
The project becomes permanent work as the programme continues
