The project is run as a portfolio rather than as a project
Tailoring & Project Context.w: A project may sit within a programme or portfolio, and a programme context is one of the influences that gives cause to tailor the method (see manual 1.5 and 2.7).

n.0: All seven principles still apply to a project within a programme; principles are not tailored away (manual ch 2).
n.2: A project remains temporary whatever its context; being in a programme does not make it business as usual (manual 1.3).
n.3: A portfolio is the wider set of an organization's investments in change; the project is still managed as a project within it (manual 1.5).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A small charity is using PRINCE2 for a six-week project. Which statement about applying PRINCE2 to it is correct?
o: Fewer principles need applying, because the risks are low
The project board can be removed to save senior time
All principles apply, but processes and products can be simplified
The initiation stage can be skipped if the business case is clear
Tailoring & Project Context.w: However small the project, all seven principles must be applied; what is scaled down is the method, for example by simplifying processes and merging management products (see manual ch 2 and 2.7).

n.0: Principles are not tailored; a project that leaves one out is not a PRINCE2 project, whatever its risk level (manual ch 2).
n.1: A project board is still needed to direct the project and be accountable to the business; roles can be combined within the rules, but direction remains (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: Manage by stages requires an initiation stage before delivery work starts, even on a small project (manual 2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: On a small project with one delivery team, which roles may the project manager also perform?
o: Team manager and project support
Executive and team manager
Project assurance and project support
Project assurance and team manager
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Depending on the project's scale, complexity, skills and capacity, the project manager may also perform the team manager and project support roles (see manual 6.2.4).

n.1: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role, however small the project (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance cannot be done by the project manager or project support, and must be kept separate from support (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team manager is acceptable, but project assurance must be independent of the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A director wants to run a very short internal project with as few stages as PRINCE2 allows. What is the minimum number of management stages?
o: One: a single stage covering initiation and delivery
Two: an initiation stage followed by one delivery stage
Three: initiation, delivery and a separate closing stage
Four: one stage for each level of the organization
Tailoring & Project Context.w: A PRINCE2 project has at least two stages: the initiation stage, which is always first, and at least one delivery stage (see manual 2.4).

n.0: Initiation is a stage in its own right so that the project is properly set up before delivery work begins (manual 2.4).
n.2: Closing a project happens within the final delivery stage; it is not a separate stage (manual ch 19).
n.3: The four organizational levels describe who directs, manages and delivers; they do not set the number of stages (fig 6.2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
On a small, low-value project, the project brief and the [?] may be merged into one simple document.
o: project plan
lessons report
stage plan
business case
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Small, low-value projects may merge the project brief and the business case into one simple business case document (see manual 5.4.5).

n.0: The project plan is created in initiating a project, after the project brief; the recognized small-project merger is brief and business case (manual 5.4.5, 15.4.4).
n.1: The lessons report passes on lessons at a stage or project end; it is not combined with the project brief (manual 19.4.4).
n.2: Stage plans are produced for each stage, the first in starting up and later ones in managing a stage boundary; they are not merged with the brief (manual 2.4, ch 18).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: To keep a small project lean, the finance director proposes being both executive and project manager. Why is this unacceptable?
o: Because the executive must come from outside the business
Because a small project is directed by the business layer
Because the senior user appoints the project manager
Because executive and project manager roles must stay separate
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Roles can be combined to suit a small project, but the rules still apply: the executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role (see manual 2.7 and 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive is usually a senior person from the business who can secure funding; there is no requirement for an outsider (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project; even a small project is directed by its project board (fig 6.2, 6.2.1).
n.2: The executive appoints the rest of the project management team, with the business layer accountable; the senior user does not appoint the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Which two statements about tailoring PRINCE2 for a small project are correct?
1. Project assurance may be carried out by project support to save effort.
2. Reports to the board may be less frequent and less formal.
3. The project still needs a business justification.
4. Closing a project may be run as a separate stage after delivery.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Statement 2 is correct: controls such as the frequency and formality of reports are fitted to the project's scale. Statement 3 is correct: continued business justification applies to every project, though a small project may keep it in one simple document (see manual 2.1, 2.7 and 5.4.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: project assurance cannot be assigned to project support, and the two must be kept separate (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: closing a project takes place within the final stage rather than as a stage of its own (manual ch 19).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: assurance must stay separate from support, and closure happens inside the final stage (manual 6.2.4, ch 19).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: On a small project, the project manager plans fortnightly email updates to the board instead of formal weekly highlight reports. Which statement is correct?
o: It is acceptable tailoring of reporting frequency and formality
It is not allowed, as highlight reports follow a set weekly cycle
It departs from 'manage by exception', so needs an exception report
It is acceptable once the business layer has reissued the mandate
Tailoring & Project Context.w: Making controls fit the project's scale includes adjusting the frequency and formality of reports and reviews; agreed lighter reporting is normal tailoring for a small project (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Highlight reports are time-driven at a frequency agreed for the project; there is no fixed weekly cycle (manual 2.7, ch 11).
n.2: Changing report frequency does not breach any tolerance, so no exception report is needed; exception reports are for forecast tolerance breaches (manual 2.5).
n.3: Reporting arrangements are agreed as project controls in initiation and recorded in the PID; the mandate does not need to be reissued (manual 15.4.3).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: The board decides to close a small project early because its business case is no longer valid. The project manager suggests skipping closing a project. What should happen?
o: The project stops at once, with no closure activities needed
A final managing a stage boundary replaces closing a project
Closing a project is still run, tailored to the situation
The project manager closes it and tells the board afterwards
Tailoring & Project Context.w: When a project is brought to a premature close, the closing a project process must still be carried out, although it may be tailored to the situation, so the project closes in an orderly way (see manual 19.3).

n.0: A premature close still needs an orderly closure, for example salvaging useful work and making products safe (manual 19.4.2).
n.1: Managing a stage boundary is not used to close a project; closure is handled by closing a project (manual ch 18, ch 19).
n.3: The project manager prepares closure, but the board authorizes it in directing a project, so it cannot be told only after the event (manual ch 19).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which statement best describes the 'tailor to suit the project' principle?
o: Delegated authority is limited by setting tolerances against plans
The method is adapted to the project's size, complexity and risk
The project concentrates on defining and delivering its products
The project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The 'tailor to suit the project' principle means the method is applied and adapted to the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Setting limits of delegated authority through tolerances describes the 'manage by exception' principle, not tailoring (manual 2.5).
n.2: Defining and delivering products and their quality requirements describes the 'focus on products' principle (manual 2.6).
n.3: Planning, monitoring and controlling stage by stage describes the 'manage by stages' principle (manual 2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: Which is a purpose of tailoring PRINCE2?
o: To decide which of the seven principles the project will apply
To replace the business's own processes with PRINCE2 processes
To move accountability from the executive to the project manager
To make the method used appropriate to the project and its context
Tailoring & Project Context.w: One purpose of tailoring is to make the project management method appropriate to the project, for example by aligning it with the business processes that govern and support the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: All seven principles must be applied for a project to be a PRINCE2 project; tailoring adapts the method, not the principles (manual ch 2, 2.7).
n.1: Tailoring aligns the method with the business processes that govern and support the project rather than replacing them (manual 2.7).
n.2: The executive's accountability cannot be delegated, and tailoring does not move it to the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

Tailoring & Project Context.q: A project board agrees that a small, low-risk project will have shorter, less frequent highlight reports than the organization's large projects. Which purpose of tailoring does this serve?
o: Fitting project controls to the project's scale, complexity and risk
Aligning the method with the business processes governing the project
Making sure no more work is done than the agreed products need
Making sure lessons from earlier projects reach the lessons log
Tailoring & Project Context.w: One purpose of tailoring is to make project controls fit the project's scale, complexity, importance, team capability and risk; the frequency and formality of reports and reviews is the typical example (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Aligning the method with business processes is the other purpose of tailoring, but the change here is to the frequency and formality of a project control (manual 2.7).
n.2: Doing no more work than the agreed products need is part of the 'focus on products' principle, not a purpose of tailoring (manual 2.6).
n.3: Capturing lessons from earlier projects belongs to the 'learn from experience' principle, not to adjusting reporting (manual 2.2).

Tailoring & Project Context.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
Tailoring makes sure that the project management [?] used is appropriate to the project, for example by aligning it with the business processes that govern and support the project.
o: strategy
portfolio
method
mandate
Tailoring & Project Context.w: The first purpose of tailoring is that the project management method fits the project, for example by aligning it with the business processes that govern and support it (see manual 2.7).

n.0: 'Strategy' was the 6th edition word for documents now called management approaches; the purpose of tailoring refers to the method as a whole (manual 2.7).
n.1: A portfolio is the organization's wider set of investments in change; it is not what tailoring makes appropriate to a project (manual 1.5).
n.3: The project mandate is the trigger for starting up a project provided by the business layer; it is not the thing being tailored (manual ch 13).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A project to merge two hospital pharmacies involves the hospital trust, the pharmacists who will use the new system and an external software supplier. Each has its own structures and culture. What does PRINCE2 call the temporary arrangement of people, relationships and ways of working created where these interests meet?
o: The organizational ecosystem
The business layer
The project ecosystem
The project management team structure
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Where the business, user and supplier interests come together for the project, a temporary project ecosystem is created, made up of people, relationships, structures and ways of working (see manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

n.0: The organizational ecosystem is the existing trust, user and supplier organizations themselves, which continue after the project ends (manual 3.1).
n.1: The business layer is the commissioning level outside the project management team; here it would be part of the trust (manual 6.2).
n.3: The project management team structure is the set of roles in the project; the project ecosystem is wider, covering relationships and ways of working across the three interests (manual 3.1, 6.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about ecosystems in PRINCE2 are correct?
1. The organizational ecosystem is created at initiation and dissolved when the project closes.
2. At closure, the project's products, people and learning move into the organizational ecosystem.
3. A project can affect people from across the organizational ecosystem, not just its own team.
4. The project ecosystem consists of the project board and the project manager.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
3 and 4
2 and 3
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 2 is correct: the final step of organizational design and development transitions the project's products, people and learning into the organizational ecosystem. Statement 3 is correct: projects impact people from across the organizational ecosystem (see manual 3.2.2, 6.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the organizational ecosystem is the existing set of organizations; it is the project ecosystem that is temporary (manual 3.1).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both wrong: the organizational ecosystem already exists, and the project ecosystem includes far more people and relationships than the board and project manager (manual 3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the project ecosystem covers the people, relationships, structures and ways of working across the business, user and supplier interests (manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Why does PRINCE2 recommend that the project management team understands the organizational ecosystem before designing the project ecosystem?
o: Because the project must work within the existing structures, governance and policies
Because the organizational ecosystem is replaced by the project ecosystem during delivery
Because the business layer is a member of the project management team
Because the organizational ecosystem sets the tolerances for each management stage
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The first step of the organizational design and development technique is to understand the organizational ecosystem (its structures, governance, decisions needing business approval and policies) so the project ecosystem can be designed to fit it (see manual 6.3.1, fig 6.5).

n.1: The organizational ecosystem continues throughout; the temporary project ecosystem sits within it and is transitioned back into it at closure (manual 6.3.1).
n.2: The business layer sits outside the project management team, which is made up of the directing, managing and delivering levels (manual 6.2).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board; the business layer sets project tolerances (manual 6.2, 11.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement about the organizational ecosystem is correct?
o: It is the temporary structure the project board creates during initiation
It includes the users and suppliers as well as the business, each with its own culture
It is made up of the people who hold formal roles in the project management team
It is described in full in the project management team structure within the PID
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The organizational ecosystem is made up of the existing organizations involved, including the business, users and suppliers, each with its own structures, governance, culture and people (see manual 3.1, fig 3.1).

n.0: A temporary structure created for the project describes the project ecosystem, not the organizational ecosystem (manual 3.1).
n.2: People with formal project roles form the project management team; the organizational ecosystem is much wider than that (manual 3.1, 6.2.3).
n.3: The project management team structure describes who is involved in the project and how they work together, not the whole set of existing organizations (manual ch 6).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: In PRINCE2 7, who does the 'people' element cover?
o: The members of the project management team and their reporting lines
Those working on the project, their relationships, and those it affects
The users who will operate the products once they have been handed over
The stakeholders listed in the communication management approach
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 uses 'people' to mean those working on the project and the relationships between them, together with those impacted by the project (see manual ch 3 introduction, 3.1).

n.0: The project management team is part of the picture, but the people element also covers relationships and everyone affected by the project (manual ch 3).
n.2: Users are one affected group; the people element also covers everyone working on the project and their relationships (manual ch 3).
n.3: The communication management approach records stakeholders for communication purposes; the people element is defined by who works on or is affected by the project, not by a list (manual ch 3, 3.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A bank's project will introduce a new loan system. Which of these people is affected by the project but does not work within the project team?
o: The team manager building the loan screens
The senior user representing the lending department
A branch adviser who will process loans on the new system
The project support officer maintaining the registers
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: A branch adviser who will use the new system is affected by the project's outputs but holds no role in the project team, so is one of the people affected by the project rather than working within it (see manual 3.1, 3.3.1).

n.0: A team manager holds a role at the delivering level, so works within the project team (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior user is a project board member, so works within the project team even though they represent the users (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Project support is a role in the project management team, so this person works within the project (manual 6.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: How may people who are affected by a project, but who do not work within the project team, contribute to it?
o: By approving requests for change within a delegated change budget
By setting the tolerances for the work packages in their area
By preparing checkpoint reports on their area's progress
By integrating the new products into their own area of the business
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: People in the business who are affected by the project but are outside the project team may contribute by integrating the new products into their part of the organization (see manual 3.3.1).

n.0: Approving requests for change within a change budget is done by a change authority, a role delegated by the project board (manual 10.2.4).
n.1: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager, who is within the project team (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are prepared by team managers, who work within the project team (manual ch 11).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

A project must involve people with formal roles in the project team and also key people who are impacted by the project or [?], even if they hold no formal role.
o: critical to its success
named in the project mandate
appointed by the executive
members of the business layer
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 says a project needs to involve both those with formal roles and key people who are impacted by it or critical to its success, who may hold no formal role (see manual 3.2.2).

n.1: The project mandate is the business layer's trigger for the project; being named in it is not the test PRINCE2 uses for involving people (manual ch 13).
n.2: People appointed by the executive hold formal roles in the project management team, so they are not the group without formal roles (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The business layer commissions the project; the guidance is about key people impacted by, or critical to, the project, wherever they sit (manual 3.2.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Why should a project manager pay attention to people who are affected by the project but are not part of the project team?
o: Because they are accountable for the business case and the project's funding
Because they must approve each stage plan before the next stage can start
Because they take over the senior user's duties after the products are handed over
Because the change will alter their routines, so its success depends on them
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: A project delivers change that affects people's business-as-usual activities, routines and responsibilities; how well that change is implemented depends partly on the people it impacts (see manual ch 3 introduction, 3.2.1).

n.0: The executive is accountable for the business case and secures funding; affected people outside the team hold no such accountability (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Stage plans are approved by the project board in directing a project, not by people outside the project team (manual ch 14).
n.2: The senior user stays responsible for adoption and benefits realization after closure; affected people do not take over that role (manual 6.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about people within and affected by a project are correct?
1. Members of the project board are people working within the project.
2. Someone who perceives that they will be affected by the project is a stakeholder.
3. People affected by a project fall outside the scope of the people element.
4. People with no formal role should be kept out of decisions about new ways of working.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 1 is correct: board members hold roles in the project management team, so they work within the project. Statement 2 is correct: a stakeholder includes anyone who perceives themselves to be affected by the project (see manual 3.1, 3.2.2).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: the people element explicitly covers those impacted by the project as well as those working on it (manual ch 3).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: PRINCE2 encourages co-creating products and ways of working with users and key influencers, many of whom hold no formal role (manual 3.3).
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong: affected people are part of the people element and should be involved in shaping the change (manual ch 3, 3.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement explains the difference between people within a project and people affected by it?
o: People within the project are employees of the business; affected people are external to it
People within the project hold roles in the project team; affected people may have no formal role
People within the project are the users; affected people are the suppliers and their staff
People within the project sit on the board; affected people are the team managers and teams
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: People within the project hold roles in the project team, while people affected by it may sit anywhere in the organizational ecosystem and may hold no formal role (see manual 3.1, 3.3.1).

n.0: Affected people can be inside the business, for example staff who integrate the new products into their area, and project team members can come from external suppliers (manual 3.3.1).
n.2: Users and suppliers can both be within the project (senior user, senior supplier, team members) and both can also be affected by it (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: Team managers and team members work within the project at the delivering level; they are not just affected by it (manual 6.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A council project will change how refuse collectors plan their daily routes. The collectors will not work on the project. Which project board role represents their interests?
o: Executive
Senior supplier
Senior user
Project manager
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The user interest covers those who will use, operate, maintain or be impacted by the products, and it is represented on the board by the senior user (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: The executive represents the business interest and owns the business case; the users' interests are represented by the senior user (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: The senior supplier represents those who design and deliver the products, not those who will use or be impacted by them (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: The project manager is not a project board role; the manager runs the project day to day on the board's behalf (manual 6.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: How does PRINCE2 7 define change management?
o: The procedure for assessing and approving changes to the project baseline
The process of moving a project from one management stage to the next
The means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state
The technique for capturing, assessing and deciding on issues raised in the project
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: In PRINCE2 7, change management is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Assessing and approving changes to the baseline is change control, which belongs to the issues practice (manual 10.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Moving from one stage to the next is handled by managing a stage boundary and directing a project, not by change management (manual ch 14, ch 18).
n.3: Capturing, assessing and deciding on issues is the issue management technique of the issues practice (manual 10.3.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: According to PRINCE2 7, what is required to deliver organizational change successfully?
o: A change authority with its own change budget
A separate change project run after closure
A fixed set of interim states for every project
Effective leadership
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 states that effective leadership is required to deliver the change from the current state to the target state (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: A change authority and change budget relate to approving changes to the baseline under the issues practice, not to leading organizational change (manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).
n.1: The change is planned within the project through the change management approach; PRINCE2 does not call for a separate change project after closure (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: Interim states are used where needed: the business moves to the target state through any interim states, so there is no fixed set (manual 3.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The change management approach plans how the business will move from the current state to the target state, through any [?] states.
o: interim
baseline
exception
tolerance
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach establishes the target organizational state and how the business will shift from the current state through any interim states (see manual 3.2.1).

n.1: A baseline is the approved version of products under change control (issues practice), not a step in an organizational transition (manual 10.1).
n.2: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance handled by the progress practice, not a state in a transition (manual 11.2.6).
n.3: Tolerance is the permitted deviation from a plan's targets (progress practice), not a state the organization passes through (manual 11.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Why is change management important to a PRINCE2 project?
o: Because it replaces the business case once the target state has been agreed
Because a project exists to deliver change that alters people's routines and responsibilities
Because it sets the tolerances that the project board delegates to the project manager
Because it controls which versions of products form the current project baseline
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The purpose of a project is to deliver change, which affects people's business-as-usual activities, routines and responsibilities; how well that change lands drives how well the project performs (see manual ch 3 introduction, 3.2.1).

n.0: The business case remains in place throughout the project; the principle of continued business justification still applies (manual 2.1, ch 5).
n.2: Tolerances are set through the progress practice (manage by exception), not by change management (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Controlling which product versions form the baseline is change control under the issues practice (manual 10.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A retailer's project delivered a new stock app on time and to specification. Six months later, store staff still record stock on paper and the expected cut in waste has not appeared. What does this show about change management?
o: Benefits depend on people adopting new ways of working as well as on delivered outputs
The project should have raised an exception report when the app was handed over
The issue management approach failed to control changes to the app's specification
The senior supplier is responsible for realizing the planned reduction in waste
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Outputs lead to benefits through outcomes, which are changes in how people work. Change management plans the move to the target state so that people adopt the new ways of working and benefits can be realized (see manual 3.2.1, fig 5.1).

n.1: The app was delivered on time and to specification, so no tolerance was forecast to be exceeded and no exception report was needed (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: The specification was met, so change control of the baseline was not the problem; the gap is in adoption by staff (manual 10.2.3, 3.2.1).
n.3: The senior user, not the senior supplier, specifies the benefits and is responsible for their realization after handover (manual 6.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about change management in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. It covers the move from the current state to the target state.
2. It is the procedure for approving requests for change to baselined products.
3. The organization may pass through interim states before reaching the target state.
4. It begins once the project has been closed and the products handed over.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 1 is correct: change management is how the organization transitions from the current state to the target state. Statement 3 is correct: the change management approach plans the move through any interim states (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: approving requests for change to baselined products is change control in the issues practice (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: approving requests for change is change control, and change management is planned in initiation as part of the PID (manual 10.2.3, 3.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the change management approach is agreed during initiating a project, long before closure (manual 15.4.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement about the target state in PRINCE2 change management is correct?
o: It is the position the project board sets for the end of the initiation stage
It is the set of baselined products held under change control by project support
It is the organizational state needed for the project to meet its objectives
It is the forecast position of the project at the end of the current stage
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach establishes the target organizational state required for the project to meet its objectives, and how the business will reach it (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: The end of initiation is a decision point for the board (authorize the project); the target state describes the organization after the change, not a stage end (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: Baselined products under change control form the project baseline, which belongs to the issues practice (manual 10.1).
n.3: Forecasts of the stage's end position are part of progress control and reporting, not the target organizational state (manual 11.2.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: According to PRINCE2 7, how well a change is implemented, and therefore how well the project performs, depends on which factors?
o: The number of stages and the level of detail in each stage plan
The size of the change budget and the limits of delegated authority
The format of reports and the frequency of highlight reporting
The team's capabilities, its relationships and the people impacted
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 7 explains that the success of the change, and so the project's performance, depends on the capabilities of the project team, the strength of their relationships and the people impacted by the change (see manual ch 3 introduction).

n.0: The number of stages and planning detail are decided through the plans practice and manage by stages; they are not what PRINCE2 names as driving how well change lands (manual ch 7).
n.1: The change budget and delegated authority govern approval of changes to the baseline under the issues practice (manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).
n.2: Report formats and frequency are progress controls that can be tailored; they are not the people factors PRINCE2 links to successful change (manual 11.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: What is the purpose of the change management approach?
o: To describe how issues will be captured and how changes to the baseline will be controlled
To define the means and frequency of communication with stakeholders across the ecosystem
To define the actions that will ensure outcomes are achieved and benefits are confirmed
To establish the target organizational state and how the business will move to it
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach establishes the target organizational state the project needs in order to meet its objectives, and how the business will shift from the current state through any interim states (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Capturing issues and controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.1: The means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, the project ecosystem is the purpose of the communication management approach (manual 3.4).
n.2: Ensuring outcomes are achieved and benefits are confirmed is the purpose of the benefits management approach (manual 5.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Of which management product does the change management approach form part?
o: The project initiation documentation
The project brief
The daily log within the project log
The project product description
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach is one of the nine management approaches, all of which form part of the project initiation documentation (PID) (see manual 3.2.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project; the management approaches are agreed later, in initiating a project, and form part of the PID (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: The daily log is part of the project log and records informal issues and actions; it does not hold the management approaches (manual ch 10, ch 11).
n.3: The project product description describes the project's main product, the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria; it is not where the management approaches are kept (manual 8.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: During which process is the change management approach created?
o: Starting up a project
Initiating a project
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: All nine management approaches, including the change management approach, are created in initiating a project, in the 'agree the management approaches' activity (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project brief and initiation stage plan; the management approaches come later, in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if needed, updates the management approaches; it does not first create them (manual ch 18).
n.3: In directing a project the board approves the PID, including the approaches, in 'authorize the project'; it does not create them (manual ch 14).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The change management approach describes the [?] before, during and after the transition, such as consultation, trials, training and a help line.
o: quality review steps
risk responses
enabling activities
tolerance levels
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: A typical content area of the change management approach is the enabling activities planned before, during and after the transition, such as consultation, trials, training and a help line (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Quality review steps belong to the quality practice and its quality management approach (manual ch 8).
n.1: Risk responses are recorded against specific risks in the risk register under the risk practice (manual ch 9).
n.3: Tolerance levels are set through the progress practice and documented in the plans and approaches they apply to (manual 11.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which is NOT one of the factors PRINCE2 suggests considering when deciding how much detail to include in the change management approach?
o: The skills and capabilities needed during and after the transition
The size of the change budget delegated to the change authority
The areas of the organizational ecosystem likely to be impacted
The key relationships and the evolving culture
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change budget belongs to the issues practice and funds approved requests for change. The factors PRINCE2 lists for the change management approach are skills and capabilities, impacted areas, key relationships, the evolving culture and how best to transition (see manual 3.2.1, 10.2.5).

n.0: Skills and capabilities needed during and after the transition are a listed factor for the level of detail (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: The areas of the organizational ecosystem likely to be impacted are a listed factor (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Key relationships and the evolving culture are both listed factors (manual 3.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about the change management approach are correct?
1. It is created in starting up a project as part of the project brief.
2. It forms part of the project initiation documentation.
3. It defines how requests for change to baselined products will be approved.
4. It may be adapted at stage boundaries as the project's needs change.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 2 is correct: like all nine management approaches, it forms part of the PID. Statement 4 is correct: the change management approach is adapted at stage boundaries, which is how the organizing practice applies manage by stages (see manual 3.2.1, tab 6.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the approach is created in initiating a project, not starting up a project, and is not part of the project brief (manual 15.4.2).
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: it is created in initiation, and approving requests for change is covered by the issue management approach (manual 15.4.2, 10.5).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: how requests for change are assessed and controlled is described in the issue management approach (manual 10.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A project manager is writing a description of how claims handlers work today, including their routines, team structure and skills. Under which content area of the change management approach does this belong?
o: Enabling activities before the transition
Enabling activities during the transition
The communications schedule for each group
Characteristics of the current state
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach describes the characteristics of each state, highlighting routines, practices, culture, structure, responsibilities and capabilities. A description of how people work today is a current-state characteristic (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Enabling activities are the actions that help people move, such as consultation and training; describing today's routines is not an action (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: Enabling activities during the transition are things like trials and a help line, not a description of the current way of working (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: A communications schedule sets out messages, channels and frequency for stakeholder groups, and belongs in the communication management approach (manual 3.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which management approach should explain how staff will be supported as they move to a new way of working, for example through trials and a help line?
o: Change management approach
Communication management approach
Issue management approach
Quality management approach
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Supporting people through the transition with activities such as trials, training and a help line is an enabling activity, which the change management approach sets out (see manual 3.2.1).

n.1: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication and feedback, not the planned activities that move people to the new way of working (manual 3.4).
n.2: The issue management approach covers capturing issues and controlling changes to the baseline (manual 10.5).
n.3: The quality management approach covers how products will meet their quality requirements, not how people are supported through the change (manual ch 8).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: How does PRINCE2 7 define a stakeholder?
o: Any person, group or organization that can affect, or is or feels affected by, the project
Any person or group that holds a formal role in the project management team or business layer
Any organization that supplies resources or expertise to the project under a contract
Any person who is named in the communications schedule for the project
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: A stakeholder is any individual, group or organization that can affect, be affected by, or perceives itself to be affected by the project (see manual 3.2.2).

n.1: Stakeholders include people with no formal role at all; holding a role in the project management team or business layer is not the test (manual 3.2.2).
n.2: Suppliers can be stakeholders, but so can users, the business and anyone else who can affect or is affected by the project (manual 3.2.2).
n.3: The communications schedule is planned for stakeholders who have been identified; being named in it is not what makes someone a stakeholder (manual 3.2.2, 3.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement about stakeholder relationships is correct, according to PRINCE2 7?
o: They are fixed once the stakeholder analysis has been approved in the PID
They change over time, so engagement continues as the project progresses
They are managed by the business layer rather than the project management team
They are important during initiation and are left to the business after stage one
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Relationships with stakeholders change over time, so engagement is ongoing, with ways of working set up so that all impacted areas stay involved as the project progresses (see manual 3.2.2).

n.0: Approving the PID does not freeze relationships; PRINCE2 expects them to change and the approaches to be reviewed at stage boundaries (manual 3.2.2, tab 6.5).
n.2: The project management team builds relationships with internal and external stakeholders; the board manages the interface with the organizational ecosystem (manual 2.3, 6.2.4).
n.3: Stakeholder engagement continues throughout the project; stages often mark changes in influencers and key relationships (manual 3.5.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Stakeholder engagement starts by identifying the stakeholders and the key [?] who can shape whether the change succeeds.
o: risk owners
change authorities
influencers
suppliers
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 stakeholder engagement involves identifying stakeholders and key influencers, then building relationships with them (see manual 3.2.2).

n.0: Risk owners manage specific risks under the risk practice; they are not the people stakeholder engagement seeks out (manual ch 9).
n.1: A change authority approves requests for change within delegated limits under the issues practice (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Suppliers are one stakeholder group; the term PRINCE2 uses for people who can shape the change is key influencers (manual 3.2.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: In which management product does PRINCE2 record the stakeholder analysis?
o: Risk management approach
Sustainability management approach
Business case
Communication management approach
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The communication management approach includes a stakeholder analysis: who is impacted by the outcome or the delivery, and who can influence the project's success or failure (see manual 3.4).

n.0: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed (procedures, scales and responsibilities), not who the stakeholders are (manual ch 9).
n.1: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls for meeting the project's sustainability targets (manual 5.5).
n.2: The business case documents the justification (costs, benefits and risks), not the stakeholder analysis (manual ch 5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: In a project to merge two council call centres, a long-serving supervisor with no formal project role openly criticizes the new rota, and many colleagues follow her lead. What does PRINCE2 recommend?
o: Leave her out of project communications so her views do not spread further
Ask the executive to instruct her formally to support the new rota
Raise an exception report, because her resistance threatens the stage
Find out why she resists and involve her as a key influencer in the change
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Resistance shows where engagement should be focused. PRINCE2 asks the project to understand why a stakeholder resists and to involve key influencers, who may have no formal role, in shaping the change (see manual 3.2.2, 3.4).

n.0: Sidelining a resisting stakeholder works against PRINCE2 guidance: pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused (manual 3.4).
n.1: PRINCE2 favours persuading, influencing and co-creating over formal instruction; the supervisor's influence comes from her relationships, not her role (manual 3.3, 3.2.2).
n.2: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; nothing here says a tolerance will be exceeded (manual 11.2.6).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about stakeholder engagement in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. Stakeholders are limited to people who hold a formal role in the project.
2. Regular meetings and working groups help build shared understanding across interfaces.
3. Stakeholder engagement is complete once the project initiation documentation is approved.
4. Stage boundaries are a useful point to review key relationships and influencers.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 2 is correct: regular meetings and working groups build shared understanding of perspectives across interfaces. Statement 4 is correct: stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so they are good points to review them (see manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: stakeholders include anyone who can affect or is affected by the project, many of whom have no formal role (manual 3.2.2).
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: stakeholders go well beyond formal roles, and engagement continues as relationships change (manual 3.2.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: relationships change over time, so engagement carries on throughout the project (manual 3.2.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: What does the stakeholder analysis identify in PRINCE2?
o: The roles that will approve each request for change and the limits on their authority
Who is impacted by the outcome or the delivery, and who can influence success or failure
The current, interim and target states and the activities that support each transition
The products to be delivered, their quality criteria and the people who will review them
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The stakeholder analysis in the communication management approach identifies who is impacted by the outcome or the delivery process, and who can influence the project's success or failure (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Who approves requests for change, and within what limits, is set out in the issue management approach (manual 10.2.4, 10.5).
n.2: States and enabling activities are described in the change management approach (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Products, their quality criteria and reviewers are set out in product descriptions and the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: According to PRINCE2 7, what do pockets of resistance among stakeholders indicate?
o: Where communication efforts should be focused
That the project should be closed prematurely
That a request for change should be raised
That a stage tolerance has been exceeded
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused, so the project can understand and address the reasons behind them (see manual 3.4).

n.1: Premature closure is a project board decision, for example when the business justification is lost; resistance alone does not call for it (manual ch 19).
n.2: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline; resistance is a people matter addressed through engagement and communication (manual 10.1, 3.4).
n.3: Tolerance breaches are measured against plan targets; resistance does not itself mean a tolerance has been exceeded (manual 11.2.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: How does PRINCE2 7 define culture?
o: The agreed procedures and standards set out in the management approaches
The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group
The ability to relate to and work across different cultures in the ecosystem
Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 7 defines culture as the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Procedures and standards in the management approaches are the project's defined ways of working; culture is how people actually think and behave (manual 3.2.3).
n.2: The ability to relate and work across cultures is cultural intelligence, a leadership capability, not culture itself (manual 3.3.1).
n.3: Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working is the PRINCE2 definition of management (manual 3.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Team members on a project keep bypassing the agreed process for logging defects. According to PRINCE2 7, what does this persistent non-compliance suggest?
o: The agreed ways of working may no longer fit the emerging culture
A stage tolerance has been breached and must be escalated to the board
An off-specification has occurred and must go to the change authority
The team manager role should be combined with the project support role
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 treats persistent non-compliance with project processes as a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer match the emerging culture, so feedback should be gathered and acted on (see manual 3.2.3).

n.1: Not following a process is not, in itself, a forecast breach of stage tolerance, so there is nothing to escalate as an exception (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; bypassing a process is a ways-of-working matter (manual 10.1, 3.2.3).
n.3: Combining roles is a tailoring decision about capacity and skills; it does not address a mismatch between processes and culture (manual 2.7, 3.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Gathering and acting on [?] helps keep the project's defined ways of working aligned with how people actually work.
o: checkpoint reports
quality records
exception reports
feedback
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 recommends gathering and acting on feedback so that the defined ways of working stay aligned with the way people really work (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Checkpoint reports give the project manager the status of a work package; they are not the mechanism PRINCE2 names for aligning ways of working with culture (manual ch 11).
n.1: Quality records are evidence that quality activities were carried out on products (manual ch 8).
n.2: Exception reports warn the board of a forecast breach of tolerance (manual 11.2.6).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Why is culture considered in the change management approach?
o: Because culture determines the tolerances that the board sets for each stage
Because culture cannot change, so the products must be designed around it
Because culture is one of the things that changes between current and target states
Because culture problems are logged in the issue register as off-specifications
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The change management approach describes the characteristics of each state, including culture, and the evolving culture is one of the factors in deciding how much detail it needs (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Stage tolerances are set by the project board through the progress practice; culture is not what determines them (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: PRINCE2 refers to an evolving culture: culture shifts as the change takes place, which is why it is described for each state (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Off-specifications concern products that will not meet their quality specifications; cultural matters are handled through the people element (manual 10.1, 3.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Site engineers must complete a new online checklist before each customer visit. They find it slow, and many now phone bookings through to the office instead. What should the project manager do, in line with PRINCE2 7 guidance on culture?
o: Announce that bookings phoned through to the office will no longer be accepted
Record each phoned booking as an off-specification in the issue register
Use the engineers' feedback to review and simplify the checklist
Ask the project board to replace the engineers who keep phoning bookings
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Persistent workarounds show the defined ways of working do not fit how people actually work. PRINCE2 7 recommends gathering and acting on feedback so the ways of working stay aligned with the culture (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Enforcing the process without understanding the reason ignores the leading indicator; PRINCE2 asks the project to act on the feedback instead (manual 3.2.3).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; phoned bookings are a ways-of-working matter (manual 10.1).
n.3: Replacing people does not address why the agreed ways of working no longer fit; acting on feedback does (manual 3.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements about culture in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. Culture is defined in the project mandate and stays fixed for the project.
2. Non-compliance with project processes is best handled by escalating it to the business layer.
3. Each organization in the organizational ecosystem may have its own culture.
4. Behaviours and culture are hard to document and are best learned socially.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 3 is correct: the organizations in the organizational ecosystem each bring their own culture. Statement 4 is correct: behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to document and are best learned through social learning (see manual 3.1, 3.5.1).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong: culture evolves during a change, and non-compliance is a signal to gather and act on feedback, not to escalate to the business layer (manual 3.2.1, 3.2.3).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: PRINCE2 refers to an evolving culture, and the mandate is not where culture is defined (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: persistent non-compliance is a leading indicator that ways of working need adapting through feedback (manual 3.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which principle is applied when a project recognizes that behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to document and are best learned through social learning?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Applying learn from experience to people means recognizing that valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem and that behaviours, culture and relationships are best learned socially in a knowledge-sharing environment (see manual 3.5.1).

n.1: Manage by exception, applied to people, means making decisions at the most local level where the knowledge resides (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships is about addressing people factors through clear roles and relationships across the lifecycle, not social learning (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Tailor to suit the project adapts the method to the project's context; it is not the principle behind social learning (manual 2.7).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A project's reporting process was agreed at initiation. By stage 3, teams from three suppliers have developed their own habits and the process is widely ignored. Which action BEST reflects PRINCE2 7 guidance?
o: Keep the process unchanged, because it was approved as part of the PID
Gather feedback and adapt the ways of working to fit the emerging culture
Record the ignored process as a threat in the risk register and monitor it
Let each supplier follow its own process, as their cultures cannot be aligned
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Persistent non-compliance is a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer fit the emerging culture, so the project should gather feedback and adapt them (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Approval in the PID does not freeze ways of working; they can be reviewed and updated, for example at stage boundaries (manual 3.2.3, ch 18).
n.2: The non-compliance is already happening, so it is not an uncertain future event; PRINCE2 treats it as a signal to act on feedback (manual 9.1, 3.2.3).
n.3: PRINCE2 seeks shared ways of working across the project ecosystem; feedback is used to align them, not to abandon alignment (manual 3.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: In PRINCE2 7, which practice covers change control of the project baseline?
o: Change
Progress
Issues
Plans
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project baseline; in PRINCE2 7 issue management encompasses change control (see manual 10.1).

n.0: 'Change' was a 6th edition theme; PRINCE2 7 has no change practice, and change control now sits in the issues practice (manual 10.1).
n.1: The progress practice monitors and controls performance against plans and handles exceptions, not change control of the baseline (manual 11.1).
n.3: The plans practice sets out how, when and by whom products will be delivered; it does not run change control (manual ch 7).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: What is change control in PRINCE2 7?
o: The means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state
The approach for planning communication with stakeholders affected by the change
The process of handing products into operational use and supporting their adoption
The procedure ensuring changes to the baseline are identified, assessed and decided
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Change control is the procedure that ensures changes to the project baseline are identified, assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: Moving the organization from its current state to a target state is change management, part of the people element (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: Planning communication with stakeholders is covered by the communication management approach (manual 3.4).
n.2: Handing products into use and supporting adoption relates to closing the project and the senior user's adoption responsibilities, not change control (manual 6.2.4, ch 19).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A board member asks which management product explains how the organization's staff will move from the old way of working to the new one. Which product should the project manager point to?
o: Issue management approach
Change management approach
Issue register
Project product description
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Moving staff from the current to the target way of working is change management, planned in the change management approach (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: The issue management approach covers capturing issues and controlling changes to the baseline, not the organizational transition (manual 10.5).
n.2: The issue register records formal issues and their status; it does not plan how staff will move to new ways of working (manual 10.5).
n.3: The project product description defines the project's main product, quality expectations and acceptance criteria, not the transition of staff (manual 8.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

In PRINCE2 7, how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled is described in the [?].
o: issue management approach
change management approach
communication management approach
quality management approach
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The issue management approach describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled; it replaced the 6th edition change control approach (see manual 10.5).

n.1: The change management approach plans the organizational transition from current to target state, not control of the baseline (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication and feedback (manual 3.4).
n.3: The quality management approach covers how products will meet their quality requirements, not how baseline changes are controlled (manual 8.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes change management from change control in PRINCE2 7?
o: Change management concerns the organization's transition; change control concerns baseline changes
Change management concerns baseline changes; change control concerns the organization's transition
Change management is a 6th edition term that PRINCE2 7 has replaced with change control
Change management and change control are two names for the issues practice in PRINCE2 7
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: In PRINCE2 7, change management (people element) is the organization's transition from current to target state, while change control (issues practice) handles changes to the project baseline (see manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).

n.1: This reverses the two terms: change control is about the baseline and change management is about the organizational transition (manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: Change management is a current PRINCE2 7 concept with its own management approach; it was the old 'change' theme that became the issues practice (manual 3.2.1, 10.1).
n.3: Only change control sits in the issues practice; change management belongs to the people element (manual 3.2.1, 10.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Which two statements are correct for PRINCE2 7?
1. The 6th edition 'change' theme is now covered by the issues practice.
2. The change management approach describes how requests for change are approved.
3. Change management is part of the people element.
4. A change authority approves the organization's move from the current state to the target state.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Statement 1 is correct: the old 'change' theme became the issues practice, which includes change control. Statement 3 is correct: change management is part of the people element (see manual 10.1, 3.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: how requests for change are assessed and controlled is set out in the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: requests for change are handled through the issue management approach, and a change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications (manual 10.5, 10.2.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications within delegated limits, not the organizational transition (manual 10.2.4).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A supplier proposes replacing the material specified in a baselined product description with a cheaper alternative. How is this handled in PRINCE2 7?
o: Through the change management approach, as it changes the project
Through the communication management approach, as users must be told
Through the benefits management approach, as cost affects benefits
Through the issues practice, as a request for change to a baseline
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: A proposal to change a baselined product is a request for change, an issue type handled by change control within the issues practice (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: The change management approach plans the organizational transition; changes to baselined products go through change control in the issues practice (manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Communication may follow a decision, but the request itself must be captured and assessed through change control (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: The benefits management approach covers achieving outcomes and confirming benefits; a proposed change to a baselined product is a request for change (manual 5.5, 10.1).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: A hospital project must prepare nurses to move from paper notes to tablets on the wards. Separately, the board asks for a new report to be added to the approved specification. Which pairing reflects PRINCE2 7?
o: Both through the issues practice, as each is a change to the project
Both through the change management approach, as each affects users
Nurses' move through change management; new report through change control
Nurses' move through change control; new report through change management
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: Preparing nurses for a new way of working is organizational transition, planned through change management. Adding a report to an approved specification changes the baseline, so it goes through change control in the issues practice (see manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: Moving nurses to a new way of working is not a change to the baseline; it is planned in the change management approach (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: The new report changes an approved specification, so it must go through change control in the issues practice (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: This reverses the two: people's transition is change management and baseline changes are change control (manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: In PRINCE2, which term describes the existing organizations connected with a project (the business, users and suppliers), each with its own structures, governance, culture and people?
o: Organizational ecosystem
Project ecosystem
Project management team structure
Business layer
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The organizational ecosystem is the set of existing organizations, such as the business, users and suppliers, each bringing its own structures, governance, culture and people (see manual 3.1, fig 3.1).

n.1: The project ecosystem is the temporary set of people, relationships, structures and ways of working created for the project, not the existing organizations (manual 3.1).
n.2: The project management team structure is the set of project roles (board, project manager, team managers, assurance and support), not the wider organizations (manual 6.2.3).
n.3: The business layer is the commissioning level that provides the mandate and appoints the executive; it is one part of the organizational ecosystem, not the whole of it (manual 6.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which statement describes the project ecosystem in PRINCE2?
o: The permanent structures and governance of the business that commissioned the project
The temporary people, relationships, structures and ways of working set up for the project
The list of stakeholder groups and the frequency with which each receives information
The hierarchy of all work to be done, linking the product breakdown to work packages
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The project ecosystem is temporary: it is the people, relationships, structures and ways of working created for the project where the business, user and supplier interests meet (see manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

n.0: Permanent structures and governance belong to the organizational ecosystem, which exists before and after the project (manual 3.1).
n.2: Stakeholder groups and how often they receive information are set out in the communication management approach, not the project ecosystem (manual 3.4).
n.3: A hierarchy of all work linking the product breakdown structure to work packages is the work breakdown structure (manual 6.2.5).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The project ecosystem is formed where the [?] ecosystems intersect.
o: programme, portfolio and project
directing, managing and delivering
business, user and supplier
executive, manager and team
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: PRINCE2 shows the project ecosystem as the intersection of the business, user and supplier ecosystems, the three project interests (see manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

n.0: Programmes and portfolios are possible contexts for a project, not the three ecosystems whose overlap forms the project ecosystem (manual 1.5, fig 1.2).
n.1: Directing, managing and delivering are levels of the project management team, not ecosystems (manual 6.2, fig 6.2).
n.3: Executive, project manager and team manager are roles; the project ecosystem is formed from the business, user and supplier interests (manual fig 3.2).

People: Change & Stakeholders.q: Which role is responsible for managing relationships at the interface between the organizational ecosystem and the project ecosystem?
o: Project manager
Project support
Change authority
Project board
People: Change & Stakeholders.w: The project board manages relationships where the organizational and project ecosystems meet, and monitors and supports social cohesion within the project ecosystem (see manual 6.2.4, QRG project board responsibilities).

n.0: The project manager manages relationships within the project ecosystem, while the board handles the interface with the organizational ecosystem (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Project support provides administration, such as maintaining registers and version control; it does not manage relationships between ecosystems (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: A change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications within delegated limits; it has no responsibility for the ecosystem interface (manual 10.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project manager from a supplier organization is leading a team that includes several senior specialists from the customer. Which statement is consistent with PRINCE2's guidance on leading project teams?
o: The project manager should ask the executive to direct the specialists, as they outrank the project manager
The senior specialists should be moved out of the team, as their seniority weakens the project manager's authority
The project manager should use the formal role descriptions as the basis for instructing the specialists
It is not unusual for team members to outrank the project manager, so leading by influence is needed
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 notes that it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager, so authority is harder to exercise and leadership through persuasion, influence and co-creation matters (see manual 3.3).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day on behalf of the board; asking the executive to direct team members bypasses that role and is unlikely to work for people who do not report to the executive (manual 3.3, 6.2.4).
n.1: Effective teams need a diverse mix of capabilities and perspectives; seniority is not a reason to remove people (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions do not give a temporary leader line authority over people from other organizations; leadership depends on influence and relationships (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which activity is an example of leadership rather than management, as PRINCE2 describes them?
o: Instructing a team member to carry out a task using the agreed procedure
Confirming that work was carried out in line with the agreed ways of working
Seeking regular feedback so that team members stay aligned with the objectives
Recording the current status of each product in the product register
People: Teams & Communication.w: Seeking regular feedback to keep team members aligned with the project's objectives is part of the PRINCE2 description of leadership (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Instructing the execution of a task in line with agreed ways of working is the definition of management (manual 3.3).
n.1: Checking that tasks follow the agreed ways of working is management control, not leadership (manual 3.3).
n.3: Maintaining the product register is an administrative task, typically done by project support, not an act of leadership (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements describe leadership as PRINCE2 defines it?
1. Persuading, influencing and co-creating, with a focus on key relationships.
2. Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working.
3. Motivating people to achieve the project's objectives.
4. Setting tolerances for each work package on behalf of the project board.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statements 1 and 3 are both parts of the PRINCE2 description of leadership: motivating people towards the objectives, and persuading, influencing and co-creating with a focus on key relationships (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is the definition of management, not leadership (manual 3.3).
n.2: Statement 2 defines management, and statement 4 is a control the project manager uses to manage by exception, not part of the definition of leadership (manual 3.3, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is a management control: the project manager sets work package tolerances, which is not part of the definition of leadership (manual 11.2.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Why does a project manager need to provide leadership as well as management?
o: Management directs tasks to agreed ways of working, but leading is needed to motivate and influence people
Leadership takes over from management once the team has agreed its ways of working
Management is used for people inside the project, while leadership is kept for stakeholders outside it
Combining the two allows the project manager to carry out project assurance for the board
People: Teams & Communication.w: Management instructs tasks within agreed ways of working, but on a temporary project the project manager often lacks formal authority, so leadership (motivating, persuading, influencing, co-creating) is also needed (see manual 3.3).

n.1: Leadership does not replace management at any point; both are needed throughout the project (manual 3.3).
n.2: Leadership applies to the team as well: it includes motivating team members and seeking their feedback to keep them aligned (manual 3.3).
n.3: The project manager can never carry out project assurance, which must be independent of the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which statement describes co-creation as PRINCE2 defines it?
o: A modification to any of the approved management products that make up the project baseline
Collaboration that involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working
The transfer of ownership of the completed products from the supplier to the user community
A quality review in which products are checked against their quality criteria before approval
People: Teams & Communication.w: Co-creation is a specific form of collaboration in which users and key influencers help design products and agreed ways of working, so that they are adopted (see manual 3.3).

n.0: A modification to an approved baselined management product is a change, handled through the issues practice (manual 10.1).
n.2: Transferring ownership of the project product to the users is project acceptance and handover, not co-creation (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.3: Checking products against quality criteria is quality control, for example a quality review (manual 8.2.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q: According to PRINCE2, what is the main aim of co-creating products and agreed ways of working?
o: To reduce the number of management products that the project needs
To transfer accountability for the products from the executive to the users
To ensure they are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems
To let the supplier fix the project's scope before initiation begins
People: Teams & Communication.w: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in design so that the resulting products and ways of working are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Reducing or merging management products is a matter for tailoring, not the aim of co-creation (manual 2.7).
n.1: The executive's accountability cannot be delegated, and co-creation does not move it (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Co-creation brings users and key influencers into design; it does not hand scope decisions to the supplier (manual 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
