Co-creation is a specific form of [?] that involves users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working.
o: quality assurance
delegation
governance
collaboration
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 describes co-creation as a specific form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in design (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Quality assurance is an independent check, managed outside the project management team, that the project is meeting quality requirements; it is not joint design (manual 8.2.3).
n.1: Delegation passes authority down the levels of the project; co-creation is about designing things together (manual 3.3).
n.2: Governance is the framework of authority and control; co-creation is a form of collaboration (manual 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project manager invites team members to help design the project's new procedure for reporting issues, rather than simply issuing it to them. What benefit does PRINCE2 associate with this approach?
o: People are more willing to be managed in line with ways of working they helped to create
The procedure can be left out of the issue management approach in the PID
Responsibility for maintaining the issue register passes from project support to the team
Team members become accountable for the decisions made on each issue
People: Teams & Communication.w: Co-creating ways of working with team members (and stakeholders) significantly improves their willingness to be managed in line with them (see manual 3.3).

n.1: Procedures for capturing and handling issues are still documented in the issue management approach, which forms part of the PID (manual ch 10).
n.2: Maintaining the registers remains an administrative task of project support under the project manager; co-creation does not change this (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Decisions on issues sit with the project manager, change authority or project board according to delegated authority; co-creation does not move accountability (manual 10.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: What does PRINCE2 say that co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities helps to achieve?
o: It removes the need for quality reviews, as users have already seen the products
It lets the senior supplier accept the completed products on behalf of the users
It moves responsibility for realizing benefits from the senior user to the supplier
It improves the products' adoption into the business and reduces handover risks
People: Teams & Communication.w: Co-creating products, with agreed product descriptions, unites the different perspectives of the business, user and supplier communities, improving development and adoption and reducing handover risks (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Products still go through the quality control methods in their product descriptions; involvement in design does not replace quality checks (manual 8.2.2).
n.1: Acceptance is given by or on behalf of the users, not by the supplier that built the products (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.2: The senior user remains accountable for specifying the benefits and responsible for their continued realization (manual 6.2.4.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements about collaboration and co-creation in PRINCE2 are correct?
1. Co-creation is limited to the supplier's specialist teams.
2. Leadership includes co-creating, with a focus on key relationships.
3. Regular meetings and working groups help build shared understanding across interfaces.
4. Co-creation replaces the need for agreed product descriptions.
o: 2 and 3
1 and 2
1 and 4
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 2 is correct: PRINCE2 describes leadership as including persuading, influencing and co-creating with a focus on key relationships (manual 3.3). Statement 3 is correct: regular meetings and working groups build shared understanding across interfaces (manual 3.2.2).

n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: co-creation specifically involves users and key influencers, not just supplier specialists (manual 3.3).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: co-creation involves users and key influencers, and products are co-created with agreed product descriptions rather than without them (manual 3.3, 3.5.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: PRINCE2 describes co-creating products with agreed product descriptions (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: During the 'controlling a stage' process, how should the project manager work with a team manager from a partner organization when defining a new work package?
o: Issue the work package description and ask the team manager to confirm receipt
Ask the executive to instruct the team manager to accept the work package
Build a working relationship and co-create the work package with the team manager
Let the team manager write the work package and approve it once work is under way
People: Teams & Communication.w: When authorizing a work package, the project manager builds a working relationship with the team manager, co-creates and reviews the work package with them, confirms acceptance and then authorizes the work (see manual 16.4.1, 3.3).

n.0: Issuing the work package one way misses the co-creation and confirmed acceptance that the activity expects (manual 16.4.1).
n.1: The project manager authorizes work packages; using the executive's authority over someone who does not report to them is unlikely to work (manual 16.4.1, 3.3.1).
n.3: The project manager defines and authorizes the work package before the team starts work; it is not approved after work is under way (manual 16.4.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Why does PRINCE2 encourage collaboration across the business, user and supplier communities rather than each community working separately?
o: So that each community can set its own tolerances for the products it delivers
So that their different perspectives are united, improving the products and their adoption
So that the supplier can take over the senior user's responsibility for requirements
So that the project can be directed without a single point of accountability
People: Teams & Communication.w: Working together unites the different perspectives of the business, user and supplier communities, which improves the development and adoption of products (see manual 3.3, 3.5.1).

n.0: Tolerances are set level by level (business layer, project board, project manager), not by each community for itself (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The senior user stays accountable for capturing user requirements; collaboration does not transfer this to the supplier (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The executive remains the single point of accountability for the project (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: According to PRINCE2, what does an effective project team require?
o: People who share the same professional background and working style
Team members drawn from one organization so that reporting lines are kept simple
A diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives matching the project's needs
The most senior people available from each of the business, user and supplier areas
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 says an effective team needs a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives that match what the project requires (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: A shared background and style works against the diversity of capabilities and perspectives that PRINCE2 says effective teams need (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Project teams typically work across organizational boundaries; the guidance is to match diverse capabilities to the project's needs, not to draw from one organization (manual 3.3, 3.3.2).
n.3: Seniority is not the test: roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, matched to the project's needs (manual 3.3.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q: What should the roles and responsibilities assigned to people on a PRINCE2 project reflect?
o: The capability, authority and availability of the person doing the work
The standard job descriptions used by the person's home organization
The person's grade and seniority within the business layer
The responsibilities written into the person's employment contract
People: Teams & Communication.w: Roles and responsibilities should reflect the capability, authority and availability of the individual, considered through their key relationships (see manual 3.3.2).

n.1: Standard, generic role descriptions are unlikely to be effective; roles should fit the individual and their relationships (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Grade and seniority are not the basis; it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager (manual 3.3, 3.3.2).
n.3: Employment contracts sit with the home organization; project roles are based on capability, authority and availability (manual 3.3.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
When a gap in a team member's competence is identified, PRINCE2 suggests mitigations such as [?] the person or shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people.
o: auditing
upskilling
escalating
rewarding
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 says competency and capability gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Auditing checks compliance; it does not close a gap in someone's skills (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Escalation is used when a decision could affect other areas or tolerances are threatened; it does not close a competency gap (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Rewards such as pay and career progression are often outside the project manager's remit and do not address a competency gap (manual 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Why does PRINCE2 warn that generic, standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective?
o: Because role descriptions are not one of the management products used in PRINCE2
Because role descriptions are agreed by the team managers rather than the project board
Because PRINCE2 requires each of its roles to be performed by a different person
Because people with the same skills perform a role differently and roles must fit them
People: Teams & Communication.w: Even people with the same capabilities perform the same role differently, so roles should reflect the individual's capability, authority, availability and key relationships rather than a standard template (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Role descriptions are a PRINCE2 management product of the organizing practice and form part of the PID (manual ch 6).
n.1: Role descriptions form part of the PID, which the project board approves when it authorizes the project (manual ch 6, 14.4.2).
n.2: One person may hold several roles and some roles can be shared, within the combination rules (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Two analysts with identical qualifications are given similar tasks, but one works far more effectively when paired with a particular designer. How does PRINCE2 explain this?
o: People with the same capabilities may perform a role differently, depending on who they work with
The analysts' role descriptions were not approved by the project board before work began
Competence comes from qualifications, so the difference must come from the work package tolerances
The less effective analyst is a threat that should be recorded and owned in the risk register
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 notes that people with the same capabilities and competencies often perform the same role differently, and the same person may perform differently depending on who they work with (see manual 3.3.2).

n.1: Approval of role descriptions does not explain why equally qualified people perform differently; PRINCE2 links this to individuals and their working relationships (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Qualifications do not settle competence, and tolerances set limits on a work package; they do not explain differences between people (manual 3.3.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: The situation concerns how people work together, which PRINCE2 addresses through team building and roles, not by registering a colleague as a risk (manual 3.3.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements about building effective teams are correct?
1. Some motivational factors, such as pay and career progression, may be outside the project manager's remit.
2. Roles are fixed at initiation and are not revisited during the project.
3. Structured team-building exercises can speed up the forming of a team.
4. Competency gaps are accepted as the team is temporary.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 1 is correct: pay and career progression are examples of motivators outside the project manager's remit (manual 3.3). Statement 3 is correct: structured exercises can accelerate team building (manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: roles should be reviewed and updated when key relationships shift (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: roles are reviewed when relationships shift, and competency gaps should be identified and mitigated (manual 3.3.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities (manual 3.3.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Midway through a stage, a key relationship in the project changes when one team manager is replaced by another. What does PRINCE2 suggest about the affected roles and responsibilities?
o: They stay as agreed in the PID until the end of the project
They are passed unchanged to the new team manager by project support
They are taken on by the executive until the next stage boundary is reached
They are reviewed against the changed relationship and updated as needed
People: Teams & Communication.w: Roles and responsibilities are viewed through the lens of key relationships and should be reviewed and updated when those relationships shift (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Freezing roles until closure ignores the guidance to review roles whenever key relationships shift (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Project support provides administration; handing roles over unchanged ignores the new person's capability, authority and availability (manual 3.3.2, 6.2.4).
n.2: The executive directs the project and does not take over a team manager's delivery responsibilities (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A team member assigned to write user training material is found to lack some of the skills needed for the task. Which action follows PRINCE2's guidance on building effective teams?
o: Record the skills gap as an off-specification and wait for the board's decision
Arrange upskilling or shift the training tasks to someone better suited
Ask the business layer to widen the project tolerances to allow for the delay
Leave the plan as it is, as building skills is the team member's responsibility
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 says gaps in competency and capability should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling the person or shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; a gap in someone's skills is not one, and no product has been delivered yet (manual 10.1).
n.2: No breach of project tolerance is forecast; the response to a competency gap is mitigation such as upskilling, not changing tolerances (manual 3.3.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: Identifying gaps and putting mitigations in place is part of building an effective team, not something left to the individual (manual 3.3.2).

People: Teams & Communication.q: What does PRINCE2 mean by cultural intelligence?
o: Knowledge of the business layer's strategy, policies and corporate standards
The ability to replace PRINCE2 terms with the organization's own terminology
An assessment of each team member's personality carried out during initiation
The ability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem
People: Teams & Communication.w: Cultural intelligence is the ability to relate and work across cultures within the organizational ecosystem, which is needed to lead people across organizational boundaries (see manual 3.3.1).

n.0: Knowing the business layer's strategy and standards is useful context, but it is not what cultural intelligence means (manual 3.3.1).
n.1: Changing terminology is a form of tailoring, not cultural intelligence (manual 2.7).
n.2: PRINCE2 does not define cultural intelligence as a personality assessment; it is a capability to relate and work across cultures (manual 3.3.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Why is leading a project team often harder than leading an established business team?
o: The team is temporary and crosses organizations, so authority is harder to exercise
The project manager is not permitted to give instructions to the team managers
Project teams have no governance arrangements until the project has been authorized
The project board leads the team directly, leaving the project manager to administer
People: Teams & Communication.w: Projects are delivered by temporary teams that typically work across organizational boundaries, so a temporary leader can find it harder to exercise authority and a different style of leadership is needed (see manual 3.3).

n.1: The project manager does instruct team managers, for example by authorizing work packages in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1).
n.2: Governance applies before authorization: the business layer appoints the executive in starting up a project, and the project board directs initiation through 'directing a project' (manual ch 13, ch 14).
n.3: The project board directs; the project manager manages and leads the team day to day on the board's behalf (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
Leading people who are beyond the project's direct authority, often across organizational boundaries, requires a degree of [?].
o: change authority
cultural intelligence
project assurance
stakeholder analysis
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 says leading people beyond the project's direct authority, often across organizational boundaries, requires cultural intelligence (see manual 3.3.1).

n.0: Change authority is delegated authority to approve requests for change and off-specifications, not a leadership capability (manual 10.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance is independent checking on behalf of the project board, not the capability needed to lead across boundaries (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Stakeholder analysis is a heading of the communication management approach that identifies who is affected or influential; it is not the capability needed to lead people across boundaries (manual 3.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which task most clearly requires the project manager to lead across organizational boundaries?
o: Updating the product register after the results of a quality review are known
Preparing the regular highlight report on stage status for the project board
Gaining commitment from a partner's specialists who report to their own director
Checking that the cost figures in the stage plan agree with the project plan
People: Teams & Communication.w: Securing commitment from people who report to another organization's director means leading people beyond the project's direct authority, which PRINCE2 says calls for cultural intelligence and influence (see manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

n.0: Updating the product register is administration within the project, often done by project support (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Producing highlight reports is part of the progress practice within the project's own reporting lines (manual 16.4.8).
n.3: Checking plan figures is a planning task within the project and does not involve leading people from other organizations (manual ch 7).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A supplier's team manager is slow to accept a work package. The project manager considers asking the executive to order the team manager to comply. Why is this unlikely to be effective?
o: The executive's role ends once the project has been authorized in directing a project
Work packages are authorized by the senior supplier rather than by the project manager
The team manager should accept work packages directly from the project board instead
The team manager does not report to the executive; a working relationship works better
People: Teams & Communication.w: Using the executive's authority over someone outside the executive's reporting line is unlikely to work; the project manager should build a working relationship and co-create the work package with the team manager (see manual 3.3.1, 16.4.1).

n.0: The executive remains accountable for the project until closure and continues to direct it (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The project manager authorizes work packages in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1).
n.2: Team managers take work packages from the project manager; the project board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual ch 17).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements about leading across organizational boundaries are correct?
1. Project teams often include people from several organizations within the organizational ecosystem.
2. It is not unusual for some team members to be more senior than the project manager.
3. The project manager gains line authority over all team members once the PID is approved.
4. Cultural intelligence concerns relations with external suppliers rather than internal departments.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 1 is correct: projects are delivered by temporary teams typically working across organizational boundaries. Statement 2 is correct: PRINCE2 notes it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager (see manual 3.3).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: approving the PID does not give the project manager line authority over people from other organizations (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: cultural intelligence covers relating across all cultures within the organizational ecosystem, including the business and users (manual 3.3.1).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: there is no line authority from PID approval, and cultural intelligence applies across the whole organizational ecosystem (manual 3.3.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project brings together a council, a building contractor and a housing association, each with its own way of working. What is the most appropriate way for the project manager to lead this team?
o: Apply the council's internal procedures to everyone, as the council funds the project
Relate to each organization's culture and collaborate to agree shared ways of working
Let each organization work in its own way and integrate the products at project closure
Ask project support to set the working practices so that the project manager stays neutral
People: Teams & Communication.w: Leading across boundaries needs cultural intelligence and collaboration, with ways of working agreed (ideally co-created) with the people involved so that they are adopted (see manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

n.0: Imposing one organization's procedures ignores the cultures of the others; PRINCE2 favours relating across cultures and agreeing ways of working together (manual 3.3.1).
n.2: Leaving integration until closure raises handover risk; agreed ways of working and co-created products reduce it (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Project support provides administrative services; ways of working are agreed with the people involved and set out in the management approaches (manual 6.2.4, 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project manager from the IT department must lead finance and HR staff who report to other directors. Which approach reflects PRINCE2's guidance?
o: Ask the finance and HR directors to transfer their staff to the IT department for the project
Escalate to the project board each time a team member disagrees with an instruction
Use persuasion and influence, building key relationships with the staff and their directors
Treat the project's role descriptions as giving line authority over these staff members
People: Teams & Communication.w: When leading people beyond the project's direct authority, PRINCE2 favours leadership through persuading, influencing and co-creating, with a focus on key relationships (see manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 expects project teams to work across organizational boundaries; moving staff between departments is not the guidance (manual 3.3).
n.1: Escalation is for decisions that could affect other areas of the project or threaten tolerances, not for everyday disagreements (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Role descriptions define project responsibilities; they do not create line authority over people who report elsewhere (manual 3.3.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: According to PRINCE2, how is social cohesion developed within a project?
o: By people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos
By placing everyone in a single team under one line manager for the project
By team members following the project's management approaches without change
By the project board approving a team charter during initiating a project
People: Teams & Communication.w: Social cohesion develops when people meet in a purposeful way on a regular basis, building trust across the project's silos (see manual 3.3.3).

n.1: Project teams typically span organizational boundaries; cohesion comes from purposeful, regular contact, not from a single line manager (manual 3.3, 3.3.3).
n.2: Following procedures unchanged is not how cohesion forms; PRINCE2 also expects ways of working to be adjusted when feedback shows they no longer fit (manual 3.2.3, 3.3.3).
n.3: PRINCE2 does not describe a board-approved team charter as the way cohesion is built; it comes from purposeful, regular contact that builds trust (manual 3.3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: In which type of team does PRINCE2 say that information tends to be shared organically through formal and informal networks?
o: A virtual team whose members work from their homes
A co-located team working together at the same site
A hybrid team that meets in person once a month
A remote team spread across several time zones
People: Teams & Communication.w: In co-located teams, information tends to flow organically through formal and informal networks; virtual, remote and hybrid teams need more deliberate methods (see manual 3.3.3, 3.4).

n.0: Virtual teams do not share information organically in the same way; social cohesion has to be built more deliberately (manual 3.3.3).
n.2: Hybrid working is one of the arrangements where cohesion needs deliberate effort, such as synchronized co-location days (manual 3.3.3).
n.3: Remote teams at a distance from each other need deliberate methods to build cohesion and share information (manual 3.3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
When a team is virtual or hybrid, building [?] needs more deliberate effort, for example by synchronizing co-location days for key people.
o: the project plan
risk tolerance
social cohesion
the product register
People: Teams & Communication.w: For virtual, remote or hybrid teams, social cohesion must be built more deliberately, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people focused on key relationships (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: The project plan is built through the plans practice in initiating a project; co-location days are about relationships, not planning (manual ch 7).
n.1: Risk tolerance is set by the project board from the business's risk appetite; it is unrelated to bringing dispersed people together (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: The product register records products and their status; it is not built through co-location days (manual ch 7).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which PRINCE2 role description includes monitoring and supporting social cohesion within the project ecosystem?
o: Project support
Team manager
Project assurance
Project board
People: Teams & Communication.w: The project board's role description includes focusing on the safety and well-being of the project team and monitoring and supporting social cohesion within the project ecosystem (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Project support provides administrative services such as registers, meetings and version control (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The team manager's description covers relationships within the team and the safety and well-being of team members, not cohesion across the whole project ecosystem (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance gives the board independent assurance in the business, user and supplier areas (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project team is split between two offices and several people working from home. Which action best follows PRINCE2's guidance on social cohesion?
o: Arrange regular co-location days for key people, focused on building key relationships
Rely on the team's informal networks to share information, as in a co-located team
Replace team meetings with written checkpoint reports to save people's time
Ask each office to run its work as a separate project with its own project board
People: Teams & Communication.w: Where teams are dispersed or hybrid, social cohesion needs deliberate methods, such as synchronized co-location days for key people focused on key relationships (see manual 3.3.3).

n.1: Organic sharing through informal networks is typical of co-located teams; a dispersed team needs deliberate methods (manual 3.3.3).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are progress controls from team managers to the project manager; they do not build trust and cohesion (manual 3.3.3, ch 11).
n.3: Splitting the work into separate projects does not address cohesion and would add governance; people should be brought together purposefully (manual 3.3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements about bringing project teams together are correct?
1. Social cohesion matters for co-located teams but not for remote teams.
2. Bringing teams together should make good use of people's time.
3. Once a team has formed, regular meetings add little to cohesion.
4. Team building helps people build trust and find compatible ways of working.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 2 is correct: bringing teams together should optimize the use of people's time while building social cohesion (manual 3.3.3). Statement 4 is correct: team building helps build trust and find compatible ways of working (manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Both statements are wrong: remote teams need cohesion built more deliberately, and cohesion depends on people meeting regularly (manual 3.3.3).
n.2: Statement 1 is wrong: social cohesion needs even more deliberate attention in remote and hybrid teams (manual 3.3.3).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: cohesion is developed by people meeting purposefully on a regular basis (manual 3.3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A project manager sets up a regular session where members of separate workstreams meet to share what they are working on and get to know each other. What is the main purpose of these sessions?
o: To collect progress information for the next highlight report to the board
To replace the checkpoint reports produced by the team managers
To build social cohesion and trust across the project's silos
To capture lessons for the lessons report at the end of the project
People: Teams & Communication.w: Bringing people from different parts of the project together purposefully and regularly builds social cohesion and trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: Highlight reports draw on checkpoint reports and the project log; the sessions described are about relationships, not progress reporting (manual 16.4.8).
n.1: Checkpoint reports are a progress control from team managers and are not replaced by informal team sessions (manual ch 11).
n.3: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log and reported through lessons reports; the sessions described are aimed at trust between workstreams (manual 3.3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which statement about the safety and well-being of team members is correct in PRINCE2 7?
o: It is a matter for each organization's HR function and outside the project's scope
It is the responsibility of project support, which keeps the related records
It is delegated to the change authority, which reviews it at each stage boundary
It is a focus for the project board, and the project manager and team managers monitor it
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 7 role descriptions give the project board a focus on the safety and well-being of the project team, and the project manager and team managers monitor and support the safety and well-being of team members (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: PRINCE2 7 places safety and well-being within the project's own role descriptions, so it is not outside the project's scope (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Project support provides administrative services; it does not hold responsibility for team well-being (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: The change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications within delegated limits; it has no well-being duty (manual 10.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: What is the purpose of the communication management approach?
o: To describe how issues are captured and how changes to the project baselines are controlled
To define the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, the project ecosystem
To establish the target organizational state and how the business will move from the current state
To describe how the project will engage the market, carry out procurement and manage contracts
People: Teams & Communication.w: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, across the project ecosystem, supporting alignment and the shaping of the project (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Capturing issues and controlling changes to baselines is the purpose of the issue management approach (manual ch 10).
n.2: Establishing the target organizational state and the route to it is the purpose of the change management approach (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Market engagement, procurement and contract management are covered by the commercial management approach (manual ch 6).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Why does PRINCE2 regard communication as important to a project?
o: It removes the need for formal progress reports to the project board
It transfers responsibility for adoption from the senior user to the stakeholders
It helps avoid misconceptions and unnecessary barriers to implementing change
It allows the project manager to approve changes without the change authority
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 explains that communication is important to avoid misconceptions and unnecessary barriers when implementing change (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Formal progress controls such as highlight and end stage reports still apply; communication does not replace them (manual ch 11).
n.1: The senior user remains responsible for handover, adoption and benefits realization; communication does not move this responsibility (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Approval of changes follows the issue management approach and delegated authority; communication does not change who approves (manual 10.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Under which heading of the communication management approach should an analytics tool that tracks how many stakeholders read the project newsletter be recorded?
o: Stakeholder analysis
Communications schedule and procedures
Resources
Supporting tools and techniques
People: Teams & Communication.w: Supporting tools and techniques covers items such as communications platforms and tools for analytics or automation (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the project or its delivery and who can influence its success; it does not record tools (manual 3.4).
n.1: The schedule and procedures set out purpose, frequency, channels and messages for each stakeholder group, not the tools used (manual 3.4).
n.2: Resources covers the resources for communication activities; an analytics tool belongs under supporting tools and techniques (manual 3.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which management product in the PID establishes a controlled, two-way flow of information to engage stakeholders?
o: Communication management approach
Change management approach
Sustainability management approach
Benefits management approach
People: Teams & Communication.w: The communication management approach supports engagement with stakeholders by establishing a controlled and bidirectional flow of information (see manual 3.4).

n.1: The change management approach sets out the target organizational state and how the business will transition to it (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls that ensure the project's sustainability targets are achieved (manual ch 5).
n.3: The benefits management approach defines the actions to ensure outcomes are achieved and benefits are confirmed (manual ch 5).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A local residents' group repeatedly raises objections to the project at public meetings. What does PRINCE2 suggest this resistance indicates?
o: That the group should be taken out of the stakeholder analysis
That the objections should be logged as risks owned by the executive
That communication with the group should be reduced to avoid conflict
That communication should focus on the group to understand its concerns
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 treats pockets of resistance as a useful indicator of where communications should be focused, so the reasons for the resistance should be understood (see manual 3.4).

n.0: A group that can affect, or feels affected by, the project is a stakeholder; removing it from the analysis sidelines it (manual 3.2.2, 3.4).
n.1: The objections are already happening, so they are not uncertain events; and logging them does not deal with the resistance through communication (manual 3.4, ch 9).
n.2: Resistance shows where communication should be focused, not reduced (manual 3.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two items would typically be included in the communication management approach?
1. An analysis of who is affected by the project and who can influence its success.
2. The purpose, frequency, channels and messages for each stakeholder group.
3. The scales used to estimate the probability and impact of each risk.
4. The prioritized acceptance criteria for the project product.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 1 is the stakeholder analysis and statement 2 is the communications schedule and procedures, both headings of the communication management approach (see manual 3.4).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: probability and impact scales belong in the risk management approach (manual ch 9).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: acceptance criteria are recorded in the project product description (manual ch 8).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: risk scales go in the risk management approach and acceptance criteria in the project product description (manual ch 8, ch 9).

People: Teams & Communication.q: In which process is the communication management approach first created, alongside the other management approaches?
o: Starting up a project
Initiating a project
Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
People: Teams & Communication.w: The management approaches, including the communication management approach, are created in initiating a project during 'agree the management approaches', and are then reviewed at stage boundaries and at closure (see manual 15.4.2, 3.4).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project brief and initiation stage plan; the management approaches are agreed in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.2: Controlling a stage uses the approach, for example for the frequency of highlight reports, but does not first create it (manual 16.4.8).
n.3: Managing a stage boundary reviews and updates the approaches; it is not where they are first created (manual ch 18).

People: Teams & Communication.q: How does the communication management approach relate to the highlight reports produced during a stage?
o: It replaces highlight reports for the stakeholders outside the project board
It is updated by the team managers each time they send a highlight report
It sets the frequency at which the project manager produces highlight reports
It lists the stage tolerances that highlight reports must be measured against
People: Teams & Communication.w: In controlling a stage, the project manager produces highlight reports at the frequency set out in the communication management approach (see manual 16.4.8).

n.0: Highlight reports are the project manager's regular status report to the project board; the communication approach does not replace them (manual 16.4.8).
n.1: Team managers send checkpoint reports to the project manager; highlight reports come from the project manager (manual 16.4.8).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board and recorded with the stage plan, not in the communication management approach (manual 11.2.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: How does the people element apply the 'focus on products' principle?
o: By making decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make them is held
By reviewing at each stage boundary how people interact with the wider organization
By co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities to aid adoption
By sharing knowledge hidden in the project ecosystem through social learning
People: Teams & Communication.w: Co-creating products, with agreed product descriptions, with the business, user and supplier communities unites their perspectives, improves development and adoption and reduces handover risks: this is how the people element applies focus on products (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Deciding at the most local level where the knowledge resides is how the people element applies manage by exception (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Using stage boundaries to review how people interact is how the people element applies manage by stages (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Drawing out hidden knowledge through social learning is how the people element applies learn from experience (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which principle does the people element apply when decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge needed to make and own them resides?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by exception
Manage by stages
Focus on products
People: Teams & Communication.w: The people element applies manage by exception by keeping decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own them resides, escalating when a decision could affect other areas (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Learn from experience is applied through knowledge sharing and social learning, not through where decisions are made (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Manage by stages is applied by using stage boundaries to review changing influencers and relationships (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Focus on products is applied by co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which is NOT one of the four parts of the PRINCE2 figure showing people central to the method?
o: Benefits realization
Leading successful change
Leading successful teams
Communication
People: Teams & Communication.w: The figure showing people central to the method has four parts: leading successful change, leading successful teams, communication, and people at the centre. Benefits realization belongs to the business case practice (see manual ch 3, fig 3.3).

n.1: Leading successful change is one of the parts of the figure (manual fig 3.3).
n.2: Leading successful teams is one of the parts of the figure (manual fig 3.3).
n.3: Communication is one of the parts of the figure (manual fig 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q: According to PRINCE2, on what does the extent of delegation within a project often depend?
o: The number of management stages shown in the project plan
The confidence and trust that exist in key relationships
The size of the change budget held by the project board
The seniority of the team managers within their own organizations
People: Teams & Communication.w: The extent of delegation often depends on the confidence and trust in key relationships, and it adapts over the project as people's skills and capabilities develop (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: The number of stages relates to manage by stages and decision points, not to how much is delegated (manual 3.5.1, ch 7).
n.2: A change budget funds approved changes; it does not set how far decisions are delegated to people (manual 10.2.5).
n.3: Seniority is not the basis: it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager, and delegation rests on trust (manual 3.3, 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
People factors such as behaviours, culture and relationships are difficult to document and are best learned through [?] learning.
o: formal
individual
social
classroom
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 explains that much valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem and that behaviours, culture and relationships are best learned through social learning, which is how the people element applies learn from experience (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Formal learning suits knowledge that can be written down; PRINCE2 says these people factors are hard to document and are learned socially (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Individual learning keeps knowledge with one person; PRINCE2 calls for a collaborative environment that shares knowledge (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Classroom learning is a form of formal teaching; people factors are best learned socially within the project ecosystem (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which statement best explains why PRINCE2 places people at the centre of the method?
o: People can take the place of the practices on small and simple projects
The people element is applied once, in initiating a project, when the team is formed
The people element is the responsibility of the senior user, who represents the users
Performance depends on the team's capabilities, its relationships and the people affected
People: Teams & Communication.w: Projects deliver change that affects people, and how well a project performs depends on the capabilities of the team, the strength of their relationships and the people impacted by the change (see manual ch 3).

n.0: The people element integrates with the principles, practices and processes; it does not replace any of them (manual 3.5).
n.1: People factors are addressed continually throughout the project lifecycle, not just once (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: People duties are spread across roles: the board, project manager and team managers all have people responsibilities (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Which two statements about how people integrate with the PRINCE2 method are correct?
1. Decisions are normally escalated to the project board so that the most senior view is applied.
2. People factors are addressed during initiation and are then left to the team managers.
3. Stage boundaries are good points to review how people interact with each other and the wider organization.
4. The project board focuses on the safety and well-being of the project team.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
People: Teams & Communication.w: Statement 3 is correct: stages often mark changes in influencers and key relationships, so boundaries are good review points (manual 3.5.1). Statement 4 is correct: the board's role includes a focus on the team's safety and well-being (manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Both statements are wrong: decisions are made at the most local level with the knowledge, and people factors are addressed throughout the lifecycle (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: decisions sit at the most local level where the knowledge resides, escalating when other areas could be affected (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: people factors are continually addressed throughout the project lifecycle (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: A team manager resolves a minor scheduling clash within the team's work package because the team has the relevant knowledge, the solution stays within tolerance and no other area is affected. Which principle does this apply?
o: Manage by exception, as decisions sit at the most local level holding the knowledge
Manage by stages, as the decision is made within the current management stage
Focus on products, as the work package defines the products to be delivered
Learn from experience, as the team is drawing on lessons from earlier projects
People: Teams & Communication.w: The people element applies manage by exception by keeping decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own them resides, escalating when other areas could be affected (see manual 3.5.1).

n.1: Manage by stages concerns planning and decision points at stage boundaries, and reviewing relationships there; the decision here is about where it is made (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Focus on products is about defining and co-creating products; the situation concerns the level at which a decision is taken (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Nothing in the situation involves earlier lessons; the point is that the decision is made locally within tolerance (manual 3.5.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: In the PRINCE2 people element, which statement defines management?
o: Motivating people to achieve the project's objectives through persuasion and influence
Instructing the execution of tasks in line with the agreed ways of working
The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices that shape how people behave
Representing the business, user and supplier interests when directing the project
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 defines management as instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working, which is distinct from leadership (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Motivating people through persuasion and influence describes leadership, not management (manual 3.3).
n.2: Shared attitudes, values, goals and practices describe culture, not management (manual 3.2.3).
n.3: Representing the three project interests is what the project board does at the directing level; it is not the definition of management (manual 6.2.4).

People: Teams & Communication.q: According to PRINCE2, how is leadership on a project best carried out?
o: Through the formal authority of the project board over each team member
Through detailed instructions issued by the project manager to each team
Through collaboration across the project ecosystem
Through the line management structure of the business layer
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 says leadership on projects is best done through collaboration across the project ecosystem, because temporary project leaders often lack formal authority over the people involved (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Project teams are temporary and span organizations, so formal authority is harder to exercise; leadership relies on collaboration and influence rather than board authority (manual 3.3).
n.1: Issuing instructions for tasks to be carried out is management, not leadership (manual 3.3).
n.3: Project teams draw people from several organizations, so the business layer's line structure does not cover them; leadership works through collaboration (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

People: Teams & Communication.q: Which statement best explains the difference between leadership and management on a PRINCE2 project?
o: Leadership is the responsibility of the project board, while management belongs to the project manager
Leadership is needed during initiation, while management is needed during the delivery stages
Leadership sets the agreed ways of working, while management motivates people to follow them
Leadership motivates and influences people, while management directs tasks to agreed ways of working
People: Teams & Communication.w: Leadership is about motivating, persuading, influencing and co-creating; management is about instructing tasks in line with agreed ways of working. Projects need both throughout (see manual 3.3).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not split the two by level: the project manager must lead people as well as manage tasks, and board members also lead (manual 3.3).
n.1: Both are needed throughout the project lifecycle; neither is tied to particular stages (manual 3.3).
n.2: This reverses the concepts: motivating people is part of leadership, while management instructs tasks within the agreed ways of working (manual 3.3).

People: Teams & Communication.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
Because project teams are temporary and often work across organizational boundaries, they need a different style of [?] from established business teams, as a temporary leader can find it harder to exercise authority.
o: leadership and management
governance and assurance
planning and control
reporting and escalation
People: Teams & Communication.w: PRINCE2 explains that temporary project teams, typically spanning organizational boundaries, need a different style of management and leadership from established teams, because a temporary leader finds authority harder to exercise (see manual 3.3).

n.1: Governance and assurance are arrangements of the organizing practice and the board; the people element's point about temporary teams concerns leadership and management style (manual 3.3).
n.2: Planning and control belong to the plans and progress practices; the difficulty of exercising authority is about leadership and management style (manual 3.3).
n.3: Reporting and escalation belong to the progress practice; they do not describe the style needed to lead a temporary team (manual 3.3).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the project initiation documentation (PID) are correct?
1. It is assembled during initiating a project and used to gain authorization for the project.
2. It is created in starting up a project to give a firm foundation for initiation.
3. The version used to gain authorization is baselined and later compared with actual performance.
4. It holds the daily log and lessons log so that they can be reviewed at each stage end.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 3
Business Case.w: Statement 1 is correct: the PID is assembled in initiating a project from the products created or updated there, and is used to gain authorization. Statement 3 is correct: the authorized version is baselined and later used to compare performance, for example when evaluating the project (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the product created in starting up a project as the foundation for initiation is the project brief, not the PID (manual 5.5).
n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the project brief, not the PID, is created in starting up a project; the PID is assembled in initiation (manual 5.5, 4.3.1).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the project brief is created in starting up a project, and the daily log and lessons log are held in the project log, not the PID (manual 4.3.2).

Business Case.q: Why is the version of the PID that is used to gain project authorization baselined and placed under change control?
o: So that actual performance can later be compared with what was originally agreed
So that the daily log and registers can be stored in it and updated every day
So that the business layer can reuse it as the project mandate for later projects
So that the project brief can be prepared from it in starting up a project
Business Case.w: The authorized PID is baselined so that it can be compared with actual performance later; for example, the end project report reviews performance against the baselined PID. Changes after that go through change control (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6, 19.4.4).

n.1: The logs and registers are dynamic records in the project log; the PID is a baselined set of products, not a daily record (manual 4.3.2).
n.2: The project mandate comes from the business layer before starting up a project; it is not created from a baselined PID (manual 13.3).
n.3: The project brief is created in starting up a project, before the PID exists; the PID supersedes the brief, not the other way round (manual 5.5).

Business Case.q: A team member mentions an informal concern to the project manager in conversation. Later the same day, a formal risk is identified that needs to be tracked. Where should each be recorded?
o: Both in the PID: the concern in the daily log and the risk in the risk management approach
Both in the project log: the concern in the issue register and the risk in the risk management approach
Both in the project log: the concern in the daily log and the risk in the risk register
Both in the business case: the concern in the lessons log and the risk under the major risks heading
Business Case.w: Informal concerns can be noted in the daily log, while formal risks are recorded in the risk register. Both records sit in the project log (see manual 4.3.2; issues and risk practices).

n.0: The PID does not hold the daily log, and the risk management approach holds procedures and scales, not specific risks; both belong in the project log (manual 4.3.2, ch 9).
n.1: An informal concern can be handled in the daily log, and specific risks go in the risk register; the risk management approach is part of the PID (manual 4.3.2, ch 9).
n.3: The business case summarizes the major risks for justification; individual risks and concerns are recorded in the project log, and the lessons log is for lessons (manual 4.3.2, 5.5).

Business Case.q: Which statement correctly explains the relationship between the PID and the project log?
o: The PID holds the registers and daily log, while the project log holds the management approaches
The PID holds the agreed direction and scope, while the project log holds records that change day to day
The PID is replaced by the project log once the project board has authorized the project
The project log is approved by the project board to authorize the project to begin
Business Case.w: The PID is an aggregation of products that sets the direction and scope and is baselined on authorization; the project log is the dynamic container for the daily log, lessons log and registers, updated throughout (see manual 4.3.1, 4.3.2).

n.0: This reverses them: the management approaches are in the PID, and the registers and daily log are in the project log (manual 4.3.1, 4.3.2).
n.2: The PID is not replaced; it is reviewed and updated at stage boundaries and used again in closing a project (manual 4.3.1, ch 18, ch 19).
n.3: The board authorizes the project by approving the PID; the project log is a working record kept by the project manager and support (manual 14.4.2, 4.3.2).

Business Case.q: What is the purpose of the business case practice?
o: To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable
To define the products to be delivered and the means of delivering them to satisfy the business case
To document the user's requirements of the products and establish the means by which they will be met
To identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect the achievement of the project's objectives
Business Case.w: The business case practice establishes mechanisms to judge whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable and achievable, so that decisions on continued investment can be made (see manual 5.1).

n.1: This is the purpose of the plans practice, which defines the what, who, how, where, when and how much (manual 7.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of the quality practice (manual 8.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of the risk practice (manual 9.1).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The business case practice establishes mechanisms to judge whether a project is desirable, viable and achievable, as a means of supporting decision-making in its continued [?].
o: quality planning
team structure
investment
delivery approach
Business Case.w: The practice supports decision-making about the project's continued investment: whether it is still worth committing money and resources to it (see manual 5.1).

n.0: Quality planning is part of the quality practice; the business case practice supports investment decisions (manual 8.1, 5.1).
n.1: The project's structure of accountability is the concern of the organizing practice (manual 6.1).
n.3: The delivery approach is chosen when selecting the project approach; the business case practice supports investment decisions (manual 13.4.5, 5.1).

Business Case.q: Which three tests does the business case practice use to judge whether a project is, and remains, worth continuing?
o: Whether it is specific, measurable and achievable
Whether it is affordable, deliverable and sustainable
Whether it is desirable, feasible and compliant
Whether it is desirable, viable and achievable
Business Case.w: The business case practice judges whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable and achievable (see manual 5.1).

n.0: This resembles an objective-setting checklist, not the PRINCE2 business case tests of desirable, viable and achievable (manual 5.1).
n.1: Affordability and sustainability are aspects of performance; the business case tests are desirable, viable and achievable (manual 1.4, 5.1).
n.2: Two of these terms are not the PRINCE2 tests; the practice judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q: At each stage boundary, a project board needs a sound basis for deciding whether to keep investing in the project. Which practice provides the mechanisms for that judgement, and why?
o: Quality, because it confirms that the products meet the users' requirements
Business case, because it judges whether the project remains worth the investment
Organizing, because it sets out who is accountable for each decision
Issues, because it assesses whether proposed changes are worth making
Business Case.w: The business case practice exists to establish mechanisms to judge whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable, supporting the board's decisions on continued investment (see manual 5.1).

n.0: The quality practice documents the user's requirements and how they will be met; it does not judge whether the investment is still worthwhile (manual 8.1).
n.2: The organizing practice establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities, the 'who', not whether the investment is worthwhile (manual 6.1).
n.3: The issues practice assesses issues and controls changes to baselines; the judgement on continued investment in the whole project comes from the business case practice (manual 10.1, 5.1).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the business case practice are correct?
1. It guarantees that the project's outcomes will cause no dis-benefits.
2. It provides the means to judge whether the project remains worth investing in as it progresses.
3. It supports decisions on continued investment throughout the project, not just at the start.
4. It defines who is accountable for delivering each of the project's products.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 2 is correct: the practice establishes mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, worthwhile. Statement 3 is correct: the judgement supports decisions on continued investment throughout the project lifecycle (see manual 5.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: dis-benefits are identified and managed in the business case; the practice does not prevent them (manual 5.1).
n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: accountability for products is part of the organizing and plans practices, not the purpose of the business case practice (manual 6.1).
n.3: Statements 1 and 4 are both wrong: dis-benefits are identified and managed, not prevented, and accountability belongs to the organizing practice (manual 5.1, 6.1).

Business Case.q: Why does the business case practice judge whether a project 'remains' desirable, viable and achievable, rather than checking this once before the project starts?
o: Because the business case is replaced by the project plan once the project board authorizes the project
Because costs, risks, benefits and circumstances change, so a project that was justified may stop being so
Because the business layer must reissue the project mandate at the start of every delivery stage
Because the senior user must specify new benefits at the start of every work package
Business Case.w: Justification established at the start can change as costs, timescales, risks and the business environment change, so it is kept under review and the project should be stopped if it is no longer justified (see manual 5.1, 2.1).

n.0: The business case is not replaced; it is maintained and checked at each stage boundary throughout the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: The mandate triggers starting up a project; it is not reissued at each stage. The board reviews justification at stage boundaries (manual 13.3, 5.3.1).
n.3: Benefits are specified for the project, not per work package; work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

Business Case.q: Which statement BEST distinguishes the purpose of the business case practice from that of the plans practice?
o: Business case defines the products to be delivered; plans judges whether those products are still worth producing
Business case controls changes to the baselines; plans compares actual achievements with what was planned
Business case sets the tolerances for each stage; plans sets the tolerances for the whole project
Business case judges whether the project is worth doing; plans defines what will be delivered and how, when and at what cost
Business Case.w: The business case practice establishes whether the project is (and remains) worthwhile, the 'why'. The plans practice defines the products and the means to deliver them (who, how, where, when, how much) to satisfy that business case (see manual 5.1, 7.1).

n.0: This reverses the two purposes: plans defines the products and the means to deliver them, and the business case judges worth (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.1: Controlling changes to baselines is the issues practice and comparing actuals with plans is the progress practice (manual 10.1, 11.1).
n.2: Tolerances are set by management levels (business layer for the project, board for stages), not by these two practices (manual 11.2.1).

Business Case.q: During a delivery stage, the forecast costs of a project rise so much that the expected benefits no longer appear to outweigh the costs and risks. What does the business case practice indicate should happen?
o: The project board should decide whether continued investment is still justified, stopping the project if it is not
The project manager should widen the benefits tolerance so that the business case stays within its limits
The senior supplier should rewrite the business case to reflect the higher supplier costs
The matter should be held until benefits are confirmed in the post-project benefits review
Business Case.w: The business case practice exists to support decisions on continued investment. If the project is no longer justified, the board should consider stopping it; closing a project that has lost its justification is not a failure (see manual 5.1, 2.1, ch 18).

n.1: The project manager does not set benefits tolerance; it is set above the project manager and documented in the benefits management approach (manual 5.2.2, 11.2.1).
n.2: The executive is accountable for the business case and the project manager prepares and maintains it; the senior supplier does not rewrite it (manual tab 5.1, 15.4.5).
n.3: Waiting until after closure defeats the purpose of judging whether the project remains justified; the board decides on continued investment now (manual 5.1, 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: How does PRINCE2 define an output?
o: The result of change, normally affecting real-world behaviour
The measurable improvement that results from an outcome
The tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity
The completed set of products needed to deliver an outcome
Business Case.w: An output is the tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity; in PRINCE2 outputs are the products the project delivers (see manual 5.1).

n.0: This defines an outcome, which arises when outputs are put to use (manual 5.1).
n.1: This defines a benefit (manual 5.1).
n.3: This defines a capability, the completed set of project outputs required to deliver an outcome (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
A [?] is a measurable decline resulting from an outcome that the investing organization perceives as negative, and which detracts from one or more business objectives.
o: risk effect
dis-benefit
off-specification
output
Business Case.w: A dis-benefit is the measurable decline resulting from an outcome perceived as negative by the investing organization, detracting from business objectives. Dis-benefits are identified and managed in the business case (see manual 5.1).

n.0: A risk effect is the impact an uncertain risk event would have on objectives; a dis-benefit is an expected, measurable decline caused by an outcome (manual 9.1, 5.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; it is a type of issue, not a decline caused by an outcome (manual 10.1).
n.3: An output is the deliverable of an activity, not a measurable decline (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q: Which term describes the completed set of project outputs that is required to deliver an outcome?
o: Capability
Benefit
Business objective
Outcome
Business Case.w: A capability is the completed set of project outputs required to deliver an outcome. Outputs combine into capabilities, which lead to outcomes and then benefits (see manual 5.1, fig 5.1).

n.1: A benefit is the measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, not the set of outputs (manual 5.1).
n.2: A business objective is a measurable outcome that shows progress against the organization's strategy (manual 5.1).
n.3: An outcome is the result of change once the capability is used, not the set of outputs itself (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q: A health clinic's project delivers an online appointment booking system. Once it is live, patients book online instead of phoning, and calls to the appointments line fall by 30%. Which of these is the outcome?
o: The online appointment booking system put live
A 30% fall in calls to the appointments line
The clinic's strategy for lower administration costs
Patients booking appointments online instead of phoning
Business Case.w: An outcome is the result of change, normally affecting real-world behaviour: here, patients changing how they book. The system is the output and the measurable fall in calls is the benefit (see manual 5.1).

n.0: The booking system is the output, the deliverable of the project's activities (manual 5.1).
n.1: A measurable improvement resulting from the outcome is a benefit, not the outcome itself (manual 5.1).
n.2: Strategy-related measures are business objectives, to which benefits contribute (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the key concepts of the business case practice are correct?
1. A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome.
2. An outcome is the deliverable produced by an activity.
3. A business objective shows measurable progress in relation to the organization's strategy.
4. A dis-benefit is a threat that has not yet occurred.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 1 is correct: a benefit is the measurable improvement from an outcome, seen as an advantage. Statement 3 is correct: business objectives are the measurable outcomes that demonstrate progress against the organization's strategy (see manual 5.1).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the deliverable of an activity is an output; an outcome is the result of change (manual 5.1).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: a deliverable is an output, and a dis-benefit is a measurable decline from an outcome, not an uncertain threat (manual 5.1, 9.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a dis-benefit is an expected measurable decline caused by an outcome; a threat is an uncertain event (manual 5.1, 9.1).

Business Case.q: Which sequence correctly shows how a project's work contributes to the organization's business objectives?
o: Outcomes, outputs, capabilities, benefits, business objectives
Outputs, benefits, outcomes, capabilities, business objectives
Outputs, capabilities, outcomes, benefits, business objectives
Capabilities, outputs, benefits, outcomes, business objectives
Business Case.w: Projects deliver outputs, which combine into capabilities; using them produces outcomes; outcomes give rise to benefits, which contribute to business objectives (see manual 5.1, fig 5.1).

n.0: Outcomes come after outputs and capabilities: they are the result of using what the project delivers (manual 5.1).
n.1: Benefits result from outcomes, so they cannot come before them, and capabilities come before outcomes (manual 5.1).
n.3: Capabilities are made up of outputs, so outputs come first, and outcomes come before benefits (manual 5.1).

Business Case.q: Why are most of a project's benefits realized after the project has closed?
o: Because benefits cannot be measured until the end project report has been approved
Because the business case is first prepared when the project is being closed
Because the senior supplier is responsible for realizing benefits after closure
Because projects deliver outputs, and benefits come from outcomes once outputs are in use
Business Case.w: A project delivers outputs; outcomes (changes in behaviour) and the benefits they produce mostly follow once the outputs are used in operations, which is why benefits are largely confirmed after closure (see manual 5.1, 5.3.1).

n.0: The end project report reviews project performance; benefits are measured when outcomes occur, and some can be realized during the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.1: The business case is developed before and during initiation (outline then full), not at closure (manual 5.2.1).
n.2: The senior user, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure (manual 6.2.4.2).

Business Case.q: A logistics firm's project automates its warehouse. The firm has measured that, once the new system is in use, its electricity costs will rise by a known amount, which it sees as a negative effect. How should this rise be described?
o: As a threat, as it is an uncertain event that would affect the objectives
As a dis-benefit, as it is a measurable decline from an outcome seen as negative
As an output, as it is a tangible result of installing the new system
As a problem, as it is an issue that has already arisen in the project
Business Case.w: A dis-benefit is a measurable decline resulting from an outcome that the investing organization perceives as negative. It is expected, not uncertain, and is included in the business case alongside the benefits (see manual 5.1).

n.0: The rise is measured and expected once the system is used, so it is not an uncertain event; a threat is a negative risk (manual 9.1, 5.1).
n.2: An output is a deliverable of an activity, such as the system itself; a measurable decline from using it is a dis-benefit (manual 5.1).
n.3: The rise happens once the system is in operational use, not as an event during the project, so it is not a project issue (manual 10.1, 5.1).

Business Case.q: When is the outline business case developed, and what is it developed from?
o: In initiating a project, using the project plan
In the first delivery stage, using the PID
In closing a project, using the end project report
In starting up a project, using the project mandate
Business Case.w: The project mandate triggers starting up a project and is used to develop the initial justification, documented in the outline business case within the project brief (see manual 5.2.1, 5.3.1, 13.4.3).

n.0: Initiation uses the project plan's time and cost figures to turn the outline into the full business case; the outline already exists by then (manual 15.4.5).
n.1: By the first delivery stage the full business case has been approved as part of the PID; the outline version comes much earlier (manual 5.2.1).
n.2: Closing a project updates the business case with actual costs and benefits; it does not develop the outline version (manual ch 19).

Business Case.q: Which process refines the outline business case into the full business case, ready for the project board to approve when it authorizes the project?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
Business Case.w: In initiating a project, the activity 'prepare the full business case' updates the outline business case with time and costs from the project plan and the aggregated risks; the board approves it when authorizing the project (see manual 5.2.1, 15.4.5).

n.1: Starting up a project produces the outline business case; the full version is prepared during initiation (manual 13.4.3, 15.4.5).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary updates an existing business case at the end of each stage; it does not create the full version (manual ch 18).
n.3: Directing a project is where the board approves the business case; the project manager prepares it in initiating a project (manual 14.4.2, 15.4.5).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In the delivery stages, the business case is [?]: updated with progress data and the latest forecasts, and then checked at the end of each stage.
o: developed
outlined
maintained
superseded
Business Case.w: Through the delivery stages the business case is maintained (updated with products delivered, costs, benefits realized and latest forecasts) and checked at each stage end before the next stage is authorized (see manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3, 5.3.1).

n.0: Developing the business case happens pre-project and in initiation, producing the outline and then the full version (manual 5.2.1).
n.1: The outline business case is produced in starting up a project, before the delivery stages (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: The business case is not superseded during delivery; it is the project brief that is superseded by the PID (manual 5.5).

Business Case.q: Where in the business case lifecycle is most of the work of confirming benefits carried out?
o: During initiation, when the project board approves the full business case
After the project has closed, in benefits reviews carried out by the business
At the end of starting up a project, when initiation is authorized
During each work package, when the checkpoint reports are reviewed
Business Case.w: Confirming benefits mostly happens after closure through post-project benefits reviews by the business; some benefits may be confirmed during the project where products are released in stages. Confirmation continues outside the project lifecycle (see manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3, 5.3.1).

n.0: Approving the full business case authorizes the project; no benefits have been realized yet to confirm (manual 14.4.2, 5.3.1).
n.2: At that point the board checks the outline business case to authorize initiation; benefits are confirmed much later (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Checkpoint reports give work package status to the project manager; they are not where benefits are confirmed (manual 11.5, 5.3.1).

Business Case.q:
