Which two statements about the business case through the project lifecycle are correct?
1. The full business case is approved in starting up a project.
2. The project board checks the outline business case before it authorizes initiation.
3. Confirming benefits ends when the project is closed.
4. Developing, maintaining and checking the business case take place within the project lifecycle.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 2 is correct: the outline business case is checked by the board when it authorizes initiation. Statement 4 is correct: develop, maintain and check happen within the project lifecycle, while confirming benefits continues beyond it (see manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3).

n.0: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: the full business case is prepared in initiation, and confirming benefits continues after closure (manual 5.2.1).
n.2: Statement 1 is wrong: starting up a project produces the outline business case; the full version is approved when the project is authorized (manual 5.3.1, 14.4.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: benefits confirmation continues after closure through post-project benefits reviews (manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3).

Business Case.q: A project is nearing the end of its second delivery stage, with a third stage still to come. What should happen to the business case at this point?
o: The project manager prepares the outline business case for the board to approve
The business layer confirms all benefits and closes the benefits management approach
The senior supplier develops a new full business case for approval in initiation
The project manager updates it, and the board checks it before authorizing the next stage
Business Case.w: At the end of each delivery stage the project manager maintains the business case (in managing a stage boundary) and the board checks it for continued justification before authorizing the next stage (see manual 5.2.1, 5.3.1).

n.0: The outline business case is prepared in starting up a project, not at the end of a delivery stage (manual 13.4.3).
n.1: Benefits are mainly confirmed after closure, and the benefits management approach is updated, not closed, at stage boundaries (manual 5.3.1, ch 18).
n.2: Initiation has already happened; the full business case was developed then, with the project manager responsible (manual 15.4.5).

Business Case.q: Why might some of a project's benefits be confirmed before the project closes?
o: Because products may be released in stages and used while the project continues
Because benefits reviews are completed before the end project report is written
Because the full business case is confirmed by the board at the end of initiation
Because the senior user hands over responsibility for benefits when the project closes
Business Case.w: Although most benefits are confirmed after closure, some may be realized and confirmed during the project when products are released iteratively or in phases and put into use (see manual 5.3.1, fig 5.3).

n.1: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after closure; the project plans them but does not complete them (manual 5.3.1, ch 19).
n.2: At the end of initiation the board checks and approves the full business case; that is not confirming realized benefits (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: The senior user remains responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure; nothing is handed over that would bring confirmation forward (manual 6.2.4.2).

Business Case.q: Which pairing of a lifecycle point with the business case work done there is correct?
o: End of initiation: the board checks the outline business case to authorize the first stage
End of each delivery stage: the project manager confirms benefits with the business layer
End of starting up a project: the board checks the outline business case to authorize initiation
After closure: the project board checks the updated business case before closing the project
Business Case.w: The board checks the outline business case at the end of starting up a project when deciding to authorize initiation, then checks the full business case at the end of initiation (see manual 5.3.1, 14.4.1).

n.0: At the end of initiation the board checks the full business case when authorizing the project, not the outline version (manual 5.3.1, 14.4.2).
n.1: At each stage end the project manager maintains the business case and the board checks it; benefits confirmation is mainly post-project (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Checking happens within the project; after closure the business confirms benefits, and the board has already authorized closure (manual 5.2.1, 14.4.5).

Business Case.q: In which management product is the project's benefits tolerance documented?
o: Sustainability management approach
Benefits management approach
Work package description
Risk management approach
Business Case.w: Benefits tolerance, the permissible deviation in benefit targets before escalation, is documented in the benefits management approach (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: The sustainability management approach documents sustainability performance targets and tolerances, not benefits tolerance (manual 5.2.2).
n.2: A work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerance is not agreed there (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The risk management approach sets out how risks will be managed; benefits tolerance sits in the benefits management approach (manual ch 9, 5.2.2).

Business Case.q: Where are the project's sustainability performance targets and tolerances documented?
o: Benefits management approach
Quality management approach
Communication management approach
Sustainability management approach
Business Case.w: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach, which supports the business case and should reference the organization's ESG goals (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: The benefits management approach documents benefits tolerance and benefits reviews, not sustainability targets (manual 5.2.2).
n.1: The quality management approach covers how quality will be achieved; sustainability targets are in the sustainability management approach (manual ch 8, 5.2.2).
n.2: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication with stakeholders (manual ch 3).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The outcomes and benefits of a project need to align with the organization's business objectives, which may include [?] goals set by the organization.
o: environmental, social and governance
planning, estimating and scheduling
supplier, contractor and procurement
stage, work package and checkpoint
Business Case.w: Outcomes and benefits must align with and contribute to business objectives, which may include environmental, social and governance (ESG) goals; sustainability targets should reference those goals (see manual 5.2.2).

n.1: Planning, estimating and scheduling belong to the plans practice; the business objectives referred to here may include ESG goals (manual 7.1, 5.2.2).
n.2: Supplier and procurement arrangements are part of commercial management; the alignment described is with ESG goals (manual ch 6, 5.2.2).
n.3: Stages, work packages and checkpoints are levels of plan, delegation and reporting, not types of business objective (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).

Business Case.q: What is benefits tolerance?
o: The permissible variation of the plan's products allowed before escalation to the next management level
The measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes for each identified risk to the project
The permissible deviation in benefit targets allowed before escalation to the next management level
The agreed limits on sustainability metrics allowed before escalation to the next management level
Business Case.w: Benefits tolerance is the permissible deviation in the benefit performance targets that is allowed before the deviation needs to be escalated to the next level of management; it is documented in the benefits management approach (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: This describes scope tolerance, the permissible variation of the plan's products (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: This describes risk tolerance, set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: This describes sustainability tolerance, documented in the sustainability management approach (manual 5.2.2, 11.2.1).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about aligning the business case to business objectives and tolerances are correct?
1. Benefits tolerance is agreed with team managers in each work package description.
2. ESG goals replace the business objectives recorded in the business case.
3. The project's sustainability performance targets should reference the organization's ESG goals.
4. The sustainability management approach supports the business case.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 3 is correct: sustainability performance targets and tolerances should reference and contribute to the organization's ESG goals. Statement 4 is correct: the sustainability management approach supports the business case (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong: work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances only, and ESG goals may form part of the business objectives rather than replacing them (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits management approach, not in work package descriptions (manual 5.2.2, 11.2.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: business objectives may include ESG goals; ESG goals do not replace them (manual 5.2.2).

Business Case.q: A retail chain has a corporate goal to halve the waste it sends to landfill. It is initiating a project to refit its stores. How should the project reflect this goal?
o: By setting targets and tolerances in the sustainability management approach that reference the goal
By adding the goal to the benefits tolerance agreed in each work package description for the refit
By recording the goal in the daily log as an informal concern for the project board to consider
By making the senior supplier accountable for meeting the retail chain's corporate waste goal
Business Case.w: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances for the project are documented in the sustainability management approach, which supports the business case and should reference and contribute to the organization's ESG goals (see manual 5.2.2).

n.1: Benefits tolerance is not agreed in work package descriptions, and sustainability targets belong in the sustainability management approach (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).
n.2: The daily log is the project manager's informal record; an organizational ESG goal shapes the project's sustainability targets in the approach (manual 4.3.2, 5.2.2).
n.3: Corporate goals sit with the business; the project contributes through its sustainability targets, and the board ensures alignment with ESG commitments (manual 5.2.2, 6.2.4).

Business Case.q: Which level of management sets the project-level tolerances, including the project's benefits tolerance, within which the project board must direct the project?
o: Project board
Business layer
Project manager
Project assurance
Business Case.w: The business layer sets project tolerances across the seven performance targets, including benefits; the board then sets stage tolerances and the project manager sets work package tolerances (see manual 11.2.1, tab 5.1).

n.0: The project board sets stage tolerances within the project tolerances it is given by the business layer (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances for team managers, not project tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Project assurance monitors and advises on behalf of the board; it does not set tolerances (manual 6.2.4, 11.2.1).

Business Case.q: Which role is responsible for ensuring that the project and its management approaches are aligned with the business's environmental, social and governance (ESG) commitments?
o: Team manager
Project support
Project board
Change authority
Business Case.w: The project board's responsibilities include ensuring business strategy is reflected in the business case and that the project and its management approaches align with the business's ESG commitments (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The team manager delivers products within work package tolerances and looks after the team's approach; ESG alignment of the project is a board responsibility (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Project support provides administration and maintains registers; it does not set the project's direction on ESG (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: A change authority approves requests for change within delegated limits; it is not responsible for ESG alignment (manual 6.2.4).

Business Case.q: What are the steps of the PRINCE2 business case management technique, in the correct order?
o: Develop, check, maintain, confirm
Develop, maintain, check, confirm
Identify, assess, plan, implement
Capture, assess, decide, confirm
Business Case.w: The business case management technique has four steps: develop, check, maintain and confirm (see manual 5.3.1).

n.1: The steps are right but the order is not: the business case is checked (for example to authorize initiation) before it is maintained in the delivery stages (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: These are steps of the risk management technique, which also includes communicate (manual ch 9).
n.3: Capture, assess and decide come from the issues technique; the business case technique is develop, check, maintain, confirm (manual ch 10, 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: When developing a business case, which three basic business options should be considered for any investment?
o: Build in-house, buy off the shelf, or contract a third party
Avoid the threat, reduce the threat, or accept the threat
Do the minimum, do more than the minimum, do the maximum
Do nothing differently, do the minimum, do more than the minimum
Business Case.w: The three basic business options are do nothing differently, do the minimum and do more than the minimum; 'do nothing differently' is the baseline for quantifying the others (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: These are choices made when selecting the project approach, not the three basic business options (manual 13.4.5).
n.1: These are risk responses, not business options for an investment (manual ch 9).
n.2: This leaves out the baseline option of doing nothing differently and adds a maximum option that is not one of the three (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: In which step of the business case technique does the project manager, at the end of each stage, update the business case with products delivered, costs, benefits realized and the latest forecasts?
o: The develop step
The maintain step
The confirm step
The check step
Business Case.w: In the maintain step, at the end of each stage the project manager updates the business case with progress data and the latest forecasts of benefits and performance targets (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Develop produces the outline business case in starting up a project and the full business case in initiation (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Confirm assesses whether intended benefits have been, or will be, realized, mostly after closure (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Check is the assessment of whether the business case still shows a justified project; updating it with progress data is the maintain step (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
The [?] step of the business case technique assesses whether the intended benefits have been realized, or will be, and is carried out mostly after the project has closed.
o: check
maintain
confirm
develop
Business Case.w: The confirm step assesses whether intended benefits have been (or will be) realized; much of it happens in post-project benefits reviews carried out by the business (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Check assesses whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable at key decision points within the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.1: Maintain updates the business case at each stage end with progress data and forecasts (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Develop creates the outline and then the full business case before and during initiation (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the business case technique are correct?
1. The 'do nothing differently' option is the baseline used to quantify the other options.
2. The project board checks the business case when assessing an exception plan.
3. The confirm step is completed before the project board authorizes the project.
4. The develop step begins with the end project report.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 1 is correct: 'do nothing differently' is the baseline against which the other options are measured. Statement 2 is correct: the board checks the business case at the end of starting up, the end of initiation, each stage end and when assessing an exception plan (see manual 5.3.1).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: confirming benefits happens mainly after closure, long after the project is authorized (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the develop step starts from the project mandate, which triggers starting up a project (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong: confirm is mainly post-project, and develop starts from the project mandate (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: Why is the 'do nothing differently' option considered first when developing a business case?
o: It is the option the project board is expected to prefer when the budget is tight
It is the option recorded under the expected dis-benefits heading of the business case
It is the option chosen when the project is compulsory under legislation or regulation
It is the baseline against which the costs and benefits of the other options are measured
Business Case.w: 'Do nothing differently' is the starting point: the difference between it and the other options shows what the investment would buy, so it is the baseline for quantifying them (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: No option is preferred by default; the options are compared to find the best overall value (manual 5.2.3, 5.3.1).
n.1: Doing nothing differently is a business option used for comparison, not a dis-benefit (manual 5.1, 5.3.1).
n.2: Compulsory projects still compare options and justify the chosen one; doing nothing differently is the baseline (manual 2.1, 5.2.3).

Business Case.q: Midway through a delivery stage, the organization changes the service targets that the project's outcomes were meant to support. The project manager reviews whether the project is still justified. Which step of the business case technique is this, and why?
o: Maintain, because the business case is updated each time a change in objectives occurs
Confirm, because the benefits expected from the project have now been changed
Check, because justification is reassessed when stakeholders' objectives change
Develop, because a new outline business case is needed when objectives change
Business Case.w: In the check step the project manager assesses the business case when assessing progress, risks and issues and when stakeholders' objectives change, to see whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Maintain is the update at the end of each stage with progress data and forecasts; reassessing justification after a change is checking (manual 5.3.1).
n.1: Confirm assesses whether intended benefits have been or will be realized, mostly after closure (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Develop produces the outline and full business case before and during initiation; this project is already in delivery (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: Which activity forms part of the develop step of the business case technique?
o: Comparing the benefits realized with the forecast benefits in a post-project benefits review
Comparing the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of benefits
Updating the business case with progress data at the end of each delivery stage
Reviewing the business case when the project board is assessing an exception plan
Business Case.w: Developing the business case includes options analysis and investment appraisal, comparing the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of the benefits over a period (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Assessing realized benefits after closure is the confirm step (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Updating with progress data at each stage end is the maintain step (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: The board's review when assessing an exception plan is part of the check step (manual 5.3.1).

Business Case.q: What is the purpose of the project brief?
o: To document the justification for the project based on costs, benefits and risks
To trigger starting up a project on behalf of the commissioning business layer
To provide a full and firm foundation for the initiation of the project
To define the benefits reviews that will confirm the project's benefits are realized
Business Case.w: The project brief provides a full and firm foundation for initiating the project. It is assembled in starting up a project, approved when the board authorizes initiation, and later superseded by the PID (see manual 5.5, 13.4.6).

n.0: This is the purpose of the business case; the outline business case is one part of the project brief (manual 5.5).
n.1: This describes the project mandate, which comes from the business layer before the brief exists (manual 13.3).
n.3: This describes the benefits management approach, created in initiating a project (manual 5.5).

Business Case.q: What is the purpose of the benefits management approach?
o: To define the actions and reviews that ensure outcomes are achieved and confirm benefits are realized
To define the actions, reviews and controls that ensure sustainability performance targets are met
To document the business justification for the project based on its costs, benefits and risks
To report the benefits realized in each stage to the project board in the end stage report
Business Case.w: The benefits management approach defines the benefits management actions and benefits reviews that will be put in place to ensure the project's outcomes are achieved and to confirm that its benefits are realized (see manual 5.5).

n.1: This is the purpose of the sustainability management approach (manual 5.5).
n.2: This is the purpose of the business case (manual 5.5).
n.3: Reporting stage performance is done in the end stage report; the approach defines benefits actions and reviews (manual 11.5, 5.5).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The [?] records the justification for undertaking a project by weighing its estimated costs against the expected benefits, offset by the associated risks.
o: project brief
benefits management approach
project mandate
business case
Business Case.w: The business case documents the business justification for the project, based on estimated costs against expected benefits, offset by associated risks (see manual 5.5).

n.0: The project brief provides a firm foundation for initiation; it contains the outline business case but is not itself the record of justification (manual 5.5).
n.1: The benefits management approach defines benefits actions and reviews; it does not weigh costs against benefits and risks (manual 5.5).
n.2: The project mandate is the trigger from the business layer for starting up a project (manual 13.3).

Business Case.q: Which management product defines the actions, reviews and controls that will be put in place to ensure the project's sustainability performance targets are achieved?
o: Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
Change management approach
Business Case.w: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls to ensure sustainability performance targets are achieved. It is part of the PID and supports the business case (see manual 5.5, 5.2.2).

n.0: The benefits management approach covers benefits actions and reviews, not sustainability performance targets (manual 5.5).
n.2: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with stakeholders, not sustainability targets (manual ch 3).
n.3: The change management approach concerns organizational transition, part of the people element (manual ch 3).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about the management products that support the business case practice are correct?
1. The benefits management approach is first created in starting up a project.
2. The project brief is superseded by the project initiation documentation.
3. The sustainability management approach is approved in closing a project.
4. The costs recorded in the business case include ongoing operations and maintenance costs.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 2 is correct: the project brief is the foundation for initiation and is superseded by the PID. Statement 4 is correct: the costs heading of the business case covers project costs plus ongoing operations and maintenance costs and their funding (see manual 5.5).

n.0: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: the benefits and sustainability management approaches are created in initiating a project and approved when the board authorizes the project (manual 5.5, 14.4.2).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: the benefits management approach is created in initiating a project, not starting up a project (manual 5.5).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the sustainability management approach is created in initiation and approved with the PID, not in closing a project (manual 5.5, 14.4.2).

Business Case.q: Why is the benefits management approach updated during closing a project?
o: To plan the post-project benefits reviews that the business will carry out after closure
To record the results of the benefits reviews that the project team completed after closure
To transfer the benefits tolerance into the end project report for the board's approval
To replace the business case as the record of the project's business justification
Business Case.w: In closing a project, benefits already realized are assessed and the benefits management approach is updated to include the post-project benefits reviews, which the business carries out after closure (see manual 5.5, ch 19).

n.1: The project team does not carry out post-project reviews; the business does, after the project team has disbanded (manual 5.5, ch 19).
n.2: The end project report reviews performance against the baselined PID; benefits tolerance is not transferred into it (manual ch 19).
n.3: The business case remains the record of justification and is updated with actual costs and benefits at closure (manual 5.5, ch 19).

Business Case.q: Under which heading of the business case is the period over which the project will run, and the period over which benefits will be realized, recorded?
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Costs
Time
Business Case.w: The 'time' heading covers both the period over which the project runs and the period over which the benefits will be realized (see manual 5.5).

n.0: The reasons heading explains why the project is needed and how it enables business objectives (manual 5.5).
n.1: Expected benefits are stated in measurable terms against the situation before the project; the periods involved are recorded under time (manual 5.5).
n.2: The costs heading covers project costs and ongoing operations and maintenance costs with their funding (manual 5.5).

Business Case.q: Which is NOT done by the project as part of managing benefits through the benefits management approach?
o: Planning when the post-project benefits reviews will happen
Carrying out the post-project benefits reviews
Defining how and when the benefits will be measured
Updating the approach with results of benefits actions at a stage end
Business Case.w: The project plans post-project benefits reviews but does not carry them out: they take place after closure and are undertaken by the business (see manual 5.5, ch 19).

n.0: The project does this: the approach is updated in closing a project to include the post-project benefits reviews (manual ch 19).
n.2: The project does this: the benefits management approach sets out benefits measurement and timing (manual 5.5).
n.3: The project does this: in managing a stage boundary the approach is updated with the results of benefits actions (manual ch 18).

Business Case.q: Which role is accountable for the business case throughout the project and for securing the funding for the project?
o: Senior user
Project manager
Senior supplier
Executive
Business Case.w: The executive secures funding and owns the business case and continued business justification, as the single point of accountability for the project (see manual 6.2.4, tab 5.1).

n.0: The senior user specifies the benefits and is responsible for showing that forecast benefits are on track, but does not own the business case or secure funding (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.1: The project manager prepares and maintains the business case on the executive's behalf; accountability stays with the executive (manual 15.4.5).
n.2: The senior supplier represents the suppliers and is accountable for the quality of products they deliver, not for the business case (manual 6.2.4).

Business Case.q: Which role is accountable for specifying the benefits and for demonstrating to the business that the forecast benefits are on track to be realized?
o: Executive
Senior user
Project assurance
Project manager
Business Case.w: The senior user specifies the benefits aligned to the business case, demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track and remains committed to realizing them after closure (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive owns the business case and secures funding; specifying benefits and showing they are on track is the senior user's role (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance monitors and advises on behalf of board members; it is not accountable for specifying benefits (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day and maintains the business case, but the benefits are specified by the senior user (manual 6.2.4).

Business Case.q: How does the business case practice support the 'ensure continued business justification' principle?
o: By setting benefits tolerances in each work package so that team managers can escalate
By defining quality specifications for each product so that the outcomes can be measured
By creating and maintaining a business case that shows the project is still worthwhile
By recording lessons from earlier projects in the lessons log for use in later stages
Business Case.w: The business case practice puts this principle into effect by creating and maintaining a business case that assesses whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable and achievable (see manual tab 5.2).

n.0: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerance is in the benefits management approach (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).
n.1: Defining quality specifications in product descriptions belongs to the quality practice (manual ch 8).
n.3: Recording lessons supports the 'learn from experience' principle through the progress practice (manual 4.3.2).

Business Case.q: In the 'prepare the full business case' activity of initiating a project, which role is responsible for preparing the full business case?
o: Project manager
Executive
Project assurance
Senior user
Business Case.w: In 'prepare the full business case' the project manager is responsible, the executive is accountable, project assurance is consulted and the business layer is not involved (see manual 15.4.5 RACI).

n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but the project manager is responsible for preparing it (manual 15.4.5).
n.2: Project assurance is consulted on the full business case, not responsible for preparing it (manual 15.4.5).
n.3: The senior user specifies benefits but is not the role responsible for preparing the full business case (manual 15.4.5, 6.2.4).

Business Case.q:
Which two statements about roles in the business case practice are correct?
1. The executive secures the funding for the project.
2. The senior supplier is responsible for realizing the benefits after closure.
3. The project manager owns the business case on behalf of the business layer.
4. The senior user's commitment to realizing benefits continues after the project closes.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Business Case.w: Statement 1 is correct: the executive secures funding and owns the business case. Statement 4 is correct: the senior user is responsible for the handover and adoption of products and for the continued realization of benefits after closure (see manual 6.2.4, tab 5.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the senior user, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.1: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong: the senior user is responsible for benefits realization, and the executive owns the business case (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: the executive owns the business case; the project manager prepares and maintains it on the executive's behalf (manual 6.2.4, 15.4.5).

Business Case.q: How does the business case practice support the 'manage by stages' principle?
o: The business case sets the tolerances the project manager uses for each work package
Decisions made at each stage boundary include checking that the project is still justified
The business case is prepared again from the project mandate at the start of each stage
The business case defines the products that each delivery stage must produce
Business Case.w: Under 'manage by stages', the decisions taken at stage boundaries are checked for continued business justification, using the updated business case (see manual tab 5.2, 5.3.1).

n.0: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager in work package descriptions; this is not the business case link to manage by stages (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The business case is developed once (outline then full) and then maintained; it is not recreated from the mandate each stage (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Defining products and their delivery is the plans practice, through stage plans and product descriptions (manual 7.1).

Business Case.q: How does the business case practice relate to the 'focus on products' principle?
o: It ensures that the products the project produces can lead to the required outcomes and benefits
It ensures that every product has quality specifications that the senior user approves
It ensures that stage tolerances are set for each product recorded in the product register
It ensures that lessons from earlier business cases are added to each product description
Business Case.w: The link between the business case practice and focus on products is that the products produced can lead to the outcomes and benefits the business case requires (see manual tab 5.2).

n.1: Quality specifications in product descriptions belong to the quality practice, not the business case link to this principle (manual ch 8).
n.2: Stage tolerances are set by the board for the stage, not per product in the product register (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Using lessons from earlier business cases relates to the 'learn from experience' principle (manual 15.4.5).

Business Case.q: A small, low-value internal project combines the project brief and the business case into a single short document. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, as the merged document is a management product
Manage by stages, as the merged document is approved at a stage boundary
Tailor to suit the project, as the products are adapted to the project's scale
Learn from experience, as small projects reuse earlier business cases
Business Case.w: Merging management products to fit a small project's scale is tailoring; the project still has a business justification, now held in a simpler document (see manual tab 5.2, 5.4.5, 2.7).

n.0: Focus on products concerns defining the products the project delivers; merging management documents for scale is tailoring (manual 2.6, 2.7).
n.1: The brief is approved when initiation is authorized; combining it with the business case is a tailoring choice, not a stage decision (manual 2.7, 14.4.1).
n.3: Nothing in the scenario involves reusing earlier lessons; adapting documents to the project's scale is tailoring (manual 2.2, 2.7).

Business Case.q: Which management product sets out the direction and scope of the project and, together with the current stage plan, acts as the 'contract' between the project manager and the project board?
o: Project brief and initiation stage plan
Project initiation documentation
Business case
Project mandate
Business Case.w: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, with the stage plan, forms the agreement between the project manager and the project board. It is assembled in initiating a project and its authorized version is baselined (see manual 4.3.1).

n.0: The project brief and initiation stage plan are approved in authorize initiation so that initiation can start; the brief is then superseded by the PID, which is the agreement used for delivery (manual 5.5, 14.4.1, 4.3.1).
n.2: The business case documents the business justification (costs against benefits and risks); it is one part of the PID rather than the overall agreement on direction and scope (manual 5.5).
n.3: The project mandate is the trigger for starting up a project, provided by the business layer; it is not a PRINCE2-created agreement between the project manager and the board (manual 13.3).

Business Case.q: Which set of records is held in the project log?
o: The daily log, the lessons log, the issue register and the nine management approaches
The business case, the project plan, the risk register and the quality register
The highlight reports, the checkpoint reports, the issue register and the lessons log
The daily log, the lessons log, and the issue, risk, quality and product registers
Business Case.w: The project log is the dynamic record of the project. It holds six records: the daily log, the lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers (see manual 4.3.2).

n.0: The management approaches belong in the PID, not the project log; the project log holds the daily log, lessons log and four registers (manual 4.3.1, 4.3.2).
n.1: The business case and the project plan are baselined products in the PID; only the registers listed belong in the project log (manual 4.3.1, 4.3.2).
n.2: Highlight and checkpoint reports are progress reports, not project log records; the log holds the daily log, lessons log and four registers (manual 4.3.2, 11.5).

Business Case.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The [?] is the dynamic record, kept up to date throughout the project, that holds the daily log, the lessons log and the project's registers.
o: project log
project initiation documentation
project brief
product register
Business Case.w: The project log is the second of the two containers for most management products: a dynamic record holding the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers (see manual 4.3.2).

n.1: The PID is the other container: an aggregation of baselined products (business case, approaches, plan and so on) used to authorize the project, not the dynamic log (manual 4.3.1).
n.2: The project brief is created in starting up a project as the foundation for initiation; it does not hold the logs and registers (manual 5.5).
n.3: The product register is one of the records held inside the project log; it does not contain the daily log or lessons log (manual 4.3.2).

Business Case.q: Which practice has the purpose of collecting and assessing issues and controlling changes to the project's baselines?
o: Progress
Change
Issues
Risk
Business Case.w: The purpose of the issues practice is to collect and assess issues and control changes to the project's baselines; in PRINCE2 7 issue management includes change control (see manual 10.1).

n.0: The progress practice monitors actual achievement against plans, forecasts and controls deviations that cause an exception; it is not the practice that controls changes to baselines (manual 11.1).
n.1: 'Change' was the 6th edition theme. In PRINCE2 7 the practices are business case, organizing, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress, and change control sits in the issues practice (manual 10.1).
n.3: The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives; issues that have already happened belong to the issues practice (manual 9.1).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the organizing practice are correct?

1. It defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities.
2. It sets out the products to be delivered and the dates on which they will be delivered.
3. It includes the business, user and supplier interests in the governance of the project.
4. It provides the mechanisms for judging whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Organizing.w: Statement 1 is the purpose of organizing, and statement 3 is correct because PRINCE2 includes the three principal stakeholder categories (business, user and supplier) in the project's governance and management arrangements (see manual 6.1, 6.2.1).

n.1: Statement 2 describes the plans practice, which defines the products and estimates when they will be delivered (manual 7.1).
n.2: Statement 2 belongs to the plans practice and statement 4 to the business case practice (manual 7.1, 5.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is the purpose of the business case practice, not organizing (manual 5.1).

Organizing.q: Which question is the organizing practice mainly designed to answer for a PRINCE2 project?
o: Why is the project worth the investment in it?
What products will be delivered, and by when?
Who is accountable and responsible for what?
How far may performance deviate before escalation?
Organizing.w: PRINCE2 describes the organizing practice as establishing the 'who': the structure of accountability and responsibilities (see manual 6.1).

n.0: The 'why' of the project is the business justification, addressed by the business case practice (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.1: The 'what' and estimates of 'when' are addressed by the plans practice (manual 7.1).
n.3: Permitted deviation before escalation is set through tolerances under the progress practice and the manage by exception principle (manual 11.2, 2.5).

Organizing.q: Which statement best describes how the organizing practice differs from the plans practice?
o: Organizing defines the products to be delivered, while plans decides who is accountable for producing each one
Organizing sets out who is accountable and responsible, while plans defines the products and the means to deliver them
Organizing replaces the plans practice once the project management team has been appointed in starting up
Organizing records actual progress against each plan, while plans sets the baselines that progress is measured against
Organizing.w: Organizing establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities (the 'who'), whereas plans defines the products (the 'what') and the means of delivering them (see manual 6.1, 7.1).

n.0: This reverses the two practices: defining products is part of plans, and accountability is set by organizing (manual 6.1, 7.1).
n.2: All seven practices apply throughout the project; organizing does not replace plans after appointments are made (manual 4).
n.3: Comparing actual achievement with plans is the progress practice, not organizing (manual 11.1).

Organizing.q: A new project brings together staff from a council, a housing association and a building contractor, each with its own line managers. What should applying the organizing practice achieve for this project?
o: A single line management chain in which every person reports through the contractor's managers
A set of tolerances for each of the seven aspects of performance at every level of plan
A schedule of the work packages showing their sequence, dependencies and durations
An agreed structure in which each person knows what is expected of them and of others
Organizing.w: Organizing gives the project an explicit structure of accountability and responsibilities, so the right people are involved and know what is expected of them and what they can expect from others (see manual 6.1, 2.3).

n.0: Organizing creates a project structure that represents the business, user and supplier interests; it does not move everyone into one organization's line management (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: Setting tolerances for the aspects of performance is part of the progress practice and manage by exception, not the purpose of organizing (manual 11.2).
n.2: A schedule of work packages is produced through the plans practice's planning technique (manual 7.3.1).

Organizing.q: PRINCE2 includes three principal categories of stakeholder in the governance and management arrangements of every project. Which are these three project interests?
o: Business, programme and customer
Business, user and supplier
Directing, managing and delivering
Executive, sponsor and supplier
Organizing.w: The three project interests are business, user and supplier, and all three are represented in the project management team through the project board (see manual 6.2.1, fig 6.1).

n.0: Programme and customer are not PRINCE2 project interests; 'customer' reflects older customer/supplier wording rather than the three v7 interests (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Directing, managing and delivering are three of the four organizational levels, not the stakeholder interests (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role or interest, and the executive is a role that represents the business interest (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: Which role represents, on the project board, the interests of those who will provide the skills, people and resources needed to deliver the project's products?
o: Project executive
Senior user
Team manager
Senior supplier
Organizing.w: The supplier interest covers those with the skills and knowledge to deliver the products, internal or external, and the senior supplier represents it on the project board (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.0: The project executive represents the business interest and is accountable for the business case, not for supplier resources (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior user represents those who will use, operate, maintain or be affected by the products (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: A team manager works at the delivering level and is not a member of the project board (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: Which of the three project interests covers the people who will use, operate or maintain the project's products, or who will be affected by them?
o: User
Business
Supplier
Corporate
Organizing.w: The user interest covers those who will use, operate, maintain or be impacted by the products; they help define the requirements and check they are met (see manual 6.2.1).

n.1: The business interest is about meeting a business need and remaining justified as value for money (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: The supplier interest is about those with the skills and knowledge to deliver the products (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: 'Corporate' comes from the older 'corporate, programme management or the customer' level, now the business layer; it is not one of the three interests (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

On the project board, the [?] represents the business interest, which requires the project to remain justified as value for money throughout its life.
o: senior user
senior supplier
executive
project manager
Organizing.w: The executive represents the business interest and is responsible for the business case and the continued business justification of the project (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.0: The senior user represents the user interest: requirements, benefits and adoption of the products (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior supplier represents the supplier interest: resources, product quality and technical integrity (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager manages the project day to day and is not a member of the project board (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the three project interests are correct?

1. Users can sit inside the business, or outside it, for example members of the public affected by the outputs.
2. Suppliers must come from outside the business that is commissioning the project.
3. The business interest requires the project to be justified as value for money throughout its life.
4. The supplier interest is represented by the executive because suppliers are paid from the project budget.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
Organizing.w: Users may be within the business or outside it as end users or people affected by the outputs (statement 1), and the business interest needs the project to stay justified as value for money for its whole life (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: suppliers may come from within the organization or be external (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both false: suppliers may be internal, and the senior supplier, not the executive, represents them (manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is false: the supplier interest is represented by the senior supplier (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: Why does PRINCE2 require the business, user and supplier interests all to be represented on the project board?
o: So that each interest can set its own project-level tolerances separately from the others
So that decisions balance justification, the users' needs and what the suppliers can deliver
So that the board members can carry out the day-to-day management of the work packages
So that the business layer no longer needs to be involved once the project is initiated
Organizing.w: A project succeeds only if it is justified for the business, meets the users' needs and can be delivered by the suppliers, so all three interests are represented in the project management team and reflected on the board (see manual 6.2.1, 2.3).

n.0: Project-level tolerances are set by the business layer, not separately by each interest on the board (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Day-to-day management is the project manager's job within constraints set by the board; the board directs (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: The business layer stays involved throughout: it sets project tolerances and decides on project-level exceptions (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: A government agency is building an online licensing service. Members of the public will apply for licences through it, and agency staff will process the applications. How does PRINCE2 treat these two groups?
o: The public are external stakeholders rather than users, so the user interest is the agency staff
Both groups belong to the business interest, which the executive represents on the project board
Both groups are part of the user interest, which the senior user represents on the project board
The agency staff are part of the supplier interest, because they will operate the new service
Organizing.w: Users can sit within the business (here, staff who will operate the service) or outside it as end users (here, the public), and the senior user represents the user interest (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 states that users can sit outside the business as end users, so the public are part of the user interest (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: The business interest concerns justification and value for money; people who use or are affected by the products form the user interest (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: Operating the products makes someone a user; suppliers are those with the skills to deliver the products (manual 6.2.1).

Organizing.q: Which statement about the supplier interest in a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: Suppliers may be internal teams or external organizations, and the senior supplier represents them
Suppliers must be external organizations, because internal teams belong to the user interest
Suppliers are represented by the team managers, who sit on the project board for that purpose
Suppliers are accountable for specifying the benefits that the project's products will deliver
Organizing.w: The supplier interest covers people with the skills and knowledge to deliver the products, whether from within the organization or external, and the senior supplier represents it (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.1: Suppliers may come from within the organization; the user interest is about using, operating or being affected by the products (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Team managers work at the delivering level and are not board members; the senior supplier represents suppliers (manual fig 6.2, 6.2.4).
n.3: Specifying benefits is the accountability of the senior user, not the supplier interest (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: How many organizational levels does PRINCE2 describe for a project, and how many of them make up the project management team?
o: Three levels, all of which make up the project management team
Four levels, all of which make up the project management team
Five levels, of which three make up the project management team
Four levels, of which three make up the project management team
Organizing.w: There are four levels: the business layer (commissioning), directing, managing and delivering. The last three form the project management team; the business layer sits outside it (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: There are four levels, not three; the fourth, the business layer, sits outside the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: The business layer is one of the four levels but is not part of the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: PRINCE2 describes four levels, not five (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: Which of the four organizational levels sits outside the project management team?
o: Directing level
Managing level
Business layer
Delivering level
Organizing.w: The business layer commissions the project and sits outside the project management team, which is made up of the directing, managing and delivering levels (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: The directing level is the project board, which is part of the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: The managing level is the project manager, who is part of the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: The delivering level (team managers) is one of the three levels that make up the project management team; only the business layer sits outside it (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: At which organizational level is the project mandate provided and the executive identified?
o: Directing (the project board)
Business layer (commissioning)
Managing (the project manager)
Delivering (the team managers)
Organizing.w: The commissioning party in the business layer provides the project mandate, identifies the executive and defines the project-level tolerances within which the board works (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: The project board directs the project; it does not exist until the executive has been identified by the business layer (manual fig 6.2, 13.4.1).
n.2: The project manager is appointed alongside the executive in starting up a project; the mandate comes from above the project (manual 13.3).
n.3: Team managers deliver products within constraints set by the project manager; they do not commission the project (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The [?] level is responsible for the day-to-day management of the project within the constraints established by the project board.
o: managing
directing
delivering
commissioning
Organizing.w: The managing level is the project manager, who manages the project day to day within the constraints set by the project board (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.1: The directing level is the project board itself, which sets the constraints rather than working within them (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The delivering level manages its own element of the work within constraints set by the project manager, not the whole project (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: The commissioning level (business layer) sets the constraints for the board; it does not manage the project day to day (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes the delivering level in the PRINCE2 organizational structure?
o: It provides the project mandate and sets the tolerances within which the project board works
It directs the project within the constraints that have been set by the commissioning party
It manages and makes decisions on its element of the work within constraints set by the project manager
It manages the whole project day to day within the constraints established by the project board
Organizing.w: Team managers and team members at the delivering level manage and make decisions on their element of the project within the constraints set by the project manager, co-creating with others where needed (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: Providing the mandate and setting project-level tolerances is the business layer (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: Directing within the constraints set by the commissioning party is the directing level, the project board (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Day-to-day management of the whole project is the managing level, the project manager (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: In the four-level structure, which level sets the tolerances for each stage, working within the project-level tolerances it has been given?
o: Directing (project board)
Business layer (commissioning)
Managing (project manager)
Delivering (team managers)
Organizing.w: The project board, at the directing level, sets stage tolerances within the project tolerances defined by the business layer (see manual 6.2.4, 11.2).

n.1: The business layer defines project-level tolerances, not the tolerances for each stage (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances for team managers, not stage tolerances (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team managers set tolerances for their team members, not for stages (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the four organizational levels are correct?

1. The business layer is part of the project management team.
2. The project manager's primary responsibility is managing relationships within the project so that it produces the required products.
3. The project board works within the project tolerances defined by the business layer.
4. Team managers work within constraints set directly by the project board.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
3 and 4
2 and 3
Organizing.w: The project manager's primary responsibility is managing relationships within the project so it delivers products in line with strategic objectives and agreed requirements (statement 2), and the board works within project-level tolerances set by the business layer (statement 3) (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the business layer sits outside the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both false: the business layer is outside the team, and team managers work within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the delivering level works within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: The project manager forecasts that the whole project will exceed its project-level cost tolerance, and the project board agrees. Which organizational level should decide how to proceed?
o: Directing, because the project board is accountable for the success of the project
Business layer, because it defined the project-level tolerances in the first place
Managing, because the project manager runs the project on behalf of the project board
Delivering, because the team managers produce the products that incur the costs
Organizing.w: The business layer defines project-level tolerances and decides on breaches of them; the board escalates a forecast breach of project tolerance to the business layer (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2, 11.2).

n.0: The board is accountable for success but can decide only within the project tolerances it was given; a forecast breach of them goes to the business layer (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The project manager escalates forecast breaches of stage tolerance to the board; decisions on project tolerance are made above the board (manual 11.2).
n.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances and escalate to the project manager; they do not decide on project-level breaches (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: Which statement defines the project board in PRINCE2?
o: Accountable to the business for the project's success, with authority to direct it within the remit the business sets
Responsible for running the project day to day on behalf of the business, within the agreed project tolerances
The full set of roles, including assurance and support, that together hold the authority to direct the project
The commissioning party that provides the mandate and decides on any breach of the project-level tolerances
Organizing.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the success of the project and has the authority to direct it within the remit set by the business (see manual 6.2.1).

n.1: Running the project day to day within tolerances is the project manager's role, on behalf of the board (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: This describes the project management team structure, which PRINCE2 says does not have authority to direct the project (manual 6.2.3).
n.3: Providing the mandate and deciding on breaches of project tolerance is the business layer, which sits above the board (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: Which roles make up the project board in a PRINCE2 project?
o: Executive, project manager and senior supplier(s)
Executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s)
Senior user(s), senior supplier(s) and project assurance
Executive, senior user(s) and team manager(s)
Organizing.w: The project board consists of the executive (one person), the senior user(s) and the senior supplier(s), so that the business, user and supplier interests are all represented (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.0: The project manager works at the managing level and is not a board member; the senior user role is missing (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Project assurance is a board responsibility, not a board role, and the executive is missing (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team managers work at the delivering level, not on the board (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: Which statement about the project management team structure is correct?
o: It holds the authority to direct the project within the remit set by the business layer
It includes the business layer, because the business layer appoints the project executive
It is another name for the board of executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s)
It covers the board, project manager, team managers, and assurance and support roles
Organizing.w: The project management team structure is composed of the project board, project manager, team managers, and the project assurance and project support roles (see manual 6.2.3).

n.0: PRINCE2 states that the project management team structure does not itself have authority to direct the project; the board does (manual 6.2.3, 6.2.1).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project management team, even though it appoints the executive (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The executive, senior users and senior suppliers make up the project board, which is only one part of the wider project management team structure (manual 6.2.3).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The project board is accountable to the [?] for the success of the project and has authority to direct the project within the remit that has been set for it.
o: project manager
senior user
business
project assurance
Organizing.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the success of the project, and directs it within the remit set by the business (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: The project manager is accountable to the project board, not the other way round (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior user is a member of the project board, not the party the board answers to (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Project assurance is carried out on behalf of the board members; the board is not accountable to it (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: Which is a responsibility of the project board?
o: Setting work package tolerances and constraints for the team managers
Setting stage tolerances and establishing the change budget for the project
Providing the project mandate and defining the project-level tolerances
Maintaining the project registers and providing version control of products
Organizing.w: The project board sets stage tolerances to enable management by exception and establishes tolerances and the change budget to support decision-making (see manual 6.2.4, appendix B).

n.0: Setting work package tolerances for team managers is the project manager's responsibility (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Providing the mandate and project-level tolerances is the business layer's responsibility (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Maintaining registers and version control are project support services (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: A team manager says that, because she is a member of the project management team, she can approve a change to the current stage plan. Which statement is correct?
o: She is right, because every role in the project management team shares the board's authority
She is right, because team managers work at the directing level of the project's organization
She is wrong, because changes to a stage plan are approved by the business layer, not the board
She is wrong, because the authority to direct the project rests with the project board
Organizing.w: The project management team structure is a set of roles and does not itself have authority to direct the project; that authority sits with the project board (see manual 6.2.3, 6.2.1).

n.0: Being in the project management team structure gives no authority to direct; PRINCE2 states the structure does not have that authority (manual 6.2.3).
n.1: Team managers work at the delivering level, within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Stage plans are approved by the project board in directing a project; the business layer handles project-level matters (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the project board and the project management team are correct?

1. The project board is made up of the executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s).
2. The project board is accountable to the project manager for directing each stage.
3. The project management team structure includes project assurance and project support roles.
4. The project board manages the work packages day to day on behalf of the team managers.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Organizing.w: The board comprises the executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s) (statement 1), and the project management team structure includes the assurance and support roles as well as the board, project manager and team managers (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.3).

n.1: Statement 2 is false: the board is accountable to the business, and the project manager is accountable to the board (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both false: the board answers to the business, and day-to-day management is done by the project manager and team managers (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the board directs; it does not manage work packages day to day (manual fig 6.2).

Organizing.q: A hospital is replacing its patient booking system as a PRINCE2 project. Which person is outside the project team?
o: The head of outpatients, who is the senior user for the project
The supplier's team manager, who leads the system configuration work
A ward clerk who will use the new system but has no project work
A project support officer who maintains the project's registers
Organizing.w: People in the business who are affected by the project but do not work within it sit outside the project team, although they may later help integrate the new products into their area (see manual 3.3.1, 6.2.3).

n.0: The senior user is a member of the project board and so is inside the project team (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Team managers deliver work packages and are part of the project management team structure (manual 6.2.3).
n.3: Project support is one of the roles in the project management team structure, so this officer works within the project (manual 6.2.3).

Organizing.q: Which role is appointed as the single point of accountability for the project, is ultimately accountable for its success and secures its funding?
o: Senior user
Senior supplier
Executive
Project manager
Organizing.w: The executive is appointed by the business as the single point of accountability, is ultimately accountable for the project's success and secures its funding (see manual 6.2.4.1).

n.0: The senior user represents the users and is accountable for requirements and benefits specification, not overall success and funding (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for supplier product quality and technical integrity (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day on the board's behalf; ultimate accountability stays with the executive (manual 6.2.4.5).

Organizing.q: Which role is accountable for the quality of the products delivered by the suppliers and for the technical integrity of the project?
o: Project executive
Senior user
Team manager
Senior supplier
Organizing.w: The senior supplier represents the supplier community, commits supplier people and resources, and is accountable for the quality of supplier products and the project's technical integrity (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive is accountable for the project's overall success and business case, not specifically for supplier product quality (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.1: The senior user monitors products against the users' requirements, but supplier product quality and technical integrity sit with the senior supplier (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: A team manager delivers products to the agreed specifications but is not accountable for the project's technical integrity (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: An insurer's project is delivering a new customer portal. Someone on the project board must show the business that the forecast benefits are on track and keep the user community committed to realizing them after the project closes. Which role is responsible for this?
o: Senior user
Executive
Senior supplier
Project manager
Organizing.w: The senior user is responsible for specifying the benefits and for demonstrating to the business that forecast benefits are on track; this commitment continues after closure (see manual 6.2.4.2).

n.1: The executive owns the business case and is accountable for the project's success, but specifying and demonstrating benefits is the senior user's responsibility (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.2: The senior supplier is accountable for supplier product quality and technical integrity, not benefits (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day and is not a board role responsible for benefits (manual 6.2.4.5).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

PRINCE2 defines [?] rather than jobs, so one person may hold more than one of them, and some of them may be shared between people.
o: positions
roles
grades
posts
Organizing.w: PRINCE2 assigns roles, not jobs: one person can hold several roles within the rules, and a role can be shared, except the executive and project manager roles (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not define organizational positions; it defines roles that people from any position can fill (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Grades are an employment concept; PRINCE2 roles are independent of seniority grades (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Posts are permanent jobs in the line structure; PRINCE2 defines temporary project roles (manual 6.2.4).

Organizing.q: Which combination of roles is NOT permitted in a PRINCE2 project?
o: Executive and project manager held by one person
Project manager and team manager held by one person
Senior user role shared between two department heads
Project manager and project support held by one person
Organizing.w: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role (see manual 6.2.4.1, 6.2.4.5).

n.1: Depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity, the project manager may also perform the team manager role (manual 6.2.4.5).
n.2: More than one person may represent the users, depending on the scale and complexity of the user community (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.3: The project manager may also perform the project support role (manual 6.2.4.5).

Organizing.q: A regional rail project affects three user departments, and the executive proposes involving the director of each department on the project board. How can PRINCE2 accommodate this?
o: All three directors can share the executive role, each accountable for one department's benefits
All three directors can act as senior users, because more than one person may represent the users
One director becomes senior user and the other two become team managers for their departments
The directors can jointly hold the project manager role, so that each department has daily control
Organizing.w: Depending on the scale and complexity of the user community, more than one person may represent users in the senior user role (see manual 6.2.4.2).

n.0: There can only be one executive; the role cannot be shared (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.2: Team managers deliver work at the delivering level and do not represent users on the board; several people may hold the senior user role instead (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager role should not be shared, so that the project has a single focus for day-to-day management (manual 6.2.4.5).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about PRINCE2 roles are correct?

1. The executive can delegate accountability for the project's success to the project manager.
2. On a small project, the project manager may also perform the team manager role.
3. The senior user is accountable for the approach taken to capture user requirements.
4. The senior supplier is responsible for the business case and continued business justification.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Organizing.w: The project manager may also perform the team manager role depending on scale and capacity (statement 2), and the senior user is accountable for the approach to capturing user requirements (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.4.2, 6.2.4.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the executive's accountability cannot be delegated (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both false: executive accountability cannot be delegated, and the business case belongs to the executive (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the executive, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the business case (manual 6.2.4.1).

Organizing.q: A chief operating officer is described as the 'sponsor' of a new project being run with PRINCE2. How does PRINCE2 treat this sponsor?
o: PRINCE2 adds a sponsor role to the project board, next to the executive and senior user
The sponsor becomes the project manager, because the sponsor owns the outcome of the project
The sponsor takes the senior supplier role, because the sponsor funds the suppliers' work
PRINCE2 has no sponsor role; a sponsor typically becomes, or sits above, the executive
Organizing.w: PRINCE2 has no role called sponsor; a sponsor or senior responsible owner typically becomes the executive or sits above the executive in the business layer (see manual 6.2.4, appendix B).

n.0: The board has three roles only: executive, senior user and senior supplier; PRINCE2 does not add a sponsor role (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: The project manager manages day to day on the board's behalf; a senior sponsor maps to the executive, and the two roles cannot be combined (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.2: The senior supplier represents those delivering the products; securing funding is an executive responsibility (manual 6.2.4.1).

Organizing.q: On a PRINCE2 project, who is accountable for the project assurance of the user interest, even when the assurance work is delegated to someone else?
o: Project manager
Senior user
Project support
Executive
Organizing.w: Each board member is accountable for assurance of their own area: the senior user for the user interest. Delegating the assurance tasks does not transfer that accountability (see manual 6.2.4.7).

n.0: Project assurance cannot be assigned to the project manager, because it monitors the project independently of the project manager (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Project assurance cannot be assigned to project support, which must be kept separate from assurance (manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).
n.3: The executive is accountable for assurance of the business interest, not the user interest (manual 6.2.4.7).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes project support in PRINCE2?
o: Administrative and advisory services that are the project manager's responsibility and can be delegated
Independent monitoring of all aspects of the project's performance on behalf of the project board members
Approval of requests for change and off-specifications within limits and a budget delegated by the board
A business function, independent of the project, that checks the organization's quality system is followed
Organizing.w: Project support provides services such as administration, facilitating meetings and workshops, tool advice and planning support. It is the project manager's responsibility and can be delegated, for example to a project office or team members (see manual 6.2.4.8).

n.1: Independent monitoring on behalf of the board members is project assurance, not project support (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Approving changes within delegated limits and a change budget is the change authority role (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: A business function independent of the project management team that checks the quality system is quality assurance, a quality practice concept (manual 8.2.3).

Organizing.q: Which statement about project assurance in a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: It can be assigned to project support, because support already maintains the project's registers
It is the project manager's responsibility, and the project manager can delegate it to a project office
It can be carried out by board members, by people from the wider business or by an external party
It is another name for quality assurance, which the business manages from outside the project
Organizing.w: Depending on who has the knowledge, skills and capacity, assurance tasks can be done by the board member themselves, by someone appointed from the wider business, or by an external party (see manual 6.2.4.7).

n.0: Project assurance cannot be assigned to project support; the two are kept separate to protect the independence of assurance (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.1: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and cannot be assigned to the project manager; it is project support that the project manager is responsible for (manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).
n.3: Project assurance is a board responsibility within the project, whereas quality assurance is independent of the project management team; they are different (manual 8.2.3, 6.2.4.7).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications, but it may delegate their approval, within agreed limits, to a [?].
o: team manager
project assurance
