project support
change authority
Organizing.w: A change authority is a person or group to whom the project board delegates approval of requests for change and off-specifications, within limits and usually with a change budget (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).

n.0: Team managers implement agreed work within their work packages; PRINCE2 names the change authority (or the project manager) as the delegate for approving changes (manual 10.2.4).
n.1: Project assurance gives the board members independent advice and monitoring; it is not a body that approves changes (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Project support administers the issue and change procedure for the project manager; it does not approve changes (manual 6.2.4.8).

Organizing.q: Which person is NOT permitted to perform a project assurance role on a PRINCE2 project?
o: An external auditor engaged by the project board
A member of staff appointed from the wider business
A senior user checking the user interest personally
The project support officer working on the project
Organizing.w: Project assurance roles cannot be assigned to the project manager, project team members or project support (see manual 6.2.4.7).

n.0: Assurance can be selected from an external party (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.1: Assurance can be appointed from the wider business (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Board members can undertake assurance of their own area themselves (manual 6.2.4.7).

Organizing.q: Why must project support be kept separate from project assurance?
o: Because project support is funded from the change budget, while assurance is funded from the risk budget
Because project support reports to the business layer, while assurance reports to the project manager
Because project support works for the project manager, so combining them would weaken independent assurance
Because project support is an optional role, while assurance has to be carried out by external auditors
Organizing.w: Project support is the project manager's responsibility, whereas assurance monitors the project independently of the project manager on behalf of the board, so keeping them apart maintains that independence (see manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).

n.0: The change and risk budgets fund approved changes and risk responses; they are not why support and assurance are separated (manual 7.3.1, 10.2.5).
n.1: This reverses the lines: support is the project manager's responsibility, and assurance acts for the board members (manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).
n.3: Assurance can be done by board members or people from the wider business as well as external parties; the reason for separation is independence (manual 6.2.4.7).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about project assurance, project support and change authority are correct?

1. When a board member delegates assurance tasks, that board member remains accountable for assurance.
2. Project support is the responsibility of the project board.
3. The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change, but may delegate their approval.
4. A change authority is responsible for implementing approved changes in the work packages.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Organizing.w: Delegating assurance does not move the board member's accountability (statement 1), and the board is the ultimate authority for changes but may delegate approval to a change authority or the project manager (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.4.7, 10.2.4).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: project support is the project manager's responsibility (manual 6.2.4.8).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both false: support belongs to the project manager, and delegation to a change authority concerns approving changes, not implementing them (manual 6.2.4.8, 10.2.4).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: delegated change authority is about approving changes, not carrying them out (manual 10.2.4).

Organizing.q: A water company's project board expects many minor requests for change during the next stage and does not want to meet for each one. Which arrangement is consistent with PRINCE2?
o: Delegate approval of minor changes to a change authority, with defined limits and a change budget
Ask project support to approve minor changes, as support already administers the issue register
Delegate approval of all changes to project assurance, as assurance is independent of the manager
Ask the business layer to approve each request for change so that the board keeps its independence
Organizing.w: The board may delegate approval of requests for change to a change authority (or the project manager) within defined limits, ideally with a change budget, and reviews this at each stage boundary (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).

n.1: Project support provides administration for the project manager; it is not given authority to approve changes (manual 6.2.4.8, 10.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance advises and monitors on behalf of the board members; approving changes is a delegated change authority role (manual 6.2.4.7, 10.2.4).
n.3: The business layer deals with project-level matters such as project tolerances; routine requests for change are handled by the board or its delegated change authority (manual fig 6.2, 10.2.4).

Organizing.q: Which statement defines the work breakdown structure (WBS) in PRINCE2?
o: A hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan, from the major products downwards
A diagram showing the sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them
A chart showing the roles in the project management team and the lines of authority between them
A hierarchy of all the work to be done in a project, linking the product breakdown to the work packages
Organizing.w: The WBS is a hierarchy of all the work to be done during a project, forming the link between the product breakdown structure and the work packages (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: A hierarchy of all the products of a plan is the product breakdown structure, created in the plans practice's planning technique (manual 7.3.1).
n.1: A diagram of product sequence and dependencies is the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: A chart of roles and lines of authority belongs in the project management team structure (manual 6.5).

Organizing.q: In PRINCE2, the work breakdown structure forms a link between which two things?
o: The business case and the benefits management approach
The product breakdown structure and the work packages
The project mandate and the project brief for the project
The risk register and the issue register in the project log
Organizing.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure (what is to be produced) to the work packages (how the work is allocated and delivered) (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: The business case and benefits management approach are linked through the business case practice, not by the WBS (manual 5.5).
n.2: The project brief is built from the mandate in starting up a project; the WBS is not involved (manual 13.4).
n.3: The risk and issue registers are records in the project log; the WBS is a hierarchy of work (manual 4.3.2, 6.2.5).

Organizing.q: How does the work breakdown structure help the project manager when organizing the project?
o: It sets the tolerances that each team manager is allowed when delivering a work package
It shows which board member is accountable for the assurance of each of the project interests
It helps decide how to structure the project teams and the boundaries between those teams
It records the status of every product and the version of it that is currently baselined
Organizing.w: By setting out all the work, the WBS supports the project manager in deciding how to structure project teams and where the boundaries between them should lie (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager in the work package description, not by the WBS (manual 6.2.4.5).
n.1: Each board member is accountable for assurance of their own interest; this is a role rule, not something the WBS shows (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.3: Product status and versions are recorded in the product register in the project log (manual 4.3.2).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The work breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the work to be done during a project, and it forms a link between the product breakdown structure and the [?].
o: work packages
stage plans
team plans
product descriptions
Organizing.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages (see manual 6.2.5).

n.1: Stage plans are one level of plan; the WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages rather than to a plan level (manual 6.2.5).
n.2: Team plans are optional plans produced by team managers; they are not what the WBS links to (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Product descriptions describe each product in the product breakdown structure; the WBS goes further, to the work packages (manual 6.2.5, 7.3.1).

Organizing.q: What is the main difference between the product breakdown structure and the work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS covers management products, while the WBS covers the specialist products
The PBS breaks down the products, while the WBS breaks down the work needed to deliver them
The PBS is produced by the team managers, while the WBS is produced by the business layer
The PBS is created in closing a project, while the WBS is created in starting up a project
Organizing.w: The product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of the products of a plan; the WBS is a hierarchy of all the work needed, linking those products to the work packages (see manual 6.2.5, 7.3.1).

n.0: Both structures relate to the products of the plan; the distinction is products versus the work to deliver them, not management versus specialist products (manual 6.2.5, 7.3.1).
n.2: The business layer commissions the project and sets project tolerances; it does not produce the WBS, which is developed as part of organizing and planning the project's work (manual fig 6.2, 6.2.5).
n.3: Product breakdown structures are created during planning, not in closing; the WBS supports organizing the teams that do the work (manual 7.3.1, 6.2.5).

Organizing.q: A project manager uses the work breakdown structure to agree which elements of the work an external supplier will deliver. In which management product should this delivery model be described?
o: Commercial management approach
Communication management approach
Quality management approach
Benefits management approach
Organizing.w: The commercial management approach includes the delivery model, which identifies which elements of the WBS will be delivered by external suppliers (see manual 6.5, 6.3.2.1).

n.1: The communication management approach sets out how and when the project communicates with stakeholders, not which work suppliers deliver (manual 3.4).
n.2: The quality management approach describes how quality will be managed, not the commercial delivery model (manual 8.5).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed, not which suppliers deliver the work (manual 5.5).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the work breakdown structure are correct?

1. It is a hierarchy of all the products of a plan.
2. It is used by the business layer to set the project-level tolerances.
3. It links the product breakdown structure to the work packages.
4. It helps the project manager decide how to structure teams and the boundaries between them.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Organizing.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages (statement 3) and supports the project manager in structuring teams and their boundaries (statement 4) (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: Statement 1 describes the product breakdown structure, and statement 2 is false: project tolerances are not derived from the WBS (manual 7.3.1, fig 6.2).
n.1: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 1 describes the product breakdown structure, not the WBS (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is correct, but statement 2 is false: the business layer sets project tolerances, and the WBS is a tool for structuring work and teams (manual fig 6.2, 6.2.5).

Organizing.q: A project manager has a product breakdown structure for a new visitor centre and now needs to allocate responsibility for the work to teams. What should the work breakdown structure enable?
o: Approval of each product against its quality specifications before handover to the users
Measurement of the benefits once the visitor centre has opened to members of the public
Grouping of all the required work into work packages that can be allocated to teams
Selection of the executive and senior user who represent the interests on the board
Organizing.w: The WBS sets out all the work needed to deliver the products and links it to work packages, so that responsibility can be allocated to teams with clear boundaries (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: Checking products against quality specifications is quality control under the quality practice (manual 8.2).
n.1: Measuring benefits after the project is covered by the benefits management approach in the business case practice (manual 5.5).
n.3: The executive is appointed by the business layer and the rest of the board by the executive in starting up; the WBS is not used for this (manual 13.4.1, 13.4.4).

Organizing.q: What is the first step of the PRINCE2 organizational design and development technique?
o: Understand the organizational ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
Organizing.w: The technique starts by understanding the organizational ecosystem: the existing structures, governance, decision rights, people management and policies of the organizations involved (see manual 6.3.1.1, fig 6.5).

n.1: Designing the project ecosystem is the second step, and it depends on first understanding the organizational ecosystem (manual 6.3.1.2).
n.2: Developing the project ecosystem is the third step, carried out as needs and team members change (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.3: Transitioning the project into the organizational ecosystem is the fifth and final step, at closure (manual fig 6.5).

Organizing.q: During which step of the organizational design and development technique would new team members be onboarded, for example through a site visit, an induction or a certification?
o: Design the project ecosystem
Understand the organizational ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Organizing.w: Developing the project ecosystem is ongoing work in response to changing needs, team members and relationships, and includes onboarding people through site visits, inductions or certification (see manual 6.3.1.3).

n.0: Designing the project ecosystem decides how to organize work and people: the people and resources needed, integrated working practices, behaviours and culture (manual 6.3.1.2).
n.1: Understanding the organizational ecosystem examines the existing structures and governance of the organizations involved (manual 6.3.1.1).
n.3: Managing ongoing changes concerns changing capabilities over the lifecycle, moving people on and off the project and a robust change management procedure (manual 6.3.1.4).

Organizing.q: Which step of the organizational design and development technique involves determining the people and resources needed and implementing integrated working practices?
o: Develop the project ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
Understand the organizational ecosystem
Transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
Organizing.w: Designing the project ecosystem concerns how to organize work and people: determining people and resources, implementing integrated working practices and developing project behaviours and culture, shaped by the WBS and the commercial management approach (see manual 6.3.1.2).

n.0: Developing the project ecosystem is the ongoing development that follows the design, such as onboarding and skills assessment (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.2: Understanding the organizational ecosystem looks at the existing organizations before any project design is done (manual 6.3.1.1).
n.3: Transitioning the project hands products, people and learning back to the business at closure (manual fig 6.5).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The final step of the organizational design and development technique is to [?] the project into the organizational ecosystem.
o: reintegrate
close
embed
transition
Organizing.w: The fifth step is to transition the project into the organizational ecosystem, handing products, people and learning back to the business (see manual 6.3.1, fig 6.5).

n.0: The step is named 'transition', which covers handing products, people and learning back; 'reintegrate' is not the technique's term (manual fig 6.5).
n.1: Closing the project is a process (closing a project); the technique step is named 'transition the project into the organizational ecosystem' (manual fig 6.5).
n.2: 'Embed' is not the name of the technique step; PRINCE2 calls it transitioning the project into the organizational ecosystem (manual fig 6.5).

Organizing.q: Why does the organizational design and development technique begin by understanding the organizational ecosystem?
o: Because the project's products need business approval before any design work on them starts
Because the business layer has to agree the stage tolerances before the board can be appointed
Because projects bring together people from organizations with their own structures and governance
Because the project ecosystem replaces the organizational ecosystem for the life of the project
Organizing.w: Projects unite people from organizations that already have structures and governance requirements, so these must be understood before the project organization can be designed as a distinct entity (see manual 6.3.1.1).

n.0: Product approval is part of quality and change control, not the reason the technique starts with the organizational ecosystem (manual 8.2, 6.3.1.1).
n.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board, not the business layer, and are unrelated to this step (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project ecosystem is a temporary entity that exists alongside the organizational ecosystem and is transitioned back into it at closure; it does not replace it (manual 6.3.1.1, fig 6.5).

Organizing.q: Midway through a project, the capabilities required change: some specialists must join the project and others must leave it, and the commercial arrangements must support this. Which step of the organizational design and development technique addresses this?
o: Step 2: design the project ecosystem
Step 3: develop the project ecosystem
Step 5: transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
Step 4: manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Organizing.w: Managing ongoing changes to the project ecosystem recognizes that required capabilities change over the lifecycle: the commercial management approach must support this and people are transitioned onto and off the project (see manual 6.3.1.4).

n.0: Designing the project ecosystem sets up the initial organization of work and people; it is not the step for capability changes during the lifecycle (manual 6.3.1.2).
n.1: Developing the project ecosystem covers activities such as onboarding and skills assessment, while changing capabilities and moving people on and off is the next step (manual 6.3.1.3, 6.3.1.4).
n.2: Transition hands the project's products, people and learning back to the business at closure, not midway through (manual fig 6.5).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements about the organizational design and development technique are correct?

1. The design step is shaped by the work breakdown structure and the commercial management approach.
2. The transition step hands products, people and learning back to the business at closure.
3. The technique has four steps, ending with developing the project ecosystem.
4. The develop step is carried out once, in starting up a project, and is not repeated.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Organizing.w: The design step is shaped by the WBS and the commercial management approach (statement 1), and the final step transitions products, people and learning back into the organizational ecosystem (statement 2) (see manual 6.3.1, fig 6.5).

n.1: Statement 3 is false: the technique has five steps and ends with transitioning the project into the organizational ecosystem (manual fig 6.5).
n.2: Statement 4 is false: developing the project ecosystem is ongoing as needs, team members and relationships change (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.3: Both are false: there are five steps, and the develop step continues throughout the project (manual fig 6.5, 6.3.1.3).

Organizing.q: A project manager sets up a robust change management procedure so that the effect of decisions on different parts of the project ecosystem is considered before they are made. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is being applied?
o: Step 3: develop the project ecosystem
Step 4: manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Step 5: transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
Step 1: understand the organizational ecosystem
Organizing.w: In managing ongoing changes to the project ecosystem, the project manager ensures a robust change management procedure so that impacts on different areas of the project ecosystem are considered in decision-making (see manual 6.3.1.4).

n.0: Developing the project ecosystem covers onboarding, skills assessment and similar development activities, not the change management procedure (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.2: Transition takes place at closure, when products, people and learning return to the business (manual fig 6.5).
n.3: Understanding the organizational ecosystem examines existing structures and governance before the project is designed (manual 6.3.1.1).

Organizing.q: A project's environmental manager is to be held accountable for meeting the project's carbon-reduction target. In which management product should this accountability be recorded?
o: Project management team structure
Product description
Role descriptions
Benefits management approach
Organizing.w: Role descriptions set out the roles in the project management team and their specific responsibilities, and should include accountability for sustainability targets (see manual 6.5).

n.0: The project management team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and how they will work together, not each role's specific accountabilities (manual 6.5).
n.1: A product description sets out a product's purpose, composition, derivation and quality specifications, not a person's accountabilities (manual 8.5).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed; individual role accountabilities belong in role descriptions (manual 5.5, 6.5).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the commercial management approach?
o: To describe how the project will communicate with its stakeholders, including its suppliers
To set out who is in the project management team and how its members will work together
To describe how the benefits will be measured and reviewed, including after the project closes
To describe how commercial agreements will be secured, serviced and maintained for the project
Organizing.w: The commercial management approach sets out the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities for securing, servicing and maintaining the project's commercial agreements, covering market engagement, procurement and contract management (see manual 6.5).

n.0: How the project communicates with stakeholders is set out in the communication management approach (manual 3.4).
n.1: Who is involved and how they will work together is the project management team structure (manual 6.5).
n.2: Measuring and reviewing benefits is covered by the benefits management approach (manual 5.5).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes a 'thin client' delivery model in the commercial management approach?
o: Most of the work, including much of the project management, is carried out by suppliers
Most of the work is carried out by the business, with suppliers giving specialist input
The work is split evenly between the business and one external supplier under a joint contract
The supplier's director takes the executive role so that the supplier owns the business case
Organizing.w: Delivery models range from thin client, where suppliers do most of the work including much of the project management, to thick client, where the business does most of the work (see manual 6.3.2.1, 6.5).

n.1: Most of the work being done by the business describes a thick client model (manual 6.3.2.1).
n.2: Thin and thick client describe how much work suppliers do rather than the business; an even split is not the definition of thin client (manual 6.3.2.1).
n.3: The executive represents the business interest and owns the business case; the delivery model does not change who holds that role (manual 6.2.4.1).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The organizing practice supports the '[?]' principle by adapting the project management team structure, role descriptions and the commercial, communication and change management approaches at stage boundaries.
o: learn from experience
manage by stages
tailor to suit the project
manage by exception
Organizing.w: Adapting the team structure, role descriptions and the commercial, communication and change management approaches at each stage boundary is how organizing supports manage by stages (see manual 6.7, tab 6.5).

n.0: Organizing supports learn from experience by using lessons to inform the team structure, the WBS and a healthy project ecosystem (manual tab 6.5).
n.2: Organizing supports tailoring by creating a team suited to the project's needs and the capability of the people and organizations involved (manual tab 6.5).
n.3: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and escalation; the stage boundary review of the organizing products supports manage by stages (manual 2.5, tab 6.5).

Organizing.q: How does the organizing practice support the 'learn from experience' principle?
o: By adapting the role descriptions and the management approaches at each stage boundary
By creating a project management team suited to the capability of the people involved
By developing an explicit team structure so that everyone knows their responsibilities
By using lessons to inform the team structure, the WBS and a healthy project ecosystem
Organizing.w: Organizing applies learn from experience by using lessons to shape the project management team structure, the work breakdown structure and a healthy project ecosystem, so the right people are in the right roles at the right time (see manual 6.7, tab 6.5).

n.0: Adapting role descriptions and approaches at stage boundaries is how organizing supports manage by stages (manual tab 6.5).
n.1: A team suited to the project's needs and people's capability is how organizing supports tailor to suit the project (manual tab 6.5).
n.2: An explicit team structure that makes responsibilities clear is how organizing supports define roles, responsibilities and relationships (manual tab 6.5).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes the project management team structure as a management product?
o: It lists each role's specific responsibilities, including accountability for sustainability targets
It shows who is involved in the project, their relationships and how they will work together
It sets out how market engagement, procurement and contract management will be carried out
It records lessons from earlier projects about how their project teams were organized
Organizing.w: The project management team structure, part of the PID, shows who is involved in the project, their relationships and how they will work together (see manual 6.5).

n.0: Each role's specific responsibilities, including sustainability accountability, are recorded in role descriptions (manual 6.5).
n.2: Market engagement, procurement and contract management are covered by the commercial management approach (manual 6.5).
n.3: Lessons from earlier projects are recorded in the lessons log and lessons reports, not the team structure (manual 4.3.2).

Organizing.q:
Which two statements correctly describe how the organizing practice supports the principles?

1. Tailor to suit the project: the team is designed to fit the project's needs and the capability of the people and organizations involved.
2. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships: roles are agreed informally within each team as the work develops.
3. Manage by stages: the team structure and role descriptions are reviewed and adapted at stage boundaries.
4. Learn from experience: lessons about the team are recorded in the commercial management approach.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Organizing.w: Organizing supports tailoring by building a team that fits the project's needs and capabilities (statement 1), and manage by stages by adapting the team structure and role descriptions at stage boundaries (statement 3) (see manual 6.7, tab 6.5).

n.0: Statement 2 is false: organizing supports this principle with an explicit team structure so everyone knows their responsibilities and relationships (manual tab 6.5).
n.1: Both are false: roles are defined explicitly, and lessons are recorded in the lessons log and used to inform the team structure and WBS (manual tab 6.5, 4.3.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: lessons go in the lessons log and inform the team structure, the WBS and the project ecosystem (manual tab 6.5).

Organizing.q: A council is deciding how much of a new leisure centre project, including some of its management, will be carried out by an external contractor rather than by its own staff. Under which heading of the commercial management approach should this be described?
o: Delivery model
Responsibilities
Resources
Communication procedures
Organizing.w: The delivery model heading describes which elements of the work external suppliers will deliver, on a range from thin client (suppliers do most of the work) to thick client (the business does most of it) (see manual 6.5, 6.3.2.1).

n.1: The responsibilities heading records who is responsible for market engagement, procurement and contract management, not how the work is split (manual 6.5).
n.2: The resources heading covers the resources needed for the commercial activities, not which work suppliers deliver (manual 6.5).
n.3: Communication procedures belong in the communication management approach, which is not a heading of the commercial management approach (manual 3.4).

Organizing.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the organizing practice in PRINCE2?
o: To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable
To facilitate communication and control by defining the products to be delivered and the means to deliver them
To define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities
To establish mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements against those that were planned
Organizing.w: The organizing practice exists to define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, often summarized as the 'who' of the project (see manual 6.1).

n.0: Judging whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable is the purpose of the business case practice (manual 5.1).
n.1: Defining the products and the means to deliver them, to aid communication and control, is the purpose of the plans practice (manual 7.1).
n.3: Monitoring and comparing actual achievements against those planned is part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).

Organizing.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The organizing practice defines and establishes the project's structure of [?] and responsibilities, which PRINCE2 describes as the 'who' of the project.
o: accountability
communication
deliverables
tolerances
Organizing.w: The purpose of the organizing practice is to define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (see manual 6.1).

n.1: Communication with stakeholders is planned through the communication management approach in the people element; it is not the structure the organizing practice establishes (manual 3.4, 6.1).
n.2: Deliverables (products) are the 'what' of the project, defined through the plans and quality practices, not the 'who' (manual 7.1).
n.3: Tolerances are the permitted deviations set at each level of management under the progress practice, not what the organizing practice structures (manual 11.2).

Organizing.q: Which practice establishes who is accountable for the project, who has the authority to direct it and who is responsible for each area of its management?
o: Plans
Progress
Business case
Organizing
Organizing.w: Organizing is the practice that sets out the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, including the project board's authority to direct and the project manager's day-to-day responsibility (see manual 6.1, 6.2).

n.0: Plans defines the products and the means to deliver them (what, how, where, when, how much); it does not establish the accountability structure itself (manual 7.1).
n.1: Progress establishes mechanisms to monitor actual against planned performance and to control deviations, not the structure of accountability (manual 11.1).
n.2: Business case establishes mechanisms to judge whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable; it does not define who is accountable for what (manual 5.1).

Organizing.q: Why does a PRINCE2 project need its own structure of accountability and responsibilities instead of relying on the existing line management structure?
o: Because line management structures are designed for stage-by-stage control, which projects do not normally use
Because project work often spans functions, organizations and locations that normal line structures do not cover
Because every one of the project's products must be fully defined before any people can be assigned to the work
Because a separate structure allows the project board to set the project-level tolerances for the project itself
Organizing.w: Day-to-day line structures are often unsuited to projects, which are cross-functional, may involve several organizations, mix part-time and full-time staff and work across locations, so organizing sets up a temporary structure of accountability (see manual 2.3, 6.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 projects are managed by stages, so stage-by-stage control is a feature of projects, not a reason to reject line structures (manual 2.4).
n.2: Focusing on products does not require every product to be defined before people are assigned; the need for a project structure comes from the cross-functional nature of project work (manual 2.6, 2.3).
n.3: Project-level tolerances are set by the business layer, not the project board, so this is not why the project needs its own structure (manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about what a plan defines are correct?
1. It defines who will deliver the products and how and where they will be delivered.
2. It states why the project is worth undertaking, so a separate business case is not needed.
3. It includes estimates of when the products will be delivered and how much they will cost.
4. It is the product used to judge whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: a plan defines the products and the means of delivering them (who, how and where) with estimates of when and how much (see manual 7.1).

n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: that judgement is made using the business case (manual 5.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: the why is held in the business case, which the plan must satisfy (manual 7.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.
n.3: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong. Statement 2 is wrong: the why is held in the business case, which the plan must satisfy (manual 7.1). Statement 4 is wrong: that judgement is made using the business case (manual 5.1).

Plans.q: How does the plans practice support the control of a project through the progress practice?
o: Plans record the actual cost and completion date of each product as it is handed over
Approved plans are the baseline that actual progress is compared with
Plans set the business's risk appetite that the board uses to judge progress
Plans hold the lessons log entries that are reviewed when each stage ends
Plans.w: Plans facilitate control: once approved, a plan is the baseline that the progress practice compares actual achievement with, so that deviations can be controlled (see manual 7.1, 11.1).

n.0: Actual progress is captured in progress reports and the product register, not in the plan itself (manual 11.5, 4.3.2).
n.2: Risk appetite is set by the business, not by a plan (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: The lessons log is part of the project log, not a plan (manual 4.3.2).

Plans.q: A project manager drafts a plan that lists target dates, costs and team members but does not identify any of the products to be delivered. Which part of the purpose of the plans practice has been missed?
o: Defining why the project is justified
Defining who directs the project
Defining what is to be delivered
Defining how quality is assured
Plans.w: The plans practice defines the products to be delivered (the what) as well as the means of delivering them. A plan with dates, costs and people but no products has missed the what (see manual 7.1).

n.0: The why is held in the business case, not the plan, so it is not a gap in this plan (manual 7.1, 5.1).
n.1: Who directs the project is set by the organizing practice; the plan already names team members (manual 6.1).
n.3: Quality assurance is part of the quality practice and is independent of the project management team; it is not the missing part of the plan's purpose (manual 8.2).

Plans.q: Why does a plan include estimates of time and cost as well as describing the products to be delivered?
o: So that the plan can take the place of the business case once the project is authorized
So that benefits tolerances can be passed to team managers in work package descriptions
So that the project board can set the risk appetite of the business for the project
So the means of delivery can be checked against the business case that it must satisfy
Plans.w: A plan defines the products and the means of delivering them, including estimates of when and how much, so that the business case is satisfied. The estimates let the board check the plan against the business case (see manual 7.1, 7.7).

n.0: The business case remains the record of the why and is maintained throughout; a plan satisfies it but does not replace it (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.1: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Risk appetite is set by the business, not derived from a plan's estimates (manual 9.2.1).

Plans.q: Which list gives the four types of plan used in PRINCE2?
o: Project plan, stage plan, work package plan and exception plan
Project plan, stage plan, team plan and exception plan
Project plan, initiation plan, delivery plan and closure plan
Business plan, project plan, stage plan and team plan
Plans.w: PRINCE2 uses four types of plan: the project plan, stage plans, team plans and exception plans (see manual 7.1.1).

n.0: There is no 'work package plan'; work is passed to teams in a work package description, and a team manager may produce a team plan (manual 7.1.1, 7.5).
n.2: These are not PRINCE2 plan types; initiation and delivery stages each have a stage plan, and closure is planned in the final stage plan (manual 7.1.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.3: A business plan belongs to the business, not the project, and this list leaves out the exception plan (manual 7.1.1).

Plans.q: Which type of plan is a high-level plan showing the major products of the project and when, how and at what cost they will be delivered?
o: Stage plan
Team plan
Project plan
Exception plan
Plans.w: The project plan is the high-level plan for the whole project, showing its major products and when, how and at what cost they will be delivered (see manual 7.2.2.1).

n.0: A stage plan is the detailed plan used as the basis for project management control throughout one stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.1: A team plan is an optional plan made by a team manager to organize and control a team's work on one or more work packages (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: An exception plan follows an exception report and replaces the stage or project plan it covers (manual 7.2.2.4).

Plans.q: Which statement about team plans is correct?
o: They are required for every work package and are approved in directing a project
They are produced by the project manager to control each management stage
They are replaced by an exception plan when work package tolerances are exceeded
They are optional and are produced by a team manager for one or more work packages
Plans.w: A team plan is produced by a team manager to organize and control the work of a team on one or more work packages. Team plans are optional in PRINCE2 (see manual 7.2.2.3).

n.0: Team plans are optional, and the project board does not direct work at team level (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.1: The project manager controls a stage using the stage plan; team plans are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.2, 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Exception plans replace stage or project plans, not team plans; work package deviations are handled by the project manager (manual 7.2.2.4).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
When the project board decides to address an exception, the [?] is prepared and, once approved, replaces the plan it covers from the current position to the end of that stage or project.
o: exception plan
next stage plan
team plan
project plan
Plans.w: An exception plan follows an exception report. If the board decides to address the exception, it is prepared and, once approved, replaces the stage or project plan from the current position (see manual 7.2.2.4).

n.1: A next stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage for the following stage; it does not replace a plan after an exception (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: A team plan covers a team's work on work packages and is never used to replace a stage or project plan (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: The project plan is updated at stage boundaries; the plan prepared in response to an exception is the exception plan (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.4).

Plans.q: In which process is the stage plan for the initiation stage created?
o: Initiating a project, alongside the project plan
Starting up a project, by the project manager
Managing a stage boundary, at the end of the first stage
Directing a project, by the project board
Plans.w: The initiation stage plan is created in starting up a project ('plan the initiation stage'). Every later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, in managing a stage boundary (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Initiation cannot start until its stage plan is approved, so that plan is made earlier, in starting up a project; the project plan is the one created in initiation (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary prepares the plan for the next stage; the initiation stage plan exists before initiation begins (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.3: The board approves the initiation stage plan when it authorizes initiation; the project manager creates it in starting up a project (manual 7.2.2.2, 14.4.1).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about when PRINCE2 plans are produced are correct?
1. The project plan is created in initiating a project and baselined when the project board approves it.
2. An exception plan is prepared in controlling a stage as soon as an exception report is sent.
3. Team plans are prepared for every work package and are approved by the executive.
4. Each stage plan after initiation is prepared near the end of the stage before it.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 4 are correct. The project plan is created in initiating a project and baselined on approval by the board; each later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when its work happens (see manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the exception report is raised in controlling a stage, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary if the board decides to address the exception (manual 7.2.2.4). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: team plans are optional and are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.3). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.3: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong. Statement 2 is wrong: the exception report is raised in controlling a stage, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary if the board decides to address the exception (manual 7.2.2.4). Statement 3 is wrong: team plans are optional and are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.3).

Plans.q: A project has an initiation stage followed by three delivery stages, and no exceptions occur. How many stage plans will the project manager prepare in managing a stage boundary?
o: Four stage plans
Two stage plans
One stage plan
Three stage plans
Plans.w: The initiation stage plan is made in starting up a project. Each of the three delivery stages has its stage plan prepared near the end of the stage before it, in managing a stage boundary, giving three (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Four counts the initiation stage plan, which is made in starting up a project, not in managing a stage boundary (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.1: Two misses the plan for the first delivery stage, which is prepared at the end of the initiation stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: One would apply to a project with a single delivery stage; here each of the three delivery stages needs a stage plan (manual 7.2.2.2).

Plans.q: Where are the activities for closing the project planned?
o: In the stage plan for the final stage
In a separate closure stage plan approved at the last stage boundary
In a team plan produced by project support
In an exception plan prepared at the end of the final stage
Plans.w: Closing a project is not a separate stage. Its activities are planned in, and carried out within, the final stage, so they appear in the final stage plan (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.1: There is no closure stage; closing a project happens within the final stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: Team plans are produced by team managers for work packages, and closure is planned by the project manager (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Exception plans respond to exceptions; they are not how planned closure is arranged (manual 7.2.2.4).

Plans.q: In the plans practice, what is meant by the planning horizon?
o: The total duration of the project from its mandate to closure
The point at which the project board next reviews the business case
The period ahead for which it is possible to plan accurately
The latest date by which the project plan must be approved
Plans.w: The planning horizon is the period for which accurate planning is possible: only the near future can be planned in detail, so detail falls away further ahead (see manual 7.2.1).

n.0: The planning horizon is usually much shorter than the whole project; that is why the project plan is high level and detail is added stage by stage (manual 7.2.1).
n.1: That describes a decision point such as a stage end, not the planning horizon (manual 7.2.3).
n.3: This is not a PRINCE2 concept; the planning horizon concerns how far ahead detailed planning is possible (manual 7.2.1).

Plans.q: Why does PRINCE2 combine a high-level project plan with a detailed stage plan for the current stage?
o: Because the project plan is fixed at initiation and cannot be updated during the project
Because the board approves stage plans while the business layer approves the project plan
Because team managers prepare the stage plans and the project manager prepares the project plan
Because only the near future can be planned in detail, so detail is added one stage at a time
Plans.w: The planning horizon limits how far ahead detailed planning is possible. PRINCE2 therefore uses a high-level project plan for the whole project and a detailed stage plan for the current stage (see manual 7.2.1, 7.2.2).

n.0: The project plan is updated at each stage boundary and at closure, so it is not fixed (manual 7.2.2.1).
n.1: The project board approves the project plan when it authorizes the project; the reason for two levels is the planning horizon (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.1).
n.2: The project manager prepares both the project plan and stage plans; team managers prepare team plans and work package schedules (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q: What is the minimum number of management stages in a PRINCE2 project, and what are they?
o: Two: an initiation stage and at least one delivery stage
One: a single delivery stage that includes initiation
Three: initiation, delivery and a closure stage
Two: a starting up stage and a delivery stage
Plans.w: A PRINCE2 project has at least two management stages: the initiation stage and one or more delivery stages. A simple project may need only initiation plus a single delivery stage (see manual 7.2.3).

n.1: Initiation is always a separate management stage, so a project cannot have fewer than two stages (manual 7.2.3).
n.2: Closing a project is not a stage; it takes place within the final delivery stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.3: Starting up a project happens before the project begins and is not a management stage; the first stage is initiation (manual 7.2.3).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
When deciding the number and length of management stages, the project manager considers the planning horizon, where key decisions are needed, the level of [?] and the complexity of the project.
o: lessons
risk
tolerance
reporting
Plans.w: The number and length of stages depend on the planning horizon, the decision points needed, the level of risk and the complexity of the project (see manual 7.2.3).

n.0: Lessons help improve estimates, but the level of risk is the factor listed for deciding the number and length of stages (manual 7.2.3, 7.7).
n.2: Tolerances are set for each stage once the stages are defined; the factor listed here is risk (manual 7.2.3, 7.2.4).
n.3: Reporting frequency is agreed for highlight and checkpoint reports; it is not one of the factors for setting stages (manual 7.2.3, 11.2).

Plans.q: How might the project plan for an iterative-incremental project arrange its delivery stages?
o: As a single delivery stage, because acceptance criteria cannot change once initiation is complete
As delivery stages with no initiation stage, because the product backlog replaces the project initiation documentation
As several delivery stages in which quality and acceptance criteria are refined alongside the products using a product backlog
As one management stage per iteration, each authorized by a team manager instead of the board
Plans.w: For an iterative-incremental project, the project plan may provide several delivery stages, with quality and acceptance criteria refined in parallel with developing the products through a product backlog (see manual 7.2.3).

n.0: Iterative-incremental projects refine acceptance criteria during delivery, and they may use several delivery stages (manual 7.2.3).
n.1: Every PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage that produces the project initiation documentation (manual 7.2.3, 4.3.1).
n.3: Management stages are authorized by the project board in directing a project, not by team managers (manual 7.2.3).

Plans.q: How does the planning horizon affect when each stage plan after initiation is prepared?
o: All of them are prepared in initiation so that the board can approve them together
Each is prepared by a team manager once the first work package in that stage has started
Each is prepared during closure to record what that stage actually delivered
Each is prepared near the end of the stage before it, when its work can be planned in detail
Plans.w: Because only the near future can be planned in detail, each later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when the work will be done (see manual 7.2.1, 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Initiation produces the project plan; later stage plans are prepared near the end of each preceding stage (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.1: Stage plans are prepared by the project manager before the stage starts; team managers prepare team plans (manual 7.2.2.2, 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Stage plans are forward-looking plans for control; actual performance is reported in end stage and end project reports (manual 7.2.2.2, 11.5).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about management stages are correct?
1. The end of each management stage gives the project board a decision point on whether to continue.
2. Closing a project is run as a separate management stage after the final delivery stage.
3. Stage boundaries can be placed where key decisions about the project are needed.
4. Every project must have at least three management stages, including initiation.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Stage ends are decision points for the board, and the number and length of stages take account of where key decisions are needed (see manual 7.2.3).

n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: the minimum is two stages, initiation plus one delivery stage (manual 7.2.3). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: closing a project takes place within the final delivery stage, not as a stage of its own (manual 7.2.2.2). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.
n.3: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong. Statement 2 is wrong: closing a project takes place within the final delivery stage, not as a stage of its own (manual 7.2.2.2). Statement 4 is wrong: the minimum is two stages, initiation plus one delivery stage (manual 7.2.3).

Plans.q: A project manager is planning a project with high levels of risk. Why might she propose more management stages of shorter length than for a low-risk project?
o: PRINCE2 sets a maximum stage length of three months for any high-risk project
Stage length should reflect risk, and more stage ends give the board more decision points
Shorter stages mean that no exception plan is needed if a stage tolerance is breached
Stage length is set by the business layer in the project mandate for high-risk projects
Plans.w: The number and length of stages depend on risk among other factors. Each stage end is a decision point, so more, shorter stages let the board review a risky project more often (see manual 7.2.3).

n.0: PRINCE2 sets no fixed stage length; the number and length of stages are judged on the planning horizon, decisions, risk and complexity (manual 7.2.3).
n.2: An exception plan may still be needed whatever the stage length (manual 7.2.2.4).
n.3: The project manager proposes the stages in the project plan for the board to approve; the business layer does not set stage length (manual 7.2.3, 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q: In PRINCE2 7, for which aspects of performance can tolerances be set to manage a project's constraints?
o: Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope and risk
Cost, time, quality, scope, risk and stakeholder satisfaction
Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, risk and resources
Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk
Plans.w: PRINCE2 7 provides tolerances for seven aspects: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk. Sustainability is new in PRINCE2 7 (see manual 7.2.4).

n.0: This is the older list of six; PRINCE2 7 adds sustainability as a seventh aspect (manual 7.2.4).
n.1: Stakeholder satisfaction is not a tolerance area, and the list misses benefits and sustainability (manual 7.2.4).
n.2: Resources are not a tolerance area; the seventh aspect is sustainability (manual 7.2.4).

Plans.q: Which statement describes a tolerance in PRINCE2?
o: The permitted deviation from a plan's target before escalation to the next management level
Money held back in a plan to pay for responses to the project's threats and opportunities
Money, or agreed constraints, reserved in a plan to pay for approved changes to the baseline
How much risk, and of what kind, the business is prepared to accept to meet its objectives
Plans.w: A tolerance is the permitted deviation above or below a plan's target that is allowed before the matter needs to be escalated to the next level of management (see manual 7.2.4).

n.1: This describes a risk budget, which funds risk responses; it is not a permitted deviation (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: This describes a change budget, which funds approved changes (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: This describes risk appetite, which is set by the business (manual 9.2.1).

Plans.q: Who sets the tolerances for the project as a whole, and where are they documented?
o: The executive, in each stage plan as it is approved by the project board
The business layer, in the project mandate or confirmed to the board for the project brief
The project manager, in the project plan that is prepared during initiating a project
Project assurance, in the quality management approach agreed during initiation
Plans.w: The business layer sets project tolerances and documents them in the project mandate, or confirms them to the project board for inclusion in the project brief (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: The executive defines tolerances for each stage; project-level tolerances come from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances, not project tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 11.2).
n.3: Project assurance reviews progress against agreed tolerances; it does not set them (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In the plans practice, the [?] defines the tolerances for each stage and approves the stage plans.
o: senior user
project manager
executive
business layer
Plans.w: Among the planning areas of focus, the executive defines tolerances for each stage and approves stage plans (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: The senior user makes sure plans remain consistent with the user perspective; stage tolerances are defined by the executive (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.1: The project manager prepares stage plans and sets work package tolerances; the executive defines stage tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The business layer sets tolerances for the project as a whole, not for each stage (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q: Which tolerances are agreed with a team manager in a work package description?
o: Scope, cost, time and quality
Benefits, cost and time
Cost, time, risk and sustainability
Scope, cost and time
Plans.w: A work package description carries tolerances for scope, cost and time. Benefits, quality, risk and sustainability tolerances are not set at work package level (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Quality is controlled at work package level through the product descriptions, not through a quality tolerance in the work package description (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Benefits are not managed at work package level; the tolerances are scope, cost and time (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Risk and sustainability tolerances are not set in a work package description, and this list leaves out scope (manual 11.2.1).

Plans.q: Why is it important to understand which of a project's constraints take precedence when planning?
o: It guides the choice of approach and how much tolerance is set for each aspect
It decides which role approves the project plan in directing a project
It lets the project manager change the business case targets without approval
It determines how many team plans each team manager must produce
Plans.w: Understanding which constraints take precedence is crucial to choosing the right approaches and setting tolerances, for example a tight time tolerance where a fixed date matters most (see manual 7.2.4).

n.1: The project board approves the project plan when it authorizes the project, whatever the constraints (manual 7.2.2.1).
n.2: The project manager cannot change approved targets; deviations beyond tolerance are escalated (manual 7.2.4).
n.3: Team plans are optional; the reason for understanding constraints is to guide the approach and tolerances, not to fix how many team plans exist (manual 7.2.2.3, 7.2.4).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about tolerances in the plans practice are correct?
1. A team manager who forecasts that a work package will exceed its tolerances raises it with the project manager.
2. The project manager sets the tolerances for each stage and records them in the project mandate.
3. An exception exists when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not just after it has been exceeded.
4. Quality tolerance is set in the work package description together with cost and time tolerance.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. A team manager escalates a forecast work package breach to the project manager, who instructs corrective action; and an exception is a forecast deviation beyond tolerance (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 11.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: stage tolerances are defined by the executive, and the project mandate comes from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; quality tolerance is not one of them (manual 11.2.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: stage tolerances are defined by the executive, and the project mandate comes from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

Plans.q: What does a sustainability tolerance set limits on in PRINCE2 7?
o: The plan's aggregated risks
The permissible variation of the plan's products
The agreed metrics for sustainability
The over- or under-delivery of benefits
Plans.w: A sustainability tolerance sets limits on the agreed sustainability metrics, alongside the other six tolerance areas (see manual 7.2.4, 11.2).

n.0: Limits on a plan's aggregated risks are risk tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).
n.1: Variation in the plan's products is scope tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).
n.3: Under- or over-delivery of benefits is benefits tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).

Plans.q: In product-based planning, what is the starting point for building a plan?
o: Defining and analysing the products that the plan must deliver
Listing the activities and tasks that the teams will carry out
Agreeing the budget and cost tolerances with the executive
Identifying the team managers who will accept the work packages
Plans.w: Product-based planning starts from defining and analysing the required products, and derives the rest of the plan, such as the work breakdown structure, estimates and schedule, from the product descriptions (see manual 7.2.5).

n.1: Activities are identified after the products are defined, when work packages are organized; they are not the starting point (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1.2).
n.2: Preparing the budget comes late in the planning technique, after products, estimates and schedule (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: Work packages are organized and allocated after the products have been defined and analysed (manual 7.3.1.2).

Plans.q: When defining and analysing the products for the project plan, which step is carried out first?
o: Create the product breakdown structure
Write the project product description
Create the product flow diagram
Write the product descriptions
Plans.w: Defining and analysing the products has four steps in order: write the project product description (project plan only), create the product breakdown structure, write product descriptions, and create the product flow diagram (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: The product breakdown structure is the second step, after the project product description (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: The product flow diagram is the last of the four steps, once the products are known (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.3: Product descriptions are written in the third step, after the products have been broken down (manual 7.3.1.1).

Plans.q: Which statement describes a product breakdown structure?
o: A diagram of the order in which the products will be developed
A hierarchy of the activities and tasks needed to deliver a plan
A hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan
A list of all the products of a plan and their current status
Plans.w: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan, breaking major products into their components (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: The order of development and the dependencies are shown in the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.1: A product breakdown structure lists products, not activities; activities are grouped into work packages later (manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).
n.3: A list of products with their status is the product register in the project log (manual 4.3.2).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The [?] shows the sequence in which products will be developed and the dependencies between them, including any external products.
o: product breakdown structure
product register
work breakdown structure
product flow diagram
Plans.w: The product flow diagram shows the sequence of development and the dependencies between products, including intermediate and external products (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: The product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of products; it does not show their sequence (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.1: The product register records the products of a plan and their status; it does not show sequence and dependencies (manual 4.3.2).
n.2: The work breakdown structure organizes the work into work packages; the sequence of products is shown in the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1.2).

Plans.q: When is the project product description written, and for which level of plan?
o: In starting up a project, for the project plan
In initiating a project, for every stage plan
In managing a stage boundary, for the next stage plan
In managing product delivery, for each team plan
Plans.w: The project product description is written in starting up a project and is used for the project plan only; product descriptions are written for all levels of plan (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.1: It is written before initiation and covers the project plan; stage plans use product descriptions instead (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Next stage plans are built from product descriptions; the project product description already exists from starting up (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.3: Team plans use product descriptions; the project product description is written once, in starting up a project (manual 7.3.1.1).

Plans.q: A project manager uses the planning technique to prepare the plan for stage 3. Which step of defining and analysing the products is NOT carried out for this plan?
o: Creating the product breakdown structure
Writing the project product description
Writing product descriptions
Creating the product flow diagram
Plans.w: The project product description is written for the project plan only. For a stage plan, the project manager creates a product breakdown structure, writes product descriptions and creates a product flow diagram (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: Each plan has its own product breakdown structure of the products it will produce (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Product descriptions are written for products at all levels of plan, including stage plans (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.3: The planning technique, including the product flow diagram, is repeated for each stage plan (manual 7.3.1.1).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about defining and analysing products are correct?
1. External products are left out of the product flow diagram because they are outside the project's control.
2. Product descriptions are written for products at all levels of plan.
3. A dependency means that one product depends on another, and dependencies can be internal or external.
4. The product flow diagram is drawn before the product breakdown structure is created.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 3
2 and 4
Plans.w: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Product descriptions are written for all levels of plan, and a dependency means one product depends on another, with at least internal and external types (see manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: external products are included in the product flow diagram so that dependencies on others are visible (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: external products are included in the product flow diagram so that dependencies on others are visible (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the product breakdown structure comes before product descriptions and the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

Plans.q: In a linear-sequential project, how detailed should product descriptions be when they are written?
o: Brief, because acceptance criteria will be refined during delivery through a product backlog
Limited to the project's major products, as recorded in the project product description
Written in full for the final stage's products, with earlier products left as titles
Detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated with an appropriate level of confidence
Plans.w: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence. In iterative-incremental work, criteria are refined during delivery (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: Refining criteria during delivery through a product backlog describes an iterative-incremental project (manual 7.2.3).
n.1: The project product description covers the major products; individual product descriptions go further, down to the products of each plan (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Products are described as each plan is prepared, so earlier products need descriptions before their work starts (manual 7.3.1.1).

Plans.q: Once the delivery approach is decided, which step of the planning technique identifies the delivery activities for each product and groups them for allocation to teams?
o: Preparing the schedule
Organizing work packages
Preparing estimates
Documenting the plan
Plans.w: After the products are defined and analysed and the delivery approach is decided, the delivery activities for each product are identified and grouped into work packages (see manual 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Scheduling sets the sequence and duration of work packages once they have been organized (manual 7.3.1.4).
n.2: Estimating works out the effort, time and cost of the work; grouping activities into work packages is a separate step (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.3: Documenting the plan is the final step, recording the narrative such as assumptions and controls (manual 7.3.1).

Plans.q: What should the project manager make sure of when organizing the work into work packages?
o: Each work package corresponds to one management stage of the project
Each work package has a team plan that is approved by the project board
There is no overlap in scope between any two work packages and no gaps
Each work package includes benefits and quality tolerances for its products
Plans.w: When organizing work packages, the project manager makes sure that no two work packages overlap in scope and that nothing is left out (see manual 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Work packages are grouped around products and delivery activities, not matched one to one with stages; a stage may contain several work packages (manual 7.3.1.2, 7.3.1.4).
n.1: Team plans are optional and are produced by team managers; the board does not approve them (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Work package tolerances are for scope, cost and time; benefits and quality tolerances are not set at that level (manual 11.2.1).

Plans.q: In the plans practice, what is captured in a schedule?
o: The list of all the products of a plan together with the current status of each
The hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan
The timetable of reports and meetings agreed with the stakeholders
The sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks
Plans.w: A schedule captures the sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks; every work package for a stage must appear in that stage's schedule (see manual 7.3.1.4).

n.0: This describes the product register, which is held in the project log (manual 4.3.2).
n.1: This describes the product breakdown structure (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Reporting and communication timings belong in the communication management approach and project controls, not the plan's schedule (manual 7.3.1.4).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In PRINCE2, project managers and team managers plan using [?], which can be improved with lessons and data from earlier work.
o: estimates
baselines
change budgets
product registers
Plans.w: Project managers and team managers always plan using estimates. Techniques include top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics and expert consensus, and lessons help improve them (see manual 7.3.1.3, 7.7).

n.1: A baseline is an approved version of a plan or product; plans are built from estimates and then baselined on approval (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.3.1.3).
n.2: A change budget is an optional part of a plan's budget for approved changes; it is not the basis of planning (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: The product register records products and their status; planning is based on estimates (manual 4.3.2, 7.3.1.3).

Plans.q: A team estimates the effort for each work item by privately voting with cards and discussing differences until they agree. Which kind of estimating technique is this?
o: Parametric, applying known rates to measured units
Expert consensus, agreeing an estimate as a group
Top-down, splitting an overall figure across the parts
Comparative, using similar past work as a reference
Plans.w: Planning poker, like the Delphi technique, is an expert consensus approach to estimating, one of the techniques used in the preparing estimates step (see manual 7.3.1.3).

n.0: Parametric estimating applies known rates or measures to the size of the work, not group voting (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.2: Top-down estimating starts from an overall figure and splits it across the parts; it is not a voting method (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.3: Comparative estimating uses similar past work as the reference, not repeated rounds of voting (manual 7.3.1.3).

Plans.q: What is the difference between a risk budget and a change budget in a plan's budget?
o: A risk budget funds authorized changes; a change budget funds risk responses
A risk budget covers activity overspends; a change budget covers late delivery
A risk budget funds responses to risks; a change budget funds authorized changes
Both form part of cost tolerance and are used when a stage will overspend
Plans.w: A risk budget is money to fund specific responses to threats and opportunities, while a change budget is set aside to cover authorized changes. Both are optional parts of a plan's budget (see manual 7.3.1).

n.0: This reverses the two: the risk budget funds risk responses and the change budget funds changes (manual 7.3.1).
n.1: Overspends and late delivery are managed through cost and time tolerances and exceptions; the risk budget funds risk responses and the change budget funds authorized changes (manual 7.2.4, 7.3.1).
n.3: Risk and change budgets are separate from cost tolerance in the budget (manual 7.3.1).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about the later steps of the planning technique are correct?
1. The schedule is prepared before the products are defined, so that dates can be fixed early.
2. Documenting the plan is the first step, done before any estimates are prepared.
3. Analysing risks runs alongside the other steps, and a plan stays in draft until its risks are addressed.
4. The budget may include a risk budget and a change budget as well as the cost of the activities.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Plans.w: Statements 3 and 4 are correct. Risk analysis runs alongside the planning steps, and the budget covers activity costs plus any risk budget, change budget and cost tolerances (see manual 7.3.1).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong. Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 2 is wrong: documenting the plan is the last step, after the budget has been prepared (manual 7.3.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.2: Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

Plans.q: What does the project plan identify that typically forms the top level of the project's work breakdown structure?
o: The proposed work packages into which delivery activities will be organized
The team plans that each team manager will prepare for the project
The product descriptions for every product of every stage of the project
The stage tolerances that the executive will set for each delivery stage
Plans.w: The project plan identifies the proposed work packages into which product delivery activities will be organized; these typically form the top level of the work breakdown structure (see manual 7.2.2.1).

n.1: Team plans are optional plans prepared later by team managers; they are not the top level of the work breakdown structure (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Product descriptions describe products; the work breakdown structure is organized around work packages (manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the executive for each stage; they are not part of the work breakdown structure (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q: What is the purpose of a work package description?
o: To describe the project's major products and how they will be accepted when the project closes
To record every product of a plan and its current status so that progress can be tracked
To describe how one or more products will be produced and to pass responsibility for the work formally to a team
To set out the major products of the whole project and when, how and at what cost they will be delivered
Plans.w: A work package description describes how one or more products will be produced and delivered, and is used to pass responsibility for that work formally to a team manager or team member (see manual 7.5).

n.0: This describes the project product description, which covers the whole project and its acceptance (manual 7.5).
n.1: This describes the product register, which is held in the project log (manual 4.3.2).
n.3: This describes the project plan, the high-level plan for the whole project (manual 7.2.2.1).

Plans.q: Which management product describes the user's quality expectations, together with the acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project?
o: Product description
Product breakdown structure
Work package description
Project product description
