Plans.w: The project product description describes the project's major products or outcomes, including the user's quality expectations and the acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project (see manual 7.5).

n.0: A product description covers one product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications, not the acceptance of the whole project (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.1: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of the products in a plan; it does not record quality expectations or acceptance criteria (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: A work package description passes a piece of work to a team; it does not hold the project's acceptance criteria (manual 7.5).

Plans.q: How is the project product description used when the project is being closed?
o: To confirm that the products meet the acceptance criteria
To pass the lessons from the project on to future projects
To set the benefits tolerances for the post-project benefits review
To record the final status of every product in the product register
Plans.w: The project product description holds the acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project, and is used during closure to confirm that the project product is acceptable (see manual 7.5).

n.1: Lessons are passed on through the lessons report, not the project product description (manual 11.5).
n.2: Benefits tolerances are held in the benefits management approach, not the project product description (manual 5.5).
n.3: Product status is kept in the product register within the project log; the project product description defines acceptance (manual 4.3.2, 7.5).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The [?] heading of a work package description records limits on the work, such as authorized working hours and any safety or security requirements.
o: references
constraints
techniques and procedures
agreement
Plans.w: The constraints heading of a work package description records limits such as authorized hours and safety or security requirements (see manual 7.5).

n.0: References link the work package to higher-level plans and documents; they do not set limits on the work (manual 7.5).
n.2: This heading records the methods to be used in producing the products, not limits such as working hours (manual 7.5).
n.3: The agreement heading records the initial authorization of the work and its final completion (manual 7.5).

Plans.q: Under which heading of a plan is the work in scope recorded as a work breakdown structure with its associated work package descriptions?
o: Planning assumptions
Monitoring and control
Work to be performed
External dependencies
Plans.w: A plan's 'work to be performed' heading shows the work in scope as a work breakdown structure together with the associated work package descriptions (see manual 7.5).

n.0: Planning assumptions record what the plan assumes to be true; they do not hold the work breakdown structure (manual 7.5).
n.1: Monitoring and control describes how the plan will be tracked, not the breakdown of the work itself (manual 7.5).
n.3: External dependencies record what the plan relies on from outside the project, not the work breakdown structure (manual 7.5).

Plans.q: What is recorded under the 'agreement' heading of a work package description?
o: The terms of the contract agreed with an external supplier for the work
The acceptance criteria for the project agreed with the senior user
The stage tolerances agreed between the executive and the project manager
A record of the initial authorization of the work and of its final completion
Plans.w: The agreement heading of a work package description records the initial authorization of the work and its final completion (see manual 7.5).

n.0: Supplier contracts are dealt with through the commercial management approach, not the agreement heading of a work package (manual 7.5).
n.1: The project's acceptance criteria are in the project product description (manual 7.5).
n.2: Stage tolerances belong in the stage plan; a work package carries its own scope, cost and time tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 11.2.1).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about the management products of the plans practice are correct?
1. The project product description is written in starting up a project.
2. The 'references' heading of a work package description links the work to higher-level plans and documents.
3. A work package description may set benefits tolerances for the products it covers.
4. The project product description replaces the individual product descriptions in a stage plan.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The project product description is written in starting up a project, and a work package description includes references to higher-level plans and documents (see manual 7.3.1.1, 7.5).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: stage plans use product descriptions for their products; the project product description is for the project plan only (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

Plans.q: How does the project product description link the plans practice to the quality practice?
o: It records the results of the quality reviews held during each stage
It records the quality expectations and acceptance criteria the project must meet
It sets out the quality assurance checks made independently of the project
It sets the quality tolerance for each work package description
Plans.w: The project product description records the user's quality expectations and the acceptance criteria, which set the standard the project product must meet to be accepted and feed quality planning (see manual 7.5, 8.1).

n.0: Quality activity results are recorded in the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.2: Quality assurance is a business function independent of the project management team; it is not set out in the project product description (manual 8.2).
n.3: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances, not quality tolerance (manual 11.2.1).

Plans.q: Setting tolerances at each level of plan, so that deviations beyond them are escalated, applies which PRINCE2 principle?
o: Manage by stages
Focus on products
Tailor to suit the project
Manage by exception
Plans.w: Tolerances at each level of plan are how the plans practice supports manage by exception: each level works within its tolerances and escalates forecast breaches (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Manage by stages is supported by the project plan and stage plans with stage boundaries; tolerances apply manage by exception (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.1: Focus on products is supported by product-based planning, not by setting tolerances (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.2: Tailoring is shown by adjusting the formality and detail of plans, not by setting tolerances (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

Plans.q: Which principle does product-based planning support, and how?
o: Focus on products, because planning starts by defining and analysing the products
Manage by stages, because each product is delivered in its own management stage
Learn from experience, because each product description records the lessons learned
Manage by exception, because each product description sets the tolerances for the stage
Plans.w: Product-based planning starts from the products to be delivered and derives the rest of the plan from their descriptions, which is how the plans practice supports focus on products (see manual 7.2.5, 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.1: Products are not tied one to one with stages; manage by stages is supported by the project plan and stage plans (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.2: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log; in planning, they are used to improve estimates (manual 4.3.2, 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the executive, and tolerances at each plan level support manage by exception (manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 7.7 tab 7.2).

Plans.q: In the plans practice, who is responsible for providing the planning standards required by the business?
o: Project support
The business layer
Project assurance
The project manager
Plans.w: Among the planning areas of focus, the business layer provides the planning standards required by the business and sets project tolerances (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: Project support assists with compiling plans and maintaining planning tools; it does not set the business's planning standards (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: Project assurance reviews stage and project progress against agreed tolerances; the standards come from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The project manager prepares plans in line with the business's standards and decides how stages are applied (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Using a high-level project plan together with a detailed plan for each stage, with a decision at each stage boundary, applies the [?] principle.
o: manage by exception
focus on products
manage by stages
learn from experience
Plans.w: The project plan plus stage plans, with stage boundaries as decision points, is how the plans practice supports the manage by stages principle (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Manage by exception is supported by setting tolerances at each plan level (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.1: Focus on products is supported by product-based planning (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.3: Learn from experience is supported by using lessons when estimating (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

Plans.q: How does the plans practice support the ensure continued business justification principle?
o: By setting the business's risk appetite before the project plan is approved by the board
By replacing the business case with the project plan once the project has been authorized
By recording lessons from earlier projects in each stage plan as it is prepared
By aligning plan targets with the business case and giving estimates to judge viability
Plans.w: The plans practice aligns a plan's performance targets with the business case objectives and provides estimates on which the project board can confirm that the project is viable (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Risk appetite is set by the business, not by the plans practice (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: The business case remains and is maintained throughout; plans must satisfy it, not replace it (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.2: Using lessons in estimating supports learn from experience; lessons are held in the lessons log, not the stage plan (manual 4.3.2, 7.7 tab 7.2).

Plans.q: In the plans practice, which role reviews stage and project progress against the agreed tolerances?
o: Project assurance
Project support
The team manager
The senior supplier
Plans.w: Project assurance reviews stage and project progress against agreed tolerances on behalf of the project board (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.1: Project support assists the project manager with compiling plans and planning tools; reviewing progress against tolerances is an assurance task (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: The team manager prepares schedules for each work package and reports on work package progress; it does not review the stage or project (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The senior supplier makes sure plans are consistent with the supplier perspective and commits supplier resources (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

Plans.q:
Which two statements about the areas of focus of roles in the plans practice are correct?
1. The team manager prepares schedules for each work package.
2. Project support reviews progress against tolerances on behalf of the project board.
3. The project manager instructs corrective action when work package tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.
4. The senior user approves stage plans and defines the tolerances for each stage.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Plans.w: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The team manager prepares schedules for each work package, and the project manager instructs corrective action when work-package-level tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: reviewing progress against tolerances is project assurance; project support assists with compiling plans (manual 7.6 tab 7.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the executive defines stage tolerances and approves stage plans; the senior user keeps plans consistent with the user perspective (manual 7.6 tab 7.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: reviewing progress against tolerances is project assurance; project support assists with compiling plans (manual 7.6 tab 7.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

Plans.q: A project manager uses actual figures from a similar earlier project to sharpen the estimates in a stage plan. Which principle is the plans practice supporting?
o: Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Learn from experience
Tailor to suit the project
Plans.w: Using lessons and past data to improve estimates is how the plans practice supports the learn from experience principle (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Business justification is supported by aligning plan targets with the business case; the use of past figures here is learning from experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.1: Focus on products is supported by starting planning from the products; this example is about improving estimates with experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.3: Tailoring adjusts the formality and detail of plans; drawing on past figures is learning from experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

Plans.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the plans practice?
o: To support communication and control by defining the products and the means of delivering them
To capture the user's requirements for the products and set up how those requirements will be met
To provide a means of judging whether the project is, and stays, desirable, viable and achievable
To compare actual achievement with what was planned and forecast the work still to be done
Plans.w: The plans practice exists to support communication and control. It defines what is to be delivered (the products) and the means of delivering it: who, how and where, with estimates of when and how much, so that the business case is satisfied (see manual 7.1).

n.1: This is the purpose of the quality practice, which deals with user requirements and how they will be met, not with defining the means, timing and cost of delivery (manual 8.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of the business case practice, which supports decisions on continued investment; the plan must satisfy the business case but does not judge it (manual 5.1).
n.3: This describes the progress practice, which compares achievement with the plan; the plans practice provides the plan that progress is measured against (manual 11.1).

Plans.q: A plan answers several questions about how a project will deliver its products. Which question is answered by the business case rather than by the plan?
o: What products are to be delivered
Why the products are worth delivering
Who will deliver the products, and how
When the products will be delivered
Plans.w: The plans practice defines the what, who, how, where, when and how much. The why is held in the business case, which the plan must satisfy (see manual 7.1).

n.0: Defining the products to be delivered (the what) is a core part of the plan's purpose (manual 7.1).
n.2: The means of delivery, including who and how, are defined in the plan (manual 7.1).
n.3: The plan contains estimates of when products will be delivered, as well as how much they will cost (manual 7.1).

Plans.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
A plan defines the products to be delivered and the means of delivering them, so that the [?] of the project is satisfied.
o: project product description
quality management approach
business case
risk management approach
Plans.w: The plans practice defines the what and the means of delivery in order to satisfy the business case, which holds the why (see manual 7.1).

n.0: The project product description describes the major products and their acceptance; it is one input to planning, not the justification the plan must satisfy (manual 7.5).
n.1: The quality management approach sets out how quality will be managed; the plans purpose refers to satisfying the business case (manual 7.1, 8.5).
n.3: The risk management approach describes how risks will be managed; the plan's targets must satisfy the business case (manual 7.1, 9.5).

Plans.q: Once a stage plan has been approved, the project manager compares actual progress with it so that deviations can be spotted early. Which part of the purpose of the plans practice does this mainly support?
o: Communication, because the plan gives stakeholders one shared picture
Justification, because the plan explains why the products are needed
Accountability, because the plan sets out who directs the project
Control, because the approved plan is the baseline for measuring progress
Plans.w: The plans practice facilitates communication and control. An approved plan is the baseline against which progress is measured, which is the control part of its purpose (see manual 7.1, 11.1).

n.0: Plans do support communication, but comparing actual progress with the plan to spot deviations is the control part of the purpose (manual 7.1).
n.1: The why belongs to the business case; a plan satisfies the business case but does not justify the project (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.2: The structure of accountability is defined by the organizing practice, not by comparing progress with a plan (manual 6.1).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the quality practice are correct?

1. Quality means the products meet their requirements and expectations and enable the intended benefits.
2. Requirements captured well during initiation should not change, so later changes are not planned for.
3. Product-based quality helps the project avoid work that cannot be traced to its business justification.
4. The main aim of the quality practice is to compare actual progress with the stage plan.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 1 reflects what quality means in PRINCE2, and statement 3 is correct because defining quality through products keeps the work traceable to the business justification (see manual 8.1, 8.1.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: however well requirements are captured in initiation, the quality practice expects them to change and the project must handle those changes (manual 8.1.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: requirement changes are expected (manual 8.1.2), and comparing progress with the stage plan is the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 describes the progress practice, not quality (manual 11.1).

Quality.q: During initiation of a library digitization project, the project manager says the users' requirements have been captured so thoroughly that no changes to them need to be allowed for. Which statement reflects the quality practice?
o: Requirements recorded in the project initiation documentation are fixed, so any change must close the project
Requirement changes are expected, and the team manager may agree them informally with the users during delivery
Requirement changes are handled through the quality register, which is updated by project support
Requirements are likely to change however well they were captured, so the project must expect and manage change
Quality.w: The quality practice accepts that requirements will change no matter how well they were captured in initiation, so the project should expect such changes and handle them in a controlled way (see manual 8.1.2).

n.0: A change to requirements is handled as a change to a baseline through the issue management approach; it does not mean the project must close (manual 8.2.1.6, ch 10).
n.1: Changes to baselined requirements are controlled through the issue management approach, not agreed informally between the team manager and the users (manual 8.2.1.6).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities and their results; requirement changes are controlled through the issue management approach (manual 8.5, 8.2.1.6).

Quality.q: On what does PRINCE2 base its approach to achieving the required quality in a project?
o: Defining each product and its quality specifications in a product description, then checking it against them
Inspecting the work done by each team member against a time-based schedule of activities in the team plan
Measuring the benefits achieved after closure against the forecasts in the original business case
Reviewing each stage plan's activities at every checkpoint to confirm that the work has been carried out
Quality.w: PRINCE2 takes a product-based view of quality: each product's purpose and quality specifications are defined in its product description and the product is then checked against them (see manual 8.1, 8.5).

n.1: PRINCE2 is output-oriented rather than work-oriented; quality is defined for products, not for the activities in a schedule (manual 2.6, 8.1).
n.2: Measuring benefits after closure is part of the business case practice and the benefits management approach, not the basis of quality (manual ch 5).
n.3: Checking that activities were carried out is progress monitoring; quality is judged against the product's specifications, not completion of activities (manual ch 11, 8.1).

Quality.q: A charity's board asks what the quality practice will mainly be concerned with on its new fundraising database project. Which answer is correct?
o: Whether the project's activities are carried out in the sequence shown in the stage plan
Whether the project continues to be desirable, viable and achievable at each stage
Whether the project's products are fit for purpose and meet what the users require
Whether each management level in the project has clearly defined accountabilities
Quality.w: The quality practice is concerned with products being fit for purpose: it documents what users require of the products and how those requirements will be met (see manual 8.1).

n.0: The sequence of activities is a plans and progress concern, set out in the schedule and monitored against the stage plan (manual ch 7, ch 11).
n.1: Continuing desirability, viability and achievability is the concern of the business case practice (manual 5.1).
n.3: Defining accountabilities at each management level is the concern of the organizing practice (manual 6.1).

Quality.q: Which term describes a prioritized list of measurable criteria that the project product must meet before the user will accept it?
o: User's quality expectations
Acceptance criteria
Quality specifications
Quality tolerance
Quality.w: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user accepts it; they are recorded in the project product description (see manual 8.1.1).

n.0: User's quality expectations are a high-level statement of the quality expected from the project product and are often not measurable (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: Quality specifications are the measures and levels that individual products must meet, set out in their product descriptions, not the project-level acceptance list (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality before escalation, not a list of criteria for acceptance (manual 8.2.1.2).

Quality.q: In PRINCE2, what are the user's quality expectations?
o: The measures applied by those doing quality control and the levels each finished product must reach
The permissible deviation in a product's quality before the deviation must be escalated
A need or expectation that has been documented in an approved management product
A statement about the quality expected from the project product, recorded in the project product description
Quality.w: The user's quality expectations are a statement about the quality expected from the project product; they are captured in the project product description and are typically high-level (see manual 8.1.1, 8.2.1.1).

n.0: Measures applied in quality control, with the levels to be met, are quality specifications, held in product descriptions (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: The permissible deviation in quality before escalation is quality tolerance (manual 8.2.1.2).
n.2: A need or expectation documented in an approved management product is the general definition of a requirement (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q: A project will build a new visitor centre with several separate products. Where are the quality specifications for one of those individual products documented?
o: In that product's product description
In the project product description
In the quality register
In the quality management approach
Quality.w: Quality specifications, the measures and levels a specific product must meet, are documented in that product's product description (see manual 8.1.1, 8.5).

n.1: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product as a whole, not each product's specifications (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities planned or performed and their results, not the specifications themselves (manual 8.5).
n.3: The quality management approach sets out the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the project, not the specifications of individual products (manual 8.5).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The permissible deviation in a product's quality before the deviation needs to be escalated to the next level of management is known as quality [?].
o: assurance
control
tolerance
specification
Quality.w: Quality tolerance is the permissible deviation in a product's quality before it needs to be escalated (see manual 8.2.1.2).

n.0: Quality assurance is an independent, planned activity giving confidence that products will meet their specifications, not a permitted deviation (manual 8.2.3).
n.1: Quality control is the monitoring of products against standards and the recording of results, not a permitted deviation (manual 8.2.2).
n.3: A quality specification is the measure and level a product must meet; tolerance is the allowed variation around it (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q: Which statement about acceptance criteria is correct?
o: They are high-level statements of the quality expected and are often not measurable
They are set for each individual product in its product description by the team manager
They record whether each quality check was passed or failed during the delivery stages
They are prioritized and measurable, and are recorded in the project product description
Quality.w: Acceptance criteria form a prioritized list of measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user accepts it, and they are recorded in the project product description (see manual 8.1.1).

n.0: High-level, often unmeasurable statements are the user's quality expectations; acceptance criteria are measurable (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: Product-level measures in product descriptions are quality specifications, not acceptance criteria for the project product (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: Pass or fail results of quality checks are recorded in the quality register (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: At the start of a staff booking system project, the senior user says the new system 'must be easy for reception staff to use'. Which term best describes this statement?
o: A user's quality expectation
A user's acceptance criterion
A product's quality specification
A product's quality tolerance
Quality.w: A broad statement of the quality expected from the project product, which is not yet measurable, is a user's quality expectation recorded in the project product description (see manual 8.1.1, 8.2.1.1).

n.1: Acceptance criteria must be measurable; 'easy to use' would need to be turned into a measurable criterion, such as a task completed within a set time (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: A quality specification is a measure with a required level for a specific product, set out in its product description; this statement has neither (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Quality tolerance is the allowed deviation from agreed quality criteria before escalation, not a statement of what the user wants (manual 8.2.1.2).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about quality terms are correct?

1. An outcome such as 'more customers return each year' is a user's quality expectation.
2. Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria.
3. Quality specifications are found in product descriptions.
4. A requirement is any need, whether or not it is documented in a management product.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 2 is the definition of acceptance criteria and statement 3 is correct because each product's quality specifications are held in its product description (see manual 8.1.1, 8.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: an outcome or benefit is not a quality expectation of the project product (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong (an outcome is not a quality expectation), and statement 4 is wrong because a requirement is a need or expectation documented in an approved management product (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is wrong: in PRINCE2 a requirement is documented in an approved management product (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q: For a new online shop, the executive suggests recording 'a 10% rise in online sales within a year' as one of the user's quality expectations. Which statement is correct?
o: It is suitable as an expectation, because it is measurable and agreed with the users
It is a benefit the online shop should enable, not a quality expectation of the shop itself
It belongs among the acceptance criteria in the project product description instead
It belongs among the quality specifications in the shop's product description instead
Quality.w: A rise in sales is an outcome or benefit that the product should help to achieve; it says nothing about the quality of the product itself, so it is not a quality expectation, an acceptance criterion or a quality specification (see manual 8.1.1).

n.0: Being measurable does not make a benefit a quality expectation; expectations describe the quality of the project product (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: Acceptance criteria are measurable attributes of the project product the user can check before accepting it; a future sales rise is a benefit (manual 8.1.1, ch 5).
n.3: Quality specifications are measures of a product's own characteristics, not the business results it later enables (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q: Which management products does quality planning produce, so that the project knows how its products will be checked?
o: The quality register entries and the results of each completed quality check
The outline business case and the project brief for the initiation stage
The product descriptions and the quality management approach for the project
The acceptance records and the end project report for the project board
Quality.w: Quality planning captures the quality specifications and produces the product descriptions and the quality management approach (see manual 8.2.1).

n.0: Recording quality checks and their results in the quality register is quality control, not quality planning (manual 8.2.2).
n.1: The outline business case and project brief are created in starting up a project under the business case practice (manual ch 5, ch 13).
n.3: Acceptance records and the end project report belong to project acceptance and closing a project, not quality planning (manual 8.3.1.3, ch 19).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

During quality planning, quality tolerances are set using the prioritized [?] and the quality specifications of the products.
o: acceptance criteria
benefits forecasts
risk responses
stage tolerances
Quality.w: Quality tolerance is set from the prioritized acceptance criteria and the quality specifications (see manual 8.2.1.2).

n.1: Benefits forecasts sit in the business case and drive benefits tolerance, not quality tolerance (manual ch 5).
n.2: Risk responses are planned under the risk practice and do not define how far a product's quality may vary (manual ch 9).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board for the stage plan; quality tolerance comes from acceptance criteria and quality specifications (manual 11.2, 8.2.1.2).

Quality.q: Which management product, agreed during initiating a project, describes how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported?
o: Product description
Project product description
Quality register
Quality management approach
Quality.w: The quality management approach, part of the project initiation documentation, focuses on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported (see manual 8.3.1.1, 8.5).

n.0: A product description sets out one product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications, not the project's quality control arrangements (manual 8.5).
n.1: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product, created in starting up a project (manual 8.1.1, ch 13).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities planned or performed and their results; it does not describe how quality control is organized (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: A project manager is about to start quality planning for a new water treatment plant. What is a primary input to this planning?
o: The results of the quality checks recorded so far in the project's quality register
The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria in the project product description
The checkpoint reports produced by the team managers during the delivery stages
The lessons report produced when the previous project was closed
Quality.w: The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria, captured in the project product description during starting up a project, are a primary input to quality planning (see manual 8.3.1.1).

n.0: Quality register results come from quality control, which happens after planning; they cannot be the starting input to it (manual 8.3.1.2).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are progress reports from team managers during delivery, not an input to planning quality (manual ch 11).
n.3: Lessons from earlier projects can inform the approaches, but the primary input to quality planning is the project product description (manual 8.3.1.1).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about quality planning are correct?

1. Quality planning records the result of every quality check in the quality register.
2. Quality planning captures the quality specifications for the project's products.
3. Quality tolerances for a product are agreed in the work package description.
4. Changes to the baselined project initiation documentation arising from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach.
o: 1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 2 is correct because quality planning captures quality specifications and produces product descriptions, and statement 4 is correct because baseline changes from lower-level planning are controlled through the issue management approach (see manual 8.2.1, 8.2.1.6).

n.0: Both are wrong: recording check results is quality control (manual 8.2.2), and a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances, not quality tolerance (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 describes quality control, not quality planning (manual 8.2.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct but statement 3 is wrong: quality tolerances are not agreed in a work package description (manual 11.2.1).

Quality.q: While preparing the next stage plan, the project manager writes product descriptions that add requirements which alter the baselined project initiation documentation. How should these changes be handled?
o: By updating the project initiation documentation directly, as the project manager owns it
By recording them in the quality register as planned quality activities for the stage
By asking quality assurance to approve the revised product descriptions for the stage
Through the issue management approach, because they are changes to an approved baseline
Quality.w: Changes to the baselined project initiation documentation that arise from lower-level planning are handled through the issue management approach, as changes to a baseline (see manual 8.2.1.6).

n.0: The project initiation documentation is approved by the project board; the project manager cannot change a baseline without going through issue and change control (manual 8.2.1.6).
n.1: The quality register records quality activities and their results; it is not the means of controlling changes to baselines (manual 8.5).
n.2: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team and checks the quality control measures; it does not approve changes to baselined products (manual 8.2.3).

Quality.q: During quality planning, why should the project product description identify all of the project's major products?
o: So that requirements outside the approved scope do not creep into the lower-level product descriptions
So that the team manager can agree a quality tolerance for each product in the work package description
So that the quality register can show the result of each quality check before the products are built
So that quality assurance can approve each major product before the project board accepts it
Quality.w: By identifying all the major products in the project product description, the project prevents requirements that are outside the approved scope from appearing in product descriptions (see manual 8.2.1.1).

n.1: A work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances only; quality tolerance is not agreed there (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The quality register records checks that are planned or have taken place; it does not show results before products exist (manual 8.5).
n.3: Quality assurance gives independent confidence in the quality control measures; it does not approve individual products before acceptance (manual 8.2.3).

Quality.q: When is the quality management approach created, and who approves it?
o: During starting up a project, and the business layer approves it with the project mandate
During initiating a project, and quality assurance approves it on behalf of the business
During initiating a project, and the project board approves it in directing a project
During the first delivery stage, and the senior supplier approves it for the suppliers
Quality.w: The quality management approach is agreed in initiating a project (agree the management approaches) and approved by the project board in directing a project (see manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project product description, not the management approaches, and the business layer does not approve them (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.1: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team; the board, not quality assurance, approves the project's management approaches (manual 8.2.3, tab 14.3).
n.3: The approach must exist before delivery starts, as part of the project initiation documentation the board approves when it authorizes the project (manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).

Quality.q: Which statement describes quality control in PRINCE2?
o: Independently checking that the project's quality control measures are appropriate for the business
Monitoring specific products and their development activities to see whether they comply with standards
Capturing the quality specifications and writing the product descriptions for the stage
Transferring ownership of the project product to the project board on behalf of the users
Quality.w: Quality control consists of the procedures that monitor specific products and the activities that develop them, to check they comply with the relevant standards and to minimize causes of unsatisfactory performance (see manual 8.2.2).

n.0: Independently checking that the quality control measures are appropriate is quality assurance, carried out outside the project management team (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Capturing quality specifications and writing product descriptions is quality planning (manual 8.2.1).
n.3: Transferring ownership of the project product is project acceptance, the final part of the quality technique (manual 8.3.1.3).

Quality.q: A team has just completed a planned inspection of a draft training manual. In which part of the project log should the inspection and its result be recorded?
o: Daily log
Product register
Issue register
Quality register
Quality.w: The quality register summarizes all quality management activities planned or performed, recording each activity and its result (see manual 8.5, 8.3.1.2).

n.0: The daily log is the project manager's informal diary of actions and informal issues, not the formal record of quality checks (manual ch 11).
n.1: The product register lists all products required by a plan and their status; it does not record individual quality checks and results (manual 8.5).
n.2: The issue register records formal issues such as requests for change and off-specifications, not routine quality check results (manual ch 10).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

As well as checking whether products comply with the relevant standards, quality control aims to [?] the causes of unsatisfactory performance.
o: minimize
transfer
tolerate
escalate
Quality.w: Quality control monitors products and their development activities for compliance with standards and seeks to minimize the causes of unsatisfactory performance (see manual 8.2.2).

n.1: Transferring is what project acceptance does with ownership of the project product, not what quality control does with causes of poor performance (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.2: Quality tolerance sets how far quality may vary; quality control does not aim to tolerate the causes of unsatisfactory performance (manual 8.2.1.2, 8.2.2).
n.3: Escalation is how deviations beyond tolerance are handled under the progress practice; quality control seeks to reduce the causes (manual ch 11, 8.2.2).

Quality.q: What is the purpose of the quality register?
o: To list all of the products required by a plan, together with their current status
To describe the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the whole project
To summarize all the quality management activities that are planned or have taken place
To set out the quality specifications and quality method for one specific product
Quality.w: The quality register summarizes all quality management activities that are planned or have taken place, and the project manager and project assurance use it to review progress (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Listing all products of a plan and their status is the purpose of the product register (manual 8.5).
n.1: The quality techniques, standards and responsibilities are described in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).
n.3: A product's quality specifications and quality method are set out in its product description (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: A software module fails its planned test, but the team expects it to pass once some minor corrections have been made. What does PRINCE2 guidance on quality control allow?
o: The product is recorded as a concession and accepted without further checks
The team manager raises an exception report directly to the project board
The failed result is deleted from the quality register once the product passes
The check is repeated, with the activity and result recorded in the quality register
Quality.w: A failed quality check may be repeated where a pass is expected, and the quality register records the activity and its result (see manual 8.3.1.2).

n.0: A concession is an off-specification accepted without corrective action, a decision for the board or change authority; here the team plans to correct the product (manual ch 10).
n.1: Exception reports go from the project manager to the board when stage or project tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; a team manager reports to the project manager (manual ch 11).
n.2: Quality records are kept as evidence; the register records activities and results rather than removing failures (manual 8.5, 8.3.1.2).

Quality.q: How do the records produced by quality control support the project board's decision at the end of a stage?
o: The quality register is checked and its records provide input to the end stage report
The quality register is attached to the next stage plan to act as its stage tolerances
The quality records are sent to quality assurance, which authorizes the next stage
The quality records replace the highlight reports for the final weeks of the stage
Quality.w: In managing a stage boundary the quality register is checked to confirm the stage's quality activities were performed, and quality records feed the end stage report on which the board bases its next-stage decision (see manual 8.3.1.2, tab 18.3).

n.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board for the stage plan; the quality register is not a set of tolerances (manual 11.2).
n.2: The project board, not quality assurance, authorizes the next stage in directing a project (manual ch 14, 8.2.3).
n.3: Highlight reports continue at the agreed frequency throughout the stage; quality records do not replace them (manual ch 11).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about the quality register are correct?

1. It records each quality activity and its result, typically pass or fail.
2. It lists every product in a plan together with its current status.
3. It is created during starting up a project, before the project brief.
4. It is updated when quality activities in a work package are completed.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 1 is correct because the register records the activity and its result, and statement 4 is correct because in managing product delivery the completed quality activities are notified and the quality register is updated (see manual 8.3.1.2, tab 17.3).

n.0: Statement 2 describes the product register, not the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.1: Statement 2 describes the product register, and statement 3 is wrong because the registers are set up in initiating a project (manual 8.5, ch 15).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct but statement 3 is wrong: the quality register is set up in initiating a project, not starting up (manual ch 15).

Quality.q: A project manager is designing the quality register. Which heading would you expect it to include?
o: Derivation, showing the source products from which an item is built
Result, showing whether the check passed or failed and any follow-up
Composition, listing the parts that together make up the product
References, naming the business's quality management system
Quality.w: The quality register records, for each quality activity, the quality method, planned and actual dates, who was responsible and the result, including the response to any failure (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Derivation is a heading of a product description, describing where the product comes from (manual 8.5).
n.2: Composition is a heading of a product description, describing what the product is made of (manual 8.5).
n.3: References, such as the business's quality management system, are a heading of the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: Which statement describes quality assurance in PRINCE2?
o: The project board's responsibility to confirm that the whole project is being conducted correctly
Checking products against their quality specifications and recording the results
A planned, systematic activity giving confidence that products will meet their quality specifications
The process by which the users take ownership of the project product at closure
Quality.w: Quality assurance is a planned, systematic activity that gives confidence that products will meet their quality specifications when tested under quality control (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Confirming the project is being conducted correctly on the board's behalf is project assurance, not quality assurance (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.1: Checking products against specifications and recording the results is quality control (manual 8.2.2).
n.3: The transfer of ownership of the project product is project acceptance in the quality technique (manual 8.3.1.3).

Quality.q: Who typically performs quality assurance for a PRINCE2 project?
o: A business or programme function that is independent of the project management team
The members of the project board, acting as project assurance for their own interests
Project support, as part of maintaining the quality register and quality records
The team managers, as part of carrying out the quality checks in each work package
Quality.w: Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team, typically by a business or programme function such as part of the business's quality management system (see manual 8.2.3).

n.1: Board members are accountable for project assurance, which is independent of the project manager but part of the project; quality assurance sits outside the project management team (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Project support is part of the project management team and administers quality records; it cannot provide independent quality assurance (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.3: Team managers carry out quality control within work packages; quality assurance is independent of the project management team they belong to (manual 8.2.2, 8.2.3).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Quality assurance is performed [?] of the project management team, typically by a function of the business or programme.
o: on behalf
as a member
at the direction
independently
Quality.w: Quality assurance is carried out independently of the project management team, often by a business or programme quality function (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Acting on behalf of the project management team would remove the independence that quality assurance needs (manual 8.2.3).
n.1: Quality assurance is not done by a member of the project management team; that would be quality control or project assurance territory (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Quality assurance is not directed by the project management team; it reviews their quality control measures independently (manual 8.2.3).

Quality.q: When quality assurance reviews a project, what is it checking?
o: That the business case remains desirable, viable and achievable at each stage
That the project's quality control measures are appropriate for its products
That each stage is forecast to finish within its agreed time and cost tolerances
That each product's quality specifications are recorded in the project product description
Quality.w: Quality assurance gives independent confidence that the project's quality control measures are appropriate, so that products tested under them will meet their specifications (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Checking ongoing business justification is the executive's concern, supported by business-focused project assurance, not quality assurance (manual ch 5).
n.2: Forecasting stage performance against time and cost tolerances is part of the progress practice (manual ch 11).
n.3: Individual product specifications are held in product descriptions, not the project product description, and checking their location is not the aim of quality assurance (manual 8.1.1, 8.2.3).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about assurance are correct?

1. Quality assurance is the responsibility of the project board.
2. Project assurance is independent of the project manager but not of the project.
3. Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team.
4. Project support can carry out project assurance on behalf of the project board.
o: 1 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 2
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 2 is correct because project assurance is the board's responsibility and is independent of the project manager, not of the project; statement 3 is correct because quality assurance sits outside the project management team (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Both are wrong: project assurance (not quality assurance) is the board's responsibility, and project support can never carry out project assurance (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.2: Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 confuses quality assurance with project assurance (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is wrong: project support must be kept separate from project assurance (manual ch 6).

Quality.q: The project board of a regional transport project is deciding who could carry out project assurance for it. Which of the following should NOT be given this responsibility?
o: A member of the project board for the area they represent
A person appointed from elsewhere in the business
An external specialist appointed by the project board
The project support officer who maintains the registers
Quality.w: Project assurance may be carried out by board members, by people appointed from the business or by external specialists, but it must be independent of the project manager, so project support, team members and the project manager cannot do it (see manual 8.2.3, ch 6).

n.0: Board members are accountable for assurance of their own area and may carry it out themselves (manual ch 6).
n.1: The board may appoint people from elsewhere in the business to carry out project assurance (manual ch 6).
n.2: The board may also use external people to carry out project assurance (manual ch 6).

Quality.q: An auditor from a manufacturer's central quality office, acting for the company's quality management system rather than for the project board, confirms that a project's planned inspections and tests are suitable. Which activity is this?
o: Quality assurance
Project assurance
Quality control
Quality planning
Quality.w: An independent check, from outside the project management team and on behalf of the business's quality management system, that the quality control measures are appropriate is quality assurance (see manual 8.2.3).

n.1: Project assurance is carried out on behalf of the project board; this auditor acts for the company's quality system instead (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Quality control is the carrying out of the inspections and tests themselves, by the project, not an independent review of them (manual 8.2.2).
n.3: Quality planning is the project's own work of defining specifications, product descriptions and the quality management approach (manual 8.2.1).

Quality.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes quality assurance from project assurance?
o: Quality assurance is the senior user's responsibility; project assurance is the executive's
Quality assurance checks the business case; project assurance checks the specialist products
Quality assurance is independent of the project management team; project assurance of the project manager
Quality assurance is carried out by project support; project assurance by the business's quality office
Quality.w: Quality assurance is independent of the whole project management team, while project assurance is the board's responsibility and is independent of the project manager but not of the project (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Project assurance is shared by all board members for their own interests, and quality assurance is not a board role at all (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.1: Quality assurance concerns the appropriateness of quality control measures, and project assurance covers business, user and supplier interests, not just products (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.3: Project support cannot provide either form of assurance, and project assurance is done on behalf of the project board (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).

Quality.q: Which elements make up the PRINCE2 quality management technique?
o: Quality planning, quality control and quality assurance
Quality planning, quality control and project acceptance
Quality expectations, acceptance criteria and quality specifications
Quality review, quality audit and quality certification
Quality.w: The quality management technique has three parts: quality planning, quality control and project acceptance (see manual 8.3.1).

n.0: Quality planning, quality control and quality assurance are the three areas of guidance for effective quality management; the technique ends with project acceptance, not quality assurance (manual 8.2, 8.3.1).
n.2: Quality expectations, acceptance criteria and quality specifications are key quality concepts, not the steps of the technique (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Reviews and audits are examples of quality methods or assurance activities, not the elements of the PRINCE2 technique (manual 8.3.1).

Quality.q: In the quality management technique, what does project acceptance typically achieve?
o: It transfers ownership of the project product from the users to the supplier
It confirms that the quality management approach can be approved by the board
It records the planned dates of quality checks in the quality register
It transfers ownership of the project product to the project board for the users
Quality.w: Acceptance of the project product typically transfers ownership or responsibility from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (see manual 8.3.1.3).

n.0: The transfer runs the other way: from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the users (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.1: The quality management approach is approved by the board during initiation, long before project acceptance (manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).
n.2: Recording planned dates of quality checks belongs to quality planning and control through the quality register, not to acceptance (manual 8.3.1.2, 8.5).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Acceptance of the project product typically transfers [?] from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user.
o: ownership
tolerance
funding
assurance
Quality.w: Project acceptance typically transfers ownership or responsibility for the project product from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (see manual 8.3.1.3).

n.1: Tolerance is delegated downwards from the board to the project manager and team managers; it is not what acceptance transfers (manual ch 11).
n.2: Funding is secured by the executive; acceptance concerns the product, not the money (manual ch 6).
n.3: Assurance is the board's responsibility throughout the project; acceptance does not transfer it (manual 8.2.3).

Quality.q: Which part of the quality management technique involves carrying out the quality methods and recording the results?
o: Quality planning
Project acceptance
Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality.w: In quality control the planned quality methods are carried out and the results are recorded in the quality register (see manual 8.3.1.2).

n.0: Quality planning defines the specifications, product descriptions and the quality management approach before any methods are carried out (manual 8.3.1.1).
n.1: Project acceptance follows the quality checks and transfers ownership of the project product (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.3: Quality assurance is an independent check that quality control measures are appropriate; it is not one of the three parts of the technique and does not carry out the methods (manual 8.2.3).

Quality.q: Within the quality planning part of the technique, what does the quality management approach focus on?
o: How benefits will be measured and reviewed after the project has closed
How issues will be captured, assessed and decided during each stage
How each product's composition, derivation and format will be described
How quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported
Quality.w: In quality planning, the quality management approach focuses on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported (see manual 8.3.1.1).

n.0: How benefits will be measured after closure is set out in the benefits management approach (manual ch 5).
n.1: Capturing, assessing and deciding on issues is covered by the issue management approach and the issues technique (manual ch 10).
n.2: Composition, derivation and format are recorded for each product in its product description, not in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: Which statement about the quality planning part of the quality management technique is correct?
o: The user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria from starting up are a primary input
It starts after the first delivery stage, once there are products to inspect and test
It is carried out by quality assurance, independently of the project manager
It produces the quality register entries that confirm the products have passed their checks
Quality.w: The project product description, with the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria captured in starting up a project, is a primary input to quality planning (see manual 8.3.1.1).

n.1: Quality planning starts in starting up and initiating a project, before delivery, so that products are built against defined specifications (manual 8.3.1.1).
n.2: Quality planning is done by the project management team; quality assurance is independent of that team and checks the resulting controls (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: Entries confirming that checks were passed are produced during quality control, not quality planning (manual 8.3.1.2).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about the quality management technique are correct?

1. Quality assurance is the third part of the quality management technique.
2. The technique consists of quality planning, quality control and project acceptance.
3. Quality control records provide input to the end stage and end project reports.
4. Project acceptance transfers ownership of the project product to the supplier.
o: 1 and 2
3 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 2 names the three parts of the technique and statement 3 is correct because quality records feed the end stage and end project reports (see manual 8.3.1, 8.3.1.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: quality assurance is part of the guidance, while the technique's third part is project acceptance (manual 8.2, 8.3.1).
n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: acceptance transfers ownership from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.3: Both are wrong: the third part of the technique is project acceptance, and ownership passes to the board, not the supplier (manual 8.3.1, 8.3.1.3).

Quality.q: A community centre's final product has passed every planned quality check during the last delivery stage. Which part of the quality management technique follows?
o: Quality planning, so that the product descriptions can be baselined for the stage
Project acceptance, so ownership passes to the project board on behalf of the users
Quality assurance, so that the board can confirm its own quality controls were used
Quality control, so that the business layer can repeat the checks before handover
Quality.w: Once the products have passed their quality control, project acceptance follows, typically transferring ownership of the project product to the project board on behalf of the users (see manual 8.3.1.3).

n.0: Quality planning comes first in the technique and was done before the products were built (manual 8.3.1.1).
n.2: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team and is not a step of the technique; the board does not assure its own controls this way (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: Quality control has already been completed; the technique moves on to acceptance rather than the business layer repeating the checks (manual 8.3.1.2, 8.3.1.3).

Quality.q: What is the purpose of a product description?
o: To summarize all of the quality activities planned or carried out on the project
To list all of the products required by a plan, together with their current status
To describe a product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications
To describe the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the whole project
Quality.w: A product description describes a product's purpose, composition, derivation and format, together with its quality specifications, quality method and quality responsibilities (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Summarizing all planned and completed quality activities is the purpose of the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.1: Listing all products of a plan and their status is the purpose of the product register (manual 8.5).
n.3: The quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the project are described in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: Which management product, held in the project log, lists all of the products required by a plan together with their status?
o: Product register
Quality register
Product breakdown structure
Project product description
Quality.w: The product register, one of the records in the project log, lists all the products required by a plan and their status (see manual 8.5).

n.1: The quality register records quality activities and their results, not the status of every product (manual 8.5).
n.2: A product breakdown structure is a planning diagram showing the hierarchy of products; it does not track their status (manual ch 7).
n.3: The project product description describes the project's major products, quality expectations and acceptance criteria; it is not a status list (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The quality management approach forms part of the project [?] documentation and describes the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities to be applied.
o: assurance
completion
mandate
initiation
Quality.w: The quality management approach is one of the management approaches agreed in initiating a project and held in the project initiation documentation (see manual 8.5, 15.4.2).

n.0: Project assurance is a board responsibility carried out by people, not a set of documents; the approaches sit in the project initiation documentation (manual 8.2.3, 15.4.2).
n.1: Documents produced at completion, such as the end project report, review performance at the end; the approach is set at the start (manual ch 19).
n.2: The project mandate comes from the business layer to trigger starting up a project; it does not contain the management approaches (manual ch 13).

Quality.q: Which management product describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied, and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality?
o: Product description
Quality management approach
Quality register
Project product description
Quality.w: The quality management approach describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality specifications and acceptance criteria (see manual 8.5).

n.0: A product description defines one product, including its quality specifications, not the project's overall quality techniques and standards (manual 8.5).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities and results; it does not set the techniques and standards to be used (manual 8.5).
n.3: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product, not the techniques and responsibilities (manual 8.1.1).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about the quality practice's management products are correct?

1. A product description includes the quality specifications for the product.
2. The quality management approach records the result of each quality check.
3. The product register describes the format and composition of each product.
4. The quality register is one of the records held in the project log.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 1 is correct because a product description holds the product's quality specifications, and statement 4 is correct because the quality register is one of the project log records (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: check results are recorded in the quality register, not the quality management approach (manual 8.5).
n.2: Both are wrong: results go in the quality register, and format and composition are headings of a product description (manual 8.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct but statement 3 is wrong: format and composition belong in a product description, while the product register tracks product status (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: An events company insists that every supplier on its new venue project must operate a recognized quality policy. In which management product should this requirement be recorded?
o: The product description of the first deliverable
The quality register
The product register
The quality management approach
Quality.w: A requirement that all suppliers hold a quality policy is a project-wide quality standard and responsibility, so it belongs in the quality management approach (see manual 8.5).

n.0: A product description covers a single product's purpose, composition and quality specifications, not a rule applying to all suppliers (manual 8.5).
n.1: The quality register records quality activities and their results, not project-wide quality requirements (manual 8.5).
n.2: The product register lists products of a plan and their status; it is not where quality standards are set (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: A project manager is drafting the quality management approach. Which heading would you expect it to contain?
o: Supporting tools and techniques, such as testing, inspection and prototyping
Derivation, such as the source products that the deliverable is built from
Dates, showing when each quality check was planned and when it was actually held
Status, showing whether each product is in development or approved
Quality.w: The quality management approach includes headings for references, responsibilities, supporting tools and techniques (for example testing, inspection and prototyping) and standards (see manual 8.5).

n.1: Derivation is a heading of a product description (manual 8.5).
n.2: Planned and actual dates of each check are recorded in the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.3: The status of each product is tracked in the product register (manual 8.5).

Quality.q: When a team manager returns a completed work package, how does the project manager confirm that each product has gained the approval it requires?
o: By checking the acceptance criteria recorded in the project product description
By asking quality assurance to sign off each product before it is handed over
By checking the quality and sustainability responsibilities in each product description
By checking the quality tolerances agreed for it in the work package description
Quality.w: When receiving a completed work package, the project manager ensures each product has gained its requisite approval as defined by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description (see manual 16.4.3, 8.5).

n.0: Acceptance criteria in the project product description are for accepting the project product as a whole, not for approving each work package product (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team and does not sign off individual products (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: A work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances, not quality tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

Quality.q: On a construction project using two external contractors, which role is accountable for the quality of the products the suppliers deliver and for their technical integrity?
o: Senior user
Senior supplier
Project executive
Team manager
Quality.w: The senior supplier represents the suppliers on the project board and is accountable for the quality of products delivered by suppliers and their technical integrity (see manual ch 6, tab 8.2).

n.0: The senior user represents the users, specifying their requirements and benefits; the senior user does not answer for supplier quality (manual ch 6).
n.2: The executive owns the business case and is ultimately accountable for the project, but supplier product quality is the senior supplier's accountability (manual ch 6).
n.3: A team manager produces products to specification within a work package, but is not a board role and is not accountable for supplier quality overall (manual ch 6).

Quality.q: Which principle does the quality practice most directly apply when each product's quality specifications are defined in a product description?
o: Manage by stages
Learn from experience
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Quality.w: Focus on products centres the project on defining and delivering products, in particular their quality expectations and requirements; product descriptions with quality specifications are its main tool (see manual 2.6, tab 8.3).

n.0: Manage by stages is about planning, monitoring and controlling the project stage by stage with decision points, not defining product specifications (manual 2.4).
n.1: Learn from experience is about seeking, recording and applying lessons, not specifying products (manual 2.2).
n.2: Ensure continued business justification is about the project remaining justified, recorded in the business case, not specifying each product (manual 2.1).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Quality tolerances support the principle of manage by [?], because a product's quality may vary within agreed limits before the deviation has to be escalated.
o: exception
stages
objectives
results
Quality.w: Quality is one of the seven aspects for which tolerances are set; working within tolerance and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception (see manual 2.5, 8.2.1.2).

n.1: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and control with decision points, not the limits of delegated authority (manual 2.4).
n.2: 'Manage by objectives' is not a PRINCE2 principle; tolerances apply manage by exception (manual 2.5).
n.3: 'Manage by results' is not a PRINCE2 principle; tolerances apply manage by exception (manual 2.5).

Quality.q: Which role usually maintains the quality register and the quality records on behalf of the project manager?
o: Project assurance
Quality assurance
Project support
Senior supplier
Quality.w: Project support, which is the project manager's responsibility, maintains registers such as the quality register and administers quality records (see manual ch 6, tab 8.2).

n.0: Project assurance works for the project board and must be kept separate from the administrative work of project support (manual ch 6).
n.1: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team, so it does not maintain the project's registers (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: The senior supplier is a board role providing supplier resources and accountable for supplier quality, not an administrator of registers (manual ch 6).

Quality.q: How does the quality practice support the principle of tailor to suit the project?
o: By setting tolerances so that quality deviations are escalated to the right level of management
By recording lessons about quality methods so that later projects can learn from them
By ensuring that every product can be traced back to the project's business justification
By requiring only the quality activities appropriate to the delivery approach and products
Quality.w: The quality practice supports tailoring by requiring only those quality activities that suit the delivery approach and the characteristics of the products (see manual tab 8.3, 2.7).

n.0: Setting tolerances and escalating deviations applies manage by exception, not tailoring (manual 2.5).
n.1: Recording and passing on lessons applies learn from experience, not tailoring (manual 2.2).
n.2: Keeping products traceable to the business justification supports ensure continued business justification, not tailoring (manual 2.1, 8.1.2).

Quality.q: Which role is accountable for capturing the users' requirements and for monitoring that the products being delivered meet them?
o: Senior user
Senior supplier
Executive
Project manager
Quality.w: The senior user represents those who will use the products and is accountable for capturing user requirements and monitoring that the products meet them (see manual ch 6).

n.1: The senior supplier is accountable for the quality of products delivered by suppliers, not for capturing user requirements (manual ch 6).
n.2: The executive owns the business case and secures funding; capturing user requirements is the senior user's accountability (manual ch 6).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day and documents what is needed, but accountability for capturing user requirements rests with the senior user on the board (manual ch 6).

Quality.q:
Which two statements about quality roles and principles are correct?

1. Project assurance can be carried out by the project manager on behalf of the project board.
2. The senior supplier is accountable for the quality of products delivered by suppliers.
3. Defining quality specifications in product descriptions applies the focus on products principle.
4. Setting quality tolerances is mainly an application of the manage by stages principle.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Quality.w: Statement 2 is correct because supplier product quality is the senior supplier's accountability, and statement 3 is correct because product descriptions with quality specifications apply focus on products (see manual ch 6, 2.6).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: project assurance must be independent of the project manager (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.1: Both are wrong: the project manager cannot carry out project assurance, and tolerances apply manage by exception (manual ch 6, 2.5).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is wrong: tolerances apply manage by exception, not manage by stages (manual 2.5).

Quality.q: How does the quality practice support the principle of manage by stages?
o: Product descriptions for every product are written in full during initiation, before any stage plan
The quality register is checked at each stage end and feeds the end stage report for the next decision
Project acceptance of the project product takes place at the end of each delivery stage in turn
Quality assurance approves each stage plan before the project board authorizes the next stage
Quality.w: At each stage boundary the quality register is checked to confirm the stage's quality activities took place, and this feeds the end stage report the board uses at its stage decision point (see manual 2.4, tab 18.3).

n.0: Product descriptions are written for each stage as it is planned in managing a stage boundary, not all in full at initiation; this does not support stage-by-stage control (manual 2.4, ch 18).
n.2: Project acceptance concerns the project product as a whole and happens when the project closes, not at every stage end (manual 8.3.1.3, ch 19).
n.3: The project board approves stage plans in directing a project; quality assurance is independent and does not approve them (manual ch 14, 8.2.3).

Quality.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the quality practice in PRINCE2?
o: To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable
To identify, assess and control uncertainty so that the project's chances of success are improved
To document the user's requirements of the project's products and establish the means by which they will be met
