To establish mechanisms to monitor actual achievements against those planned and to control any deviations
Quality.w: The quality practice exists to document what the user requires of the project's products and to establish how those requirements will be met, so that the products are fit for purpose (see manual 8.1).

n.0: Judging whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable is the purpose of the business case practice (manual 5.1).
n.1: Identifying, assessing and controlling uncertainty is the purpose of the risk practice (manual 9.1).
n.3: Monitoring actual against planned achievement and controlling deviations is the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).

Quality.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The quality practice documents the user's [?] of the project's products and establishes the means by which they will be met, so that the products are fit for purpose.
o: requirements
benefits
tolerances
dependencies
Quality.w: The purpose of the quality practice is to document the user's requirements of the project's products and to establish how they will be met (see manual 8.1).

n.1: Benefits are the measurable improvements the business case practice justifies and tracks; the quality practice is about what the products must be like (manual 5.1, 8.1).
n.2: Tolerances are the permitted deviations set under the progress practice; quality tolerance is one tool of the quality practice, not what it documents from the user (manual 11.2, 8.2.1.2).
n.3: Dependencies between products are identified by the plans practice when sequencing the work, not documented as the user's needs (manual ch 7).

Quality.q: A new hospital outpatients project is being set up. Which practice is concerned with documenting what the users need from the project's products and establishing how the project will meet those needs?
o: Plans
Business case
Progress
Quality
Quality.w: Documenting the user's requirements of the products and establishing the means of meeting them is the purpose of the quality practice (see manual 8.1).

n.0: Plans defines the products to be delivered and the means, timing and cost of delivering them; it does not document the users' quality requirements (manual 7.1).
n.1: Business case judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable; it does not set out what the users need from each product (manual 5.1).
n.2: Progress monitors actual against planned performance and controls deviations; it does not document the users' requirements (manual 11.1).

Quality.q: How does the quality practice help the project to deliver value to the business that commissions it?
o: It sets the benefits tolerance that the project board uses to judge whether the project is still viable
It defines products that meet the users' requirements and expectations so they can enable the benefits
It replaces the business case as the basis on which the project board authorizes each delivery stage
It measures the benefits achieved after closure by recording them in the quality register
Quality.w: In PRINCE2, quality means the products meet their requirements and expectations and so enable the benefits the business wants; this is why the quality practice matters to value (see manual 8.1).

n.0: Benefits tolerance is set through the business case practice and recorded in the benefits management approach, not set by the quality practice (manual 5.1, 11.2).
n.2: The business case remains the basis for the board's stage decisions; the quality practice does not replace it (manual 5.1, ch 14).
n.3: The quality register records quality activities and their results; benefits after closure are reviewed under the benefits management approach (manual 8.5, 5.5).

Risk.q: A project manager tells the board: 'Our risk register is thorough, so we can be certain the project will meet its objectives.' Why is this view inconsistent with the purpose of the risk practice?
o: A thorough register shows that the project is not viable, so the board should consider closing it early
Managing risk improves the project's chance of success but cannot guarantee that the agreed objectives will be met
The risk register records events that have already happened, so it says little about future uncertainty
Risk management deals with opportunities, so a register of threats cannot show whether the project will succeed
Risk.w: The risk practice improves the ability of the project to succeed; it does not guarantee that the agreed objectives will be met (see manual 9.1).

n.0: The number of risks recorded does not by itself show that the project is unviable; viability is judged through the business case (manual 5.1, 9.1).
n.2: The risk register records identified risks, which are uncertain future events; events that have happened go to the issue register or daily log (manual 9.5, 10.1).
n.3: The risk practice deals with both threats and opportunities, and threats are a central part of it (manual 9.1).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the risk practice are correct?
1. It identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty that would affect the project's objectives.
2. It collects issues and controls changes to the project's baseline.
3. It improves the ability of the project to succeed.
4. It makes sure that every threat is removed before a stage is authorized.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Risk.w: Statement 1 is the core of the purpose, and statement 3 is its result: controlling uncertainty improves the project's ability to succeed (see manual 9.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is the purpose of the issues practice, not the risk practice (manual 10.1).
n.2: Statement 2 describes the issues practice, and statement 4 is wrong because threats cannot all be removed; many are reduced, accepted or covered by contingent plans (manual 9.1, 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the practice does not require every threat to be removed before a stage is authorized, and removal is not possible for many threats (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which practice is concerned with an uncertain event that, if it occurred, would have a positive effect on the project's objectives?
o: Issues, because a business opportunity is one of the types of issue that the project records
Risk, because an uncertain event with a positive effect on objectives is an opportunity
Business case, because the effect on objectives would change the project's expected benefits
Progress, because the effect on objectives would be reported in the next highlight report
Risk.w: An opportunity is an uncertain event that would have a positive effect on objectives, and opportunities are managed by the risk practice (see manual 9.1).

n.0: A business opportunity issue is an event that has already arisen and needs consideration; an uncertain future event with a positive effect is a risk (manual 9.1, 10.2).
n.2: The business case reflects the project's aggregated risk, but uncertain events themselves are identified and controlled by the risk practice (manual 5.1, 9.1).
n.3: Reports communicate risks, but identifying, assessing and controlling the uncertainty is the work of the risk practice (manual 9.1, 9.3.1).

Risk.q: A team reports that a key supplier might go out of business before delivery, and also that a test server has failed. How should these be treated?
o: The possible supplier failure is a risk; the server failure, which has happened, is an issue
Both are risks, because each of them would affect the achievement of the project's objectives
Both are issues, because each of them is an event that needs project management consideration
The server failure is a risk, because its full effect on the stage is not yet known
Risk.w: A risk is an uncertain event that may occur; something that has already happened is an issue and is handled by the issues practice (see manual 9.1, 10.1).

n.1: The server failure has already happened, so it is not uncertain; it is an issue, even though it affects objectives (manual 10.1).
n.2: The supplier failure has not happened and may not happen, so it is an uncertain event: a risk (manual 9.1).
n.3: Uncertainty about the size of the effect does not make an event that has already occurred into a risk; it is an issue to be assessed (manual 10.1).

Risk.q: In the risk practice, what is a risk owner?
o: The person nominated to own a specific agreed action that responds to a risk
The person who maintains the risk register and keeps its entries up to date
The person who sets the threshold beyond which a risk must be escalated
The person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a particular risk
Risk.w: A risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a risk; they may ask a risk action owner to carry out agreed actions (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This describes the risk action owner, also called the risk actionee, who carries out agreed actions for the risk owner (manual 9.2).
n.1: Maintaining the register is an administrative task usually given to project support; it does not make them responsible for responding to a risk (manual 9.5, appendix B).
n.2: Thresholds for risk are risk tolerances, set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite; that is not the risk owner's role (manual 9.2.1).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The person nominated to own agreed actions to respond to a risk, also known as the risk actionee, is the [?].
o: risk action owner
risk owner
issue owner
project assurance
Risk.w: The risk action owner (risk actionee) owns the agreed actions taken in response to a risk, on behalf of the risk owner (see manual 9.2).

n.1: The risk owner is responsible for responding to the risk as a whole and may nominate a risk action owner for specific actions (manual 9.2).
n.2: An issue owner manages an issue that has already arisen; the term for owning agreed risk actions is risk action owner (manual 9.2, 10.2).
n.3: Project assurance reviews how the project is run for the board; it is not the named owner of agreed risk actions (manual 6.2.4.7, 9.2).

Risk.q: How does PRINCE2 recommend that each risk is described?
o: In terms of its cause, the uncertain event, and the effect it would have on objectives
In terms of its probability, its proximity, and the response category chosen for it
In terms of the objective at risk, the risk owner, and the date it was first registered
In terms of the threat, the matching opportunity, and the overall risk exposure
Risk.w: Describing a risk by its cause (the source), event (the uncertain occurrence) and effect (the impact on objectives) makes it clear and comparable (see manual 9.2.1).

n.1: Probability, proximity and response category are assessed and recorded for a risk, but they do not describe what the risk is (manual 9.2.2, 9.5).
n.2: Owner and date are register details; the description itself sets out cause, event and effect (manual 9.2.1, 9.5).
n.3: A risk is either a threat or an opportunity; overall exposure is assessed across risks and is not part of a single risk's description (manual 9.1, 9.2).

Risk.q: What is the difference between a threat and an opportunity?
o: A threat would have a negative effect on objectives if it occurred; an opportunity a positive one
A threat is likely to occur soon; an opportunity is likely to occur later in the project
A threat affects the project's objectives; an opportunity affects the business layer's objectives
A threat is recorded in the risk register; an opportunity is recorded in the issue register
Risk.w: PRINCE2 uses 'threat' for an uncertain event with a negative effect on objectives and 'opportunity' for one with a positive effect (see manual 9.1).

n.1: When a risk might occur is its proximity; it does not decide whether the risk is a threat or an opportunity (manual 9.1, 9.2).
n.2: Both threats and opportunities are defined by their effect on the project's objectives (manual 9.1).
n.3: Both threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register (manual 9.5).

Risk.q: A risk is written as: 'Because the venue has a single access road, the road may be closed by roadworks, which would delay equipment delivery by two days.' Which part is the risk event?
o: The venue having a single access road
The two-day delay to equipment delivery
The supplier that will deliver the equipment
The possible closure of the road by roadworks
Risk.w: The event is the uncertain occurrence: the road may be closed. The single access road is the cause, and the two-day delay is the effect (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: This is a current fact that gives rise to the risk, so it is the cause, not the uncertain event (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: This is what would happen to objectives if the event occurred, so it is the effect (manual 9.2.1).
n.2: The supplier is not part of the cause, event and effect described; the event is the possible road closure (manual 9.2.1).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about risk owners and risk action owners are correct?
1. The risk owner is responsible for responding to the risk.
2. The risk action owner is responsible for managing the risk as a whole.
3. The risk action owner carries out agreed actions to respond to the risk.
4. Project support is the risk owner for each risk in the register.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Risk.w: Statement 1 matches the definition of the risk owner, and statement 3 matches the risk action owner, who owns agreed actions for the risk owner (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: overall responsibility for responding to the risk sits with the risk owner, not the risk action owner (manual 9.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: the risk owner, not the action owner, responds to the risk, and project support administers the register rather than owning risks (manual 9.2, appendix B).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: project support provides risk administration but is not assigned as owner of every risk (manual 9.2, appendix B).

Risk.q: Which statement best reflects how PRINCE2 treats opportunities?
o: They are managed with the same discipline as threats and are recorded in the risk register
They are recorded in the issue register as business opportunities as soon as they are identified
They are passed to the business layer, as they affect benefits rather than project objectives
They are noted in the daily log, while threats are entered in the risk register
Risk.w: Opportunities are risks with a positive effect on objectives, so they go through the same technique as threats and are recorded in the risk register (see manual 9.1, 9.5).

n.1: An uncertain future opportunity is a risk and belongs in the risk register; a business opportunity issue is an event that has already arisen (manual 9.5, 10.2).
n.2: Opportunities are managed by the project's risk practice; they are defined by their positive effect on objectives (manual 9.1).
n.3: Both threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register; the daily log is for informal issues and notes (manual 9.5).

Risk.q: A draft risk register entry reads: 'The supplier is already two weeks late with the design.' Why is this not a well-formed risk?
o: It names a supplier, and a risk must be described without reference to any party outside the project
It does not state a probability, and each risk description must start with its probability
It is a threat, and threats are recorded in a separate register from opportunities
It describes something that has already happened, so it is an issue or a cause rather than an uncertain event
Risk.w: A risk is uncertain. A situation that is already true is an issue, or it may be the cause of a risk, for example a late design that may delay testing (see manual 9.1, 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk descriptions may refer to external parties; the problem is that the event has already happened (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: Probability is assessed and recorded separately; the description sets out cause, event and effect (manual 9.2.1, 9.2.2).
n.2: Threats and opportunities are both recorded in the risk register (manual 9.5).

Risk.q: In the risk practice, what is meant by risk proximity?
o: How quickly a risk would affect objectives once it occurs
How likely it is that a risk will occur during the project
How near in time a risk might occur
How far a particular objective is at risk overall
Risk.w: Risk proximity is how near in time a risk might occur; it helps decide when responses are needed (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk velocity, a separate measure of how fast the impact would arrive after the event (manual 9.2).
n.1: This is risk probability, the estimated chance of occurrence (manual 9.2).
n.3: This is risk exposure, the degree to which an objective is at risk (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: What does risk velocity describe?
o: How near in time a risk might occur during the project
How quickly a risk would have an impact on objectives should it occur
The estimated chance that a risk will occur in the current stage
The rate at which new risks are added to the risk register
Risk.w: Risk velocity, a concept added in PRINCE2 7, is how quickly a risk would affect objectives once it occurs (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk proximity: when the risk might happen, not how fast its effect would follow (manual 9.2).
n.2: This is risk probability, the estimated likelihood or frequency of occurrence (manual 9.2).
n.3: Velocity is a property of a single risk's impact after it occurs, not a count of new risks (manual 9.2).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Risk [?] is the estimated effect on objectives should a risk occur, and it is expressed in the same units as the objective affected.
o: impact
probability
exposure
proximity
Risk.w: Risk impact is the estimated effect on objectives if a risk occurs, for example in days or pounds when those are how the objectives are measured (see manual 9.2, 9.3.1.2).

n.1: Probability is the estimated chance that a risk will occur, not its effect on objectives (manual 9.2).
n.2: Exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk overall, rather than the estimated effect of one risk occurring (manual 9.2).
n.3: Proximity is how near in time a risk might occur (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: What is meant by risk probability?
o: The estimated effect on the project's objectives if the risk were to occur
The degree to which a particular objective of the project is at risk overall
The measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes of each objective at risk
The estimated chance that a risk will occur, judged from its likelihood or frequency
Risk.w: Risk probability is the estimated chance of a risk occurring, often estimated from its probability or frequency of occurrence (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk impact, which is measured in the units of the objective affected (manual 9.2).
n.1: This is risk exposure, a neutral measure that can be positive or negative (manual 9.2).
n.2: This is risk tolerance, set by the project board (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).

Risk.q: Which statement about risk exposure is correct?
o: It is the degree to which an objective is at risk, and it applies to threats as opportunities carry no exposure
It is how near in time a risk might occur, and it is recorded as a heading for each risk in the register
It is the amount and type of risk the business will take, and it is set by the business layer
It is the degree to which an objective is at risk, and it is neutral as it can be positive or negative
Risk.w: Risk exposure is the degree to which a particular objective is at risk. It is a neutral concept because exposure can be negative (threats) or positive (opportunities) (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Exposure is neutral: opportunities create positive exposure just as threats create negative exposure (manual 9.2).
n.1: How near in time a risk might occur is proximity; exposure for an individual risk is not a register heading (manual 9.2, 9.5).
n.2: This describes risk appetite, which is set by the business (manual 9.2).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about the measures used to assess risks are correct?
1. Proximity describes when a risk might occur.
2. Velocity describes the estimated chance that a risk will occur.
3. Impact is estimated in the units used for the affected objective, such as days or pounds.
4. Exposure is a negative concept, as it applies to threats.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Risk.w: Statement 1 is the definition of proximity, and statement 3 reflects how impact is estimated in the same units as the objective (see manual 9.2, 9.3.1.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the estimated chance of occurrence is probability; velocity is how quickly the impact would be felt (manual 9.2).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: exposure is neutral and can be positive or negative (manual 9.2).
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: velocity is how quickly a risk would affect objectives once it occurs, not its probability (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: A threat might arise in nine months' time, but if it occurred it would stop all work within hours. Which statement correctly describes this threat?
o: It has a high proximity, as its impact would arrive within hours
It has a low probability, as it may not occur for nine months
It is not near in time, but it has a high velocity
It has a low impact, as the project has time to prepare for it
Risk.w: Nine months away describes its proximity (not near). Stopping work within hours of occurring describes a high velocity, so a contingent plan may be needed well in advance (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Proximity is how near in time the risk might occur (nine months here); the speed of the impact is velocity (manual 9.2).
n.1: Timing does not set probability; how likely the threat is to occur is a separate estimate (manual 9.2).
n.3: Impact is the effect on objectives if it occurs; halting all work is a severe effect whatever the timing (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: When assessing risks, what does the project compare with the risk tolerance and the business's risk appetite?
o: The proximity of the individual risk that is nearest in time
The velocity of the fastest-acting threat in the register
The impact of the most severe individual threat
The combined risk exposure across all of the project's risks
Risk.w: In the assess step the project assesses the combined risk profile: the aggregated exposure of all risks, compared with risk tolerance and appetite (see manual 9.3.1.2).

n.0: Proximity helps prioritize individual risks; the comparison with tolerance and appetite uses the aggregated exposure (manual 9.3.1.2).
n.1: Velocity is used to prioritize single risks; tolerance applies to the plan's aggregated risks (manual 9.2, 9.3.1.2).
n.2: One threat's impact does not show the overall position; risk tolerance relates to the aggregated risks (manual 9.3.1.2).

Risk.q: In the risk practice, what is risk appetite?
o: A measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes of each objective at risk
A sum of money set aside to fund specific responses to threats and opportunities
The amount and type of risk the business is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives
The degree to which a particular objective is at risk from the project's risks
Risk.w: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk taking: the amount and type of risk it will accept in pursuit of its objectives (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk tolerance, which the project board sets based on the business's appetite (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).
n.1: This is the risk budget, which funds responses such as contingent plans (manual 9.2).
n.3: This is risk exposure, a neutral measure of how far an objective is at risk (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: What is risk tolerance?
o: The amount and type of risk that the business is willing to take to meet its objectives
A sum of money held to cover the cost of contingent plans if a risk occurs
A measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes for each objective at risk
The estimated chance that the project's risks will occur over its life
Risk.w: Risk tolerance is a measurable threshold representing the tolerable range of outcomes for each objective at risk, in the same units used to measure that objective (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk appetite, set by the business; tolerance turns it into measurable thresholds for the project (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).
n.1: This is the risk budget (manual 9.2).
n.3: This describes probability, which is estimated for each risk; it is not a threshold (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: Who sets the risk tolerance for a project?
o: The business layer, as part of the project mandate it provides
The project manager, when writing the risk management approach
Project assurance, after it has reviewed the risk register
The project board, based on the business's overall risk appetite
Risk.w: Risk tolerance is set by the project board, based on the overall risk appetite determined by the business (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: The business layer determines the risk appetite; the project board applies it by setting the project's risk tolerance (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: The project manager drafts the approach, which records the tolerance, but the tolerance itself is set by the project board (manual 9.2.1).
n.2: Project assurance reviews risk management on behalf of the board; it does not set the tolerance (manual 6.2.4.7, 9.2.1).

Risk.q: What is the risk budget used for?
o: To fund approved requests for change to the project's baseline during the current stage
To absorb overspends on a stage that stay within the cost tolerance agreed by the board
To fund specific responses to threats and opportunities, such as contingent plans
To pay for quality assurance that the business carries out on the project
Risk.w: The risk budget is money set aside to fund specific management responses to threats and opportunities, for example the cost of a contingent plan if a risk occurs (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Approved changes to the baseline are funded from the change budget, which is a separate budget prepared in the planning technique (manual 7, 9.2).
n.1: Cost tolerance is the permitted variation from the budget; the risk budget is for specific risk responses (manual 9.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: Quality assurance is a business function; the risk budget funds responses to threats and opportunities (manual 8.2.3, 9.2).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Risk [?] is determined by the business, and the project board applies it when setting measurable risk thresholds for the project.
o: tolerance
exposure
budget
appetite
Risk.w: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the business is willing to take; the board bases the project's risk tolerance on it (see manual 9.2, 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk tolerance is the measurable threshold itself, set by the project board, rather than the business's attitude it is based on (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: Risk exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk; it is assessed, not determined by the business (manual 9.2).
n.2: The risk budget funds responses to risks; it is not the basis for setting tolerance (manual 9.2).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about risk appetite and risk tolerance are correct?
1. Risk appetite reflects the business's attitude to taking risk.
2. Risk tolerance is expressed in the same units used to measure the objective at risk.
3. Risk appetite is a measurable threshold set by the project manager for each stage.
4. Risk tolerance is a sum of money used to fund contingent plans.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Risk.w: Statement 1 describes risk appetite, set by the business. Statement 2 describes risk tolerance, a measurable threshold in the objective's own units (see manual 9.2).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: appetite is the business's attitude to risk; measurable thresholds are tolerances, set by the project board (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: money to fund contingent plans is the risk budget, not risk tolerance (manual 9.2).
n.3: Both are wrong: appetite is not a threshold set by the project manager, and tolerance is not a sum of money (manual 9.2).

Risk.q: During a stage, the project manager forecasts that the aggregated risk on the stage will go beyond the agreed risk tolerance. What should happen?
o: The project manager should increase the risk budget to restore the tolerance
The business layer should revise its risk appetite to match the forecast
The situation should be escalated to the project board as an exception
The team manager should raise a concession for the stage's risk position
Risk.w: Risk is one of the seven tolerance areas, covering the plan's aggregated risks. A forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated to the board through an exception report, applying manage by exception (see manual 2.5, 9.2.1, 11.2.1).

n.0: The risk budget funds specific responses; the project manager cannot use it to change the tolerance the board has set (manual 9.2).
n.1: A forecast breach of stage tolerance goes to the project board; appetite is the business's standing attitude to risk and is not adjusted to fit one stage (manual 9.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: A concession is an off-specification accepted without corrective action; it does not apply to risk tolerance (manual 10.2).

Risk.q: Why does PRINCE2 keep the risk budget separate from the change budget?
o: The risk budget funds new user requirements, while the change budget funds contingent plans for threats
The risk budget is held by the business layer, while the change budget is held by the team manager
The risk budget funds responses to risks, while the change budget funds approved changes to the baseline
The risk budget is spent during initiation, while the change budget is spent in later delivery stages
Risk.w: The risk budget pays for specific risk responses, such as contingent plans. The change budget pays for authorized changes to the baseline. Keeping them apart stops one being used up by the other (see manual 7 (preparing the budget), 9.2).

n.0: This reverses the two: new requirements are changes funded by the change budget, and contingent plans are funded by the risk budget (manual 9.2).
n.1: Both budgets are part of the project's planned budget and are controlled within the project; team managers do not hold the change budget (manual 7, preparing the budget).
n.3: Both can be used in any stage; the difference is what they fund, not when they are spent (manual 7, 9.2).

Risk.q: Which response to a threat makes the uncertain situation certain by removing the risk, for example by removing its cause?
o: Reduce
Transfer
Accept
Avoid
Risk.w: Avoid removes the threat, often by removing its cause, so the uncertain situation becomes certain (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.0: Reduce takes definite action now to change the probability or impact, so some residual risk remains (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Transfer passes part of the financial impact to a third party, such as an insurer; the threat itself remains (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Accept takes the chance and monitors the risk, with no action now to remove it (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which pair shows a threat response and its matching opportunity response?
o: Avoid a threat and share an opportunity
Transfer a threat and exploit an opportunity
Accept a threat and enhance an opportunity
Reduce a threat and enhance an opportunity
Risk.w: Reduce and enhance are the matching pair: both take definite action now to change probability or impact. The other pair-specific match is avoid and exploit (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.0: Avoid is paired with exploit, as both make the situation certain; share is used for threats and opportunities alike (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Transfer is used for threats and opportunities alike, and exploit pairs with avoid, not with transfer (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Accept is used for threats and opportunities alike; enhance is the opportunity match for reduce (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: What does the 'prepare contingent plans' response involve?
o: Taking definite action now to change the probability or impact of the risk
Planning actions now that will be carried out if the risk occurs
Passing part of the financial impact of the risk to a third party
Taking the chance and monitoring the risk with no further plans made
Risk.w: Preparing contingent plans means deciding now what to do, and putting it in place to be used if the risk occurs; it is often funded from the risk budget (see manual 9.2, 9.2.3.1).

n.0: This describes reduce (for a threat) or enhance (for an opportunity) (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: This describes transfer, for example through insurance or a contract (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: This describes accept; a contingent plan is a prepared set of actions (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: A building project takes out insurance so that an insurer will pay for repairs if a crane collapses on site. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer the risk
Share the risk
Reduce the threat
Avoid the threat
Risk.w: Transfer passes all or part of the financial impact of a risk to a third party, such as an insurer (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.1: Share is a pain and gain arrangement with a partner, common in customer and supplier contracts; insurance is a transfer (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Insurance does not change the probability that the crane collapses or the physical damage; it moves the financial impact (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: The threat still exists after insurance is bought, so it has not been avoided (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which is NOT a response type that can be used for an opportunity?
o: Avoid
Exploit
Share
Prepare contingent plans
Risk.w: Avoid is a threat response. The opportunity responses are exploit, enhance, transfer, share, accept and prepare contingent plans (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.1: Exploit is the opportunity response that makes the opportunity certain (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Share applies to both threats and opportunities, for example through a gain-share contract (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Contingent plans can be prepared for opportunities as well as for threats (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about risk responses are correct?
1. Exploit makes an opportunity certain to happen.
2. Enhance removes the uncertainty from an opportunity.
3. A reduce response can leave a residual risk.
4. Share passes the whole financial impact of a risk to an insurer.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
Risk.w: Statement 1 describes exploit, which makes the situation certain. Statement 3 is right because reducing a threat rather than removing it leaves residual risk (see manual 9.2.3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: enhance changes probability or impact but leaves the opportunity uncertain; making it certain is exploit (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: passing financial impact to an insurer is transfer; share is a pain and gain arrangement with a partner (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: removing the uncertainty from an opportunity is exploit, not enhance (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: A software project assigns its most experienced tester to raise the chance that the product passes certification a month early. Which response is this?
o: Exploit, because it acts now to make sure the opportunity will happen
Enhance, because it acts now to increase the probability of the opportunity
Share, because the tester and the project both gain from passing early
Accept, because the project is waiting to see whether the pass happens early
Risk.w: Enhance takes definite action now to increase the probability or positive impact of an opportunity. Passing early is still uncertain, so it is not exploit (see manual 9.2.3.1).

n.0: Exploit makes the opportunity certain; extra testing effort raises the chance of an early pass but does not guarantee it (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Share is a pain and gain arrangement, usually in a contract with a partner; assigning a team member is not sharing (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Accept takes no action now; assigning a tester is definite action to change the probability (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which statement about choosing risk responses is correct?
o: Avoidance should be chosen for each threat where possible, as it gives the project the lowest exposure
Threats and opportunities use identical response types, so one response list covers both of them
The best response depends on the situation and type of risk, and threats and opportunities can differ
Accept is reserved for opportunities, as each threat needs definite action from the risk owner
Risk.w: PRINCE2 says the best response depends on the particular situation and type of risk, and it gives different response types for threats and opportunities (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.0: Avoiding every threat can be costly or impossible; the choice depends on the situation and type of risk (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Some responses are specific: avoid and reduce for threats, exploit and enhance for opportunities (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Accept applies to threats as well as opportunities; taking the chance and monitoring can be the right choice (manual 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which decision bias describes a mindset that values avoiding a loss more than making a gain?
o: Optimism bias
Groupthink
Loss aversion
Proximity bias
Risk.w: Loss aversion is a mindset that values avoiding loss over making a gain. It is one of the decision biases PRINCE2 names under risk culture (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk on the assumption that things will turn out well (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: Groupthink values cohesion within a group over voicing a different view or reaching the right decision (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Proximity bias makes situations closer in time seem riskier and more important than later ones (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q: In the risk practice, what is optimism bias?
o: A mindset that values avoiding a loss more highly than making an equivalent gain
A mindset that values the cohesion of a group more than voicing a different view
A mindset in which situations closer in time are seen as riskier and more important
A mindset that discounts disadvantageous risk, assuming that things are likely to succeed
Risk.w: Optimism bias leads people to discount risks that could harm them, on the assumption that things will be successful for them (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: This describes loss aversion (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: This describes groupthink (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: This describes proximity bias, not optimism bias (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q: How does PRINCE2 describe decision bias in its guidance on risk culture?
o: As a failing that a mature risk culture removes from the project's decision-making
As a concern for the business layer rather than for the project management team
As natural and largely positive, though it can sometimes lead to less effective decisions
As a problem that affects how threats are judged but not how opportunities are judged
Risk.w: Decision bias is natural and largely positive, because it lets people make rapid decisions every day; sometimes, though, it leads to less effective decision-making (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Bias is natural and mostly helpful; the guidance is to understand it, not to remove it (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: Decision bias affects decisions at every level of the project, so the project management team needs to understand it (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Bias can affect any risk decision; loss aversion, for example, can stop people pursuing a gain (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The decision bias known as [?] makes people value cohesion within a group more than expressing a different view or reaching the right decision.
o: loss aversion
groupthink
optimism bias
proximity bias
Risk.w: Groupthink is the bias in which keeping the group together matters more than challenging a view or reaching the right decision (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Loss aversion values avoiding loss over making a gain (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk on the assumption of success (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Proximity bias treats nearer situations as riskier and more important (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q: In a risk workshop, the team spends most of its time on a minor supplier delay due next week, because it is soon, and gives little attention to a serious regulatory threat six months away. Which bias is most likely affecting them?
o: Optimism bias
Proximity bias
Groupthink
Loss aversion
Risk.w: Proximity bias is a mindset in which situations closer in time seem riskier and more important than those further in the future (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Optimism bias discounts risk on the assumption of success; here the team's attention follows how soon each risk is (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: Groupthink is about keeping group cohesion rather than voicing other views; nothing suggests people are suppressing disagreement (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Loss aversion values avoiding loss over gains; the team's focus here is driven by nearness in time (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about risk culture and decision bias are correct?
1. Decision bias lets people make rapid decisions and is largely positive.
2. Groupthink drives people to discount risks on the assumption of success.
3. Bias can sometimes result in less effective decisions about risk.
4. Loss aversion makes people see near-term situations as more important.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
Risk.w: Statements 1 and 3 together summarize the guidance: bias is natural and largely positive, but it can sometimes lead to less effective decisions (see manual 9.2.4).

n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: seeing near-term situations as more important is proximity bias; loss aversion values avoiding loss over gain (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: discounting risk on the assumption of success is optimism bias, not groupthink (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Both are wrong: statement 2 describes optimism bias and statement 4 describes proximity bias (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q: How does PRINCE2 7 suggest that data can support the risk practice?
o: Analytics can replace the risk owner by choosing and carrying out the responses to each risk
Data analysis can set the business's risk appetite on behalf of the business layer
Data is gathered after closure to confirm which risks occurred, for the benefits review
Data and analytics can help the project identify and assess risks, giving evidence for its decisions
Risk.w: PRINCE2 7 encourages the use of data and analytics to identify and assess risks, for example to forecast exposure, which also helps to counter decision bias (see manual 9.3.2.6).

n.0: Data informs decisions, but risk owners and risk action owners are still identified and agreed for each risk (manual 9.3.1.4).
n.1: Risk appetite is determined by the business; data supports identifying and assessing risks (manual 9.2, 9.3.2.6).
n.2: The guidance is about using data during the project to identify and assess risks, not about a post-project check (manual 9.3.2.6).

Risk.q: A project board hesitates to approve a low-cost trial that could deliver a large saving, mainly because it fears losing the small trial budget. Which bias does this show?
o: Groupthink
Proximity bias
Loss aversion
Optimism bias
Risk.w: Loss aversion values the avoidance of a loss more than making a gain, so a small possible loss outweighs a larger possible saving (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Groupthink concerns valuing group cohesion over dissent; the hesitation here comes from fear of a loss (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: Proximity bias is about nearness in time; the board is weighing loss against gain (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Optimism bias would make the board discount the risk and assume success, the opposite of what happens here (manual 9.2.4).

Risk.q: What is the correct order of the first four steps of the PRINCE2 risk management technique?
o: Identify, assess, plan, implement
Identify, plan, assess, implement
Assess, identify, plan, implement
Identify, assess, implement, plan
Risk.w: The technique runs identify, assess, plan and implement in sequence, with communicate running alongside all four (see manual 9.3.1, figure 9.2).

n.1: Risks must be assessed and prioritized before responses are planned (manual 9.3.1).
n.2: A risk cannot be assessed until it has been identified (manual 9.3.1).
n.3: Responses are planned before they are implemented (manual 9.3.1).

Risk.q: Which statement about the communicate step of the risk management technique is correct?
o: It runs in parallel with the other four steps throughout the project
It follows the implement step, once the planned responses have been actioned
It comes before the identify step, to agree the project's context with stakeholders
It takes place at each stage end, when the end stage report is being prepared
Risk.w: Identify, assess, plan and implement are carried out in sequence, while communicate runs alongside all of them, using the project's existing reports and channels (see manual 9.3.1, figure 9.2).

n.1: Communicate is not a final step: risk information is shared throughout, including while risks are still being identified and assessed (manual 9.3.1).
n.2: Defining context and objectives is part of identify; communicate runs alongside all the steps rather than preceding them (manual 9.3.1, 9.3.1.1).
n.3: The end stage report is one channel, but communication is continuous and uses checkpoint and highlight reports too (manual 9.3.1).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Within the [?] step of the risk management technique, the project defines its context and objectives so that there is a common understanding of what is at risk.
o: assess
plan
communicate
identify
Risk.w: Identify has two parts: define the context and objectives, then identify the threats and opportunities, describing each as cause, event and effect (see manual 9.3.1.1).

n.0: Assess prioritizes the identified risks and assesses the combined risk profile (manual 9.3.1.2).
n.1: Plan identifies and evaluates responses to the risks (manual 9.3.1.3).
n.2: Communicate keeps stakeholders informed throughout; defining context and objectives belongs to identify (manual 9.3.1, 9.3.1.1).

Risk.q: In which step of the risk management technique are responses to threats and opportunities identified and evaluated?
o: Plan
Assess
Implement
Identify
Risk.w: The plan step identifies and evaluates the right responses to remove or reduce threats and to maximize opportunities (see manual 9.3.1.3).

n.1: Assess prioritizes risks and assesses the combined risk profile; it does not choose responses (manual 9.3.1.2).
n.2: Implement carries out the responses already planned and reviews how well they work (manual 9.3.1.4).
n.3: Identify sets the context and finds the threats and opportunities (manual 9.3.1.1).

Risk.q: Which activity takes place in the 'assess' step of the risk management technique?
o: Prioritizing risks and assessing the combined risk profile of the project
Defining the context and objectives that shape the risk management approach
Carrying out the planned responses and reviewing how effective they are
Evaluating response options to reduce threats and maximize opportunities
Risk.w: Assess has two parts: prioritize the risks (using probability, impact, proximity and velocity) and assess the combined risk profile (see manual 9.3.1.2).

n.1: This is the first part of the identify step (manual 9.3.1.1).
n.2: This is the implement step (manual 9.3.1.4).
n.3: This is the plan step (manual 9.3.1.3).

Risk.q:
Which two statements about the 'implement' step of the risk management technique are correct?
1. Planned responses are actioned and their effectiveness is reviewed.
2. The combined risk profile is compared with risk tolerance.
3. The risk owner and risk action owner for each risk are identified and agreed.
4. Business policies and standards are examined to shape the approach.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Risk.w: In implement, planned responses are actioned and reviewed, with corrective action where needed, and the risk owner and risk action owner are identified and agreed for each risk (see manual 9.3.1.4).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: assessing the combined risk profile is part of the assess step (manual 9.3.1.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: statement 2 belongs to assess and statement 4 to identify, when context and objectives are defined (manual 9.3.1.1, 9.3.1.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: examining business policies and standards is part of defining context and objectives in identify (manual 9.3.1.1).

Risk.q: How is information about risks communicated in the risk management technique?
o: Through a separate risk report that the project manager sends to the business layer at each stage end
Through the risk register, which is issued to all stakeholders after the plan step is complete
Through an exception report, which the project manager raises each time a new risk is identified
Through existing reports such as checkpoint, highlight and end stage reports, and to stakeholders as needed
Risk.w: Communicate uses the project's existing reports (for example checkpoint, highlight, end stage and end project reports) to share risk information within the project ecosystem and with external stakeholders as needed (see manual 9.3.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not add a separate risk report; risk information travels through the existing reports (manual 9.3.1).
n.1: The register is a project log record, not a communication product, and communication runs throughout rather than after one step (manual 9.3.1, 9.5).
n.2: An exception report is raised for a forecast breach of tolerance, not for each new risk (manual 9.3.1, 11.5).

Risk.q: In the identify step, why does the project manager review the organization's risk policy, standards and procedures?
o: They show which risks have already occurred and so need to be recorded as issues
They set the project board's risk tolerance for each stage of the project
They shape the project's risk management approach and the context for identifying risks
They provide a ready-made response for each threat, so the plan step is not needed
Risk.w: Defining context and objectives means understanding what is at risk and forming a suitable risk management approach, which is shaped by the business's environment, policies, standards and procedures (see manual 9.3.1.1).

n.0: Policies and standards do not record events; they shape how risk will be managed (manual 9.3.1.1).
n.1: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's appetite, not by the standards reviewed in identify (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: Responses are still identified and evaluated in the plan step for each risk (manual 9.3.1.3).

Risk.q: What is the purpose of the risk management approach?
o: To keep a record of the identified risks related to the project, including their status and history
To describe how issues will be captured and how changes to the project baseline will be controlled
To describe how risk will be managed, including the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities
To describe how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project
Risk.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed: the specific procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities to be applied. It contains no specific risks (see manual 9.5).

n.0: This is the purpose of the risk register, which is part of the project log (manual 9.5).
n.1: This is the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.3: This is the digital and data management approach (manual 11.5).

Risk.q: What is the purpose of the risk register?
o: To keep a record of identified risks related to the project, including their status and history
To describe the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities for managing risk
To record informal issues and actions that the project manager needs to keep track of
To record the quality activities that are planned for products and the results of each
Risk.w: The risk register is part of the project log and records each identified threat and opportunity with its status and history (see manual 9.5).

n.1: This is the risk management approach, part of the PID (manual 9.5).
n.2: This describes the daily log (manual 11.5).
n.3: This describes the quality register (manual 8.5).

Risk.q: Where is the risk register held?
o: In the project initiation documentation, alongside the management approaches
In the business case, under the heading that summarizes the project's risks
In the project log, alongside the issue, quality and product registers
In the risk management approach, as an appendix listing the known risks
Risk.w: The risk register is one of the six records in the project log, with the daily log, lessons log and the issue, quality and product registers (see manual 4.3.2, 9.5).

n.0: The PID holds the risk management approach, but the register of specific risks is a dynamic record in the project log (manual 4.3.1, 9.5).
n.1: The business case summarizes the main risks for the investment decision, but the register itself is part of the project log (manual 5.5, 9.5).
n.3: The risk management approach describes how risk is managed and contains no specific risks (manual 9.5).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The risk management approach forms part of the [?], which the project board reviews when it authorizes the project.
o: project log
PID
project brief
business case
Risk.w: The risk management approach is one of the management approaches held in the PID, and the board approves it in directing a project (see manual 9.5, 4.3.1, table 14.3).

n.0: The project log holds the risk register, not the risk management approach (manual 4.3.2, 9.5).
n.2: The project brief is created in starting up a project; the management approaches are agreed in initiation and held in the PID (manual 4.3.1).
n.3: The business case is a separate product within the PID; it does not contain the risk management approach (manual 5.5, 9.5).

Risk.q: A project manager adds a list of the ten most serious threats to the risk management approach. Why is this inappropriate?
o: Threats belong in the issue register until the project board has approved a response for them
Specific risks belong in the business case, which records each threat under its own heading
The approach covers opportunities, while threats are recorded in the stage plan
Specific risks belong in the risk register; the approach holds the procedures and responsibilities
Risk.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed and does not contain specific risks; individual threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register (see manual 9.5).

n.0: Threats are risks, not issues, and are recorded in the risk register once identified, before responses are approved (manual 9.5).
n.1: The business case summarizes the main risks for the investment decision; the record of individual risks is the risk register (manual 5.5, 9.5).
n.2: The approach covers neither specific threats nor specific opportunities; both are recorded in the risk register (manual 9.5).

Risk.q:
Which two statements describe how the risk practice supports the PRINCE2 principles?
1. Setting risk tolerance supports manage by exception.
2. Recording risks in the daily log supports focus on products.
3. Weighing aggregated risk in the business case supports ensure continued business justification.
4. Letting the team manager set risk appetite supports define roles, responsibilities and relationships.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Risk.w: Risk is one of the seven tolerance areas, so risk tolerance applies manage by exception (statement 1). The business case weighs benefits against costs and the associated risks, so aggregated risk informs continued business justification (statement 3) (see manual 2.1, 2.5, 9.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the daily log is not where identified risks are managed, and focus on products is about defining products and their quality (manual 2.6, 9.5).
n.2: Both are wrong: risks are recorded in the risk register, and risk appetite is set by the business, not by a team manager (manual 9.2, 9.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: risk appetite is determined by the business, and the project board sets tolerance from it (manual 9.2.1).

Risk.q: How does the risk practice support the 'tailor to suit the project' principle?
o: Risk tolerances are set for each level so that forecast breaches are escalated
Lessons about risks from previous projects are reviewed when the project starts
The risk management approach is made proportionate to the project's scale and risk
Risks are reviewed at each stage end before the board authorizes the next stage
Risk.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's scale, complexity, importance, team capability and level of risk; the risk management approach is made proportionate to the project (see manual 2.7, 9.7).

n.0: Setting tolerances and escalating forecast breaches applies manage by exception, not tailoring (manual 2.5).
n.1: Using lessons from earlier projects applies learn from experience (manual 2.2).
n.3: Reviewing risks at stage boundaries applies manage by stages (manual 2.4, 18.1).

Risk.q: A project manager reviews the lessons logs of similar past projects to find threats that affected them. Which principle does this apply to the risk practice?
o: Manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Learn from experience
Risk.w: Seeking lessons from previous projects, here about the threats they met, applies the learn from experience principle to identifying risks (see manual 2.2, 9.7).

n.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and authorizing the project a stage at a time, not drawing on past projects (manual 2.4).
n.1: This principle concerns keeping the project desirable, viable and achievable, not using lessons from earlier projects (manual 2.1).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products that meet quality requirements (manual 2.6).

Risk.q: What is the purpose of the risk practice?
o: To collect and assess issues and control changes to the project's baseline, so keeping the agreed products under control
To identify, assess and control uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives, so improving its ability to succeed
To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable, so supporting decisions
To define and implement the means by which the project will verify that its products are fit for use, so meeting expectations
Risk.w: The risk practice exists to identify, assess and control uncertainty that would affect the project's objectives, and in doing so it improves the project's ability to succeed (see manual 9.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of the issues practice, which deals with events relevant to the project and with changes to the baseline, not with uncertainty about objectives (manual 10.1).
n.2: This describes the business case practice, which supports decisions about investment; the risk practice controls uncertainty affecting objectives (manual 5.1, 9.1).
n.3: This describes the quality practice, which deals with quality specifications and fitness for use rather than with uncertain events (manual 8.1, 9.1).

Risk.q: Which statement best describes what the risk practice can achieve for a project?
o: It guarantees that the agreed objectives will be met by removing the uncertainties before delivery starts
It resolves events that have already happened and are now affecting the project's approved baseline
It improves the ability of the project to succeed by controlling the uncertainties that affect its objectives
It confirms at each stage boundary that the project is still desirable, viable and achievable
Risk.w: Controlling uncertainty improves the chance of success, but the agreed objectives cannot be guaranteed: some uncertainty always remains (see manual 9.1).

n.0: The risk practice cannot guarantee that objectives will be met; it improves the ability to succeed by managing uncertainty throughout the project (manual 9.1).
n.1: Events that have already happened are issues, handled by the issues practice; risks are uncertain events that may happen (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Confirming that the project remains desirable, viable and achievable is the role of the business case practice, although risks feed into it (manual 5.1).

Risk.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The purpose of the risk practice is to identify, assess and [?] uncertainties that would affect the project's objectives.
o: eliminate
control
transfer
accept
Risk.w: The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty, which improves the project's ability to succeed (see manual 9.1).

n.0: Uncertainty cannot be eliminated from a project; the practice controls it, and it cannot guarantee the objectives will be met (manual 9.1).
n.2: Transfer is one of the response types for an individual risk, used for passing financial impact to a third party; it is not part of the practice's purpose (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Accept is one of the response types for an individual risk; the purpose of the practice is to control uncertainty, not to accept it (manual 9.1, 9.2.3.1).

Risk.q: Which statement about the scope of the risk practice is correct?
o: It covers both threats and opportunities, as uncertainty can affect objectives negatively or positively
It covers threats to the project, while opportunities are handled through the business case practice
It covers uncertainties after they have occurred, so that their effect on the baseline can be assessed
It covers threats with a high probability, while low-probability threats are passed to the business layer
Risk.w: A risk can have a negative effect on objectives (a threat) or a positive effect (an opportunity), and the risk practice manages both (see manual 9.1).

n.1: Opportunities are uncertain events with a positive effect on objectives and are managed by the risk practice alongside threats (manual 9.1).
n.2: Once something has occurred it is an issue, not a risk; the risk practice deals with events that might occur (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: All identified threats and opportunities are assessed and controlled by the project; probability is one measure used to prioritize them (manual 9.2.2).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the issues practice are correct?
1. It collects and assesses issues, which can be raised by anyone involved at any time.
2. It starts once the first delivery stage begins, after the project plan is approved.
3. It controls changes to the approved versions of management products and project products.
4. It sets how much risk the business is willing to take on the project.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 is correct: issues can be raised by anyone at any time and are collected and assessed by the practice. Statement 3 is correct: the practice controls changes to the project baseline, which is made of approved management and project products (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issues are noted from starting up a project (in the daily log) and the issue register is set up in initiation, before any delivery stage (manual ch 13, ch 15).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: issues are handled from starting up a project, and risk appetite is set by the business, not by the issues practice (manual 9.2.1, ch 13).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: risk appetite is determined by the business and applied through the risk practice, not the issues practice (manual 9.2.1).

Issues.q: A supplier confirms that a component will arrive three weeks late. Which practice deals with this first, and why?
o: The issues practice, because the event has already happened and needs management consideration
The risk practice, because the late delivery is an uncertain event that may affect objectives
The quality practice, because the component will no longer meet its quality specifications
The plans practice, because the delay must be scheduled before the event can be assessed
Issues.w: The delay has happened and needs project management consideration, so it is an issue to be captured and assessed through the issues practice; a certain event is an issue, not a risk (see manual 10.1, 9.1).

n.1: A risk is an uncertain event; the supplier has confirmed the delay, so it is no longer uncertain and is handled as an issue (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.2: Nothing suggests the component fails its quality specifications; the problem is its timing, not its quality (manual 8.1, 10.1).
n.3: Plans may later be updated, but the event must first be captured and assessed as an issue to see whether and how it affects the project (manual 10.3.1).

Issues.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the issues practice from the risk practice?
o: Issues are uncertain events that may happen later; risks are events that have already occurred
Issues need management consideration now; risks are uncertain events that may affect objectives
Issues are raised by team managers; risks are identified by the project board and the executive
Issues concern specialist products; risks concern management products such as plans and reports
Issues.w: An issue is a relevant event that requires project management consideration, whereas a risk is an uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect objectives (see manual 10.1, 9.1).

n.0: This reverses the two definitions: risks are the uncertain future events and issues are the events that need consideration now (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.2: Issues can be raised by anyone at any time, and risks can be identified by anyone in the project too; the difference is certainty, not who raises them (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Both issues and risks can relate to any product, management or project; the distinction is between a present event and an uncertain one (manual 9.1, 10.1).

Issues.q: Which outcome shows that the purpose of the issues practice is being achieved?
o: Issues are escalated to the project board so that the board makes each decision about them
Requests for change are refused once the project plan has been baselined and approved
Issues are recorded when the project closes so they can be included in the lessons report
Changes to approved products are made after their impact is assessed and they are authorized
Issues.w: The practice exists to assess issues and control changes to the baseline, so a sign of success is that approved products change only after their impact has been assessed and the change authorized (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: The board may delegate authority for changes and the project manager handles issues within tolerance, so escalating everything defeats manage by exception (manual 10.2.4, 2.5).
n.1: Change control does not forbid change; requests for change are assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: Issues are captured and assessed as they arise, not stored up until closure; lessons are a separate record (manual 10.3.1, 11.5).

Issues.q: The marketing manager on a website project asks for an extra page to be added to the site map that the project board has already approved. Which type of issue is this?
o: Off-specification
Concern
Business opportunity
Request for change
Issues.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline. The approved site map is part of the baseline, so asking to add to it is a request for change (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; nothing here says a product is failing its specification (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed; this is a clear proposal to change an approved product (manual 10.1).
n.2: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or user organization, not a request to alter an approved product (manual 10.1).

Issues.q: During a stage, a team manager reports that a completed training module will not meet the quality specifications set out in its product description. Which type of issue should the project manager record?
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Event external to the project
Business opportunity
Issues.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications, which is exactly what the team manager has reported (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.1: A request for change proposes altering a baseline; here the product simply falls short of its existing specification (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: The shortfall arises inside the project's own work, not from an event outside the project (manual 10.1).
n.3: A business opportunity brings unanticipated positive consequences; a product failing its specification is not a positive event (manual 10.1).

Issues.q: A key server used by the project team fails overnight, and work on two products has stopped this morning. Which type of issue has an immediate and negative impact such as this?
o: Concern
Problem
Off-specification
Request for change
Issues.w: A problem is an issue with an immediate and negative impact on the project, such as work stopping because a server has failed (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed; here the impact is already immediate and known (manual 10.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; the failed server is not a product failing its specification (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: Nobody is proposing a change to a baseline; the event is a failure that has already happened (manual 10.2.3).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
A [?] is an issue whose timelines and impact still need to be assessed before the project manager can decide how serious it is.
o: problem
off-specification
concern
request for change
Issues.w: A concern is an issue whose timelines and impact need to be assessed; it is the issue type for matters whose seriousness is not yet clear (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A problem has an immediate and negative impact, so its effect is already evident rather than still to be assessed (manual 10.1).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline (manual 10.2.3).

Issues.q: A new team member asks what PRINCE2 means by the word 'issue'. Which definition should the project manager give?
o: An uncertain event that, should it occur, will affect the achievement of the project's objectives
An event relevant to the project that requires project management consideration
A situation where a deviation beyond the agreed tolerance levels can be forecast
A modification to an approved product that forms part of the project baseline
Issues.w: An issue is an event relevant to the project that requires project management consideration, and it can be raised by anyone at any time (see manual 10.1).

n.0: This defines a risk, which is uncertain; an issue is an event that needs consideration now (manual 9.1).
n.2: This defines an exception, which is handled through the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: This defines a change; a change may arise from an issue, but the two terms are not the same (manual 10.1).

Issues.q: A team manager finds that a records database already built for the project can also be used by a second department with no extra work, giving that department benefits nobody had expected. Which type of issue is this?
o: Business opportunity
Request for change
Off-specification
Event external to the project
Issues.w: A business opportunity is an issue representing unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization, as with the unexpected extra use of the database (see manual 10.1).

n.1: No change to an approved product is being proposed; the database can be reused as it is (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: The database is not failing its quality specifications; the event is positive (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: The discovery comes from the project's own work on the database, not from an event outside the project (manual 10.1).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about the types of issue in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed.
2. A request for change is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.
3. A business opportunity is an uncertain event that could have a positive effect on objectives.
4. An event external to the project that may affect it is one of the types of issue.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 correctly defines a concern. Statement 4 is correct: an event external to the project that may affect it is one of the types of issue the QRG lists, alongside problem, concern, business opportunity, request for change and off-specification (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a product that will not meet its quality specifications is an off-specification; a request for change proposes a change to a baseline (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: statement 2 describes an off-specification, and statement 3 describes a risk (an opportunity) because it is uncertain (manual 9.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: an uncertain positive event is an opportunity in the risk practice; a business opportunity is an issue that has already arisen (manual 9.1, 10.1).

Issues.q: The government announces new accessibility rules that will apply to a public website the project is building, and the project manager records this in the project log. Which type of issue is this?
o: Request for change
Off-specification
External event
Business opportunity
Issues.w: A rule change announced by government arises outside the project and may affect it in some way, which makes it an event external to the project (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; the announcement itself is an outside event, which may later lead to such a request (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: No product has yet been found to miss its quality specifications; the issue is a new outside requirement (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: A business opportunity brings unanticipated positive consequences; new rules that add constraints are not described as a benefit here (manual 10.1).

Issues.q: In PRINCE2 7, what is the project baseline?
o: The current approved versions of the management and project products that are under change control
The original versions of the plans, kept unchanged so that later progress can be compared with them
The tolerances for the seven aspects of performance agreed for each stage of the project
The list of all the products required by a plan, together with the current status of each one
Issues.w: The project baseline is the current approved versions of the management products and project products that are subject to change control (see manual 10.1).

n.1: The baseline is the current approved version, not a frozen original: each approved change creates a new baselined version (manual 10.1, 10.2.1).
n.2: Tolerances are limits of delegated authority set under manage by exception; they are not the baseline itself (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.3: A list of a plan's products and their status describes the product register in the project log, not the baseline (manual 4.3.2, 10.1).

Issues.q: A project manager updates the approved stage plan after the project board agrees to bring forward a delivery date. Which PRINCE2 term describes a modification to an approved product that forms part of the project baseline?
o: Concession
Change
Off-specification
Exception
Issues.w: A change is a modification to any of the approved management or project products that make up the project baseline (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A concession is an off-specification that is accepted without corrective action; it is not the general term for altering a baselined product (manual 10.3.1, tab 10.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications, not a modification to an approved product (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: An exception is a forecast deviation beyond agreed tolerance levels, handled through the progress practice (manual 11.1).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
[?] is the procedure that ensures changes to the project baseline are identified and assessed, and then approved, rejected or deferred.
o: Quality control
Exception management
Change control
Change management
Issues.w: Change control is the procedure by which changes to the baseline are identified, assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred; in PRINCE2 7 it is part of the issues practice (see manual 10.2.3).

n.0: Quality control checks whether products meet their quality specifications; it does not decide on changes to the baseline (manual 8.2).
n.1: Exception management deals with forecast breaches of tolerance, escalated to the level above (manual 11.3).
n.3: In PRINCE2 7, change management means the organizational transition covered by the people element, not control of baselines (manual ch 3).

Issues.q: When setting up baselines for a project, which action reflects the guidance on baselines in the issues practice?
o: Baseline every product at the same level of detail, whatever the size and complexity of the project
Replace each product when a change is approved, removing the version it supersedes from the records
Ask the business layer to approve each new version of a baselined product before it is used
Decide the level at which products are baselined and check their status against their authorized state
Issues.w: The guidance is to decide the appropriate level at which products are baselined and to check periodically that the actual status of products matches their authorized state, looking for discrepancies (see manual 10.2.1).

n.0: The project management team decides the appropriate level of baselining to suit the project, rather than applying one level to everything (manual 10.2.1).
n.1: Configuration control keeps a record of changes and an archive of superseded versions, so earlier versions are kept (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.2: Approval of changes rests with the project board or the authority it delegates, not with the business layer for each version (manual 10.2.4).

Issues.q: Why does the project management team periodically compare the status of products with the versions the board approved?
o: To find any discrepancies between what has been authorized and what actually exists
To release the change budget so that approved changes can be funded and delivered
To decide which change authority should be appointed for the next delivery stage
To confirm that the benefits in the business case have been realized as forecast
Issues.w: Periodically verifying that the actual status of products reflects their authorized state reveals discrepancies; it is part of the baselines guidance and helps the team understand product status (see manual 10.2.1).

n.1: The change budget is what enables approved changes to be funded; checking product status does not release it (manual 10.2.5).
n.2: The project board decides on delegating change authority, reviewing it at stage boundaries; a status check does not make that decision (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Benefits are reviewed through the benefits management approach, not by checking product versions against their authorized state (manual 5.5).

Issues.q: An approved change to a baselined product has been made. What should happen to the baseline for that product?
o: The original version stays current and the change is noted in the daily log
A new version becomes the baseline and the superseded version is archived
The baseline is frozen until the next stage boundary, when the change is applied
The issue report describing the change replaces the product in the baseline
