Issues.w: Each approved change creates a new baselined version. Records of change are kept and superseded versions are archived, which is configuration control (see manual 10.2.1, 10.3.1.5).

n.0: Once an approved change is implemented, the affected product and baseline are updated; keeping the old version as current would defeat change control (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.2: Approved changes are implemented when decided, through work packages, not held until the next stage boundary (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.3: The issue report describes the issue and recommends a decision; it does not become part of the product baseline (manual 10.5).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about baselines and change are correct?
1. The project baseline holds the current approved versions of products subject to change control.
2. Once a product has been baselined it cannot be changed for the rest of the project.
3. A change is a modification to an approved product that forms part of the project baseline.
4. Draft products still being developed in a work package form part of the project baseline.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 defines the project baseline and statement 3 defines a change: a modification to an approved product in that baseline (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: baselined products can change, through change control, with each approved change creating a new version (manual 10.2.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: baselined products can be changed under change control, and drafts are not yet approved, so they are not in the baseline (manual 10.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the baseline holds approved versions, so a draft still in development is not part of it (manual 10.1).

Issues.q: A delivered product differs from the approved version in the project baseline. How should this discrepancy be handled?
o: Recorded as a lesson and left in place, because the product has already been delivered
Recorded as a new threat in the risk register so that it can be monitored in later stages
Corrected by the team manager as routine work, with the baseline left as it is
Treated as an off-specification and taken through the change control procedure
Issues.w: An off-specification is a discrepancy between the approved baseline and the delivered products, and it must be addressed through the change control procedure (see manual 10.2.3).

n.0: A lesson may be learned, but the discrepancy itself is an off-specification that must go through change control (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: The discrepancy already exists, so it is an issue rather than an uncertain future event for the risk register (manual 9.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: Off-specifications go through change control and a decision by the right authority, rather than being fixed as routine team work (manual 10.2.3, 10.2.4).

Issues.q: A project has a change authority with a small change budget, and the project manager also holds limited authority to approve minor changes. Which role is the ultimate authority for approving requests for change and off-specifications?
o: The change authority
The project board
The project manager
The senior supplier
Issues.w: The project board is the ultimate authority for reviewing and approving requests for change and off-specifications, although it may delegate some of that authority (see manual 10.2.4).

n.0: A change authority holds only the authority the board delegates to it, within limits; it is not the ultimate authority (manual 10.2.4).
n.2: The project manager can approve changes only within any authority the board delegates (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: The senior supplier is one member of the board; the authority rests with the project board as a whole (manual 6.2, 10.2.4).

Issues.q: What is a change budget?
o: Money set aside to fund the planned responses to specific threats and opportunities
The cost tolerance allowed for a stage before an exception has to be raised
Money or authorized constraints set aside to cover the cost of approved changes
The total cost of the project, as shown in the investment appraisal of the business case
Issues.w: A change budget is money, or a set of authorized constraints, set aside in a plan to cover changes, allocated by those with delegated authority so that authorized changes can be delivered (see manual 10.2.5).

n.0: Money for responses to threats and opportunities is the risk budget, not the change budget (manual 9.2).
n.1: Cost tolerance is the permitted deviation in cost before escalation; it is not a fund for approved changes (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The project's total cost appears in the business case; the change budget is a separate amount reserved for approved changes (manual 5.5, 10.2.5).

Issues.q: A delivered brochure uses a slightly different shade of the brand colour from the one specified. The board decides that this is acceptable and that no rework is needed. What is this decision called?
o: Approving a request for change
Extending the stage tolerance
Reducing the project scope
Granting a concession
Issues.w: A concession is an off-specification that is accepted without corrective action; granting one is a decision option for an off-specification (see manual 10.3.1.4, tab 10.1).

n.0: A request for change proposes altering the baseline; here a product already falls short of its specification and is accepted as it is (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: Tolerances relate to forecast deviations beyond plan limits; accepting a product that misses its specification is not a tolerance change (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Nothing is removed from the scope; the product is still delivered and accepted despite the shortfall (manual 10.3.1.4).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The project board may delegate authority for approving requests for change and off-specifications to a [?], which acts within the limits the board sets.
o: change authority
project assurance role
quality assurance function
team manager
Issues.w: The board may delegate approval of requests for change and off-specifications to a change authority, a person or group acting within limits set by the board (see manual 10.2.4).

n.1: Project assurance advises the board and checks that the project is being run properly; it is not the body delegated to approve changes (manual 6.2, 10.2.4).
n.2: Quality assurance is a function independent of the project management team; it does not approve the project's changes (manual 8.2).
n.3: A team manager implements corrective actions in work packages; delegated approval goes to a change authority or the project manager (manual 10.2.4, 10.6).

Issues.q: Why should delegated change authority be accompanied by a change budget?
o: So that the change authority can extend stage tolerances without referring to the board
So that the changes the change authority approves can be funded and then implemented
So that the responses planned for threats can be paid for without escalating them
So that the project manager can add new products without recording them as issues
Issues.w: Delegated authority should come with an appropriate change budget; applying the change budget is what allows approved changes to be funded and therefore implemented (see manual 10.2.5).

n.0: A change budget funds approved changes; it does not let anyone extend the tolerances that the board sets (manual 10.2.5, 11.2.1).
n.2: Funding responses to threats is the purpose of a risk budget, not a change budget (manual 9.2).
n.3: New products still go through change control and are recorded; the budget funds approved changes rather than bypassing the procedure (manual 10.2.3).

Issues.q: Which statement about delegating authority for changes is correct?
o: Delegation lets the change authority carry out the changes it approves within its own team
Once delegated, change authority stays fixed for the whole project and is not revisited
The board decides whether to delegate, and the delegation is reviewed at stage boundaries
The business layer appoints the change authority when it issues the project mandate
Issues.w: The project board decides whether to delegate authority for changes and to whom; the arrangement is reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change (see manual 10.2.4).

n.0: Delegation concerns approving changes, not implementing them; implementation is done by the project manager through work packages (manual 10.2.4, 10.3.1.5).
n.1: Delegated change authority is reviewed at stage boundaries or when tolerances change (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Delegating change authority is a project board decision recorded in the issue management approach, not something set in the mandate (manual 10.2.4, 10.5).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about change authority and the change budget are correct?
1. The project board may give the project manager authority to approve some changes.
2. A change authority can approve changes of any size once it has been appointed.
3. A change budget can be a set of authorized constraints within which trade-offs may be made.
4. The change budget is the same fund as the risk budget and pays for responses to threats.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
Issues.w: Statement 1 is correct: the board may delegate authority for changes to a change authority or to the project manager. Statement 3 is correct: a change budget is usually money but can be a set of authorized constraints for trade-offs (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a change authority acts within the limits the board delegates, not without limit (manual 10.2.4).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: delegated authority has limits, and the risk budget is a separate fund for risk responses (manual 9.2, 10.2.4).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the risk budget funds responses to risks, while the change budget funds approved changes (manual 9.2, 10.2.5).

Issues.q: A change authority approves a request for change that will cost money to implement. According to the change control guidance, where should the funding for the change come from?
o: The approved change budget, or additional funding from the customer
The risk budget, because the change removes a threat to the stage
The cost tolerance of the current stage, treated as normal stage spending
The team manager's budget for the work package, agreed in the team plan
Issues.w: If a change has a cost, the source of funding must be identified as either the approved change budget or additional funding from the customer (see manual 10.2.3).

n.1: The risk budget pays for responses to identified risks, not for approved changes (manual 9.2, 10.2.3).
n.2: Cost tolerance is a margin for deviation in planned work, not the funding source for approved changes (manual 10.2.3, 11.2.1).
n.3: A work package budget covers its agreed products; new changes are funded from the change budget or extra customer funding (manual 10.2.3).

Issues.q: A project manager is writing a one-page guide for team managers that shows how an issue moves from being raised to being resolved. In what order are the steps of the PRINCE2 issues technique carried out?
o: Capture, recommend, assess, decide, implement
Identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate
Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
Capture, assess, decide, recommend, implement
Issues.w: The issues technique runs capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement: an issue is registered, its impact assessed, options evaluated and a recommendation made, a decision taken by the right authority, and the change then implemented (see manual 10.3.1, fig 10.1).

n.0: A recommendation cannot be made before the issue's impact has been assessed, so assess comes before recommend (manual 10.3.1).
n.1: These are the five steps of the risk technique, not the issues technique (manual 9.3.1).
n.3: The recommendation is made to the person or group with authority so that they can decide, so recommend comes before decide (manual 10.3.1.3, 10.3.1.4).

Issues.q: A team manager telephones the project manager about a fault found in a product. The project manager decides it is a problem, sets its priority and enters it in the issue register. Which step of the issues technique is this?
o: Assess
Recommend
Decide
Capture
Issues.w: Capture covers determining the issue type, determining its severity or priority and registering it; issues can be captured through formal or informal channels such as a phone call (see manual 10.3.1.1, fig 10.1).

n.0: Assess looks at whether and how the issue affects the project, such as its impact on the business case and risk profile; it follows registration (manual 10.3.1.2).
n.1: Recommend identifies and evaluates options and recommends one to the authority; no options have been considered yet (manual 10.3.1.3).
n.2: Decide is when the person or group with authority approves, rejects or otherwise responds to the recommendation (manual 10.3.1.4).

Issues.q: After an issue has been registered, the project manager moves on to the assess step of the issues technique. Which two questions is this step trying to answer?
o: Does this issue affect the project? If so, how?
Who raised the issue? When was it first raised?
Should the change be approved? Who will implement it?
Is the issue a threat? What is its probability?
Issues.w: When reviewing issues in the assess step, the aim is to answer whether the issue affects the project and, if it does, how: for example its impact on targets and tolerances, the business case, other products and the risk profile (see manual 10.3.1.2).

n.1: Who raised the issue and when are details recorded at capture; they do not establish its effect on the project (manual 10.3.1.1).
n.2: Whether to approve the change is settled in the decide step, and implementation follows it (manual 10.3.1.4, 10.3.1.5).
n.3: Probability belongs to assessing risks in the risk technique; an issue is an event that needs consideration now (manual 9.3.1, 10.1).

Issues.q: A trainee project manager is listing the steps of the PRINCE2 issues technique for an exam revision card. Which is NOT one of the steps of the issues technique?
o: Recommend
Identify
Implement
Decide
Issues.w: Identify is the first step of the risk technique. The issues technique has five steps: capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement (see manual 10.3.1, 9.3.1).

n.0: Recommend is the third step of the issues technique, where options are evaluated and a recommendation made (manual 10.3.1.3).
n.2: Implement is the fifth step, where corrective action is taken and records and baselines updated (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.3: Decide is the fourth step, where the person or group with authority makes the decision (manual 10.3.1.4).

Issues.q: The project manager assesses a request for change and finds that it would cost more than the delegated authority allows. Who should make the decision on this request?
o: The team manager who would deliver the extra products in a work package
Project support, because it maintains the issue register for the project
The project board, or a change authority with enough authority
Project assurance, acting on behalf of the senior user and the executive
Issues.w: In the decide step, an issue beyond the decision-maker's delegated authority is escalated; decisions are made by the project board, a change authority or the project manager within the authority each holds (see manual 10.3.1.4, 10.2.4).

n.0: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not approve requests for change (manual 10.6).
n.1: Project support administers the procedures by maintaining the issue register; it has no decision authority over changes (manual 10.6).
n.3: Project assurance supports the board; it does not take decisions on requests for change on the board's behalf (manual 6.2, 10.2.4).

Issues.q: A request for change reaches the decide step of the issues technique. Which set lists typical decision choices available to the person or group with authority?
o: Avoid, reduce, transfer or share the matter with another party
Accept the matter, enhance it, exploit it or prepare a contingent plan
Escalate it to the business layer, close it, or record it as a lesson
Approve, reject, ask for an exception plan or request more information
Issues.w: Typical decisions on a request for change are to approve it, reject it, ask for an exception plan or request more information (see manual 10.3.1.4, tab 10.1).

n.0: Avoid, reduce, transfer and share are risk responses to threats, not decisions on a request for change (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Accept, enhance, exploit and contingent plans are also risk responses, chosen in the risk technique (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: The project board escalates to the business layer only where project tolerance is threatened, and an unresolved request is not closed or turned into a lesson (manual 10.3.1.4, 11.3).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about the issues technique are correct?
1. In the recommend step, options are identified and evaluated before a recommendation is made.
2. The assess step is best carried out by the project manager working alone, without input from others.
3. A recommendation should make clear the consequences of both approving and rejecting the request.
4. In the implement step, the project board carries out the corrective action itself.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 is correct: options are identified and evaluated in the recommend step. Statement 3 is correct: the recommendation goes to whoever has the authority, with the consequences of approval and rejection made clear (see manual 10.3.1.3).

n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: corrective action is taken by the project manager, typically through work packages, not by the board (manual 10.3.1.5, 10.6).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: assessment is best done cooperatively, drawing on team members and stakeholders (manual 10.3.1.2).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: assessment is a cooperative activity, and the board decides rather than implements (manual 10.3.1.2, 10.3.1.5).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In the [?] step of the issues technique, corrective action is taken and the project log, the affected management products and, where necessary, the baseline are updated.
o: decide
implement
recommend
assess
Issues.w: The implement step takes corrective action and updates records and the project baseline where necessary; approved changes are recorded in the project log and reflected in the affected products (see manual 10.3.1.5, fig 10.1).

n.0: Decide is where the authority approves, rejects or responds otherwise; the action and updates follow in the next step (manual 10.3.1.4).
n.2: Recommend evaluates options and proposes a resolution; nothing is changed yet (manual 10.3.1.3).
n.3: Assess examines whether and how the issue affects the project; it does not change products or baselines (manual 10.3.1.2).

Issues.q: A team manager mentions that a supplier's delivery note was missing some details. The project manager sorts it out with a quick phone call and decides it does not need formal handling. Where should the project manager record it?
o: Daily log
Issue register
Lessons log
Risk register
Issues.w: Issues handled informally are recorded in the daily log, the project manager's informal diary of issues, actions and observations (see manual 10.1, 11.5).

n.1: The issue register holds issues being managed formally; this matter has been dealt with informally (manual 10.5).
n.2: The lessons log records lessons for this or future projects, not the day-to-day handling of an informal issue (manual 11.5).
n.3: The risk register records uncertain future events; this matter has already happened and been resolved (manual 9.5, 10.1).

Issues.q: Which issues are typically managed formally, with an issue register entry and, where needed, an issue report?
o: Notes, actions and observations from the project manager's day-to-day work on the stage
Requests for change, off-specifications and problems or concerns needing formal review
Lessons the team wants recorded so that they can be passed on to future projects
Uncertain events that could affect the project's objectives later in the stage
Issues.w: Issue reports are used for requests for change, off-specifications, business opportunities and problems or concerns that need formal review; these issues are managed formally through the issue register (see manual 10.5).

n.0: Day-to-day notes, actions and observations belong in the daily log, the project manager's informal diary (manual 11.5).
n.2: Lessons are captured in the lessons log and reported in a lessons report, not managed as formal issues (manual 11.5).
n.3: Uncertain future events are risks, recorded in the risk register and managed through the risk practice (manual 9.1, 9.5).

Issues.q: A team member privately tells the project manager about a personal conflict between two senior stakeholders that is starting to affect the project. It would be inappropriate for everyone with access to the project records to read about it. Where should the project manager record it?
o: Issue register
Highlight report
Daily log
Issue report
Issues.w: Sensitive matters, where open access to the record would be inappropriate, are recorded in the daily log rather than in the issue register (see manual 10.1, 11.5).

n.0: The issue register is for formal issues and is widely accessible, which makes it unsuitable for a sensitive personal matter (manual 10.5).
n.1: A highlight report goes to the project board and possibly other stakeholders, so it is not a place for a sensitive matter (manual 11.5).
n.3: An issue report describes a formal issue's impact and recommends a decision; it is not used to hold sensitive notes (manual 10.5).

Issues.q: A team manager asks for a quick clarification of a product description, and no baselined product needs to change. How should this be handled?
o: Formally, by raising an issue report and adding an entry to the issue register
As a request for change, to be decided by the project board at its next meeting
As an exception, escalated to the project board in an exception report
Informally, with a note of the question and the answer in the daily log
Issues.w: Judgement is needed on what to record formally: logging every minor matter as a formal issue swamps decision-making. A quick clarification that changes no baseline can be dealt with informally and noted in the daily log (see manual 10.2.2, 11.5).

n.0: Formal handling is for issues such as requests for change and off-specifications; recording every trivial query formally swamps decision-making (manual 10.2.2, 10.5).
n.1: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline, and here nothing in the baseline is changing (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: An exception report is needed only when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, which a clarification does not threaten (manual 11.5).

Issues.q: When is the daily log first available for recording issues?
o: In starting up a project, before the issue register is set up in initiating a project
In initiating a project, at the same time as the issue register and the risk register
In controlling a stage, once the first work package has been authorized for delivery
In directing a project, once the project board has authorized initiation of the project
Issues.w: The daily log is set up in starting up a project, so early issues and risks can be noted before the issue register is created in initiating a project (see manual ch 13, ch 15, 11.5).

n.1: The registers are set up in initiating a project, but the daily log already exists from starting up a project (manual ch 13, ch 15).
n.2: The daily log is in use long before delivery starts; it is created in starting up a project (manual ch 13).
n.3: The daily log is created by the project manager in starting up a project, before the board authorizes initiation (manual ch 13, 14.4.1).

Issues.q: A delivered product will not meet one of its quality specifications. How should the project manager handle this issue?
o: Informally in the daily log, because it was raised verbally by the team manager
Formally, recording it in the issue register as an off-specification
As a risk in the risk register, because its impact has not yet been measured
As an entry in the lessons log, to be reviewed when the project is closed
Issues.w: An off-specification is a discrepancy between the baseline and the delivered product and must go through change control, so it is handled formally in the issue register (see manual 10.2.3, 10.5).

n.0: Issues can be raised through informal channels, but how it was raised does not make it informal; an off-specification needs formal change control (manual 10.3.1.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: The shortfall already exists, so it is an issue, not an uncertain risk (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: A lesson may be drawn later, but the off-specification must be resolved now through change control (manual 10.2.3).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about handling issues formally or informally are correct?
1. Some matters raised as issues turn out to be risks and should be handled as risks.
2. Sensitive issues are placed in the issue register so that all stakeholders can see them.
3. Off-specifications are handled formally through the change control procedure.
4. An informal issue needs an issue report before it can be noted in the daily log.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 is correct: part of issue resolution is checking whether a matter is really a risk. Statement 3 is correct: off-specifications must be addressed through change control, so they are handled formally (see manual 10.2.2, 10.2.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: sensitive issues go in the daily log, where open access is not given (manual 10.1, 11.5).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: sensitive issues belong in the daily log, and informal issues are noted there without an issue report (manual 10.5, 11.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: issue reports are for issues needing formal review; informal issues are simply noted in the daily log (manual 10.5).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Issues that are being managed formally are recorded in the [?], which is one of the records held in the project log.
o: daily log
lessons log
risk register
issue register
Issues.w: The issue register, part of the project log, captures and maintains information on all issues that are being managed formally (see manual 10.5, 4.3.2).

n.0: The daily log is also in the project log, but it holds informal and sensitive issues rather than formal ones (manual 11.5).
n.1: The lessons log records lessons, not issues under formal management (manual 11.5).
n.2: The risk register records uncertain events, while formal issues have their own register (manual 9.5).

Issues.q: What is the purpose of the issue management approach?
o: To record each formal issue with its type, owner, priority and current status
To describe how issues are captured and reported and how baseline changes are controlled
To describe one issue's impact on the baseline and recommend a decision about it
To describe how threats and opportunities will be identified, assessed and controlled
Issues.w: The issue management approach describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled, including matters such as version control and delegated change authority (see manual 10.5).

n.0: Recording each formal issue and its details is the job of the issue register in the project log, not the approach (manual 10.5).
n.2: Describing a single issue's impact and recommending a decision is the purpose of an issue report (manual 10.5).
n.3: How threats and opportunities are managed is described in the risk management approach (manual 9.5).

Issues.q: A request for change is within the project manager's tolerances but needs a formal decision. Which management product describes the issue's impact on the project baseline, sets out ways to resolve it and recommends a decision?
o: Issue register
Exception report
Issue report
Highlight report
Issues.w: An issue report describes an issue's impacts on the project baseline, identifies ways to resolve it or address an off-specification, and recommends a decision. Where tolerance is not threatened, an issue report rather than an exception report is used (see manual 10.5).

n.0: The issue register records and tracks formal issues; it does not set out a full impact analysis and recommendation for one issue (manual 10.5).
n.1: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance, which is not the case here (manual 11.5).
n.3: A highlight report summarizes stage status for the board at agreed intervals; it is not the vehicle for one issue's recommendation (manual 11.5).

Issues.q: A large project has a dedicated project support team working for the project manager. According to the roles in the issues practice, who should maintain the issue register on this project?
o: The team manager
Project assurance
The senior user
Project support
Issues.w: Project support administers the change control and issue procedures by maintaining the issue register; the project manager does this when there is no project support (see manual 10.6, tab 10.2).

n.0: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not maintain the issue register (manual 10.6, tab 10.2).
n.1: Project assurance supports the board and must stay independent of the project manager; administering registers is project support work (manual 6.2, 10.6).
n.2: The senior user makes decisions on escalated issues, focusing on safeguarding the expected benefits, rather than keeping the register (manual 10.6, tab 10.2).

Issues.q: The project board delegates to a change authority the approval of changes up to an agreed cost, and anything above that limit is referred back to the board. Which principle does this aspect of the issues practice support?
o: Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Tailor to suit the project
Issues.w: Delegating authority for changes within defined limits, with matters beyond those limits escalated, applies manage by exception: limits of delegated authority with escalation when they would be exceeded (see manual 2.5, 10.2.4).

n.1: Business justification concerns whether the change is worth its costs and risks, not the limits on who may approve it (manual 2.1).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products; the limits of approval authority are a manage by exception mechanism (manual 2.6).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; setting delegated limits with escalation is the core of manage by exception (manual 2.5, 2.7).

Issues.q: Before deciding on a request for change, the change authority compares the extra benefit the change would bring with its extra cost and the extra risk it adds. Which principle is being supported?
o: Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by stages
Issues.w: Ensure continued business justification requires what the project delivers to stay consistent with its justification, so a request for change weighs the additional benefit against the additional cost and risk (see manual 2.1).

n.0: Manage by exception concerns delegated limits and escalation; the cost and benefit comparison is about justification (manual 2.5).
n.2: This principle concerns agreed roles and stakeholder relationships; it does not involve weighing a change's benefits against its cost and risk (manual 2.3).
n.3: Manage by stages provides decision points at stage ends; the comparison here is made for one change, on business grounds (manual 2.4).

Issues.q: On a small, low-risk project, the board agrees that minor issues will be kept in a simple shared list reviewed at weekly team meetings, while requests for change still receive an issue report. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by stages
Focus on products
Tailor to suit the project
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Issues.w: Adapting the formality of issue control and the form of management products to the project's size and risk is tailoring: controls are fitted to the project's scale, complexity and risk (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and controlling the project stage by stage; the arrangement here adjusts how formal the issue controls are (manual 2.4).
n.1: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products; the choice here is about the formality of controls (manual 2.6).
n.3: This principle concerns agreed roles and relationships; the arrangement here changes how formal the issue controls are (manual 2.3).

Issues.q:
Which two statements about the management products that support the issues practice are correct?
1. The issue register captures and maintains information on issues being managed formally.
2. An issue report is prepared for every entry that the project manager makes in the daily log.
3. The issue management approach lists the specific issues that have been raised so far.
4. The issue register records an issue owner for each issue it holds.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
Issues.w: Statement 1 is correct: the issue register captures and maintains formal issues. Statement 4 is correct: each issue on the register has an issue owner, who manages that issue while the project manager runs the procedure (see manual 10.5, 10.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issue reports are for issues needing formal review, not for informal notes in the daily log (manual 10.5).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: daily log entries do not each need an issue report, and the approach describes procedures rather than listing specific issues (manual 10.5).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: the issue management approach describes how issues and changes are handled; specific issues go in the issue register (manual 10.5).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The issues practice supports the '[?]' principle, because change control is based on clearly defined products and the approved versions held in the baseline.
o: focus on products
manage by stages
learn from experience
define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Issues.w: Focus on products underpins change control: product definitions and baselined versions make it clear what is being changed (see manual 2.6, 10.1).

n.1: Manage by stages provides stage-by-stage planning and decision points; it is not what change control of product versions rests on (manual 2.4).
n.2: Learn from experience concerns lessons; the link described here is with defined products and their baselined versions (manual 2.2).
n.3: This principle concerns roles and relationships in the project management team, not the products that change control is based on (manual 2.3).

Issues.q: A project manager briefs a new project board on handling issues. Which statement describes the purpose of the issues practice?
o: To identify, assess and control uncertainties that could affect the project's objectives
To compare actual achievement with the plan and control deviations that cause an exception
To collect and assess issues and to control changes made to the project's baseline
To document the user's requirements for the products and establish how they will be met
Issues.w: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project baseline, so that change happens in a managed way rather than by drift (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Identifying, assessing and controlling uncertainties is the purpose of the risk practice, which deals with events that have not yet happened (manual 9.1).
n.1: Comparing actual with planned achievement and controlling deviations is the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: Documenting user requirements and the means of meeting them is the purpose of the quality practice (manual 8.1).

Issues.q: How does the issues practice in PRINCE2 7 relate to change control?
o: Issue management in PRINCE2 7 encompasses change control, so the issues practice controls changes to baselines
Change control now sits in the change management approach, which the people element uses to manage baselines
Change control is a separate eighth practice that takes over once an issue has been assessed and recommended
Change control is handled by the quality practice because it concerns the quality specifications of products
Issues.w: In PRINCE2 7, issue management includes change control: the issues practice replaced the old change theme and covers controlling changes to the project baseline (see manual 10.1).

n.1: In PRINCE2 7 change management means organizational transition under the people element; it is not the control of baselines (manual ch 3, 10.1).
n.2: There are seven practices; change control is part of the issues practice rather than a practice of its own (manual ch 4, 10.1).
n.3: The quality practice defines and checks quality requirements; controlling changes to approved products belongs to the issues practice (manual 8.1, 10.1).

Issues.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The purpose of the issues practice is to collect and assess issues and to control changes to the project's [?], so that the products the board has approved are not altered without authority.
o: risk profile
baseline
tolerances
benefits
Issues.w: The issues practice controls changes to the project baseline: the current approved versions of the management and project products that are subject to change control (see manual 10.1).

n.0: The risk profile is assessed in the risk practice; it is not what the issues practice controls changes to (manual 9.1).
n.2: Tolerances are set by the level above under manage by exception; changing them is not the purpose of the issues practice (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.3: Benefits are defined and tracked in the business case practice; the issues practice controls changes to approved products (manual 5.1, 10.1).

Issues.q: A team member asks why an approved product cannot simply be improved by the team. Why are changes to the project baseline controlled?
o: Because the baseline records uncertain events that must be kept within the business's risk appetite
Because the baseline is the record of lessons that must be passed on to the business at closure
Because the baseline holds the stage tolerances that the business layer has agreed with the executive
Because it holds the approved versions of products, so changes are assessed and authorized first
Issues.w: The baseline is the set of current approved versions of products under change control. Controlling changes to it means each proposed change is identified and assessed, then approved, rejected or deferred before it is made (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: Uncertain events are recorded in the risk register and managed against risk appetite in the risk practice; they are not the project baseline (manual 9.2).
n.1: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log and reported in a lessons report; the baseline is the set of approved products (manual 11.5, 10.1).
n.2: The baseline is made of approved products, and stage tolerances are set by the project board, not agreed between the business layer and the executive (manual 10.1, 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A stage is heading for a deviation that would take it beyond the limits agreed with the project board. Which element of the purpose of the progress practice is concerned with dealing with this deviation?
o: Monitoring actual achievement against the stage plan
Forecasting the project's objectives and continued viability
Controlling any deviation that would cause an exception
Defining the products and the means to deliver them
Progress.w: The third element of the progress purpose is to control deviations that would cause an exception, for example by escalating to the level that can decide on a response (see manual 11.1, 11.2.6).

n.0: Monitoring is how the deviation is detected, but it does not deal with it; dealing with it is the control element of the purpose (manual 11.1).
n.1: Forecasting predicts that the deviation will happen; it does not by itself deal with the deviation (manual 11.1, 11.2.5).
n.3: Defining the products and the means of delivery is the purpose of the plans practice, not progress (manual 7.1).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the progress practice are correct?

1. It monitors and compares actual achievements against those that were planned.
2. It defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities.
3. It controls deviations from plan that would cause an exception.
4. It defines the products to be delivered and estimates when they will be delivered.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: Monitoring and comparing actual against planned achievement (1) and controlling deviations that cause an exception (3) are both part of the purpose of the progress practice; the third part is forecasting (see manual 11.1).

n.1: Statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is the purpose of the organizing practice (manual 6.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is the purpose of organizing (manual 6.1) and statement 4 is the purpose of plans (manual 7.1); neither describes progress.
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is the purpose of the plans practice (manual 7.1).

Progress.q: A trainer is listing the elements of the purpose of the progress practice. Which is NOT part of the purpose of the progress practice?
o: Monitoring and comparing actual achievements against those that were planned
Seeking lessons from earlier projects and passing them on to future ones
Providing a forecast for the project's objectives and continued viability
Controlling any deviations from plan that would cause an exception
Progress.w: Lessons are reviewed and reported under the progress guidance and support the learn from experience principle, but seeking and passing on lessons is not one of the three elements of the progress purpose (monitor and compare, forecast, control deviations) (see manual 11.1, 11.2.3).

n.0: This IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1), so it cannot be the answer to a NOT question.
n.2: Forecasting the objectives and continued viability IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: Controlling deviations that cause an exception IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).

Progress.q: Why does the progress practice include forecasting as well as monitoring what has already been achieved?
o: So that the project board can set the work package tolerances for each team manager in advance
So that an exception can be identified when a breach of tolerance is predicted, before it has happened
So that time-driven reports can be dropped once a stage is running in line with its plan
So that the team manager can approve changes to the stage plan without involving the project manager
Progress.w: An exception is a situation where a deviation beyond tolerance can be forecast, so forecasting lets the project manager raise it early, while the next level still has time to act (see manual 11.1, 11.2.5).

n.0: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager, not the board, and forecasting is not the means of setting them (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Time-driven monitoring and reporting are needed in every stage alongside event-driven control; forecasting does not replace them (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: The team manager works within work package tolerances and escalates to the project manager; the stage plan is the project manager's responsibility within stage tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: The project board is about to authorize the next delivery stage and must agree the limits within which the project manager may act during that stage. Which management level sets these stage tolerances?
o: The business layer
The project board
The project manager
The team manager
Progress.w: Tolerances are delegated down the management levels: the business layer sets project tolerances, the project board sets stage tolerances, and the project manager sets work package tolerances (see manual 11.2.1, fig 11.2).

n.0: The business layer sets project tolerances, normally in the mandate or brief, not the tolerances for each stage (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The project manager works within stage tolerances and sets work package tolerances for team managers (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The team manager works within the work package tolerances set by the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

When a work package is authorized, the [?] sets its tolerances, and the team manager must then deliver the work within them.
o: project board
business layer
senior supplier
project manager
Progress.w: The project manager sets work package tolerances when authorizing a work package in controlling a stage, and the team manager works within them (see manual 11.2.1, 16.4.1).

n.0: The project board sets stage tolerances for the project manager, not tolerances for individual work packages (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: The business layer sets project tolerances; it is not involved in authorizing work packages (manual 11.2.1, 16.4.1).
n.2: The senior supplier represents supplier interests on the board; work package tolerances are set by the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A project board member asks what PRINCE2 means by a tolerance. Which definition is correct?
o: The total budget that the business layer has agreed to release for the whole project, including any contingency
The overall level of risk exposure that the business is willing to accept across all of its projects and operations
The permissible deviation above and below a plan's target before escalation to the next management level is needed
A situation in which a deviation beyond the levels agreed between two levels of management can be forecast
Progress.w: A tolerance is the permissible deviation above and below a plan's target for an aspect such as time or cost, beyond which the matter must be escalated to the next level of management (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: A budget is a planned figure, not a permitted deviation; tolerance is the range above and below a target (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: This describes risk appetite, which the business determines; tolerance is a permitted deviation against a plan's target (manual 9.2.1, 11.2.1).
n.3: This is the definition of an exception, which is triggered when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 11.1).

Progress.q: A project board is agreeing tolerances for the next stage. Which set of items are all aspects for which PRINCE2 7 allows tolerances to be set?
o: Time, cost, scope and stakeholders
Time, cost, scope and sustainability
Quality, risk, benefits and resources
Benefits, risk, quality and communication
Progress.w: PRINCE2 7 recognizes tolerances for seven aspects of performance: time, cost, scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability, the last being new in this edition (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Stakeholders are not a tolerance aspect; the seven are time, cost, scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Resources are not one of the seven tolerance aspects; the other three items are (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Communication is planned through the communication management approach and is not a tolerance aspect (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A stage plan allows some lower-priority products to be left out without the project manager needing to escalate. Which type of tolerance describes this permitted variation in the plan's products?
o: Quality tolerance
Scope tolerance
Benefits tolerance
Risk tolerance
Progress.w: Scope tolerance is the permissible variation of a plan's products, for example agreeing in advance which lower-priority products may be dropped without escalation (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Quality tolerance is the permitted variation from the agreed quality criteria of products, not variation in which products are delivered (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Benefits tolerance is the permitted under- or over-delivery of benefits, not variation in the plan's products (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Risk tolerance sets limits on the plan's aggregated risks, not on which products are delivered (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about tolerances in PRINCE2 7 are correct?

1. The project board sets the tolerances for each work package.
2. The business layer sets the tolerances for the project as a whole.
3. A team manager who forecasts a work package breach escalates it directly to the project board.
4. Tolerances can be set for sustainability as well as for time and cost.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: The business layer sets project tolerances (2), and PRINCE2 7 adds sustainability to time, cost, scope, quality, benefits and risk as an aspect for tolerances (4) (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is correct, but work package tolerances are set by the project manager, not the board (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Neither is correct: the project manager sets work package tolerances, and a team manager escalates a forecast breach to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but a team manager raises a forecast work package breach with the project manager as an issue, not with the board (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A project manager is agreeing a work package description with a team manager. According to PRINCE2 7, which tolerances should the work package description contain?
o: Scope, cost and time
Scope, cost, time and benefits
Quality, cost and time
Time, cost, risk and sustainability
Progress.w: PRINCE2 7 states that the tolerances agreed in a work package description are scope, cost and time; benefits and quality tolerances are not agreed at work package level (see manual 11.2.1).

n.1: Benefits tolerances are not agreed in a work package description; they are managed at project and stage level (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Quality tolerance is not agreed in a work package description, and the scope tolerance it does carry is missing (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: This omits scope, which a work package description carries; PRINCE2 7 lists scope, cost and time as the work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A team manager forecasts that their work package will exceed its cost tolerance, although the stage as a whole is still within its tolerances. How should the team manager handle this?
o: Raise it with the project manager as an issue
Send an exception report to the project board
Prepare an exception plan for the project manager to approve
Agree new work package tolerances with the senior supplier
Progress.w: A team manager works within the work package tolerances set by the project manager and escalates a forecast work package breach to the project manager as an issue, which the project manager handles in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).

n.1: Exception reports are raised by the project manager when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not by a team manager for a work package (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager in managing a stage boundary for stage or project breaches (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager, so the senior supplier cannot change them (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: A project manager is setting up the controls for a delivery stage. Which of these is an example of a time-driven control?
o: An end stage report prepared for the project board as the stage draws to a close
An exception report raised when a breach of stage tolerance is forecast
A board review triggered by completing the project initiation documentation
A highlight report sent to the project board at intervals the board has agreed
Progress.w: Time-driven controls take place at predefined periodic intervals; highlight reports to the board and checkpoint reports on a work package are the two PRINCE2 examples (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: The end stage report is triggered by an event, the end of a stage, so it is an event-driven control (manual 11.2.2).
n.1: Creating an exception report is triggered by an event (a forecast breach), so it is event-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Completion of the PID is a specific event, so a control linked to it is event-driven (manual 11.2.2).

Progress.q: A retail company aligns a project review with the close of its accounting year so the board can confirm funding for the next year. Which type of control is this review?
o: A time-driven control, as it recurs once every year
An event-driven control, triggered by an organizational event
A time-driven control, set at the frequency in the work package
An event-driven control, triggered by a forecast tolerance breach
Progress.w: Event-driven controls occur when a specific event happens, such as the end of a stage, completion of the PID, an exception report or an organizational event such as the end of the financial year (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Although it recurs, the review is triggered by a specific organizational event, the end of the financial year, which PRINCE2 classes as event-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Frequencies in a work package apply to checkpoint reports from the team manager, not to a board review linked to the accounting year (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: The review is triggered by the end of the accounting year, not by a forecast breach of tolerance, which would lead to an exception report (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.6).

Progress.q: Which statement correctly defines an event-driven control in PRINCE2?
o: A control that takes place at predefined periodic intervals, such as every month
A control that a team manager applies informally within a work package
A control that the business layer applies when approving each management product
A control that takes place when a specific event occurs, such as the end of a stage
Progress.w: An event-driven control is triggered by a specific event, for example the end of a stage, completion of the PID, the creation of an exception report or an organizational event (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Controls at predefined periodic intervals are time-driven controls, such as highlight and checkpoint reports (manual 11.2.2).
n.1: Event-driven controls are defined by what triggers them, not by who applies them or how informally (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: The business layer sets project tolerances and decides on project-level exceptions; it does not approve each management product (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

In PRINCE2, monitoring and reporting are mainly time-driven, whereas [?], in the sense of decision-making, is event-driven.
o: forecasting
control
assurance
planning
Progress.w: PRINCE2 explains that monitoring and reporting are time-based, while control, meaning decision-making, is event-based; both are needed in every stage (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Forecasting is part of each progress review and looks forward; it is not the decision-making that PRINCE2 describes as event-driven (manual 11.2.5).
n.2: Assurance is the board's responsibility for checking the project independently of the project manager; it is not the decision-making described here (manual 6.2).
n.3: Planning belongs to the plans practice; the event-driven element of progress is control, meaning decisions (manual 11.2.2).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about the types of control in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. Highlight reports are an event-driven control.
2. Checkpoint reports are a time-driven control.
3. Completion of the project initiation documentation is a time-driven control.
4. Creating an exception report is an event-driven control.
o: 2 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
3 and 4
Progress.w: Checkpoint reports occur at a frequency set in the work package, so they are time-driven (2); creating an exception report is triggered by a forecast breach, so it is event-driven (4) (see manual 11.2.2).

n.1: Statement 2 is correct, but highlight reports are produced at intervals set by the board, so they are time-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: highlight reports are time-driven, and completion of the PID is an event, so it is event-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but completing the PID is a specific event, which makes it event-driven (manual 11.2.2).

Progress.q: Why does PRINCE2 expect both event-driven and time-driven controls to be used in every stage?
o: Time-driven controls apply in the initiation stage, while event-driven controls apply in the delivery stages
Event-driven controls are used by team managers, while time-driven controls are used by the business layer
Time-driven controls replace event-driven controls once the project team has gained experience
Periodic reports keep each level informed, while key decisions are taken when events such as a stage end occur
Progress.w: Time-driven monitoring and reporting (highlight and checkpoint reports) keep people informed between decisions, while event-driven control (for example at the end of a stage or on an exception) is where decisions are taken; both are needed in every stage (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Both types of control are needed in every stage, including initiation and delivery stages; they are not split by stage (manual 11.2.2).
n.1: The two types differ by what triggers them, not by who uses them; for example the project manager produces both highlight and exception reports (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Experience can reduce how often reports are needed, but it does not remove the event-driven decision points (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.4).

Progress.q: As a delivery stage closes, the project manager gives the project board an end stage report so that it can decide whether to authorize the next stage. Which type of control is this, and why?
o: Time-driven, because stages have a fixed length set by the board
Time-driven, because it is a report from the PM to the board
Event-driven, because it is triggered by the end of a stage
Event-driven, because it is triggered by a forecast tolerance breach
Progress.w: The end stage report is an event-driven control: the event that triggers it is the end of a stage, at which the board decides whether to continue (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Stage length is chosen to suit the project rather than fixed, and the end stage report is classed as event-driven because the end of the stage triggers it (manual 2.4, 11.2.2).
n.1: Who sends a report does not decide its type: the highlight report also goes from the project manager to the board but is time-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: A forecast breach of tolerance triggers an exception report, not an end stage report (manual 11.2.6).

Progress.q: A team manager sends a report on the status of the team's work package every Thursday, as agreed when the work package was authorized. Which time-driven control is this?
o: Highlight report
End stage report
Checkpoint report
Exception report
Progress.w: Checkpoint reports are time-driven reports from the team manager to the project manager on work package status, at the frequency defined in the work package (see manual 11.2.2, 11.5).

n.0: A highlight report is from the project manager to the project board on stage status, not from a team manager on a work package (manual 11.5).
n.1: An end stage report is event-driven, produced by the project manager at the end of a stage (manual 11.5).
n.3: An exception report is event-driven, raised by the project manager when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: According to PRINCE2 guidance on reviewing progress, what sets the limit on the level of detail at which progress can be controlled?
o: The frequency of highlight reports set by the board
The number of tolerance areas agreed for the stage
The level of detail held in the plans
The size of the change budget agreed for the stage
Progress.w: Progress can be controlled only at the level of detail contained in the plans, which is why detailed stage and team plans support the high-level project plan (see manual 11.2.3).

n.0: Reporting frequency affects how often progress is seen, but control is limited by the detail of the plans themselves (manual 11.2.3).
n.1: Tolerance areas set the limits of delegated authority, not the level of detail at which progress can be controlled (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.3).
n.3: The change budget funds approved changes; it does not limit the detail of progress control (manual 10.2, 11.2.3).

Progress.q: A project manager is starting a stage with a newly formed team that has no experience of PRINCE2. What does PRINCE2 guidance suggest about the frequency of progress reporting?
o: Report less often at first so that the new team can concentrate on building the products
Report more often at first and reduce the frequency as confidence in the team grows
Keep the reporting frequency fixed for the whole project as stated in the project mandate
Replace checkpoint reports with end stage reports until the team has gained experience
Progress.w: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required; an inexperienced team usually needs more frequent reporting, which can be relaxed as confidence grows (see manual 11.2.4).

n.0: PRINCE2 suggests the reverse: an inexperienced team needs more frequent reporting until confidence grows (manual 11.2.4).
n.2: Reporting frequency reflects the level of control needed and can be adjusted; it is agreed between management levels, not fixed in the mandate (manual 11.2.4).
n.3: End stage reports are event-driven reports to the board and cannot replace the regular checkpoint reports on work packages (manual 11.2.2, 11.5).

Progress.q: Which statement about lessons is consistent with the guidance in the progress practice?
o: Lessons are recorded by project assurance in the issue register as they arise
Lessons are one of the three elements of the purpose of the progress practice
Lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project
Lessons are reviewed in initiation and then held back for the end project report
Progress.w: The guidance on reviewing progress and lessons says lessons should be sought, recorded and actioned throughout the project, not left to the end (see manual 11.2.3).

n.0: Lessons are recorded in the lessons log, part of the project log maintained for the project manager, not in the issue register by assurance (manual 11.5).
n.1: The progress purpose is to monitor and compare, forecast and control deviations; lessons sit in its guidance, not its purpose (manual 11.1, 11.2.3).
n.3: Lessons are not held back: they are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project, including at each stage boundary (manual 11.2.3).

Progress.q: A project board and project manager are agreeing how often progress should be reported during the next stage. What should mainly determine the reporting frequency?
o: The level of control required, reflecting factors such as team experience
A standard reporting frequency that PRINCE2 sets for every type of project
The preference of each team manager, agreed with the senior supplier
The number of products listed in the product register for the stage
Progress.w: The frequency of progress reporting should reflect the level of control required, for example more frequent reports for an inexperienced team or a high-risk stage (see manual 11.2.4).

n.1: PRINCE2 does not prescribe one frequency; it is tailored to the control needed (manual 11.2.4, 2.7).
n.2: Checkpoint frequency is set in the work package by the project manager, and highlight intervals by the board; it is not left to team managers (manual 11.5).
n.3: The number of products does not determine reporting frequency; the level of control required does (manual 11.2.4).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about reporting progress in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. The intervals for highlight reports are defined by the project board.
2. The frequency of checkpoint reports is defined in the work package.
3. Changing the formality of progress reports is not a permitted form of tailoring.
4. Lessons are reported to the project board through checkpoint reports.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: Highlight reports are produced at intervals defined by the project board (1), and checkpoint reports at the frequency defined in the work package (2) (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is correct, but adjusting the frequency and formality of reports is a recognized form of tailoring (manual 2.7).
n.2: Statement 2 is correct, but checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, not to the board (manual 11.5).
n.3: Both are wrong: report formality can be tailored, and checkpoint reports are sent to the project manager, not the board (manual 2.7, 11.5).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Adjusting the frequency and formality of progress reports to suit the size and risk of a project is an example of [?].
o: forecasting
escalation
assurance
tailoring
Progress.w: The tailor to suit the project principle includes making project controls, such as the frequency and formality of reports and reviews, fit the project's scale, complexity and risk (see manual 2.7, 11.2.4).

n.0: Forecasting predicts future performance; it does not change how reports are produced (manual 11.2.5).
n.1: Escalation means referring a forecast breach of tolerance to the next level, not adjusting reporting arrangements (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Assurance is the board's independent checking of the project, not the adjustment of reporting arrangements (manual 6.2).

Progress.q: A project board whose members work in three different countries asks for highlight reports to be shared on an online dashboard instead of as a written document. How does PRINCE2 regard this change?
o: As acceptable tailoring of the format of progress reporting
As a breach of the manage by stages principle for the project
As an exception that the business layer must approve first
As removing one of the time-driven controls from the stage
Progress.w: Report formats can be tailored, for example presenting highlight reports virtually or in a dashboard for a dispersed board, while still providing the regular, time-driven reporting that the board needs (see manual 2.7, 11.2.4, 11.2.7).

n.1: Manage by stages concerns planning and controlling the project stage by stage; changing a report's format does not affect it (manual 2.4).
n.2: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance; changing a report's format is not one (manual 11.1).
n.3: The highlight report is still produced at the agreed intervals, so the time-driven control remains; only its format changes (manual 11.2.2).

Progress.q: Which statement best describes the main reporting lines used in the progress practice?
o: Team managers report work package progress directly to the project board in highlight reports
The PM reports stage progress to the business layer in checkpoint reports
Team managers report work package progress to the PM, who reports stage progress to the board
The project board reports stage progress to the PM in highlight reports
Progress.w: Checkpoint reports carry work package status from team managers to the project manager, and highlight reports carry stage status from the project manager to the project board (see manual 11.5, fig 11.2).

n.0: Team managers report to the project manager through checkpoint reports; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 11.5, 17).
n.1: Checkpoint reports come from team managers to the project manager; stage progress goes to the board in highlight reports (manual 11.5).
n.3: Highlight reports flow from the project manager to the board, not the other way round (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: A project board member asks what PRINCE2 means by an exception. Which definition is correct?
o: Any relevant event raised by a member of the project team that needs to be considered by the project manager
A deviation from the stage plan that the project manager is able to resolve within the stage tolerances
A situation where a deviation beyond the tolerance levels agreed between two management levels can be forecast
An uncertain event with a high probability of occurring that has been entered in the risk register
Progress.w: An exception is a situation where it can be forecast that there will be a deviation beyond the tolerance levels agreed between the project manager and the board, or between the board and the business layer (see manual 11.1).

n.0: An event that needs project management consideration is an issue; it becomes an exception when it is forecast to breach agreed tolerances (manual 10.1, 11.1).
n.1: A deviation that can be resolved within stage tolerance is not an exception; the project manager handles it without an exception report (manual 11.2.6).
n.3: An uncertain event is a risk; an exception is a forecast breach of agreed tolerances (manual 9.2, 11.1).

Progress.q: A project manager forecasts that the current stage will finish two weeks later than planned, but this is still within the stage's time tolerance. What should the project manager do?
o: Take corrective action within the stage, without raising an exception report
Raise an exception report so that the project board can decide on the delay
Ask the business layer to extend the project tolerances to cover the delay
Prepare an exception plan in the managing a stage boundary process
Progress.w: If the project manager can resolve an issue within stage tolerance, no exception report is needed; the project manager takes corrective action in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.6, 16.4.6).

n.1: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; a delay within tolerance is the project manager's to manage (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Project tolerances are not threatened by a delay that is within stage tolerance, and the project manager does not deal directly with the business layer on this (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: An exception plan is prepared when the board requests one after an exception report; none is needed for a deviation within tolerance (manual 11.3.1).

Progress.q: According to PRINCE2 guidance on escalating, which forecast situations should the project manager escalate to the project board?
o: Forecast breaches of work package tolerances
Forecast breaches of stage or project tolerances
Every new entry made in the issue register
Deviations the PM can correct within stage tolerance
Progress.w: Only exceptions to stage or project plans are escalated to the project board; work package exceptions are dealt with by the project manager (see manual 11.2.6).

n.0: Work package exceptions are handled by the project manager in controlling a stage, not escalated to the board (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Many issues can be handled within the project manager's authority; escalation is for forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance (manual 11.2.6).
n.3: Deviations within stage tolerance are dealt with by the project manager through corrective action, without escalation (manual 11.2.6).

Progress.q: What does PRINCE2 guidance on forecasting say that progress reviews should do?
o: Concentrate on work completed and leave prediction to the business case
Be replaced by forecasts produced by the project's data systems
Focus on recording lessons rather than predicting performance
Look forward to predict the likely outcome, as well as reviewing work done
Progress.w: Forecasting guidance says progress reviews should look forward as well as back, predicting likely future performance by extrapolation, data or judgement so that exceptions can be spotted early (see manual 11.2.5).

n.0: Progress reviews look forward as well as back; the forecasts they produce then feed the business case (manual 11.2.5).
n.1: Data and systems support forecasting, but they do not replace progress reviews or the judgement of the management levels (manual 11.2.7).
n.2: Lessons are reviewed too, but the forecasting guidance is that reviews predict future performance as well as reviewing the past (manual 11.2.3, 11.2.5).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about escalation in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. A forecast breach of work package tolerance is handled by the project manager.
2. An exception arises once a tolerance has actually been exceeded, and not before.
3. A team manager escalates a forecast work package breach directly to the project board.
4. A forecast breach of project tolerance is decided on by the business layer.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: Work package exceptions are handled by the project manager (1), and breaches of project tolerance are decided by the business layer, which sets project tolerances (4) (see manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6, 11.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is correct, but an exception is a forecast breach, so it arises before tolerance is actually exceeded (manual 11.1).
n.1: Both are wrong: an exception is based on a forecast, and a team manager escalates to the project manager, not the board (manual 11.1, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but a team manager raises a forecast work package breach with the project manager as an issue (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

When a project manager forecasts that the current stage will exceed its agreed tolerances, the situation should be [?] to the project board using an exception report.
o: escalated
delegated
tailored
baselined
Progress.w: A forecast breach of stage tolerance takes the matter beyond the project manager's authority, so it is escalated to the project board in an exception report (see manual 11.2.6).

n.1: Delegation passes authority down a level, with tolerances; a forecast breach is passed up a level (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; it is not how a forecast breach is handled (manual 2.7).
n.3: Baselining fixes an approved version of a product; it does not describe passing a forecast breach to the board (manual 4.3).

Progress.q: A project manager's forecast shows that the whole project, not just the current stage, will exceed its cost tolerance. Which level decides on the response to this forecast breach?
o: The project board, as it sets the tolerances for each stage
The executive, as the owner of the business case
The project manager, as it is within delegated authority
The business layer, as project tolerances are set at that level
Progress.w: Each level decides on breaches of the tolerances it set: the business layer sets project tolerances, so it decides how to respond to a forecast breach of them, after the board refers it upwards (see manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).

n.0: The board decides on breaches of stage tolerance; a forecast breach of project tolerance goes on to the business layer (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: The executive is accountable within the board, but project tolerances belong to the business layer, which decides on project-level exceptions (manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).
n.2: The project manager's authority is limited to stage tolerances; a forecast project-level breach is outside it (manual 11.2.1).

Progress.q: Why does PRINCE2 expect a forecast breach of tolerance to be escalated as soon as it is identified?
o: So the project manager can widen the stage tolerances in good time
So the next level of management can decide while there is still time to act
So the team manager can approve an exception plan before the stage ends
So the business layer can take over the project board's role for the stage
Progress.w: Escalating as soon as a breach is forecast alerts the next level of management early, while there are still options to respond, which is the point of managing by exception (see manual 2.5, 11.2.6).

n.0: Stage tolerances are set by the board; the project manager cannot widen them (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager and approved by the board, not by a team manager (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Escalation lets the next level decide on the exception; it does not transfer the board's role to the business layer (manual 11.2.6).

Progress.q: In the exception management technique, which management product does the project manager use to tell the project board that the stage is forecast to exceed its tolerances?
o: Issue report
Exception report
Highlight report
Exception plan
Progress.w: In the technique, the project manager forecasts a breach of stage tolerance in controlling a stage and raises an exception report to the project board (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: An issue report records the assessment of a formal issue; a forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated in an exception report (manual 10.5, 11.3.1).
n.2: Highlight reports are routine, time-driven summaries of stage status; a forecast breach is escalated through an exception report (manual 11.5).
n.3: The exception plan is prepared later, if the board requests it in response to the exception report (manual 11.3.1).

Progress.q: After reviewing an exception report, the project board asks for an exception plan. In which process does the project manager prepare the exception plan?
o: Managing a stage boundary
Controlling a stage
Directing a project
Managing product delivery
Progress.w: The project manager prepares the exception plan in managing a stage boundary ('prepare exception plan'), and the board then approves it in directing a project (see manual 11.3.1, 18).

n.1: Controlling a stage is where the exception report is raised, not where the exception plan is prepared (manual 11.3.1, 16.4.7).
n.2: Directing a project is where the board decides on the exception and later approves the exception plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Managing product delivery is the team manager's process for executing work packages (manual 17).

Progress.q: In the exception management technique, what is the project board's part once it has received an exception report?
o: To prepare the exception plan for the revised stage
To capture the issue and assess its effect on the stage
To take corrective action within work package tolerances
To decide on a response, such as requesting an exception plan
Progress.w: The board, in directing a project, decides how to respond to the exception report: for example by requesting an exception plan, giving direction or closing the project prematurely (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: The project manager prepares the exception plan in managing a stage boundary; the board approves it (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: Capturing and assessing the issue is done by the project manager in controlling a stage, before the report is raised (manual 11.3.1, 16.4.5).
n.2: Corrective action within tolerance is the project manager's job; the board is involved because tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 11.2.6).

Progress.q: A project board approves an exception plan in response to a forecast breach of stage tolerance. What happens to the plans for the current stage?
o: The exception plan is added to the affected team plan for that work
The exception plan becomes the project plan for the rest of the project
The exception plan replaces the stage plan, and a revised stage begins
The exception plan is filed and the original stage plan continues
Progress.w: When approved, the exception plan replaces the stage plan; its approval marks a stage boundary and a revised stage begins (for example stage 2 becomes stage 2a) (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: Exception plans are never used to replace a team plan; a stage-level exception plan replaces the stage plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: A stage-level exception plan replaces the stage plan, not the project plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Once approved, the exception plan takes the place of the stage plan; the original plan does not continue (manual 11.3.1).

Progress.q: Which sequence correctly reflects the exception management technique?
