o: Issue arises; exception report; board decision; exception plan prepared; plan approved
Issue arises; exception plan prepared; exception report; board decision; plan approved
Exception report; issue arises; board decision; plan approved; exception plan prepared
Issue arises; board decision; exception report; exception plan prepared; plan approved
Progress.w: The technique runs: an issue arises, the project manager forecasts a breach and raises an exception report, the board decides, the project manager prepares an exception plan, and the board approves it (see manual 11.3.1, fig 11.3).

n.1: The exception plan is prepared after the board has received the exception report and decided to request one (manual 11.3.1).
n.2: The issue comes first, and the plan must be prepared before the board can approve it (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: The board decides in response to the exception report, so the report comes before the decision (manual 11.3.1).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about the exception management technique are correct?

1. The exception plan is prepared in the controlling a stage process.
2. The exception report is raised in the controlling a stage process.
3. Approval of an exception plan marks a stage boundary.
4. The team manager approves the exception plan.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: The project manager raises the exception report in controlling a stage (2), and approval of the exception plan by the board marks a stage boundary for the revised stage (3) (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is correct, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 11.3.1).
n.2: Both are wrong: the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary and approved by the project board (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but the project board, not the team manager, approves an exception plan (manual 11.3.1).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

Once the project manager has prepared an exception plan for a stage, the project board approves it in the [?] process.
o: managing a stage boundary
controlling a stage
directing a project
closing a project
Progress.w: The board approves exception plans in directing a project, through the 'authorize a stage or exception plan' activity (see manual 11.3.1, 14).

n.0: Managing a stage boundary is where the project manager prepares the exception plan, not where the board approves it (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: Controlling a stage is where the exception report is raised (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Closing a project is for planned or premature closure, not for approving exception plans (manual 19).

Progress.q: Which statement about the exception management technique is correct?
o: Tolerances are delegated down through the levels, and forecast breaches go one level up
Each level sets its own tolerances, and forecast breaches go to the business layer
Tolerances are set by the team manager, and forecast breaches go to the project board
The board sets tolerances for every level, and forecast breaches go to project assurance
Progress.w: PRINCE2 delegates tolerances down through the four management levels (11.2.1); in the exception management technique, a level that forecasts a breach of its tolerances escalates to the level above, which set them (see manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).

n.1: Tolerances are set by the level above, and a breach goes to the next level up, which may or may not be the business layer (manual 11.3.1).
n.2: Team managers work within tolerances set by the project manager and escalate to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The board sets stage tolerances only, and breaches go to the management level that set the tolerance, not to assurance (manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).

Progress.q: A new team manager asks what a checkpoint report is for. Which statement describes the purpose of a checkpoint report?
o: To report a summary of stage status from the project manager to the project board
To tell the project board that stage tolerances are forecast to be exceeded
To summarize the stage at its end so the board can decide what to do next
To report the status of a work package from the team manager to the project manager
Progress.w: A checkpoint report is produced by the team manager for the project manager, reporting work package status at the frequency defined in the work package (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Summarizing stage status for the board is the purpose of the highlight report (manual 11.5).
n.1: Informing the board of a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance is the purpose of the exception report (manual 11.5).
n.2: A summary at the end of a stage to support the board's next decision is the end stage report (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: The project board wants a regular summary of the status of the current stage, produced at intervals it has chosen. Which management product provides this?
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
End stage report
Exception report
Progress.w: The project manager produces highlight reports for the project board (and possibly other stakeholders), summarizing stage status at intervals defined by the board (see manual 11.5).

n.1: A checkpoint report gives work package status to the project manager, not stage status to the board (manual 11.5).
n.2: An end stage report is produced at the end of a stage, not at regular intervals during it (manual 11.5).
n.3: An exception report is raised when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not at regular intervals (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: At the end of a project, the project manager prepares an end project report. Against what does this report review how the project has performed?
o: The project brief approved when initiation was authorized
The latest highlight report sent to the project board
The lessons log maintained since starting up the project
The version of the PID that was used to authorize the project
Progress.w: The end project report reviews how the project performed against the version of the project initiation documentation used to authorize it, including a review of the products (see manual 11.5, 19.4.4).

n.0: The project brief is the basis for authorizing initiation; the end project report compares performance with the PID that authorized the project (manual 11.5).
n.1: Highlight reports summarize stage status; they are not the baseline for reviewing the whole project's performance (manual 11.5).
n.2: The lessons log is reviewed for lessons to pass on; it is not the baseline for measuring the project's performance (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: During closure, the project manager reviews the project log and produces a lessons report. What is the purpose of the lessons report?
o: To record lessons informally as they are identified during the project
To pass on lessons so that they can be applied on future projects
To review the project's performance against the baselined PID
To confirm that users have accepted the project product
Progress.w: The lessons report passes on lessons that can be used by other or future projects; in closing a project it is produced from a review of the project log, in consultation with the project management team (see manual 11.5, 19.4.4).

n.0: Recording lessons as they arise is the purpose of the lessons log, part of the project log (manual 11.5).
n.2: Reviewing performance against the PID used to authorize the project is the purpose of the end project report (manual 11.5).
n.3: Confirming acceptance of the project product is done in the 'confirm project acceptance' activity of closing a project (manual 19.4.3).

Progress.q:
Which two statements about progress reports are correct?

1. An end stage report is produced by the team manager.
2. A highlight report is sent by the team manager to the project board.
3. An exception report offers options and a recommendation to the project board.
4. An end stage report gives the project board the information it needs to decide what to do next.
o: 3 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
Progress.w: An exception report sets out options and a recommendation for the board (3), and an end stage report summarizes progress so the board can decide what to do next (4) (see manual 11.5).

n.1: Both are wrong: the end stage report and the highlight report are both produced by the project manager for the board (manual 11.5).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct, but the end stage report is produced by the project manager, not the team manager (manual 11.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but highlight reports are produced by the project manager, not the team manager (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: A project manager is drafting an exception report for the project board. Which content would the project manager expect to include in it?
o: A product review covering the products delivered, their handover and any off-specifications
Follow-on action recommendations for issues and risks that remain open at closure
The consequences of the deviation for the project and the business if it is not addressed
A review of the benefits already realized by products in operational use
Progress.w: An exception report explains the deviation, including its consequences for the project and the business if not addressed, and offers options with a recommendation (see manual 11.5).

n.0: A product review of delivered products and their handover belongs in the end project report (manual 11.5).
n.1: Follow-on action recommendations are part of the end project report produced in closing a project (manual 11.5, 19.2).
n.3: A review of benefits achieved so far belongs in the end project report, not an exception report (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: When, by whom and in which process is an end stage report normally produced?
o: At regular intervals in a stage, by the project manager, in controlling a stage
Near the end of a stage, by the project manager, in managing a stage boundary
At the end of each work package, by the team manager, in managing product delivery
At the end of the project, by the project manager, in closing a project
Progress.w: The project manager prepares the end stage report as close as possible to the end of each stage, in the 'evaluate the stage' activity of managing a stage boundary (see manual 11.5, 18).

n.0: Regular reports during a stage are highlight reports, produced in controlling a stage (manual 11.5, 16.4.8).
n.2: Team managers report on work packages through checkpoint reports and notify completion to the project manager; they do not produce end stage reports (manual 11.5, 17).
n.3: The report produced at the end of the project in closing a project is the end project report (manual 11.5, 19.4.4).

Progress.q: A team manager wants to tell the project manager that the work package is on schedule and that the team has identified one new risk. Which management product should the team manager use?
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Issue report
Daily log
Progress.w: Checkpoint reports give the project manager the status of a work package, including issues and risks for that work package, at the agreed frequency (see manual 11.5, 17.4.2).

n.1: Highlight reports are produced by the project manager for the project board, not by a team manager (manual 11.5).
n.2: An issue report is prepared for a formal issue being assessed; routine work package status goes in a checkpoint report (manual 10.5, 11.5).
n.3: The daily log is the project manager's own informal diary, not a report from the team manager (manual 11.5).

Progress.q: A project manager wants somewhere to note informal issues, actions and observations that do not need formal handling. What is the purpose of the daily log?
o: To act as the project manager's diary of informal issues, actions, notes and observations
To record the formal issues that are being managed through the issue reports
To hold the list of all the products in a plan together with their current status
To record the planned quality activities for products and the results of those activities
Progress.w: The daily log, part of the project log, is the project manager's informal diary for informal issues, required actions, notes and observations, including sensitive matters (see manual 11.5).

n.1: Formal issues are recorded in the issue register and may have issue reports; the daily log holds informal ones (manual 10.5, 11.5).
n.2: Products and their status are recorded in the product register, another part of the project log (manual 4.3).
n.3: Planned quality activities and their results are recorded in the quality register (manual 8.5).

Progress.q: A project manager wants lessons from earlier, similar projects to be recorded before any detailed planning begins. In which process is the lessons log first set up?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Controlling a stage
Closing a project
Progress.w: The lessons log is set up in starting up a project as part of 'assess previous lessons', so that lessons from earlier projects can be recorded at the outset (see manual 11.5, 13).

n.0: The project log is completed in initiation, but the lessons log is first set up earlier, in starting up a project (manual 4.3, 13).
n.2: Lessons are captured during controlling a stage, but the log already exists by then (manual 13).
n.3: In closing a project the log is reviewed to produce the lessons report; it is not set up then (manual 19.4.4).

Progress.q: A project manager is agreeing the management approaches in initiation. What does the digital and data management approach describe?
o: How the project's products will be quality checked and then accepted by the users
How issues will be captured and assessed and how changes to baselines will be controlled
How data and information will be created, used and managed during and after the project
How the project's stakeholders will be engaged and kept informed during the project
Progress.w: The digital and data management approach, part of the PID, sets out how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem, through the lifecycle and afterwards, including security and privacy (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Quality checking and acceptance arrangements belong in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).
n.1: Handling issues and controlling changes to baselines is covered by the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.3: Engaging and informing stakeholders is planned in the communication management approach (manual 3.4).

Progress.q: The digital and data management approach supports the progress practice. In which management product is the digital and data management approach included?
o: The project brief from starting up a project
The end project report produced at closure
The project mandate from the business layer
The project initiation documentation
Progress.w: The digital and data management approach is one of the nine management approaches agreed in initiating a project and held in the project initiation documentation (see manual 11.5, 15).

n.0: The project brief is assembled in starting up; the management approaches are agreed later, in initiating a project, and form part of the PID (manual 15).
n.1: The end project report reviews performance at closure; it does not contain the management approaches (manual 11.5).
n.2: The project mandate is provided by the business layer to trigger starting up; it does not contain PRINCE2 management approaches (manual 13).

Progress.q: According to PRINCE2 guidance on the use of data and systems in progress management, which is a benefit of using data and technology?
o: Systems can set the tolerances for each management level from past data
Automated tracking removes the need for highlight reports to the board
Stored data on past performance can help to predict future performance
Dashboards can replace the board's decisions at the end of each stage
Progress.w: Guidance on data and systems notes that stored past performance helps predict future performance, automation saves manually consolidating data, and information can be presented in the format stakeholders prefer (see manual 11.2.7).

n.0: Tolerances are set by the management levels (business layer, board, project manager), not by data or systems (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.7).
n.1: Automation removes manual consolidation of data from different sources; the board still needs highlight reporting (manual 11.2.7).
n.3: Data supports decisions but does not replace the board's event-driven decisions at stage boundaries (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.7).

Progress.q:
Which two statements describe how the progress practice supports the PRINCE2 principles?

1. Setting tolerances and raising exception reports supports manage by exception.
2. Fixing the same reporting frequency for every project supports tailor to suit the project.
3. Recording lessons in the lessons log and passing them on supports learn from experience.
4. Producing highlight reports is how the focus on products principle is applied.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
Progress.w: Tolerances and exception reporting put manage by exception into practice (1), and the lessons log and lessons report support learn from experience (3) (see manual 2.2, 2.5, 11.7).

n.1: Statement 1 is correct, but tailoring means adjusting reporting frequency and formality to the project, not fixing one frequency for all (manual 2.7).
n.2: Both are wrong: tailoring adjusts reporting to suit each project, and focus on products concerns defining products, not highlight reporting (manual 2.6, 2.7).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but focus on products is applied by defining products and their quality requirements, not by highlight reports (manual 2.6).

Progress.q: A board member privately tells the project manager about a sensitive concern that should not yet be visible to the wider project team. Where should the project manager record it?
o: Issue register
Risk register
Lessons log
Daily log
Progress.w: Informal issues, including sensitive ones where open access through the issue register would be inappropriate, are recorded in the project manager's daily log (see manual 11.2.3, 11.5).

n.0: The issue register is open to the project team, so it is inappropriate for an informal or sensitive issue (manual 11.2.3, 11.5).
n.1: The risk register records identified risks for formal management, and is not the place for a sensitive informal concern (manual 9.5).
n.2: The lessons log records lessons for this or future projects, not current concerns (manual 11.5).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

By planning and controlling the project stage by stage, with an end stage report at each stage boundary, the progress practice supports the principle of manage by [?].
o: exception
objectives
products
stages
Progress.w: Stage-by-stage control and end stage reports at each stage boundary support the manage by stages principle (see manual 2.4, 11.7).

n.0: Manage by exception is supported by tolerances and exception reporting, not by stage-by-stage control with end stage reports (manual 2.5).
n.1: Manage by objectives is not one of the seven PRINCE2 principles (manual 2).
n.2: PRINCE2's principle is focus on products, not manage by products, and it concerns defining products (manual 2.6).

Progress.q: A new project manager asks why PRINCE2 includes a progress practice. Which statement describes the purpose of the progress practice?
o: To set up ways to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable, so that decisions on continued investment can be made
To support communication and control by defining the products to be delivered and the means, timing and cost of delivering them
To identify, assess and control the uncertainties that could affect the project's objectives, improving its ability to succeed
To set up ways to monitor and compare actual achievement with the plan, forecast objectives and viability, and control deviations causing an exception
Progress.w: The progress practice exists to provide mechanisms for monitoring and comparing actual against planned achievement, to forecast the project's objectives and continued viability, and to control deviations that would cause an exception (see manual 11.1).

n.0: Judging whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable is the purpose of the business case practice (manual 5.1), not progress.
n.1: Defining the products and the means to deliver them, to support communication and control, is the purpose of the plans practice (manual 7.1).
n.2: Identifying, assessing and controlling uncertainty is the purpose of the risk practice (manual 9.1).

Progress.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

As well as comparing what has been achieved with what was planned, the progress practice provides a [?] for the project's objectives and its continued viability.
o: baseline
tolerance
justification
forecast
Progress.w: Part of the purpose of the progress practice is to provide a forecast for the project's objectives and its continued viability, so that problems can be seen before they happen (see manual 11.1, 11.2.5).

n.0: A baseline is an approved, version-controlled product (such as a plan) used as a reference point; the progress practice compares against it rather than providing one for viability (manual 4.3, 11.1).
n.1: Tolerances are the permissible deviations set by each management level; they are not what the practice provides for objectives and viability (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Justification of the investment is judged through the business case practice (manual 5.1); progress feeds forecasts into it rather than providing the justification itself.

Progress.q: Which element of the purpose of the progress practice is concerned with looking ahead, rather than reviewing what has already been achieved?
o: Comparing the achievements made so far with those that were originally planned
Recording lessons in the lessons log as soon as they are identified
Providing a forecast for the project's objectives and continued viability
Defining the products to be delivered and estimating when they will be ready
Progress.w: Forecasting is the forward-looking element of the progress purpose: it predicts the project's objectives and continued viability so that deviations can be dealt with early (see manual 11.1, 11.2.5).

n.0: Comparing actual with planned achievement is part of the purpose, but it reviews work already done rather than looking ahead (manual 11.1).
n.1: Recording lessons is part of the guidance on reviewing progress and lessons, not part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1, 11.2.3).
n.3: Defining products and estimating when they will be delivered is the purpose of the plans practice, not progress (manual 7.1).

Progress.q: The progress practice repeatedly sets a plan, carries out the work, checks actual results against the plan and then takes action. On which cycle is the progress practice based?
o: Develop, check, maintain, confirm
Identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate
Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
Plan, do, check, act
Progress.w: The progress practice follows a plan-do-check-act cycle: work is planned, carried out, checked against the plan and corrective action taken where needed (see manual 11.1).

n.0: Develop, check, maintain and confirm are the steps of the business case technique (manual 5.3), not the cycle behind progress.
n.1: Identify, assess, plan, implement and communicate are the steps of the risk management technique (manual 9.3).
n.2: Capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement are the steps of the issues technique (manual 10.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about managing a stage boundary in the PRINCE2 lifecycle are correct?
1. It is first used towards the end of the initiation stage.
2. It is used at the end of the final stage to prepare for closure.
3. It can be used during a stage to prepare an exception plan.
4. It is carried out by the project board at the directing level.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 1 is correct: managing a stage boundary is first used near the end of initiation to plan the first delivery stage. Statement 3 is correct: it is also used whenever the board asks for an exception plan (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1, and 18.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage; closing a project is carried out within the final stage instead (manual 12).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage, and it is run by the project manager at the managing level, not by the board (manual 12, 18.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the project manager carries out managing a stage boundary; the board then decides in directing a project (manual 12, 14.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A project manager is drafting the stage structure for a new project and proposes 'Closure' as the last stage. Which statement correctly describes where closing a project sits in the lifecycle?
o: It is planned and authorized as a separate stage after the final delivery stage
It runs at the end of each delivery stage before the next one is authorized
It is the last part of the final delivery stage, not a stage of its own
It is carried out by the project board as part of directing a project
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Closing a project is not a stage. It takes place at the end of the final delivery stage, and the closure work is planned in that stage's plan (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1, and 19.1).

n.0: Closure is not planned as a separate stage; its activities are part of the final delivery stage (manual 12, 19.1).
n.1: Work at the end of each non-final stage is done in managing a stage boundary, not closing a project (manual 12, 18.1).
n.3: The project manager carries out closing a project; the board then authorizes closure in directing a project (manual 12, 14.4.5, 19.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: During the initiation stage, which combination of processes is in use?
o: Directing a project, initiating a project and managing a stage boundary
Starting up a project, initiating a project and controlling a stage
Initiating a project, controlling a stage and managing product delivery
Directing a project, initiating a project and closing a project
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In the initiation stage the board directs through directing a project, the project manager runs initiating a project, and managing a stage boundary is used near the end to plan the first delivery stage. Managing product delivery is not used in initiation (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.1: Starting up a project is pre-project, before the initiation stage begins (manual 12, 13.3).
n.2: The process model shows no managing product delivery in the initiation stage; specialist delivery starts in later stages (manual 12).
n.3: Closing a project belongs to the final delivery stage, not to initiation (manual 12, 19.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A project has four stages. In the second stage, which is not the final stage, which processes are used by the project manager and the team managers?
o: Initiating a project, controlling a stage and managing product delivery
Controlling a stage, managing product delivery and closing a project
Starting up a project, controlling a stage and managing a stage boundary
Controlling a stage, managing product delivery and managing a stage boundary
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Subsequent delivery stages use controlling a stage (project manager) and managing product delivery (team managers), with managing a stage boundary near the end to prepare for the next stage; the board directs throughout (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.0: Initiating a project is used in the initiation stage, which is the first stage, not a later delivery stage (manual 12, 15.3).
n.1: Closing a project is used in the final stage; this is not the final stage, so a stage boundary is managed instead (manual 12, 19.1).
n.2: Starting up a project is pre-project and is not repeated in delivery stages (manual 12, 13.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: What is the purpose of the starting up a project process?
o: To ensure the prerequisites for initiating are in place by asking whether there is a viable and worthwhile project
To establish solid foundations so the business understands the work before committing significant expenditure
To enable the project board to be accountable for success by making key decisions and exercising overall control
To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed and objectives are reviewed
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project makes sure the prerequisites for initiation are in place by answering one question: do we have a viable and worthwhile project? (see manual 13.1).

n.1: Establishing solid foundations before significant spend is the purpose of initiating a project, which follows starting up (manual 15.1).
n.2: Enabling the board to be accountable through key decisions is the purpose of directing a project (manual 14.1).
n.3: A fixed point for confirming acceptance of the project product is the purpose of closing a project (manual 19.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A regional director has asked for a new customer portal to be explored. What triggers the starting up a project process?
o: The project brief from the project manager
The initiation notice from the project board
The request to initiate a project from the executive
The project mandate from the business layer
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project is triggered by the project mandate, provided by the responsible authority in the business that is commissioning the project (see manual 13.3).

n.0: The project brief is an output of starting up a project, assembled by the project manager; it cannot be the trigger (manual 13.4).
n.1: The initiation notice comes from the board's authorize initiation activity and triggers initiating a project, not starting up (manual 14.4.1, 15.3).
n.2: The request to initiate is the final output of starting up a project and triggers directing a project (manual 13.4.8, 14.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which of the following is an objective of the starting up a project process?
o: To ensure there is common understanding of how baselines will be established and controlled
To ensure alternative ways of doing the work are evaluated and a project approach is agreed
To ensure the business layer has an effective connection to the project throughout its life
To produce a project plan showing how and when products will be delivered and at what cost
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: One objective of starting up a project is that the various ways of approaching the project are evaluated and a project approach is agreed (see manual 13.2).

n.0: Understanding how baselines will be established and controlled is an objective of initiating a project (manual 15.2).
n.2: Keeping the business layer connected to the project is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Understanding how and when products will be delivered and at what cost comes from the project plan prepared in initiating a project (manual 15.2, 15.4.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Starting up a project is as much about preventing [?] projects from being initiated as it is about approving the initiation of viable ones.
o: high-risk
compulsory
poorly conceived
externally funded
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: A key part of the purpose of starting up a project is to stop poorly conceived ideas from going into initiation, as well as approving viable ones (see manual 13.1).

n.0: A project with significant risk can still be viable and worthwhile; risk is assessed rather than a reason in itself to stop initiation (manual 13.1, 9.1).
n.1: Compulsory projects still go through starting up and still need the chosen option justified; they are not what the process sets out to prevent (manual 13.1, 5.2.3).
n.3: The source of funding does not make an idea poorly conceived; the test is whether the project is viable and worthwhile (manual 13.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Why is starting up a project described as a lighter process than initiating a project?
o: It does the minimum work needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile
It is run by the business layer, so the project manager has little to do
It produces the full business case, so initiation needs less detail later
It is run as a short first stage that has its own approved stage plan
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project is deliberately light: it does the minimum necessary to decide whether it is worthwhile to initiate the project, leaving detailed planning to initiation (see manual 13.1).

n.1: The project manager does most of the work in starting up, preparing the outline business case, project brief and initiation stage plan (manual 13.4).
n.2: Starting up produces the outline business case; the full business case is prepared in initiating a project (manual 13.4.3, 15.4.5).
n.3: Starting up a project is pre-project, not a stage; the first stage is the initiation stage, whose plan starting up produces (manual 12, 13.4.7).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the starting up a project process?
1. There is business justification for initiating the project, documented in an outline business case.
2. The full business case is approved so that the delivery stages can begin.
3. The individuals needed for initiation and significant project management roles are appointed.
4. The project plan is baselined so that progress can be measured against it.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 1 is correct: starting up checks there is justification for initiating, recorded in the outline business case. Statement 3 is correct: it ensures individuals are appointed to do the work of initiation and take significant project management roles (see manual 13.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the full business case is prepared in initiating a project and approved when the board authorizes the project (manual 15.4.5, 14.4.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: the full business case and the project plan come from initiating a project and are approved when the project is authorized (manual 15.4.4, 15.4.5, 14.4.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the project plan is prepared in initiating a project and baselined when the board authorizes the project (manual 15.4.4, 7.2.2.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A new project forms part of a wider programme of change. How is starting up a project likely to be affected?
o: The programme's own initiation stage replaces the starting up a project process
The programme board authorizes initiation, so the project mandate is not produced
The project manager approves the project brief on behalf of the programme
The programme may provide much of the information needed for the project brief
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: When a project is part of a programme, the programme may supply much of the content of the project brief, which reduces the work done in starting up a project (see manual 13.3).

n.0: The project still needs its prerequisites for initiation checked; the programme supplies information rather than replacing the process (manual 13.3).
n.1: The programme acts as the commissioning business and is the source of the mandate that triggers starting up, so a mandate still exists (manual 13.3).
n.2: The project brief is approved by the project board in authorize initiation, not by the project manager (manual 14.4.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement about the timing of starting up a project is correct?
o: It begins after the board has authorized the project and approved the PID
It runs alongside initiation so the project brief and PID are produced together
Its activities take place before the explicit decision to initiate the project
It begins when the board issues an initiation notice to the project manager
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The decision to start a project must be explicit, and the activities of starting up a project happen before that decision is made; the board then decides in authorize initiation (see manual 13.1, 14.4.1).

n.0: Authorizing the project and approving the PID come at the end of initiation, long after starting up is complete (manual 14.4.2).
n.1: The project brief is produced in starting up and approved before initiation begins; the PID is assembled later, in initiating a project (manual 13.4, 15.4.6).
n.3: The initiation notice is issued in authorize initiation and triggers initiating a project, after starting up has finished (manual 14.4.1, 15.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Before planning begins, a project manager wants a record of what went well and badly on earlier, similar projects. Which activity of starting up a project creates the log used for this?
o: Appoint the executive and the project manager
Plan the initiation stage
Request project initiation
Assess previous lessons
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The assess previous lessons activity creates the lessons log and gathers lessons from people and teams with experience of similar projects and from lessons reports (see manual 13.4.2).

n.0: Appoint the executive and the project manager puts the two key roles in place; it does not create the lessons log (manual 13.4.1).
n.1: Plan the initiation stage produces the initiation stage plan, drawing on lessons already captured rather than creating the log (manual 13.4.7).
n.2: Request project initiation asks the board for authority to initiate; it is the last activity and creates no log (manual 13.4.8).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: During starting up a project, the project manager consults the executive, senior user and senior supplier about what the project will deliver. In which activity is the project product description created?
o: Assemble the project brief
Prepare the outline business case
Select the project approach
Appoint the project management team
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In prepare the outline business case the project manager consults the senior user, senior supplier and executive to define what the project will deliver, and creates the project product description (see manual 13.4.3).

n.0: Assemble the project brief brings together products already created, including the project product description, rather than creating it (manual 13.4).
n.2: Select the project approach decides how the work will be approached, such as build or buy and the delivery method (manual 13.4.5).
n.3: Appoint the project management team puts the board and other key roles in place; it does not define the project's main product (manual 13.4.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which of the following products is NOT created during the starting up a project process?
o: Project brief
Initiation stage plan
Project plan
Outline business case
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The project plan is prepared in initiating a project, in the prepare the project plan activity. The brief, initiation stage plan and outline business case are all outputs of starting up a project (see manual 13.4, 15.4.4).

n.0: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project and approved in authorize initiation (manual 13.4, 14.4.1).
n.1: The initiation stage plan is created in the plan the initiation stage activity of starting up a project (manual 13.4.7).
n.3: The outline business case is created in the prepare the outline business case activity of starting up a project (manual 13.4.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In starting up a project, the [?] activity decides how the work will be tackled, for example in-house or by third parties, and which delivery method will be used.
o: select the project approach
assemble the project brief
prepare the outline business case
plan the initiation stage
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Select the project approach decides how the work of the project will be approached, including in-house or external delivery, build or buy, and the delivery method (see manual 13.4.5).

n.1: Assemble the project brief brings the starting up products together; the approach it contains is decided in select the project approach (manual 13.4).
n.2: Prepare the outline business case sets out the justification and creates the project product description, not the delivery approach (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: Plan the initiation stage plans the work of initiation, not how the whole project's work will be delivered (manual 13.4.7).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Why does starting up a project include the plan the initiation stage activity?
o: The initiation stage plan stands in for the project plan until closure
The board uses the initiation stage plan to authorize the whole project
It lets team managers begin work packages for the first delivery stage
Initiation uses time and resources, so its work must be planned and approved
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Initiating a project takes time and consumes resources, so the work is planned and approved in advance to make sure initiation is not aimless; starting up is not complete without this plan (see manual 13.4.7, 13.4.8).

n.0: The project plan is prepared during initiation and is approved when the project is authorized; the initiation stage plan covers the initiation stage (manual 15.4.4, 7.2.2.2).
n.1: The board authorizes the project on the basis of the PID at the end of initiation; the initiation stage plan supports the earlier decision to authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1, 14.4.2).
n.2: Work packages for a delivery stage are authorized in controlling a stage, after the board has authorized the project and that stage; team managers play no part in starting up (manual 12, 14.4.4, 16.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about the appoint the project management team activity are correct?
1. The project manager is accountable for appointing the project management team.
2. The team should reflect the interests of the business, users and suppliers.
3. Appointments are made after the board has authorized initiation.
4. Appointees need the authority and knowledge to work together as an effective team.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 2 is correct: the project management team should represent business, user and supplier interests. Statement 4 is correct: appointees need suitable authority, responsibility and knowledge and the ability to work as a high-performing team (see manual 13.4.4).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the business layer is accountable and the executive responsible for these appointments; the project manager is not involved (manual 13.4.4, tab 13.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: the project manager does not make these appointments, and they are made during starting up, before the board authorizes initiation (manual 13.4.4, 14.4.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the project management team is appointed during starting up a project, before the request to initiate is sent (manual 13.4.4, 13.4.8).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement correctly describes the request project initiation activity?
o: The executive asks the business layer for authority to deliver the project product
The project manager formally asks the board for authority to initiate the project
The project manager asks the board to approve the PID and the project plan
The project manager sends an initiation notice to each team manager
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Request project initiation is the last activity of starting up: the project manager formally asks the board for authority to initiate, presenting the project approach, appointments and initiation stage plan. Starting up is not complete without the initiation stage plan (see manual 13.4.8).

n.0: Authority to deliver the project comes from the project board in authorize the project, and it is requested by the project manager at the end of initiation (manual 14.4.2, 15.4.7).
n.2: The PID and project plan do not exist yet; they are produced in initiating a project and submitted through request project authorization (manual 15.4.6, 15.4.7).
n.3: The initiation notice is issued by the board in authorize initiation, not by the project manager, and team managers are not involved in starting up (manual 14.4.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: While starting up a project, the project manager identifies several key risks. The risk register has not yet been created. Where should these risks be recorded?
o: In the daily log
In the lessons log
In the risk management approach
In the issue register
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project sets up the daily log, and the initial key risks are recorded there until the risk register is created during initiation (see manual 13, tab 13.3).

n.1: The lessons log holds lessons from previous and current projects, not the project's own risks (manual 13.4.2).
n.2: The risk management approach describes procedures, scales and responsibilities; it holds no specific risks and is not agreed until initiation (manual 15.4.2, 9.5).
n.3: The issue register is set up in initiating a project and records formal issues, not risks (manual 15, tab 15.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: What is the purpose of the directing a project process?
o: To ensure the prerequisites for initiating the project are in place and that the project is viable and worthwhile
To enable the project board to be accountable for success by making key decisions while delegating day-to-day management
To assign work, monitor it, deal with issues and report progress so that the stage stays within its tolerances
To control the link between the project manager and team managers by agreeing how work is accepted and delivered
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Directing a project enables the project board to be accountable for the project's success by making key decisions and exercising overall control, while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager (see manual 14.1).

n.0: Ensuring the prerequisites for initiation are in place is the purpose of starting up a project (manual 13.1).
n.2: Assigning and monitoring work and reporting progress within stage tolerances is the purpose of controlling a stage, run by the project manager (manual 16.1).
n.3: Controlling the link between the project manager and team managers is the purpose of managing product delivery (manual 17.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: The project manager has completed the work of starting up a project. What triggers the directing a project process?
o: The project mandate from the business layer
The initiation notice from the board
The request to initiate a project
The first highlight report from the project manager
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Directing a project starts when the board receives the request to initiate a project, the final output of starting up a project (see manual 14.3, 13.4.8).

n.0: The project mandate triggers starting up a project, which comes before directing a project (manual 13.3).
n.1: The initiation notice is an output of directing a project (authorize initiation) and triggers initiating a project (manual 14.4.1, 15.3).
n.3: Highlight reports are produced in controlling a stage, long after directing a project has begun (manual 16.1, 11.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which of the following is an objective of the directing a project process?
o: To ensure there is authority to close the project
To ensure team managers are clear on the effort and timescales expected
To assure that all products in the current stage plan have been approved
To check that the users have accepted the project product
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The objectives of directing a project include ensuring there is authority to initiate, to deliver the project product and to close the project (see manual 14.2).

n.1: Making sure team managers are clear on effort, cost and timescales is an objective of managing product delivery (manual 17.2).
n.2: Assuring the board that the current stage's products are complete and approved is an objective of managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2).
n.3: Checking user acceptance of the project product is an objective of closing a project, which the board then relies on when authorizing closure (manual 19.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement best describes how the project board works during the directing a project process?
o: It authorizes work packages directly with the team managers
It prepares the next stage plan towards the end of each stage
It writes highlight reports for the business layer at agreed intervals
It manages by exception and delegates day-to-day management
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In directing a project the board manages by exception: it makes the key decisions and exercises overall control but does not carry out day-to-day management, which is delegated to the project manager (see manual 14.1, 14.3).

n.0: Work packages are authorized by the project manager in controlling a stage; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.3, 16.1).
n.1: The project manager prepares the next stage plan in managing a stage boundary; the board approves it in directing a project (manual 18.1, 14.4.4).
n.2: Highlight reports are written by the project manager for the board, not by the board for the business layer (manual 16.1, 11.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
One objective of directing a project is to ensure that the [?] has an effective connection to the project.
o: project support function
business layer
team manager
quality assurance function
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Directing a project aims to give the business layer an effective connection to the project, with the board communicating with it on the business's behalf (see manual 14.2, 14.3).

n.0: Project support works for the project manager inside the project; its connection is not an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2, 6.2).
n.2: Team managers take their direction from the project manager, not from the board, so linking them to the board is not a directing objective (manual 14.3, 17.1).
n.3: Quality assurance is an independent business function outside the project management team; the directing objective concerns the business layer as a whole (manual 14.2, 8.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about directing a project are correct?
1. The board takes part in managing product delivery so it can oversee team managers.
2. It gives the board a way to keep the project justified without hands-on management.
3. It ends when the project manager submits the end project report to the board.
4. Plans for realizing benefits after the project closes are managed and reviewed.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 2 is correct: directing a project lets the board ensure continued business justification without being overburdened by hands-on management. Statement 4 is correct: an objective is that plans for realizing post-project benefits are managed and reviewed (see manual 14.2, 14.3).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the board is not involved in managing product delivery; team managers work under the project manager (manual 14.3).
n.1: Both are wrong: the board is not involved in managing product delivery, and directing a project continues until the board authorizes closure after closing a project (manual 14.3, 14.4.5).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: directing a project runs until after closing a project, when the board authorizes project closure (manual 12, 14.4.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement describes the project board's relationship with the business layer during directing a project?
o: The board passes accountability to the business layer once initiation is authorized
The board approves the project mandate on behalf of the business layer
The board stays accountable to the business layer and acts as its link to the project
The board receives checkpoint reports and forwards them to the business layer
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the project's success and, in directing a project, communicates with the business layer so that the business has an effective connection to the project (see manual 14.2, 14.3, 6.2.1).

n.0: The board remains accountable for the project's success throughout; accountability does not move back to the business layer after initiation (manual 14.1, 6.2.1).
n.1: The project mandate comes from the business layer itself and triggers starting up, before the board exists (manual 13.3).
n.3: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager; the board receives highlight reports (manual 17.1, 11.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: When the project board approves the project initiation documentation and authorizes the project, which objective of directing a project is it meeting?
o: There is authority to deliver the project product
There is authority to initiate the project
There is authority to close the project
Users have formally accepted the completed project product
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Approving the PID in authorize the project gives the authority to deliver the project's product, one of the objectives of directing a project (see manual 14.2, 14.4.2).

n.1: Authority to initiate is given earlier, in authorize initiation, when the project brief and initiation stage plan are approved (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: Authority to close is given at the end of the project in authorize project closure (manual 14.4.5).
n.3: Confirming user acceptance of the project product is an objective of closing a project at the end of the final stage, not of approving the PID (manual 19.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: The project board has received the project brief and the initiation stage plan from the project manager. In which directing a project activity does the board review and approve them?
o: Authorize the project
Authorize a stage or exception plan
Authorize initiation
Give ongoing direction
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In authorize initiation the board reviews and approves the project brief and the initiation stage plan and confirms that investing in initiation is worthwhile (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: Authorize the project comes at the end of initiation and approves the PID, not the brief and initiation stage plan (manual 14.4.2).
n.1: Authorize a stage or exception plan approves later stage plans and exception plans; the initiation stage plan is approved with the brief in authorize initiation (manual 14.4.4, 14.4.1).
n.3: Give ongoing direction provides informal guidance and responses to exceptions during a stage; it does not approve the brief (manual 14.4.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A project manager sends the board an exception report forecasting that stage cost tolerance will be exceeded. In which directing a project activity does the board respond to the exception report?
o: Give ongoing direction
Authorize a stage or exception plan
Authorize the project
Authorize project closure
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The board responds to exception reports in give ongoing direction, for example by asking for an exception plan. Any exception plan is later approved in authorize a stage or exception plan (see manual 14.4.3, 14.4.4).

n.1: Authorize a stage or exception plan is used once an exception plan has been prepared; the first response to the report, such as requesting that plan, is given in give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.3, 14.4.4).
n.2: Authorize the project is the decision at the end of initiation to proceed with the rest of the project; it is not used to respond to a stage exception (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Authorize project closure confirms that the project can close at the end of the final stage; an exception report is handled through give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.5, 14.4.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: At the end of initiation, the board confirms there is an adequate business case, approves the PID and reviews the benefits management approach. Which directing a project activity is this?
o: Authorize initiation
Authorize a stage or exception plan
Give ongoing direction
Authorize the project
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In authorize the project the board decides whether to proceed with the rest of the project: it confirms the business case shows a viable project, approves the PID including the management approaches and project plan, and reviews the benefits management approach (see manual 14.4.2).

n.0: Authorize initiation happens at the end of starting up and approves the project brief and initiation stage plan, before any PID exists (manual 14.4.1).
n.1: Authorize a stage or exception plan approves stage plans or exception plans; approving the PID is part of authorize the project (manual 14.4.4, 14.4.2).
n.2: Give ongoing direction provides guidance and responds to exceptions during stages; it is not the formal decision to proceed with the project (manual 14.4.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In the [?] activity, the board checks that post-project benefits reviews are planned and sends a closure notification to the business layer.
o: give ongoing direction
authorize project closure
authorize the project
authorize a stage or exception plan
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In authorize project closure the board confirms that the project can close, ensures post-project benefits reviews are planned to cover the products in operational use, and notifies the business layer (see manual 14.4.5).

n.0: Give ongoing direction gives guidance during the project; it does not confirm closure or issue the closure notification (manual 14.4.3).
n.2: Authorize the project is the decision to proceed at the end of initiation, not the end of the project (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Authorize a stage or exception plan approves the next stage or an exception plan; it is not used to close the project (manual 14.4.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about the authorize initiation activity are correct?
1. It must be carried out at a formal board meeting so that the business layer can attend.
2. It approves the full business case and the project plan for the delivery stages.
3. It can be done without a formal meeting if the board agrees and the executive gives a documented instruction.
4. It confirms that the investment in initiating the project is worthwhile.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 3 is correct: authorize initiation may be done with or without a formal meeting, but all board members must agree and the project manager must receive a documented instruction from the executive. Statement 4 is correct: the board confirms the investment in initiation is worthwhile (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: Both are wrong: no formal meeting is required, and the full business case and project plan are approved later, in authorize the project (manual 14.4.1, 14.4.2).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: authorize initiation can be done without a formal meeting when board members agree and the executive documents the instruction (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: the full business case and project plan are prepared during initiation and approved in authorize the project (manual 15.4.4, 15.4.5, 14.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement about the give ongoing direction activity is correct?
o: It takes place at each stage end so that the board can approve the next stage plan
It is the activity team managers use to obtain board decisions on their work packages
Board members can give guidance individually or collectively at any time during the project
It is the activity in which the board authorizes the project's first delivery stage
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Give ongoing direction covers informal guidance and responses to requests for advice, given at any time by the board as a whole or by individual members, as well as responses to exception reports and to advice from the business layer (see manual 14.4.3).

n.0: Approving the next stage plan at a stage end is done in authorize a stage or exception plan (manual 14.4.4).
n.1: Team managers take direction from the project manager, not the board; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.3, 17.1).
n.3: Authorizing a delivery stage, including the first, is done in authorize a stage or exception plan (manual 14.4.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: When is the authorize a stage or exception plan activity used?
o: At each stage end except the final stage, and to approve exception plans
At the end of every stage including the final one, before closure is authorized
At the end of starting up a project, to approve the initiation stage plan
At regular intervals during each stage, after each highlight report is received
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: A stage starts only when the board authorizes it. The board uses authorize a stage or exception plan at the end of each stage except the last to approve the next stage plan, and whenever it needs to approve an exception plan (see manual 14.4.4).

n.1: There is no next stage after the final stage; the board uses authorize project closure instead (manual 14.4.4, 14.4.5).
n.2: The initiation stage plan is approved with the project brief in authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1).
n.3: Highlight reports keep the board informed between decision points; responses during a stage are given in give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.3, 11.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: At the end of the authorize the project activity, what does the project board issue?
o: An initiation notice
A project authorization notice
A closure notification
A request for project authorization
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Authorize the project ends with a project authorization notice, confirming that the project may proceed to its delivery stages (see manual 14.4.2).

n.0: The initiation notice is issued earlier, in authorize initiation, and triggers initiating a project (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: A closure notification is sent to the business layer in authorize project closure (manual 14.4.5).
n.3: The request for project authorization is sent by the project manager at the end of initiating a project; it is the input to authorize the project, not its output (manual 15.4.7).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: What is the purpose of the initiating a project process?
o: To establish solid foundations so the business understands the work needed before committing significant spend
To check whether there is a viable and worthwhile project before anyone commits to the work of initiation
To give the board enough information to review the current stage and decide whether to approve the next one
To control the link between the project manager and team managers so that specialist products are delivered
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so that the business understands the work needed to deliver the project product before it commits to significant expenditure or resources (see manual 15.1).

n.1: Checking whether there is a viable and worthwhile project, before initiation, is the purpose of starting up a project (manual 13.1).
n.2: Giving the board what it needs to review the current stage and prepare for the next is the purpose of managing a stage boundary (manual 18.1).
n.3: Controlling the link between the project manager and team managers is the purpose of managing product delivery (manual 17.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: The project board has just approved the project brief and the initiation stage plan. What triggers the initiating a project process?
o: The project mandate from the business layer
The request to initiate from the project manager
The project authorization notice from the board
The initiation notice from authorize initiation
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Initiating a project is triggered by the initiation notice the board issues in the authorize initiation activity of directing a project (see manual 15.3, 14.4.1).

n.0: The project mandate triggers starting up a project, which comes before the board's decision to initiate (manual 13.3).
n.1: The request to initiate is the project manager's request to the board; the board must authorize initiation before initiation starts (manual 13.4.8, 14.4.1).
n.2: The project authorization notice comes at the end of initiation, when the board authorizes the project (manual 14.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which of the following is an objective of the initiating a project process?
o: Appointment of the individuals who will carry out the work of initiation
Common understanding of how and when products are delivered and at what cost
An effective connection between the business layer and the project
Confirmation that the business can support the products after closure
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Initiating a project aims for a common understanding of, among other things, how and when the project's products will be delivered and at what cost (see manual 15.2).

n.0: Appointing the people who will do the work of initiation is an objective of starting up a project (manual 13.2).
n.2: Giving the business layer an effective connection to the project is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Ensuring the business can support the products after the project closes is an objective of closing a project (manual 19.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Initiating a project ensures there is a common understanding of how [?] will be identified, assessed and controlled.
o: stakeholders and users
lessons and benefits
risks and issues
team plans and checkpoints
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: One objective of initiating a project is a common understanding of how risks and issues will be identified, assessed and controlled, set out in the risk and issue management approaches (see manual 15.2, 15.4.2).

n.0: Stakeholders are considered through the communication management approach, which addresses who needs information, when and in what format, rather than identifying and controlling them (manual 15.2).
n.1: Lessons are gathered from starting up onwards and benefits are covered by the business case and benefits management approach; the objective names risks and issues (manual 15.2, 13.4.2).
n.3: Team plans and checkpoint reports belong to managing product delivery in later stages, not to this initiation objective (manual 17.1, 15.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about initiating a project are correct?
1. It ends with a request to the project board for authority to deliver the project.
2. It is carried out by the project board, with the project manager in support.
3. It is triggered by the project mandate provided by the business layer.
4. Near its end, managing a stage boundary is used to plan the first delivery stage.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 1 is correct: initiating a project ends with request project authorization. Statement 4 is correct: as initiation nears its end, managing a stage boundary prepares the plan for the first delivery stage (see manual 15.3, 15.4.7, fig 15.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: initiating a project is a managing-level process run by the project manager; the board directs it through directing a project (manual 12, 15.3).
n.2: Both are wrong: the project manager runs initiating a project, and it is triggered by the initiation notice, not the mandate (manual 12, 15.3).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the mandate triggers starting up a project; initiating a project is triggered by the initiation notice (manual 13.3, 15.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: How does the business case develop during the initiating a project process?
o: The outline business case is developed into a full business case for board approval
The business case is created for the first time, based on the project mandate
The full business case is summarized into an outline version for the PID
The business case is passed to the business layer, which approves it before authorization
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: During initiation the outline business case from starting up is updated with costs and timescales from the project plan and the aggregated risks, giving the full business case that the board approves when it authorizes the project (see manual 15.4.5, 14.4.2).

n.1: The business case already exists in outline form, created in starting up a project (manual 13.4.3).
n.2: The direction is the reverse: the outline version from starting up is expanded into the full business case (manual 15.4.5).
n.3: The project board approves the full business case when it authorizes the project; it is not sent to the business layer for approval (manual 14.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: During initiation, which objective of initiating a project is mainly addressed by agreeing the communication management approach?
o: How baselines will be established and controlled
How the required quality will be achieved
How risks will be identified, assessed and controlled
Who needs information, in what format and at what time
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The communication management approach sets out how information will flow to and from stakeholders, which meets the initiation objective of understanding who needs information, in what format and when (see manual 15.2, 15.4.2).

n.0: How baselines are established and controlled is addressed through the issue management approach and change control (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).
n.1: How quality will be achieved is set out in the quality management approach (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).
n.2: How risks will be identified, assessed and controlled is set out in the risk management approach (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement about who is involved in initiating a project is correct?
o: Team managers build early specialist products through managing product delivery
The business layer runs it and passes the completed PID to the project board
The project manager runs it, while the board directs it through directing a project
The board runs it day to day and the project manager provides project support
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Initiating a project is a managing-level process run by the project manager; the board keeps control through directing a project, for example giving ongoing direction and then authorizing the project (see manual 12, fig 12.1, 15.3).

n.0: The process model shows no managing product delivery in the initiation stage; specialist delivery starts in later stages (manual 12, fig 12.1).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project management team; the project manager assembles the PID and the board approves it (manual 15.4.6, 14.4.2).
n.3: The board manages by exception and does not run day-to-day work; the project manager runs initiation (manual 14.3, 15.3).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: During initiation, the project manager documents how the organization's standard project method will be adapted to suit this project, and the board agrees it. Which initiating a project activity is this?
o: Agree the management approaches
Establish project controls
Assemble the project initiation documentation
Agree the tailoring requirements
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: In agree the tailoring requirements the project decides how PRINCE2, or the business's own standard method, will be tailored to internal and external factors, and that tailoring is documented and agreed (see manual 15.4.1).

n.0: Agree the management approaches defines the nine approaches, such as risk and quality, rather than how the method as a whole is tailored (manual 15.4.2).
n.1: Establish project controls agrees the board's level of control and the mechanisms for it, not the tailoring of the method (manual 15.4.3).
n.2: Assemble the PID brings together and cross-checks products already prepared, including the tailoring decisions; it does not define them (manual 15.4.6).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A project manager agrees with the board how much control it will exercise after initiation and how, and agrees how the project manager will control the work of team managers. Which activity is this?
o: Agree the tailoring requirements
Establish project controls
Prepare the project plan
Request project authorization
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Establish project controls agrees the board's level of control after initiation and the mechanism for it, and the project manager's control over the work of team managers (see manual 15.4.3).

n.0: Agree the tailoring requirements decides how the method is adapted to the project, not the specific controls between levels (manual 15.4.1).
n.2: Prepare the project plan sets out the major products, timescales and costs; the control levels are agreed in establish project controls (manual 15.4.4).
n.3: Request project authorization asks the board for authority to deliver the project once the PID is ready (manual 15.4.7).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: In the prepare the full business case activity, what information is used to update the outline business case?
o: Actual costs from the first delivery stage and the first end stage report
Benefits figures from the project mandate and lessons from the lessons log
Time and costs from the project plan and aggregated risks from the project log
Progress figures from the checkpoint reports produced by team managers
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The outline business case is refined into the full business case using the timescales and costs from the project plan and the aggregated risks from the project log. The executive is accountable and the project manager responsible (see manual 15.4.5).

n.0: The first delivery stage has not started during initiation, so there are no actual stage costs or end stage report yet (manual 12, 15.4.5).
n.1: The mandate fed the outline business case in starting up; the full version is built from the project plan and the aggregated risks (manual 13.4.3, 15.4.5).
n.3: Checkpoint reports come from team managers during delivery stages, after initiation has finished (manual 17.1, 15.4.5).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The version of the project initiation documentation used to gain authorization for the project is [?] and placed under change control.
o: baselined
archived
closed
superseded
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: When the PID is assembled, its elements are cross-checked for compatibility and the version used to gain project authorization is baselined and placed under change control (see manual 15.4.6, 4.3.1).

n.1: The PID is not archived at authorization; it is the baseline used throughout the project and later compared with actual performance (manual 4.3.1).
n.2: The PID stays in use until the project closes; it is reviewed and may be updated at stage boundaries (manual 4.3.1, 18.2).
n.3: The PID supersedes the project brief, not the other way round; the authorized PID becomes the baseline (manual 15.4.6, 4.3.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Which two statements about the agree the management approaches activity are correct?
1. The approaches are agreed after the project plan, so they can be fitted to it.
2. The approaches reflect business strategies, standards and practices the project must follow.
3. Lessons on similar approaches used by earlier projects should be sought.
4. Seven approaches are agreed, one for each practice.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Statement 2 is correct: the approaches are derived from the business strategies, standards and practices the project must comply with, and from the users' expectations in the project product description. Statement 3 is correct: lessons on approaches from similar projects should be sought (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the approaches are defined first, and then project controls and the project plan can follow (manual 15.4.2).
n.1: Both are wrong: the approaches come before the project plan, and there are nine approaches, not one for each of the seven practices (manual 15.4.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: nine management approaches are agreed (benefits, change, commercial, communication, digital and data, issue, quality, risk, sustainability) (manual 15.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which list contains three of the management approaches agreed during initiating a project?
o: Benefits, configuration management, and quality
Change control, risk, and communication
Stakeholder engagement, quality, and risk
Benefits, commercial, and digital and data
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: The nine management approaches are benefits, change, commercial, communication, digital and data, issue, quality, risk and sustainability, so benefits, commercial, and digital and data are all among them (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: There is no configuration management approach in PRINCE2 7; control of changes to baselined products, including version control, is covered by the issue management approach (manual 15.4.2, 10.5).
n.1: There is no change control approach in PRINCE2 7: change control sits in the issue management approach, and the change management approach covers organizational change (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: There is no stakeholder engagement approach; stakeholder communication is covered by the communication management approach (manual 15.4.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Why does initiating a project agree the management approaches before preparing the project plan?
o: The plan must include the costs of the approaches, which the business layer sets in advance
The approaches set out how the project will be run, so the controls and plan can build on them
The board approves each approach separately before any planning is allowed to start
The approaches replace product descriptions, so the plan can be made without them
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Once the management approaches are defined, project controls and the project plan can follow, because they need to reflect how risk, quality, issues, communication and the other areas will be managed (see manual 15.4.2, 15.4.4).

n.0: The business layer does not set the cost of the approaches in advance; the approaches are derived from business standards and the users' expectations (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: The board approves the approaches as part of the PID in authorize the project, at the end of initiation, not before planning (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Product descriptions are still created as part of planning; the approaches describe how the project is managed, not what each product is (manual 15.4.4).
