Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which statement correctly describes the request project authorization activity?
o: The project manager asks the board for authority to deliver the project, with or without a formal meeting
The executive asks the business layer to approve the project brief and the outline business case
The project manager asks the board to approve the initiation stage plan before initiation starts
The project manager asks team managers to accept the work packages for the first delivery stage
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Request project authorization is the last activity of initiating a project: the project manager contacts the board to request authority to deliver the project, which may be done with or without a formal meeting (see manual 15.4.7).

n.1: The project brief and outline business case were approved by the board in authorize initiation, not by the business layer (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: The initiation stage plan was approved before initiation began, in authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1).
n.3: Work packages are agreed with team managers in controlling a stage after the board has authorized the project and the stage (manual 16.1, 14.4.4).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: A new project board asks which PRINCE2 process its members will use. Which process does the project board use from the end of starting up a project until after the project has been closed?
o: Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
Initiating a project
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Directing a project is the project board's process. It runs from the request to initiate at the end of starting up a project until after closing a project, when the board authorizes closure (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.0: Controlling a stage is used by the project manager at the managing level to run each delivery stage day to day; it is not the board's process (manual 12, 16.1).
n.1: Managing a stage boundary is used by the project manager near the end of each stage to prepare the information the board needs; it is a managing-level process (manual 12, 18.1).
n.3: Initiating a project is run by the project manager during the initiation stage to build the project's foundations; it is a managing-level process (manual 12, 15.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Starting up a project is unusual in the PRINCE2 process model because more than one management level takes part in it. Which levels are involved in starting up a project?
o: The directing and the managing levels
The managing and the delivering levels
The directing and the delivering levels
The delivering level and the business layer
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project is used by both the directing level (the executive appoints the project management team after being appointed by the business layer) and the managing level (the project manager prepares the outline business case, brief and initiation stage plan) (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.1: Team managers at the delivering level do not take part in starting up a project; delivery work starts with managing product delivery in later stages (manual 12).
n.2: The delivering level is not involved in starting up a project, and the project manager at the managing level does most of the preparation work (manual 12, 13.4).
n.3: Team managers are not involved, and the business layer sits outside the project management team; it appoints the executive but is not a management level of the project (manual 12, 6.2).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q: Which process takes place in the pre-project part of the PRINCE2 lifecycle, before the project board has decided to initiate the project?
o: Initiating a project
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
Starting up a project
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: Starting up a project is the pre-project process. It is triggered by the project mandate and checks whether there is a viable and worthwhile project before the board decides to initiate (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1, and 13.1).

n.0: Initiating a project is the first part of the project itself (the initiation stage) and starts after the board authorizes initiation (manual 12, 15.3).
n.1: Directing a project starts when the board receives the request to initiate from starting up a project, so it begins at the end of pre-project (manual 12, 14.3).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of the initiation stage, so it is not part of pre-project (manual 12, 18.1).

Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
A PRINCE2 project has at least [?] management stages, the first of which is the initiation stage.
o: three
two
one
four
Processes: Starting Up to Initiation.w: A PRINCE2 project has a minimum of two management stages: the initiation stage and at least one further delivery stage (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.0: Three is common, but the minimum is two: the initiation stage plus one delivery stage (manual 12).
n.2: One stage would leave no separate initiation stage; PRINCE2 requires initiation plus at least one delivery stage (manual 12).
n.3: Four is not the minimum; a project can be run in two stages, initiation and one delivery stage (manual 12).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the 'controlling a stage' process?
1. To keep the risks and issues that arise during the stage under control.
2. To prepare the next stage plan so the board can decide whether to continue.
3. To make sure the stage's agreed products meet quality expectations and are accepted.
4. To give the authority for the project product to be delivered.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Statements 1 and 3 are objectives of controlling a stage: risks and issues are controlled, and the stage's agreed products meet their quality expectations and are accepted (see manual 16.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the next stage plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong. The next stage plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2), and authority to deliver the project product is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: giving authority to deliver the project product is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: During a delivery stage, the project manager forecasts that the stage will exceed its cost tolerance. Which process does 'controlling a stage' send this to?
o: Managing product delivery, so the team manager can re-plan
Managing a stage boundary, to draw up an exception plan first
Closing a project, as the business case may no longer be viable
Directing a project, as the board set the stage tolerances
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: When stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, controlling a stage escalates it with an exception report to the project board in directing a project. The board set the stage tolerances, so the decision is the board's (see manual 16.3, 16.4.7).

n.0: Managing product delivery works to work package tolerances set by the project manager; a forecast breach of stage tolerance goes to the board (manual 16.4.7, 17.2).
n.1: An exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary only after the board has seen the exception report and asked for one (manual ch 18, 14.4.3).
n.2: A forecast cost overrun is an exception for the board to decide on; premature closure happens only if the board orders it (manual 16.4.7, 19.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Why does the 'controlling a stage' process include taking corrective action?
o: So the project manager can resolve deviations that are within stage tolerance
So the project manager can approve changes that exceed stage tolerance
So the team manager can revise the stage plan when work runs late
So the board can swap the stage plan for an exception plan mid-stage
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Part of the purpose of controlling a stage is to take corrective action so the stage stays within the tolerances set by the board. The project manager handles deviations inside those limits without referring them upwards, which reflects managing by exception (see manual 16.1, 16.4.6).

n.1: Going beyond stage tolerance is an exception that must be escalated to the board; corrective action is chosen within tolerance (manual 16.4.6, 16.4.7).
n.2: The team manager works in managing product delivery and raises issues with the project manager; the stage plan belongs to the project manager (manual 17.4.2).
n.3: An exception plan follows an exception report, is prepared in managing a stage boundary, and its approval marks a stage boundary (manual ch 18).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A delivery stage that is not the final stage is nearing its end. Which process does 'controlling a stage' lead into next?
o: Closing a project, to prepare the end project report
Initiating a project, to rebuild the initiation documentation
Managing a stage boundary, to prepare the next stage plan
Directing a project, to authorize the next stage straight away
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: As a stage boundary approaches, controlling a stage hands over to managing a stage boundary, where the next stage plan and end stage report are prepared for the board. When the project end approaches, it leads to closing a project instead (see manual 16.3).

n.0: Closing a project follows controlling a stage when the end of the project, not the end of a stage, is approaching (manual 16.3, 19.3).
n.1: Initiating a project runs once, in the initiation stage; later updates to the PID are made in managing a stage boundary (manual 15.3, 18.2).
n.3: The board authorizes the next stage only after receiving the next stage plan and end stage report from managing a stage boundary (manual 14.4.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which 'controlling a stage' activity does the project manager use to formally pass responsibility for work to a team manager?
o: Accept a work package
Authorize a work package
Evaluate work package status
Receive completed work package
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: In authorize a work package the project manager defines the work package with the team manager, confirms it is accepted and authorizes the team to start, so responsibility for the work passes formally to the team manager (see manual 16.4.1).

n.0: Accept a work package is the team manager's activity in managing product delivery, where the team manager agrees to deliver the work (manual 17.4.1).
n.2: This activity checks progress on work already handed over, using checkpoint reports and conversations with the team manager (manual 16.4.2).
n.3: This activity happens when the work is finished and handed back, not when it is handed over (manual 16.4.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which 'controlling a stage' activity produces the regular, time-driven progress report that the project manager sends to the project board?
o: Evaluate stage status
Escalate issues and risks
Evaluate the stage
Report highlights
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: In report highlights the project manager assembles checkpoint reports, the project log and stage plan revisions and produces a highlight report for the board at the agreed frequency (see manual 16.4.8).

n.0: Evaluate stage status compares actual progress with the stage plan; its findings feed the report but it does not produce it (manual 16.4.4).
n.1: This activity produces an exception report when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, which is event-driven rather than regular (manual 16.4.7).
n.2: Evaluate the stage is a managing a stage boundary activity that prepares the end stage report (manual ch 18).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
When the project manager forecasts that the stage will go beyond its tolerances, the activity [?] is used to send an exception report to the project board.
o: escalate issues and risks
take corrective action
capture issues and risks
evaluate stage status
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Escalate issues and risks is used when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: the project manager sends an exception report to the board so it can decide how to respond (see manual 16.4.7).

n.1: Corrective action is used for deviations the project manager can resolve within the stage tolerances (manual 16.4.6).
n.2: This activity registers and assesses new issues and risks before a course of action is chosen; it does not escalate them (manual 16.4.5).
n.3: This activity compares actual with planned progress and may reveal the problem, but escalation is a separate activity (manual 16.4.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In the 'receive completed work package' activity, what does the project manager make sure of for each product delivered?
o: The executive has approved it, as owner of the business case
Its benefits have been measured and recorded
It has the approval set out in its product description
The users have taken it into operational use
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: In receive completed work package the project manager checks that each product has its requisite approval, as defined by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description, then updates the product register and stage plan (see manual 16.4.3).

n.0: Approval follows the quality responsibilities in each product description; the executive is not the approver of every product (manual 16.4.3).
n.1: Benefits are assessed through the benefits management approach, including reviews after closure, not when a work package is received (manual 19.2, 14.4.5).
n.3: Products are passed into the operational and maintenance environment in closing a project, in confirm project acceptance (manual 19.4.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Which two statements about the activities of 'controlling a stage' are correct?
1. In 'evaluate work package status', the project manager may talk informally with the team manager as well as reviewing checkpoint reports.
2. In 'authorize a work package', the project manager co-creates and reviews the work package with the team manager.
3. In 'report highlights', the team manager produces the highlight report for the project board.
4. In 'take corrective action', the project manager may choose actions forecast to exceed stage tolerance.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Evaluate work package status includes informal conversations with the team manager and reviewing checkpoint reports, and a work package is co-created and reviewed with the team manager before it is authorized (see manual 16.4.1, 16.4.2).

n.1: Statement 4 is wrong: corrective action is selected within tolerance, and a forecast breach is escalated to the board (manual 16.4.6, 16.4.7). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: the highlight report is produced by the project manager (manual 16.4.8). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong. The project manager produces the highlight report (manual 16.4.8), and actions forecast to exceed stage tolerance must be escalated (manual 16.4.7).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A user raises a request for change with the project manager during a delivery stage. Which 'controlling a stage' activity should deal with it first?
o: Take corrective action, to change the work in progress
Escalate issues and risks, to send it to the board
Capture issues and risks, to register and assess it
Authorize a work package, to pass it to a team
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: New issues, including requests for change, enter controlling a stage through capture issues and risks, where each one is registered and then assessed before a course of action is decided (see manual 16.4.5).

n.0: Corrective action is chosen after an issue has been registered and assessed, not before (manual 16.4.5, 16.4.6).
n.1: Escalation is used when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; the request has not yet been assessed (manual 16.4.7).
n.3: New work would follow a decision on the request; it is not the first step when an issue arrives (manual 16.4.1, 16.4.5).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Apart from the start of a new stage, what can trigger the 'authorize a work package' activity?
o: A team manager notifying that a work package is complete
The project board ordering a premature close
The business layer issuing a revised project mandate
A corrective action that needs new or amended work
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Authorize a work package is triggered at the start of a stage and also by corrective action, which is put into effect through new or amended work packages (see manual 16.4.1, 16.4.6).

n.0: Notice of a completed work package triggers receive completed work package, not authorization of new work (manual 16.4.3).
n.1: A premature close notice from the board triggers closing a project, where work is made safe rather than newly authorized (manual 19.4.2).
n.2: The project mandate triggers starting up a project; it does not trigger work packages within a stage (manual 13.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: During 'evaluate stage status', the project manager finds a slippage that can be fixed within stage tolerance. What should happen next?
o: Escalate it to the board in an exception report
Take corrective action, using new or amended work packages
Hold it for the next stage plan at the stage boundary
Ask the team manager to widen the work package tolerance
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Where evaluate stage status shows a deviation within tolerance, the project manager takes corrective action, collecting information, choosing a solution within tolerance and putting it into effect through authorize a work package (see manual 16.4.4, 16.4.6).

n.0: An exception report is needed only when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; this slippage is within tolerance (manual 16.4.7).
n.2: Deviations within tolerance are dealt with during the stage by corrective action, not deferred to managing a stage boundary (manual 16.4.6).
n.3: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager, and the team manager cannot change them; corrective action is the route (manual 16.4.6, 17.2).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'managing product delivery' process?
o: To control the link between the project manager and the team manager for specialist work
To assign and monitor work and take corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance
To let the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management
To set solid foundations before significant resources are committed
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the team manager by agreeing the requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery of specialist products (see manual 17.1).

n.1: This is the purpose of controlling a stage, the project manager's process for running the stage (manual 16.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of directing a project, the project board's process; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of initiating a project, which runs in the initiation stage (manual 15.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which role uses the 'managing product delivery' process to carry out its work?
o: The project manager, who authorizes and receives work packages
The senior supplier, who directs supplier teams for the board
Project support, which keeps the registers for the team
The team manager, who agrees and delivers work packages
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Managing product delivery is the delivering level of the process model: it is the team manager's view of the work, while controlling a stage is the project manager's view (see manual 12, 17.3).

n.2: Project support helps the project manager with administration; it is informed of work package completion but does not run the process (manual 17.4.4).

exception

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which is an objective of the 'managing product delivery' process?

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: While executing a work package, a team manager identifies a new risk to the team's products. What should the team manager do?

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: What happens in the 'accept a work package' activity of 'managing product delivery'?

n.2: Checkpoint reporting happens once work is under way, in execute and evaluate a work package (manual 17.4.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A project uses an external supplier whose teams follow their own delivery method. How does 'managing product delivery' still give the project manager control?

n.1: The board is not involved in managing product delivery; the team manager reports to the project manager (manual 17.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: To assign and monitor work and take corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance
To give the board enough information to review the stage and confirm continued justification
To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed
To ensure the prerequisites for initiating a project are in place
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Managing a stage boundary lets the project manager give the board enough information to review the success of the current stage, see the next stage plan and the updated project plan, and confirm continued business justification and acceptable risks (see manual 18.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of controlling a stage, which runs the work during the stage (manual 16.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of closing a project, used within the final stage (manual 19.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of starting up a project, which comes before initiation (manual 13.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: When in a project is the 'managing a stage boundary' process used for the first time?

At the start of the first delivery stage, to authorize its work
Near the end of the initiation stage, to plan the first delivery stage
Near the end of the final stage, to plan the closure activities

n.1: Work in a delivery stage is authorized through controlling a stage, after the board has authorized the stage (manual 16.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:

n.2: A team plan is an optional plan made by a team manager in managing product delivery (manual 17.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which is an objective of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: To give the project manager accurate progress information at an agreed frequency
To check that the users accept the project product before closure

To assure the board that all products in the stage plan are complete and approved

n.1: This is an objective of closing a project (manual 19.2).
n.2: This is an objective of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?

1 and 3

n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong. Highlight reporting is part of controlling a stage (manual 16.4.8), and the next stage is authorized by the board in directing a project (manual 14.4.4).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the project manager requests the next stage, and the board authorizes it in directing a project (manual 14.4.4). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which feature of a PRINCE2 project makes the 'managing a stage boundary' process possible?
o: Each stage delivers benefits that can be measured at the end of the stage
The project has a fixed end date that is set by the business layer
Every team works to a team plan that is re-approved at each stage end
The project is divided into management stages, each ending in a decision point
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Managing a stage boundary rests on the project being divided into management stages. Each stage end gives the board a point to review the stage and decide whether to continue (see manual 18.3).

n.1: Stage boundaries depend on the project being divided into stages, not on a fixed end date (manual 18.3).
n.2: Team plans are optional and are not approved at stage boundaries; the board reviews stage and project plans (manual 17.4.1, 18.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: At a stage boundary, the project board decides that the business case is no longer viable and stops the project. How does PRINCE2 view this decision?

As sound management, as stopping an unjustified project is not a failure
As a breach of project tolerance that is referred to the business layer first
As a decision that must wait until the end of the final stage

n.2: The board has the authority to stop the project at a stage boundary; a loss of justification is not handled as a tolerance breach (manual 18.3).
n.3: The board can decide to stop at any stage boundary; waiting would waste money on an unjustified project (manual 18.3, 19.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A stage is forecast to exceed its stage tolerance and the board asks for an exception plan. Which processes prepare and approve the exception plan?

n.1: Controlling a stage raises the exception report, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 16.4.7, 18.3).
n.2: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process and cannot approve plans for the board (manual 14.4.4).
n.3: The board does not prepare plans; for a stage-level exception it approves the plan prepared by the project manager (manual 14.4.4, 18.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which 'managing a stage boundary' activity produces the end stage report for the project board?

Update the project plan
Report highlights
Evaluate the stage

n.1: This activity adds actuals and forecasts to the project plan; it does not produce a report (manual ch 18).
n.2: Report highlights is a controlling a stage activity that produces highlight reports during the stage (manual 16.4.8).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In which 'managing a stage boundary' activity are the actuals from the finishing stage and the forecasts for the next stage added to the project plan?
o: Update the project plan
Prepare next stage plan
Update the business case
Evaluate the stage
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Update the project plan brings in actual progress from the finishing stage and forecasts from the next stage plan or exception plan, and the revised costs and dates feed the business case (see manual ch 18).

n.1: This activity produces the detailed plan for the next stage; the project plan is then updated to reflect it (manual ch 18).
n.2: The business case takes its revised costs and dates from the updated project plan; it does not update the plan (manual ch 18).
n.3: This activity reviews the stage's performance in the end stage report (manual ch 18).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
At a stage boundary, a change to the forecast benefits of the project is dealt with in the activity [?].
o: prepare exception plan
update the project plan
update the business case
request next stage

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: What triggers the 'prepare exception plan' activity in 'managing a stage boundary'?

A new issue raised by a team manager during the work
The need to plan the closure work for the final stage

n.2: New issues are captured and assessed in controlling a stage; they do not trigger an exception plan (manual 16.4.5).

1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4

n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: post-project benefits reviews are planned during the project and carried out by the business after closure (manual 19.2, 14.4.5). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong. The board authorizes the next stage in directing a project (manual 14.4.4), and post-project benefits reviews happen after closure (manual 19.2).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Why is the business case updated after the project plan in 'managing a stage boundary'?

Revised costs and dates in the project plan feed it
The plan sets the benefits it is judged against
The business layer reissues it at every stage end

n.3: The business case is maintained by the project for the board's decision; the business layer does not reissue it each stage (manual ch 18).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: When an exception plan is prepared, what does PRINCE2 say about producing an end stage report?

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'closing a project' process?
o: To give the board enough information to review the stage and confirm continued justification
To ensure the prerequisites for initiating a project are in place
To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed
To let the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management

n.0: This is the purpose of managing a stage boundary, used at the end of every stage except the final one (manual 18.1).
n.1: This is the purpose of starting up a project, used before initiation (manual 13.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of directing a project, the board's process (manual 14.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Where does the 'closing a project' process sit in the project lifecycle?
o: As a closure stage after the final delivery stage
As the last part of the final stage
After the board has disbanded, run by the business
At each stage end, alongside managing a stage boundary

n.2: The project manager prepares closure and the board authorizes it in directing a project, so the board is still in place (manual 19.3, 14.4.5).
n.3: Closing a project is used once, at the end of the project; stage ends use managing a stage boundary (manual 12).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:

o: project manager
team manager
change authority

n.2: This is an objective of managing product delivery (manual 17.2).
n.3: This is an objective of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).

1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4

n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong. Post-project benefits reviews happen after closure (manual 19.2), and next stage plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: next stage plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary, which is not used at the end of the final stage (manual 18.2). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A project is being closed prematurely. What does the 'closing a project' process aim to achieve in this case?
o: That every planned product is finished before closing
That the remaining budget is passed to operational use
That the business case is rewritten for a restart
That the project is closed in an orderly way, not abandoned
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: For a premature close, closing a project makes sure the project is closed in an orderly way rather than simply abandoned (see manual 19.1, 19.2).

n.1: The budget is not transferred to operations; the aim is an orderly close of the project (manual 19.1).
n.2: A premature close follows a board decision to stop; the process does not rewrite the business case to restart it (manual 19.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Why does PRINCE2 prefer a clear end to a project rather than letting it drift into operational use?
o: Costs stop, ownership passes to the business and the team disbands
The benefits can all be realized before the team is released
The board can carry out the post-project benefits reviews
The team can resolve every open issue before handover

n.2: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after closure, not by the board during the project (manual 19.2).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In a planned close, which process leads into 'closing a project', and which process authorizes the closure?
o: Managing a stage boundary leads in; directing a project authorizes it
Directing a project leads in; the business layer authorizes it
Controlling a stage leads in; directing a project authorizes it
Controlling a stage leads in; the project manager authorizes it

n.0: Managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage; controlling a stage leads into closure (manual 16.3, 19.3).
n.1: Directing a project leads in only for a premature close, and closure is authorized by the board, not the business layer (manual 19.3, 14.4.5).
n.3: The project manager prepares closure and requests it, but the board authorizes it (manual 19.3, 19.4.5).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which 'closing a project' activity produces the end project report for the project board?
o: Evaluate the project
Confirm project acceptance
Request project closure
Prepare planned closure

n.1: This activity hands the products to the operational and maintenance environment and confirms acceptance (manual 19.4.3).
n.2: This activity briefs the board and asks it to authorize closure, using the end project report already prepared (manual 19.4.5).
n.3: This activity confirms the project can close, updates the project plan with actuals and closes the project log (manual 19.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In which 'closing a project' activity are the products passed to the operational and maintenance environment?
o: Prepare planned closure
Prepare premature closure
Confirm project acceptance
Request project closure
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: In confirm project acceptance the products are handed into the operational and maintenance environment, in one release or in phases, and acceptance is confirmed (see manual 19.4.3).

n.0: This activity checks that the project can close and secures and archives project information (manual 19.4.1).
n.1: This activity deals with an early close, salvaging useful work and making products safe (manual 19.4.2).
n.3: This activity briefs the board after acceptance has been confirmed (manual 19.4.5).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In 'prepare premature closure', the project manager records the request to close early, makes products safe and [?] any work that may still be useful.
o: abandons
salvages
re-baselines
authorizes
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Prepare premature closure records the premature close request, salvages anything useful, makes products safe and agrees what is completed and what is abandoned (see manual 19.4.2).

n.0: The point of the activity is to keep useful work, not to abandon it; the project must not simply be abandoned (manual 19.2, 19.4.2).
n.2: Baselines are reviewed against performance at closure, not re-set for work that is being stopped (manual 19.4.4).
n.3: New work is authorized through work packages in controlling a stage, not during premature closure (manual 16.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In 'evaluate the project', what does the project manager compare the project's performance against?
o: The project mandate issued by the business layer
The outline business case approved at initiation
The most recent highlight report sent to the board
The baselined PID and its current approved version
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Evaluate the project compares what was achieved with the original baselined PID and its current approved version, and analyses estimates against actuals to improve future estimating (see manual 19.4.4).

n.0: The mandate triggers starting up a project; performance is measured against the baselined PID (manual 19.4.4).
n.1: The outline business case was developed into the full business case in the PID, which is the baseline used (manual 15.4.5, 19.4.4).
n.2: A highlight report shows stage status at one point; it is not the baseline for evaluating the project (manual 16.4.8).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which of the following is NOT done within the 'closing a project' process?
o: Checking that post-project benefits reviews are planned
Closing the project log and archiving project information
Carrying out the post-project benefits reviews
Producing a lessons report in consultation with the team
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Post-project benefits reviews are planned within the project, but carrying them out is not a project activity: the business does it after closure (see manual 19.2, 19.4).

n.0: This is done in closing a project, for example by the senior user in confirm project acceptance (manual 19.4.3).
n.1: This is part of prepare planned closure (manual 19.4.1).
n.3: This is part of evaluate the project (manual 19.4.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Which two statements about the activities of 'closing a project' are correct?
1. In 'request project closure', the project manager authorizes closure and notifies the business layer.
2. In 'confirm project acceptance', the team manager raises an exception report if products are rejected.
3. In 'prepare planned closure', the project manager updates the project plan with actuals from the final stage.
4. In 'evaluate the project', the project manager produces a lessons report and the end project report.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Statements 3 and 4 are correct. Prepare planned closure updates the project plan with actuals, and evaluate the project produces the lessons report and end project report (see manual 19.4.1, 19.4.4).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong. The board authorizes closure and notifies the business layer (manual 14.4.5), and team managers do not raise exception reports (manual 16.4.7).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: the project manager requests closure and the board authorizes it (manual 19.4.5, 14.4.5). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: exception reports are raised by the project manager to the board (manual 16.4.7). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: In 'request project closure', what might the project manager recommend to the project board?
o: Extending the project until all benefits have been measured
Recognizing success and naming a strong supplier for future work
Moving the unspent project budget into the risk budget
Delaying acceptance until every open issue is resolved
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Request project closure briefs the board on performance, confirms readiness to close and highlights concessions; it may recommend celebrating success and recognizing a high-performing supplier or team manager for future work (see manual 19.4.5).

n.0: Benefits continue to be reviewed after closure through the benefits management approach; the project is not extended for them (manual 19.2).
n.2: The risk budget funds risk responses during the project; closure does not move money into it (manual ch 9, 19.4.5).
n.3: Open issues and risks are handed on with follow-on action recommendations (manual 19.2).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: What happens to the product register and quality register in 'closing a project'?
o: They are checked and then closed
They pass to team managers to maintain
They are reopened for benefits reviews
They are merged into the business case
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: When the project closes, the product register and quality register are checked and closed, and the project log is closed (see manual 19.4.1, 19.7).

n.1: Team managers' work ends with their work packages; the registers are closed with the project log (manual 19.4.1).
n.2: Benefits reviews after closure follow the benefits management approach, not the project registers (manual 19.2).
n.3: The business case is updated with actual costs and benefits; the registers are not merged into it (manual 19.7).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Following a project from mandate to closure, which process creates the project brief that the board reviews before authorizing initiation?
o: Initiating a project
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
Starting up a project
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project and is then reviewed by the board, with the initiation stage plan, in authorize initiation (see manual 13.4, 14.4.1).

n.0: Initiating a project uses the project brief to build the PID; it starts only after the brief has been approved (manual 15.3).
n.1: The board reviews and approves the brief in authorize initiation but does not create it (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of initiation, after the brief has served its purpose (manual 18.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which process and activity produce the highlight report sent to the project board during a stage?
o: Managing product delivery: evaluate a work package
Controlling a stage: report highlights
Managing a stage boundary: evaluate the stage
Directing a project: give ongoing direction
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: The project manager produces highlight reports for the board in controlling a stage, in report highlights, at the agreed frequency (see manual 16.4.8).

n.0: This activity produces checkpoint reports from the team manager to the project manager (manual 17.4.3).
n.2: This activity produces the end stage report, not regular highlight reports (manual ch 18).
n.3: The board receives and validates highlight reports but does not produce them (manual 14.4.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
The [?] is assembled in 'initiating a project' and, together with the current stage plan, forms the contract between the project manager and the project board.
o: project brief
project product description
project initiation documentation
communication management approach
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, with the current stage plan, forms the contract between the project manager and the board. It is assembled in initiating a project (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6).

n.0: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project and is superseded by the PID (manual 13.4, 4.3.1).
n.1: The project product description is created in starting up a project and is one input to the PID, not the contract itself (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: This approach is one part of the PID; on its own it does not form the contract with the board (manual 4.3.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: A project has an initiation stage and three delivery stages. Which process creates the stage plan for the second delivery stage?
o: Managing a stage boundary, near the end of the first delivery stage
Starting up a project, along with the initiation stage plan
Initiating a project, along with the project plan
Controlling a stage, at the start of the second delivery stage
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Every stage plan after initiation is prepared in managing a stage boundary near the end of the previous stage, so the plan for the second delivery stage is made at the end of the first (see manual 18.1).

n.1: Starting up a project plans only the initiation stage; later stage plans are made at stage boundaries (manual 13.4.7, 18.1).
n.2: Initiating a project creates the project plan; each delivery stage plan is made near the end of the stage before it (manual 15.4.4, 18.1).
n.3: A stage cannot start until the board has approved its plan, which must already exist (manual 14.4.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Which two statements about the project log are correct?
1. The project log is baselined when the project is authorized and put under change control.
2. The project log holds the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers.
3. The project log is passed to the business after closure so that its registers stay open.
4. The project log is started in starting up a project and completed during initiation.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Statements 2 and 4 are correct. The project log is the dynamic record holding the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers; it is set up in starting up a project and completed in initiation (see manual 4.3.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: it is the PID that is baselined and placed under change control; the project log is a dynamic record (manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong. The PID, not the project log, is baselined (manual 15.4.6), and the project log is closed in closing a project (manual 19.4.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the project log is closed in closing a project (manual 19.4.1). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: What happens to the project initiation documentation in the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: It is replaced by the end stage report as the board's reference
It is created for the first time to support the next stage request
It is closed and archived together with the project log
It is reviewed and, where needed, updated for the next stage
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: One objective of managing a stage boundary is to review and, if necessary, update the PID, in particular the business case, project plan, management approaches, team structure and role descriptions (see manual 18.2).

n.0: The end stage report reviews the stage; the PID remains the reference and is updated where needed (manual 18.2).
n.1: The PID is assembled in initiating a project, before the first delivery stage (manual 15.4.6).
n.2: Project information is archived in closing a project, not at a stage boundary (manual 19.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which management products does a team manager produce in the 'managing product delivery' process?
o: Checkpoint reports and, if needed, a team plan
Work package descriptions and highlight reports
Exception reports and the issue register
End stage reports and lessons reports
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: In managing product delivery the team manager may produce a team plan when accepting a work package and sends checkpoint reports to the project manager (see manual 17.4.1, 17.4.3).

n.1: Both are produced by the project manager in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1, 16.4.8).
n.2: Exception reports come from the project manager, and the issue register is maintained for the project manager, updated with team input (manual 16.4.7, 17.7).
n.3: These are prepared by the project manager in managing a stage boundary or closing a project (manual ch 18, 19.4.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: The project board reviews the end project report to decide whether the project can close. Which process and activity is the board using?
o: Closing a project: request project closure
Directing a project: authorize project closure
Managing a stage boundary: request next stage
Closing a project: confirm project acceptance
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: The project manager prepares the end project report in evaluate the project and requests closure; the board then reviews it and authorizes closure in directing a project (see manual 14.4.5, 19.4.4).

n.0: In request project closure the project manager asks the board to close; the decision is taken in directing a project (manual 19.4.5, 14.4.5).
n.2: This activity asks for the next stage to be authorized; it is not used at the end of the final stage (manual ch 18).
n.3: This activity hands products into operational use and confirms acceptance before closure is requested (manual 19.4.3).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'controlling a stage' process?
o: To control the link between the project manager and the team manager for specialist work
To give the board enough information to review the stage and confirm continued justification
To assign and monitor work and take corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance
To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Controlling a stage exists so the project manager can assign work, monitor it, deal with issues, report progress to the project board and take corrective action, keeping the stage within the tolerances the board has set (see manual 16.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of managing product delivery, the team manager's view of work packages, not the project manager's control of the whole stage (manual 17.1).
n.1: This describes managing a stage boundary, which is used at or near the end of a stage rather than to run the work within it (manual 18.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of closing a project, which confirms acceptance of the project product within the final stage (manual 19.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: The 'controlling a stage' process is used throughout each delivery stage. Which role carries out its activities day to day?
o: The project manager, within the stage tolerances set by the board
The team manager, within the work package tolerances set by the project manager
The executive, within the project tolerances set by the business layer
Project assurance, on behalf of the board members it reports to
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Controlling a stage sits at the managing level: the project manager assigns and monitors work and keeps the stage within the stage tolerances set by the project board (see manual 12, 16.1).

n.1: The team manager works in managing product delivery, accepting and executing work packages; controlling a stage is the project manager's process (manual 12, 17.3).
n.2: The executive directs through directing a project and manages by exception; the board does not run the stage day to day (manual 14.3).
n.3: Project assurance checks the project for the board members, independently of the project manager; it does not run the stage's activities (manual 6.2.4).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
The 'controlling a stage' process begins when the project board authorizes a stage or [?], and it is used in every delivery stage, including the final stage.
o: a work package
the project brief
a team plan
an exception plan
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: Controlling a stage is triggered when the board, in directing a project, authorizes a stage or an exception plan. It then runs through each delivery stage, the final stage included (see manual 16.3).

n.0: Work packages are authorized by the project manager within controlling a stage, so authorizing one does not start the process (manual 16.4.1).
n.1: The board approves the project brief when it authorizes initiation, which starts initiating a project, not controlling a stage (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: A team plan is an optional plan produced by a team manager in managing product delivery; the board does not authorize it (manual 17.4.1).

Processes: Delivery & Closure.q: Which is an objective of the 'controlling a stage' process?
o: To assure the board that all products in the stage plan are complete
To keep the business case under review during the stage
To make the team clear about the effort, cost and timescales expected
To check that the users accept the project product
Processes: Delivery & Closure.w: One objective of controlling a stage is that the business case is kept under review during the stage, along with controlling risks and issues and focusing on delivery of the stage's products (see manual 16.2).

n.0: This is an objective of managing a stage boundary, which reviews the stage once its products are complete (manual 18.2).
n.2: This is an objective of managing product delivery, which concerns the team manager and the team (manual 17.2).
n.3: This is an objective of closing a project, which runs as part of the final stage (manual 19.2).
